Convex Optimization School

From convex sets to robots, in three weeks · v1.1 (2026-10-26)
A three-week course
Convex optimization, without the fog.

21 lessons of about an hour each. Week 1 shows what makes an optimization problem easy. Week 2 opens up the algorithms inside every solver. Week 3 goes past convexity and into robots and self-driving cars. Plain language, real numbers, interactive widgets, and sources you can check.

How to use this course

  1. One day per sitting. Read the lesson from top to bottom. Each day builds on the one before.
  2. Play with every widget. Each one is a small optimization running in your browser, not a picture.
  3. Take the quiz, then mark the day done. Progress is saved on this device only.
  4. Use the other tabs. Algorithms has one card per method. Papers explains the robotics papers from Week 3. Glossary lets you look up any term.
  5. Open the sources. The small chips after sentences (like this one CO4A) link to the original.

What you need to know first

Some high-school algebra, what a derivative is, and the basics of vectors and matrices: adding them, the dot product, and multiplying a matrix by a vector. You do not need to read proofs. About the sources

Weeks 1 and 2 follow the Korean open textbook 모두를 위한 컨벡스 최적화 (Convex Optimization for All, "CO4A"), released under the MIT License (© 2021 CONVEX-OPTIMIZATION-FOR-ALL Team). CO4A is based on CMU's 10-725 course (Fall 2016, taught by Javier Peña and Ryan Tibshirani) and on Boyd & Vandenberghe's Convex Optimization (2004). This course rephrases and simplifies that material in English. It reorders some topics, moves proofs into optional boxes, and adds widgets and worked numbers. Week 3 draws on the original papers and on official solver documentation. Every lesson links the CO4A chapters it covers. All sources were checked on 2026-10-26, and fast-moving facts are marked "as of Oct 2026".

Week 1 · Day 1

Why convex?

After today you can say what an optimization problem is, tell a convex problem from a nonconvex one, and explain why 'every local minimum is global' makes convex problems easy to solve.

About 60 min · No prerequisites · CO4A chapter 1

Today's big idea

An optimization problem asks for the best choice that obeys some rules. In general, a search can stall in a dip that is not the deepest one. Convex problems have no such false dips: a point that no small step can improve is the best point anywhere, so computers can solve them reliably.

1. Knobs, a score, and rules

Every optimization problem has the same three parts. Think of planning a drive home. You choose the turns, you want the trip to be short, and you must obey the one-way streets.

The things you choose are the optimization variables. We stack them into one vector x = (x1, …, xn) in ℝn. The score you want small is the objective function f(x), also called the cost. The rules are the constraints.

A point that obeys every rule is called feasible. The set of all feasible points is the feasible set. Written out, every problem in this course has the same shape. "s.t." is short for "subject to". CO4A 1-1 CMU 10-725 2016

minimize f(x)
s.t. gi(x) ≤ 0, i = 1, …, m
hj(x) = 0, j = 1, …, r

Each gi is an inequality constraint ("at most"). Each hj is an equality constraint ("exactly"). Any rule can be moved into this form. For example, x ≤ 1 becomes g(x) = x − 1 ≤ 0.

The best score you can reach is the optimal value, written p*. A feasible point that reaches it is an optimal solution, or minimizer, written x*. Keep the two apart: p* is a number, and x* is a point.

Here is a problem with one knob. Minimize (x − 2)2 subject to x ≤ 1. Without the rule, the best choice would be x = 2, with a score of 0. The rule forbids it, so the best allowed point sits on the edge: x* = 1, with p* = (1 − 2)2 = 1.

Some rules are not written down at all. They hide inside the formula. Take the problem: minimize f(x) = x − log x. The logarithm only exists for x > 0, so x > 0 is a hidden rule, called an implicit constraint. Setting the slope f′(x) = 1 − 1/x to zero gives x* = 1 and p* = 1 − log 1 = 1. CO4A 1-1

A problem with no written-down constraints is an unconstrained problem. The example above counts as unconstrained, even though it hides the rule x > 0.

In practice you describe the three parts to a modelling tool and let a solver do the rest. Here is the one-knob problem in CVXPY, a free Python library. Day 4 explains how it checks that a problem is convex before it solves it.

import cvxpy as cp

x = cp.Variable()                          # the knob
objective = cp.Minimize(cp.square(x - 2))  # the score
constraints = [x <= 1]                     # the rule
problem = cp.Problem(objective, constraints)
problem.solve()
print(x.value, problem.value)              # about 1.0 and 1.0

2. Optimization is everywhere

Once you look for knobs, a score and rules, you find optimization problems everywhere. The table lists some from daily life, driving, robotics and machine learning. The last column previews today's main question: is the problem convex? Sections 3 and 4 explain how to tell.

ProblemKnobs (variables)Score (objective)Rules (constraints)Convex?
Cheapest grocery basketamount of each foodtotal priceenough protein and caloriesyes (a linear program, Day 5)
Fitting a line to dataslope and interceptsum of squared missesnoneyes (least squares)
Investing savingsmoney in each assetrisk (variance)budget, minimum expected returnyes CO4A 1-1
Route homewhich roads to take (yes or no)travel timeroads must connect, one-way streetsno as written: yes-or-no knobs (Day 15)
Car speed plan, next 5 sspeed at each momentharsh braking and accelerationspeed limit, gap to the car aheadyes, with linear rules (Day 17)
Robot arm reaching a pointjoint anglesdistance from hand to targetjoint limitsno (sines and cosines)
Training a modelthe model's weightsaverage error on the dataoften nonelinear models yes, deep networks no

Fitting a line. Suppose you measure three points: (0, 1), (1, 3) and (2, 4). You want the line y = ax + b that passes closest to them. The score adds up the squared vertical misses:

f(a, b) = (b − 1)² + (a + b − 3)² + (2a + b − 4)²

This score is a bowl over the two knobs a and b. Its lowest point is a = 1.5 and b ≈ 1.17, where the total squared miss is 0.167. Every "least squares" fit in statistics and machine learning is a bigger version of this bowl. Day 6 shows gradient descent finding its bottom.

Planning a car's speed. A self-driving car re-plans its speed many times a second. The knobs are its speeds over the next few seconds. The score adds up how hard it brakes and accelerates, so the ride stays smooth. The rules keep it under the speed limit and a safe distance behind the car ahead.

Distance travelled is a sum of speed × time, so "stay 10 m behind the car ahead" is a linear rule in the speeds. With linear rules and a squared score, the problem is convex. It is called a quadratic program, and Day 17 builds one step by step. Boyd and Vandenberghe's course slides say that convex solvers generated as code now run in milliseconds, and cite the landing of SpaceX's Falcon 9 rocket. Boyd EE364a slides

A robot arm, which is not convex. Picture an arm with two links, each 1 m long, trying to touch the point (1, 1). Two poses reach it exactly. "Elbow down" puts the shoulder at 0° and bends the elbow 90°. "Elbow up" puts the shoulder at 90° and bends the elbow −90°.

Now blend the two answers. The halfway pose has the shoulder at 45° and a straight elbow (0°). It puts the hand at (1.41, 1.41), which misses the target by 0.59 m. Two perfect answers, and the point halfway between them is bad. Section 4 shows that this cannot happen in a convex problem.

Machine learning. Training a model means choosing its weights to make the average error on the data small. For linear regression and logistic regression this problem is convex. Boyd & Vandenberghe 2004 For a deep neural network it is not, which is one reason training one needs careful starting points and tuning. Day 16 and Day 20 come back to this.

3. Convex sets and convex functions, one picture each

Two shapes carry the whole subject. Today you only need a rough picture of each. Day 2 and Day 3 treat them properly.

A set with no dents. Pick any two points inside a shape and draw the straight path between them. If the path never leaves the shape, whichever two points you pick, the shape is a convex set. A disk passes. A crescent moon fails, because the path between its two tips cuts across the empty bite.

To write "every point on the path", blend the two points x and y with a weight θ between 0 and 1. θ = 1 gives x, θ = 0 gives y, and θ = 0.5 gives the midpoint. Such a weighted average is called a convex combination. A set C is convex when CO4A 1-2

x, y ∈ C and θ ∈ [0, 1] ⇒ θx + (1 − θ)y ∈ C

A number check. The halfspace of points (p, q) with p + 2q ≤ 4 contains x = (0, 0) and y = (4, 0). With θ = 0.25 the blend is 0.25·(0, 0) + 0.75·(4, 0) = (3, 0). Since 3 + 2·0 = 3 ≤ 4, the blend is inside too.

A function shaped like a bowl. Stretch a string between any two points on the graph of a function. If the string never dips below the graph, the function is a convex function. On a bumpy curve, some strings pass under a hump.

f(θx + (1 − θ)y) ≤ θf(x) + (1 − θ)f(y)

The left side is the height of the graph at the blended point. The right side is the height of the string there. Take f(x) = x2, x = −1, y = 3 and θ = 0.5. The blended point is 1, where the graph has height f(1) = 1. The string has height (1 + 9)/2 = 5 there. Since 1 ≤ 5, the string is above the graph, by 4.

The two ideas are linked. Paint everything on or above the graph of f. That painted region is the epigraph of f. A function is convex exactly when its epigraph is a convex set. CO4A 1-2 Boyd & Vandenberghe 2004

Check it on f(x) = |x|. The points (−1, 1) and (1, 1) lie on its graph. Their midpoint (0, 1) has height 1, which is above |0| = 0, so it lies inside the painted region, as convexity requires.

4. What makes a problem convex

Now put the pieces together. A convex optimization problem needs three things. The objective f is a convex function. Each inequality function gi is convex. Each equality function hj is affine, meaning flat: hj(x) = ajTx + bj, a linear part plus a constant. CO4A 1-2 CMU 10-725 2016

Why these rules? A convex gi is a bowl, and the region where it is at most 0 is the part of the bowl under the water line: a convex blob. A flat hj makes the region where it equals 0 a flat line or plane. Overlapping convex pieces gives a convex feasible set (Day 2 shows why). A bowl-shaped score over a convex feasible set is the whole recipe.

Example A, convex. Minimize x2 subject to 1 − x ≤ 0, which means x ≥ 1. The objective is a bowl and the rule is flat. The feasible set is the ray [1, ∞), with no gaps. The answer is x* = 1 with p* = 1.

Example B, not convex. Minimize x2 subject to x2 − 1 = 0. The equality is curved, not flat. Its feasible set is just two points, −1 and 1. The path between them runs through 0, which is not allowed.

Example C, not convex. Minimize x2 subject to x2 ≥ 1, written as 1 − x2 ≤ 0. Here g(x) = 1 − x2 is an upside-down bowl. Its feasible set, everything outside (−1, 1), has a gap in the middle.

Two more facts. Maximizing a concave function, an upside-down bowl, is also a convex problem, because it is the same as minimizing its negative. And modelling tools check the rules before solving. CVXPY raises an error if you ask it to solve example B, because "x² == 1" is not an affine equality. CVXPY docs

The robot arm from section 2 fails for the same kind of reason. In a convex problem, the set of best points is itself convex, so the blend of two best answers is also a best answer. The arm's two perfect poses blend into a pose that misses by 0.59 m, so its problem cannot be convex.

5. The payoff: every local minimum is global

Imagine a hiker in thick fog who wants the lowest point of a valley. She can only feel the ground under her boots. She steps downhill until every direction goes up, and then she stops.

Where she stops is a local minimum: no nearby point is lower. What she wants is a global minimum: no point anywhere is lower. In mountains these can differ, and she may stop in a small hollow high on a slope.

On a convex bowl they cannot differ. There is only one valley, so "nothing nearby is lower" already means "nothing anywhere is lower". This is the most useful fact in the course: CMU 10-725 2016 Boyd & Vandenberghe 2004

if f(x) ≤ f(y) for every feasible y with ‖y − x‖2 ≤ ρ,
then f(x) ≤ f(y) for every feasible y

Here x is a feasible point, ρ > 0 is the radius of "nearby", and ‖y − x‖2 is the ordinary straight-line distance. The reason fits in one line. If a better point y existed far away, a short step from x toward y would already be better, because the string to y lies above the bowl. The box at the end of this section works it through with numbers.

For a smooth function with no constraints, the test gets even simpler. If f is convex and differentiable, then ∇f(x) = 0 holds exactly at the global minimizers. CMU 10-725 2016 For f(x) = (x − 1)2, setting f′(x) = 2(x − 1) to zero gives x = 1, and that is the bottom of the bowl.

The simplest computer version of the hiker is gradient descent. It repeats one move: step against the slope, scaled by a step size η (the Greek letter eta). See the gradient descent card for more.

xk+1 = xk − η f′(xk)

Run it on f(x) = (x − 1)2 with η = 0.1, starting at x0 = 2. The slope there is 2, so x1 = 2 − 0.1·2 = 1.8. Each step shrinks the distance to the bottom by a factor of 0.8. After 21 steps the ball is within 0.01 of x = 1.

Try it: tap either curve to start both balls there and watch them roll, or set x0 with the slider and press Roll. Both balls use the same rule from the same start. Then move x0 left of 0.13 and roll again. Finally, push the bowl's step size above 1.

Notice: from the default start x0 = 2.00, the bowl's ball settles at x = 1.000 after 66 steps. The bumpy ball settles after 48 steps at x = 1.347, where g = −2.619. That is only a local minimum. The global minimum, g = −5.444 at x = −1.473, lies beyond the hilltop at x ≈ 0.126, and the ball never sees it.

Analogy

Drop a marble anywhere in a salad bowl and it ends at the same bottom. Drop it into an egg carton and it ends in whichever cup is nearest, deep or shallow. Convex problems are salad bowls. Many real problems are egg cartons, and a marble cannot tell which cup is deepest.

Going deeper (optional): why local means global, with numbers

Take f(x) = (x − 1)2 and suppose someone claims x = 3 is a local minimum, with "nearby" meaning within ρ = 0.5. A better point exists: y = 1, with f(1) = 0 < f(3) = 4.

Step a little from x toward y, by θ = ρ / (2‖y − x‖2) = 0.5/4 = 0.125. That gives z = 3 + 0.125·(1 − 3) = 2.75, which is 0.25 from x, so it counts as nearby. The string inequality says f(z) ≤ 0.125·f(1) + 0.875·f(3) = 3.5, which is less than f(3) = 4. (Indeed f(2.75) = 3.0625.) A nearby point beats x, so the claim was false.

The same steps work for any convex problem. The feasible set is convex, so z is feasible, and the string inequality makes z better than x. The full proof is in Boyd & Vandenberghe §4.2.2. Boyd & Vandenberghe 2004

6. Why convex problems are the "easy" ones

Most algorithms are like the hiker. They only look at the ground near the current point. On a nonconvex problem that local view can mislead them, as the bumpy ball showed.

Boyd and Vandenberghe put it bluntly. For general nonlinear problems there is no effective general method, and even some problems with about ten variables are very hard. Boyd & Vandenberghe 2004

The usual fallback is local optimization: start somewhere, go downhill, and hope. It needs a good starting guess and some tuning. It also cannot tell you how far you are from the true best. The book calls it "more art than technology". Global search does find the true best, but its worst-case cost grows exponentially with the number of variables.

Convex problems escape this trap. Usually there is no formula for the answer. But interior-point methods solve them reliably, almost always in 10 to 100 iterations. In the book's words, once you have formulated a problem as convex, solving it is "(almost) technology". Boyd & Vandenberghe 2004 Day 12 opens up these methods.

So the hard part moves from solving to formulating. Your job is to recognise, or rewrite, a problem as convex. That skill is what Week 1 trains.

This also corrects an old rule of thumb, "linear is easy, nonlinear is hard". The better dividing line is convex versus nonconvex. A curved bowl is just as easy as a flat plane, and only the bumps make problems hard. Boyd EE364a slides CMU 10-725 2016

Convex does not mean any method will do, though. Tibshirani's first lecture cleans up a noisy image by solving one convex problem with three methods. A specialised ADMM needed 20 iterations, proximal gradient needed 1,000, and coordinate descent needed 10,000 cycles. CMU 10-725 2016 CO4A 1-3

The lesson is not "ADMM is best". ADMM won here because its steps matched the problem's structure. On another problem a different method wins. Choosing the method is the theme of Week 2.

The ideas are older than computers, and the table gives the main steps. CO4A 1-4 Boyd EE364a slides

WhenWhat happened
c. 1900–1970Convex analysis develops as pure mathematics.
1947Dantzig's simplex method solves linear programs.
1960sEarly interior-point methods.
1970sThe ellipsoid and subgradient methods.
1984Karmarkar's interior-point method solves linear programs in polynomial time.
1994Nesterov and Nemirovski extend such methods to general convex problems.
1990 onwardUse spreads to control, signal processing and circuit design; since the 2000s, machine learning, statistics and finance.

7. The road ahead

The course has three weeks. Week 1 teaches you to recognise convex problems: convex sets (Day 2), convex functions (Day 3), convex problems (Day 4), and the standard families from linear programs up to semidefinite programs (Day 5). Week 2 opens up the solvers. You will meet gradient descent, subgradients, proximal methods, duality, the KKT conditions, Newton's method, interior-point methods, ADMM, Frank–Wolfe and coordinate descent (Days 6–14). Week 3 leaves the safe bowl. It covers yes-or-no decisions, general nonlinear problems, and robots and cars: model predictive control, trajectory optimization, collision avoidance, safety filters, and solvers in practice (Days 15–21).

Explain it to a 10-year-old

You are in a dark room and want to put a ball at the lowest spot on the floor. You can't see, but you can feel which way the floor tilts. If the floor is shaped like one big bowl, just keep walking downhill and you will reach the bottom for sure. If the floor has lots of little dips, you might stop in a small one and never know a deeper one is across the room.

Common misunderstandings

  • "Convex means exactly one minimizer." No. Convexity says every local minimizer is global, not that there is only one. f(x) = max(0, |x| − 1) is convex, and every x in [−1, 1] is a minimizer. Uniqueness needs strict convexity (Day 3).
  • "A convex problem has a formula for its answer." Usually not. What it has is algorithms that reliably find the answer. Boyd & Vandenberghe 2004
  • "Smooth equality constraints are fine." No. Equalities must be affine. The smooth rule x2 = 1 already breaks convexity, leaving only the two points −1 and 1.
  • "Convex means any step size works." No. On f(x) = (x − 1)2, gradient descent with η = 1.05 from x0 = −2.2 reaches x = −7.30 after 10 steps, moving away from the answer. Convexity removes false valleys; it does not fix a bad step size.
  • "Zero slope means I found the answer." Only for convex problems. On the bumpy curve the slope is also zero at the local minimum x ≈ 1.347 and at the hilltop x ≈ 0.126.

Check yourself

Q1. Which of these is a convex optimization problem?

(x − 2)² is a bowl and x ≤ 1 is flat, so it is convex (answer x* = 1). x² = 1 is a curved equality. −x² is an upside-down bowl, and minimizing it is not convex. x² ≥ 1 leaves a gap in the feasible set.

Q2. In a convex problem, each equality constraint h(x) = 0 must have h…

An equality must be flat. "Convex" sounds right but is not enough: h(x) = x² − 1 is convex, yet h(x) = 0 leaves only the two points −1 and 1.

Q3. Why does "every local minimum is global" matter in practice?

Local methods only see nearby points, and convexity guarantees that what they find is the true best. It does not promise a unique minimizer (max(0, |x| − 1) has many), a formula, or safety from big steps.

Q4. Gradient descent on g(x) = x⁴ − 4x² + x, started at x0 = 1 with η = 0.02, ends near…

x0 = 1 is right of the hilltop at 0.126, so the ball rolls into the right-hand dip and stops at 1.347. The deeper dip at −1.473 (g ≈ −5.44) is never reached. Set x0 = 1 in the widget to watch it.

Q5. A two-link arm reaches a target exactly in two poses, but the pose halfway between them misses by 0.59 m. What does this show?

In a convex problem the set of minimizers is convex, so the blend of two minimizers is also a minimizer. Here it misses by 0.59 m. The arm is long enough, since both poses reach the target exactly.

Q6. According to Boyd and Vandenberghe, what is usually the hard part of convex optimization?

Once a problem is written in convex form, solving it is "(almost) technology". Starting points and local-versus-global worries are what make nonconvex problems hard.

Recap: things to remember

  1. An optimization problem has variables (knobs), an objective (score) and constraints (rules). x* is the best point, and p* is the best score.
  2. A problem is convex when the objective and each "≤" function are convex and each "=" function is affine.
  3. In a convex problem every local minimum is global. With no constraints and a smooth f, ∇f(x) = 0 is enough.
  4. Nonconvex problems can trap local methods. On the bumpy curve, starts right of x ≈ 0.126 stop at g ≈ −2.62, not at −5.44.
  5. The real dividing line is convex versus nonconvex, not linear versus nonlinear. Formulating is the hard part, and the choice of algorithm still matters.

Week 1 · Day 2

Convex sets

After today you can recognise convex sets (lines, halfspaces, balls, polyhedra, cones, the PSD cone), build new ones with convexity-preserving operations, and explain what separating and supporting hyperplanes guarantee.

About 60 min · Needs Day 1 · CO4A chapter 2

Today's big idea

A set is convex when the straight segment between any two of its points stays inside it. A few basic shapes pass this test: lines, halfspaces, balls, polyhedra and cones. Safe moves such as intersection build every other convex set you will need. And two convex sets that do not overlap can always be split by a flat wall.

1. Blending two points: lines, segments and rays

Picture a slider between two points x and y. At one end you sit on x, at the other on y. Let the slider run past both ends and you trace the whole line through them.

The slider position is a number θ. The point it gives is a blend of x and y. CO4A 2-1-1

z = θx + (1 − θ)y = y + θ(x − y)

Read the second form as a recipe: start at y and move θ of the way toward x. θ = 0 gives y, θ = 1 gives x, and θ = 0.5 gives the midpoint.

The range of θ decides the shape. If θ can be any real number, you get the line through x and y. If 0 ≤ θ ≤ 1, you get the line segment between them. If θ ≥ 0, you get a ray: it starts at y, passes through x, and goes on forever.

A number check with x = (1, 0) and y = (0, 1). θ = 0.5 gives 0.5·(1, 0) + 0.5·(0, 1) = (0.5, 0.5), the midpoint, on the segment. θ = 3 gives 3·(1, 0) − 2·(0, 1) = (3, −2). That point is on the line, far past x, but not on the segment.

2. Affine sets and convex sets

Some sets are flat and endless, like a point, a line or a plane. An affine set contains the whole line through any two of its points: the blend θx + (1 − θ)y stays inside for every real θ. The solutions of linear equations, {x : Ax = b}, are the typical example. CO4A 2-1-2

Blends of more than two points work the same way. A sum θ1x1 + … + θkxk whose weights add up to 1 is an affine combination. The weights may be negative. An affine set contains every affine combination of its points.

Take C = {x ∈ ℝ2 : x1 + x2 = 1}, a line. It contains (1, 0) and (0, 1), and also their blend (3, −2) from above, since 3 − 2 = 1. Slide C by (1, 0) toward the origin and you get the line x1 + x2 = 0 through the origin. Every affine set is a subspace slid away from the origin like this.

A convex set asks for less. Only the segment has to stay inside, not the whole line. This is the test from Day 1: no dents and no holes. CO4A 2-1-3 Boyd & Vandenberghe 2004

x, y ∈ C and θ ∈ [0, 1] ⇒ θx + (1 − θ)y ∈ C

A weighted average θ1x1 + … + θkxk with every θi ≥ 0 and weights adding up to 1 is a convex combination. A convex set contains every convex combination of its points, not only blends of two at a time.

Stretch a rubber band around a set of points and let it snap tight. The region inside the band is the convex hull, the smallest convex set that contains them. It is also the set of all their convex combinations.

For example, the convex hull of (0, 0), (2, 0), (0, 2) and (1, 1) is the triangle with corners (0, 0), (2, 0) and (0, 2). The fourth point adds nothing. It is 0.5·(2, 0) + 0.5·(0, 2), so it already lies on an edge.

Every affine set is convex, because the segment is part of the line. The reverse fails: a disk is convex, but the line through two of its points runs out of the disk. The edge matters too. A square that keeps its top corners but not the middle of its top edge is not convex.

Try it: pick a shape, then drag P and Q (or tap to move the nearer one). The segment is solid green where it stays inside and dashed red where it leaves. "Find a bad pair" lets the computer search 2,000 random pairs for a leak.

Notice: in the default crescent both handles are inside, P = (−0.20, 0.90) and Q = (−0.20, −0.90). Yet the points θP + (1 − θ)Q leave the set for θ from 0.285 to 0.715, where the segment crosses the bite. One leaking segment proves the crescent is not convex. On the disk, square or cut disk, no pair you drag ever leaks.

Analogy

A convex set is like a room where everyone can see everyone else. Put a pillar in the middle, or make the room L-shaped, and some pairs of people lose sight of each other. The segment test simply asks whether every pair of points can "see" each other without the line of sight leaving the room.

3. Cones: rays from the origin

Think of a flashlight beam with the bulb at the origin. If a point is lit, so is every point farther out along the same ray. A set C is a cone if x ∈ C and θ ≥ 0 always give θx ∈ C. CO4A 2-1-4

A convex cone also contains all nonnegative sums: x, y ∈ C and θ1, θ2 ≥ 0 give θ1x + θ2y ∈ C. In the plane it looks like a pie slice with its tip at the origin, running on forever.

The quarter-plane ℝ2+, where both coordinates are ≥ 0, is a convex cone. From (1, 2) and (3, 0), the sum 2·(1, 2) + 1·(3, 0) = (5, 4) is still in it.

A cone does not have to be convex. The two coordinate axes together form a cone, since stretching a point on an axis keeps it there. But (1, 0) + (0, 1) = (1, 1) is on neither axis, so this cone is not convex. CMU 10-725 2016

4. A gallery of basic convex sets

A few shapes appear in almost every problem. Learn to spot them the way you spot a circle. The figure shows them, and the paragraphs below give formulas and number checks. CO4A 2-2-1 CMU 10-725 2016

Hyperplanes and halfspaces. A hyperplane {x : aTx = b}, with a ≠ 0, is a flat wall. The vector a, called the normal, sticks straight out of the wall. A halfspace {x : aTx ≤ b} is one side of the wall, wall included. It is convex but not affine. Take a = (1, 2) and b = 4. The point (2, 1) gives 2 + 2 = 4, so it is on the wall. (0, 0) gives 0 ≤ 4, inside. (4, 4) gives 12 > 4, outside.

Balls. The Euclidean ball with centre c and radius r is every point within distance r of c: {x : ‖x − c‖2 ≤ r}. With c = (1, 1) and r = 2, the point (2, 2) is √2 ≈ 1.414 away from the centre, so it is inside.

Ellipsoids. Stretch a ball along some directions and you get an ellipsoid: {x : (x − c)TP−1(x − c) ≤ 1}. Here P is a symmetric positive definite matrix (all eigenvalues > 0). The semi-axis lengths are the square roots of P's eigenvalues. With P = diag(4, 1) and c = 0, the set is x12/4 + x22 ≤ 1, with semi-axes 2 and 1. A ball is the special case P = r2I. Boyd & Vandenberghe 2004

Norm balls. You can measure length in other ways than the straight-line distance. The p-norm is

‖x‖p = (|x1|p + … + |xn|p)1/p

The absolute values matter: without them, negative entries would break the formula. The norm ball ‖x‖p ≤ 1 is a diamond for p = 1, a disk for p = 2, and a square for p = ∞, where the norm is the largest |xi|. All of these are convex.

The formula only gives a true norm, and a convex ball, when p ≥ 1. Try p = ½, where the "ball" is √|x1| + √|x2| ≤ 1. The points (1, 0) and (0, 1) are in it. Their midpoint (0.5, 0.5) scores √0.5 + √0.5 ≈ 1.414 > 1, so it is outside. The shape is a four-pointed star, and you can drag across its dent in the widget.

Polyhedra. A polyhedron is what remains after cutting space with finitely many flat walls: {x : Ax ⪯ b, Cx = d}. The sign ⪯ means "≤ in every entry". Each row of A ⪯ b is one halfspace, and each row of Cx = d is one hyperplane. A bounded polyhedron is a polytope.

For example, x1 ≥ 0, x2 ≥ 0 and x1 + x2 ≤ 1 cut out a triangle. In matrix form, the rows of A are (−1, 0), (0, −1) and (1, 1), and b = (0, 0, 1).

Simplices. A simplex is the convex hull of affinely independent points (no point is an affine combination of the others): a segment, a triangle, a tetrahedron. The probability simplex holds the vectors with entries ≥ 0 that add up to 1, such as (0.2, 0.3, 0.5): every possible list of probabilities or mixing weights.

5. Three cones you will meet again

The ice-cream cone. The second-order cone is {(x, t) : ‖x‖2 ≤ t}, where x ∈ ℝn and t is a number. Each horizontal slice at height t is a disk of radius t, so the slices grow as you go up. CO4A 2-2-2

Check three points. (3, 4, 5) is on the surface, since ‖(3, 4)‖2 = 5. (3, 4, 6) is inside, and (3, 4, 4) is outside.

This cone describes friction. A box on a floor will not slide while the sideways force stays within μ times the pushing-down force, where μ is the friction coefficient. With μ = 0.5 and 10 N pressing down, any sideways force up to 5 N, in any direction, is safe. Legged robots and grasping hands keep their contact forces inside such cones. Day 5 builds second-order cone programs from them.

The PSD cone. A symmetric matrix X is positive semidefinite (PSD), written X ⪰ 0, when all its eigenvalues are ≥ 0. Equivalently, vTXv ≥ 0 for every vector v. The PSD matrices of size n form the PSD cone Sn+.

It is a convex cone for a one-line reason. If vTXv ≥ 0 and vTYv ≥ 0, then vT(θ1X + θ2Y)v ≥ 0 for any θ1, θ2 ≥ 0.

For 2×2 matrices there is a quick test:

[a b; b c] ⪰ 0 ⇔ a ≥ 0, c ≥ 0, ac ≥ b²

[2 1; 1 1] passes, since 2·1 = 2 ≥ 1. Its eigenvalues are 0.382 and 2.618. [2 1.5; 1.5 1] fails, since 2·1 = 2 < 2.25. One of its eigenvalues is −0.081.

Every covariance matrix is PSD, including the uncertainty a car's localisation keeps about its own position. Problems over PSD matrices are semidefinite programs, also on Day 5.

6. Building new convex sets: the safe moves

Checking the segment test by hand gets tiring for complicated sets. Instead, build them from the basic shapes with moves that keep convexity. Boyd's slides list three ways to prove a set convex: the definition, convex functions (Day 3), or safe moves from simple sets. Boyd EE364a slides CO4A 2-3

Move 1: intersection. If a segment stays inside each of two sets, it stays inside their overlap. So the intersection of convex sets is convex, even of infinitely many. The unit disk intersected with the halfspace x2 ≤ 0.5 is a "cut disk", one of the widget's shapes. In fact every closed convex set is the intersection of all the halfspaces that contain it. Boyd & Vandenberghe 2004

Move 2: affine maps. An affine map f(x) = Ax + b scales, rotates, shears, shifts or projects. It sends segments to segments. So the image of a convex set is convex, and so is the preimage {x : f(x) ∈ D} of a convex set D.

For example, A = diag(2, 1) stretches the unit disk into the ellipse x12/4 + x22 ≤ 1, with semi-axes 2 and 1. A preimage example: the set {x : x1A1 + … + xkAk ⪯ B}, called a linear matrix inequality, is convex. It is the set of x for which the affine map x ↦ B − ΣxiAi lands in the PSD cone. CMU 10-725 2016

Move 3: the perspective map. A pin-hole camera divides by depth. The perspective function P(z, t) = z/t, defined for t > 0, does the same. Images and preimages of convex sets under it are convex. For example, P(2, 4, 2) = (2/2, 4/2) = (1, 2). A convex object in front of a camera therefore shows up as a convex blob in the picture.

Following an affine map by the perspective gives a linear-fractional function f(x) = (Ax + b)/(cTx + d), defined where cTx + d > 0. It also keeps convex sets convex.

Not a safe move: union. Two disks side by side are each convex, but together they are not. In the widget's "two disks" shape, the midpoint of the two centres lies outside both.

A driving example. A planner for a self-driving car has to describe the free space it may drive into. The simplest pieces are halfspaces, one per straight edge: the two road edges, the lane line, and a line some metres behind the car ahead. Intersect a few of them and you get a convex piece of free space.

Here region A is the road with x ≤ 20, which keeps 10 m behind the car ahead. Region B is the road with y ≥ 1.75, the left lane. Each is a polyhedron, so each is convex.

The free space as a whole is "A or B", a union, and it is not convex. The point p = (15, 0) is in A and q = (45, 3.5) is in B. At x = 25 their segment has y ≈ 1.17: still in the right lane, but past the 20 m line. It is in neither region.

Planners handle this by picking a convex piece, or a chain of them, and optimizing inside it. Picking is a yes-or-no decision (Day 15). Day 19 builds whole planners this way, following the IRIS paper and graphs of convex sets.

7. Separating and supporting hyperplanes

Picture two fields that do not overlap. If both are convex, you can always build a straight fence between them. If one has a dent that wraps around the other, a straight fence may be impossible.

That is the separating hyperplane theorem. If C and D are nonempty convex sets with no common point, then there are a ≠ 0 and b such that Boyd & Vandenberghe 2004 CO4A 2-5

aTx ≤ b for all x ∈ C, and aTx ≥ b for all x ∈ D

For example, take the disks of radius 1 centred at (−2, 0) and (2, 0). The wall x1 = 0, meaning a = (1, 0) and b = 0, separates them. Every point of the left disk has x1 ≤ −1, and every point of the right disk has x1 ≥ 1.

Now lay a ruler against a convex pebble. At any point on its edge, the ruler can touch the pebble with the whole pebble on one side. That is a supporting hyperplane. If C is convex and x0 is on its boundary, there is an a ≠ 0 with aTx ≤ aTx0 for every x ∈ C.

For example, take the unit disk and x0 = (1, 0). The vertical line x1 = 1, with a = (1, 0), supports it: every point of the disk has x1 ≤ 1.

Read the separating theorem in one direction only. The sets C = D = {0} on the number line share a point, yet the "wall" x = 0 satisfies both inequalities. And a wall with a gap on both sides is not guaranteed. Two disjoint closed convex sets can creep arbitrarily close to each other, leaving no room for a gap. Boyd & Vandenberghe 2004

These two theorems are the geometry behind duality (Day 9) and behind linear classifiers, which look for a wall between two classes of data points. CO4A 2-5

Robot planners use the same fact. A car's footprint and an obstacle, both convex polygons, are apart exactly when some straight line separates them with a gap. Day 19 and the OBCA paper turn this into constraints a solver can handle.

Going deeper (optional): cones as a way to compare vectors

Numbers can always be compared, but vectors cannot. A cone K gives a partial ordering: say x ⪯K y when y − x ∈ K. With K = ℝ+, the nonnegative numbers, this is the usual ≤. K must be a proper cone: convex, closed, with a nonempty interior, and containing no whole line. CO4A 2-4

With K = ℝ2+, (1, 2) ⪯ (2, 3), because (1, 1) ∈ K. But (1, 3) and (2, 2) cannot be compared, since neither (1, −1) nor (−1, 1) is in K.

Take S = {(1, 3), (2, 2), (3, 1), (3, 3)}. No point is below all the others, so S has no minimum. But (1, 3), (2, 2) and (3, 1) are minimal: nothing in S is below them. (3, 3) is not, since (2, 2) is below it. Minimal points are the Pareto-optimal trade-offs.

Weights find them: minimizing λTz over S with λ = (2, 1) picks (1, 3). Such weights live in the dual cone K* = {λ : λTx ≥ 0 for all x ∈ K}. CO4A 2-6-1 Boyd & Vandenberghe 2004

Explain it to a 10-year-old

Draw a shape. Put two dots anywhere inside it and join them with a ruler. If the line never leaves the shape, whichever two dots you pick, the shape is "convex". A pizza slice passes. A star or a doughnut fails, because some lines poke outside or cross the hole.

Common misunderstandings

  • "Convex means round." No. Squares, triangles and halfspaces are convex. The test is about segments, not smoothness.
  • "A union of convex sets is convex." No. Intersection is safe, union is not. Two separate disks fail, and so does the two-lane free space in section 6.
  • "Any p-norm ball is convex." Only for p ≥ 1. For p = ½, the midpoint of (1, 0) and (0, 1) scores ≈ 1.414 > 1 and sits outside.
  • "If a separating hyperplane exists, the sets are disjoint." No. C = D = {0} share a point, and x = 0 still "separates" them. Also, disjoint convex sets cannot always be separated with a gap.
  • "Every cone is convex, and a cone can't be affine." Both are false. The two coordinate axes form a cone that is not convex. And any subspace, such as a line through the origin or ℝn itself, is both a cone and an affine set. (CO4A 2-1-4 states the second claim; it is a slip.)

Check yourself

Q1. Which set is NOT convex?

The ring has a hole: (0.75, 0) and (−0.75, 0) are in it, but their midpoint (0, 0) is not. An intersection of convex sets is always convex, even though a union need not be.

Q2. The ray that starts at y and passes through x is θx + (1 − θ)y with…

θ = 0 is y, θ = 1 is x, and larger θ goes past x forever. Any real θ gives the whole line, and 0 ≤ θ ≤ 1 gives only the segment.

Q3. The p-norm ball {x : ‖x‖p ≤ 1} is convex when…

For p ≥ 1 the formula is a norm and its ball is convex: diamond, disk, square, and everything in between. For p = ½ the midpoint of (1, 0) and (0, 1) scores 1.414 and leaves the "ball".

Q4. Is the matrix [2 1.5; 1.5 1] positive semidefinite?

The 2×2 test needs a ≥ 0, c ≥ 0 and ac ≥ b². The third condition fails. Positive diagonal entries and symmetry are necessary, but not enough.

Q5. Which operation can turn convex sets into a set that is not convex?

Two separate disks are each convex, but their union is not. Intersection, affine maps and the perspective map always keep convex sets convex.

Q6. What does the separating hyperplane theorem guarantee?

Both sets must be convex; a crescent can wrap around a point so that no straight wall works. The wall need not leave a gap, and the reverse direction fails: C = D = {0} share a point but are "separated" by x = 0.

Recap: things to remember

  1. z = θx + (1 − θ)y gives the line (any θ), the segment (0 ≤ θ ≤ 1) and the ray (θ ≥ 0). A set is convex when it contains the segment between any two of its points.
  2. Know the basic convex sets on sight: hyperplanes, halfspaces, balls, ellipsoids, norm balls with p ≥ 1, polyhedra, simplices, the second-order cone and the PSD cone.
  3. Intersection, affine images and preimages, and perspective maps keep sets convex. Union does not.
  4. Two disjoint convex sets can be split by a hyperplane, and every boundary point of a convex set has a supporting hyperplane.
  5. Free space for a car or robot is often a union of convex pieces, each an intersection of halfspaces. Planners optimize inside one piece at a time.

Week 1 · Day 3

Convex functions

After today you can test whether a function is convex (chord, tangent-line and second-derivative tests), build convex functions from simple pieces with convexity-preserving rules, and recognise strongly convex, quasiconvex and log-convex functions.

About 60 min · Needs Day 2 · CO4A chapter 3

Today's big idea

A convex function is shaped like a bowl: a straight string stretched between any two points of its graph never dips below the graph. Three tests check this (the chord, the tangent line and the curvature), and a short list of safe rules builds big convex costs out of small ones without testing anything. The payoff is the one from Day 1: on a bowl, a flat spot is the lowest point anywhere.

1. The chord test: what "convex" means for a function

Draw the graph of a function. Pick two points on it and stretch a string between them. If the string never passes below the graph, wherever you pick the points, the function is convex. A bowl-shaped valley passes. A road over a hill fails, because some string would cut through the hill.

The string is called a chord. To write it down, call the two inputs x and y. Every point between them is θx + (1 − θ)y for some weight θ ∈ [0, 1]: θ = 1 gives x, θ = 0 gives y, and θ = ½ gives the midpoint. The chord's height above that point is the same blend of the two heights, θf(x) + (1 − θ)f(y).

A function f is a convex function if its domain dom f (the inputs where it is defined) is a convex set and the curve never rises above the chord: CO4A 3-1-1 Boyd & Vandenberghe 2004 §3.1.1

f(θx + (1 − θ)y) ≤ θf(x) + (1 − θ)f(y)

This must hold for all x and y in dom f and every θ ∈ [0, 1]. A worked pair: f(x) = x², x = −1, y = 3 and θ = ½. The midpoint is 1, where the curve is at f(1) = 1. The chord there is at (1 + 9)/2 = 5. The gap, chord minus curve, is 4, so this pair passes.

One passing pair proves nothing, because the rule covers every pair. One failing pair, though, settles the question. Take f(x) = x⁴ − 2x² with x = −1 and y = 1. Both ends sit at height −1, so the chord is flat at −1, but the curve at the midpoint is f(0) = 0. The curve is 1 above the chord, so this f is not convex.

Turn the picture upside down for the mirror idea. A function is a concave function if −f is convex: the chord never passes above the graph, like a dome. A straight line f(x) = aTx + b (where aTx = a₁x₁ + … + aₙxₙ) turns the inequality into an equality, so affine functions are both convex and concave. CO4A 3-1-1

With θ = ½ the chord test reads "f of the average ≤ the average of f". Extended to many points and to expected values, this is Jensen's inequality, f(E[X]) ≤ E[f(X)]. If X is 0 or 2 with equal odds and f(x) = x², then f(E[X]) = f(1) = 1, while E[f(X)] = (0 + 4)/2 = 2. CO4A 3-1-3 Boyd & Vandenberghe 2004 §3.1.8

Day 2 gives a second picture of the same idea. Shade everything on or above the graph. That region is the epigraph, epi f = {(x, t) : f(x) ≤ t}, where t stands for a height. A function is convex exactly when its epigraph is a convex set. The chord test is Day 2's segment test applied to two points on the graph: a chord that dips below the graph leaves the shaded region. CO4A 3-1-3 Boyd & Vandenberghe 2004 §3.1.7

Try it: pick a function and drag the two points (or use the sliders). The θ slider moves the pair of dots that compare chord and curve. Press Hunt for a bad chord to scan 41 × 41 pairs of points with 11 weights each. The coloured strip under the plot shows the sign of f″, which section 3 explains.

Notice that the default, x² with a = −1 and b = 3, shows a gap of 4.000 at x = 1 (chord 5.000 − curve 1.000) and a lowest gap of 0.000, so the chord is green. Switch to x³: its default chord from 0 to 2 is green as well, but Hunt finds a chord from −2 to 1.1 that dips 3.98 below the graph.

Explain it to a 10-year-old

Think of a slide shaped like a smile. Hold a straight stick so that it touches the slide at two spots. Wherever you choose the spots, the stick is above the slide or touching it. Now think of a slide shaped like a W, with a bump in the middle. Put the stick's ends on both sides of the bump, and the bump pokes up through the stick. A marble on the smile always rolls to the one lowest point. On the W it can get stuck on the wrong side of the bump.

2. The tangent test: one slope gives a floor everywhere

Lay a ruler against a bowl so that it touches at one spot. The ruler touches the bowl there and nowhere cuts into it. For a convex function the tangent line is that ruler: it touches the graph at one point and stays on or below the graph everywhere else.

In symbols, write ∇f(x) for the gradient, the vector of slopes ∂f/∂x₁, …, ∂f/∂xₙ, which points uphill. The tangent at x predicts f(y) ≈ f(x) + ∇f(x)T(y − x). The first-order condition says that a differentiable f on a convex domain is convex exactly when this prediction never overshoots: CO4A 3-1-3 Boyd & Vandenberghe 2004 §3.1.3

f(y) ≥ f(x) + ∇f(x)T(y − x) for all x, y

A number check. For f(x) = x² at x = 1 the slope is 2, so the tangent line is 1 + 2(y − 1) = 2y − 1. At y = 3 the tangent says 5 and the true value is 9, so the floor holds. Now take sin x at x = 0. Its tangent is the line through the origin with slope 1. At y = 1 the line says 1, but sin 1 ≈ 0.841 is lower. The tangent has poked above the graph, so sin is not convex.

Here is why this matters. Suppose the gradient is zero at some point x*. The floor then reads f(y) ≥ f(x*) for every y, so nothing anywhere beats x*. For a convex function, a flat spot is a global minimum, not just a local one. That is Day 1's "local equals global", seen through tangents. Boyd and Vandenberghe call the first-order condition "perhaps the most important property of convex functions". Boyd & Vandenberghe 2004 §3.1.3

For a planner this is a guarantee you can act on. If a car's cost is convex in its plan and there are no constraints, a zero gradient means the best plan, not just a nearby dip. With constraints, the zero-gradient test becomes the KKT conditions of Day 10. A kink, like |x| at 0, has no single tangent, but it still has many lines that act as floors; Day 7 calls their slopes subgradients.

Going deeper (optional): why the tangent test works

Take one variable. Convexity on the short chord from x to x + t(y − x) gives f(x + t(y − x)) ≤ (1 − t)f(x) + t·f(y) for t ∈ (0, 1]. Subtract f(x) from both sides and divide by t:

[f(x + t(y − x)) − f(x)] / t ≤ f(y) − f(x)

As t shrinks to 0, the left side becomes f′(x)(y − x), and that is the tangent inequality. For n variables, run the same argument along the line through x and y. The converse (tangent floors everywhere imply convexity) is also short; Boyd and Vandenberghe give both directions. Boyd & Vandenberghe 2004 §3.1.3

3. The curvature test: second derivatives and the Hessian

Drive along the graph from left to right. On a convex function the steering wheel only ever turns left (the road bends upward) or stays straight. It never turns right. Bending upward means the slope keeps growing.

The rate at which the slope grows is the second derivative f″. So a function of one variable, twice differentiable on an open interval, is convex exactly when f″(x) ≥ 0 everywhere. Boyd & Vandenberghe 2004 §3.1.4 For −log x on x > 0, f′ = −1/x and f″ = 1/x² > 0, so −log x is convex. For x⁴ − 2x², f″ = 12x² − 4, which is negative for |x| < 0.577. There the graph bends down, and that is exactly where the chord in the first figure failed.

With several variables, curvature becomes a matrix. The Hessian ∇2f(x) is the table of all second derivatives; its entry (i, j) is ∂²f/∂xᵢ∂xⱼ. "Bends up in every direction" means the Hessian is positive semidefinite, written ∇2f(x) ⪰ 0: all its eigenvalues are ≥ 0, or equivalently vT∇2f(x)v ≥ 0 for every direction v. The second-order condition, for f twice differentiable on a convex open domain, is the n-variable version of f″ ≥ 0: CO4A 3-1-3 Boyd & Vandenberghe 2004 §3.1.4

f convex ⇔ ∇2f(x) ⪰ 0 for every x in dom f

Two quadratics that look alike show the difference. Write a matrix row by row, with ";" between rows. f(x) = x₁² + x₁x₂ + x₂² has the constant Hessian [2 1; 1 2], with eigenvalues 1 and 3. Both are positive, so f is a bowl. g(x) = x₁² + 4x₁x₂ + x₂² also has only positive coefficients, but its Hessian [2 4; 4 2] has eigenvalues −2 and 6. One negative eigenvalue makes g a saddle: up in one direction, down in another.

You can see the saddle without eigenvalues. Walk through the origin along the direction v = (1, −1), so that x = (t, −t). Then g = t² − 4t² + t² = −2t², a parabola that opens downward. A convex function must be convex along every line, so g is not convex. This trick, restricting to a line, turns any n-variable question into a one-variable one. B&V slides 3.7 CMU 10-725 2016

Try it: start from the saddle, then pick the bowl, or slide q₁₂ toward 0 and watch the verdict turn convex once |q₁₂| ≤ 1. With q₁₁ = q₂₂ = 1 the Hessian eigenvalues are 2 − 2q₁₂ and 2 + 2q₁₂.

Notice that the default saddle, x₁² + 4x₁x₂ + x₂², has Hessian eigenvalues −2 and 6. Its contours are hyperbolas, and the slices read f = 6t² along (1, 1) but f = −2t² along (1, −1), the same −2t² as in the text.

How curved is curved enough? Convexity allows straight stretches: the chord of |x| from 1 to 3 lies on the graph, gap 0. A function is strictly convex if the chord lies strictly above the graph between any two different points (for 0 < θ < 1). Then it cannot have two lowest points, because the midpoint between them would be lower still. A quick test: if ∇2f(x) has all eigenvalues > 0 everywhere, f is strictly convex. The converse fails: x⁴ is strictly convex, yet f″(0) = 0. CO4A 3-1-1 Boyd & Vandenberghe 2004 §3.1.4

A function is strongly convex with parameter m > 0 if it is at least as curved as the bowl (m/2)‖x‖₂², where ‖x‖₂ = √(x₁² + … + xₙ²) is ordinary length. Formally, f(x) − (m/2)‖x‖₂² must still be convex. CO4A 3-1-1 The Hessian of that difference is ∇2f(x) − mI, where I is the identity matrix. So for twice-differentiable f, strong convexity means ∇2f(x) ⪰ mI: every eigenvalue of the Hessian is at least m, at every x.

Some numbers. x² is strongly convex with m = 2: x² − x² = 0 is still convex, while m = 3 would leave −½x². The bowl x₁² + x₁x₂ + x₂² has smallest Hessian eigenvalue 1, so m = 1. x⁴ is strictly but not strongly convex, because its curvature 12x² falls to 0 at x = 0. So strongly convex ⇒ strictly convex ⇒ convex, and neither arrow reverses. CMU 10-725 2016 Why care? Strong convexity puts a curved floor under f instead of a flat one, f(y) ≥ f(x) + ∇f(x)T(y − x) + (m/2)‖y − x‖₂². Day 6 uses this floor to show that gradient descent then shrinks its error bound by a constant factor at every step.

Analogy

Picture a skateboard bowl. The chord test: a plank laid between any two points of the surface never goes underground. The tangent test: a plank resting on the surface at one spot never pokes into it anywhere else. The curvature test: as you roll across, the surface under your wheels only ever curves up. A bowl with a flat floor is convex but not strictly convex. A bowl that curves up everywhere by at least some fixed amount is strongly convex.

4. A catalogue of convex functions

Most convexity proofs end with "and this piece is a function we already know". So it pays to recognise a dozen on sight, the way you read road signs without reading the words. The table lists the standard ones, each with a one-line reason. CO4A 3-1-2 Boyd & Vandenberghe 2004 §3.1.5 CMU 10-725 2016

FunctionFormulaConvex onWhy, or a number
Exponentialeax, any aall of ℝf″ = a²eax ≥ 0
Powersxax > 0, when a ≥ 1 or a ≤ 0f″ = a(a − 1)xa−2 ≥ 0; for 0 ≤ a ≤ 1 it is concave (√x)
Negative log−log xx > 0f″ = 1/x² > 0
Negative entropyx log xx > 0f″ = 1/x > 0
Absolute powers|x|p, p ≥ 1all of ℝp = 1 is |x|: convex, not strictly
AffineaTx + bℝnflat, so convex and concave
Quadratic½xTPx + qTx + rℝn, if P ⪰ 0its Hessian is P
Least squares‖Ax − b‖₂²ℝn, any AHessian 2ATA ⪰ 0
Norms‖x‖p = (Σ|xᵢ|p)1/p, p ≥ 1; ‖x‖∞ = maxᵢ|xᵢ|ℝntriangle inequality; x = (3, −4) gives 7, 5, 4 for p = 1, 2, ∞
Maximummax{x₁, …, xₙ}ℝna maximum of linear functions
Log-sum-explog(ex₁ + … + exₙ)ℝnHessian ⪰ 0; x = (1, 2, 3) gives 3.408
IndicatorIC(x): 0 on C, +∞ off Cℝn, if C is convexturns "x ∈ C" into a cost

A norm ‖x‖ measures the length of a vector. Three are common: ‖x‖₁ = |x₁| + … + |xₙ| (city-block length), ‖x‖₂ (straight-line length) and ‖x‖∞ = maxᵢ|xᵢ| (the largest entry). For x = (3, −4) they give 7, 5 and 4. Every norm is convex for a one-line reason: scaling (‖θx‖ = θ‖x‖ for θ ≥ 0) and the triangle inequality (‖u + v‖ ≤ ‖u‖ + ‖v‖) together give ‖θx + (1 − θ)y‖ ≤ θ‖x‖ + (1 − θ)‖y‖, which is the chord test. In a planner, the distance ‖p − pgoal‖₂ from a car's position p to its goal is therefore convex in p.

A quadratic f(x) = ½xTPx + qTx + r, with P a symmetric matrix, has the same Hessian P at every point. So it is convex exactly when P ⪰ 0. Least squares, ‖Ax − b‖₂², is the case P = 2ATA. It is always convex, because vTATAv = ‖Av‖₂² ≥ 0 for every v.

Log-sum-exp, lse(x) = log(ex₁ + … + exₙ), is a smooth version of the maximum: max xᵢ ≤ lse(x) ≤ max xᵢ + log n. At x = (1, 2, 3) it is 3.408, between 3 and 3 + log 3 ≈ 4.099. Its Hessian is diag(z) − zzT, where zᵢ = exᵢ/Σⱼexⱼ are the softmax weights and diag(z) is the diagonal matrix holding them. At x = (0, 0) that is [0.25 −0.25; −0.25 0.25], with eigenvalues 0 and 0.5, so it is positive semidefinite. Boyd & Vandenberghe 2004 §3.1.5 CMU 10-725 2016

Finally, the indicator function of a set C, IC(x) = 0 for x in C and +∞ outside, turns a constraint "x ∈ C" into a cost. It is convex exactly when C is a convex set, which ties today back to Day 2. CO4A 3-1-2

5. Building convex functions from safe pieces

Checking a Hessian by hand gets painful fast. Engineers instead build costs like Lego, from catalogue pieces joined by moves known to keep convexity. Five moves cover almost everything. CO4A 3-2 Boyd & Vandenberghe 2004 §3.2

  1. Nonnegative weighted sums. If f₁, …, fₘ are convex and every weight αᵢ ≥ 0, then α₁f₁ + … + αₘfₘ is convex: add up their chord inequalities. Example: 3x² + 2|x| + ex. A negative weight can break it: x² − 2x⁴ has f″ = 2 − 24x², which is negative for |x| > 0.29.
  2. Affine composition. If f is convex, so is f(Ax + b) for any matrix A and vector b, because a straight line in x maps to a straight line in Ax + b. Example: ‖Ax − b‖ is convex for every norm.
  3. Pointwise maximum. The pointwise maximum f(x) = max{f₁(x), …, fₘ(x)} of convex functions is convex, and so is a supremum over infinitely many. Picture the upper edge of several bowls: still one bowl. Example: f(x) = max(2x + 1, −x + 4) has a kink at x = 1 with f(1) = 3, and the chord from x = 0 (f = 4) to x = 2 (f = 5) passes above it at 4.5. The same rule makes a worst-case cost convex: the largest of several convex costs, one for each guess about what the car ahead will do.
  4. Partial minimization. If f(x, y) is convex in x and y jointly and C is a convex set, then g(x) = infy ∈ C f(x, y) is convex, as long as g stays above −∞. This is partial minimization. Example: the distance to a convex set, dist(x, C) = miny ∈ C ‖x − y‖. For C = [0, 1] it equals max(0, −x, x − 1), so dist(3, [0, 1]) = 2. How far a car's position lies outside a convex lane corridor is therefore a convex penalty. Boyd & Vandenberghe 2004 §3.2.5
  5. Composition. For f(x) = h(g(x)), convex pieces are not enough; the direction in which the outer function h slopes matters too. The composition rule comes from the chain rule f″ = h″(g)·g′² + h′(g)·g″: when both terms are ≥ 0, f is convex. The table lists the four cases. CMU 10-725 2016 Boyd & Vandenberghe 2004 §3.2.4
Outer hInner gh(g(x)) isExample
convex, nondecreasingconvexconvexeg(x), such as ex²
convex, nonincreasingconcaveconvex1/g(x) for g concave and > 0, such as 1/(1 − x²) on (−1, 1)
concave, nondecreasingconcaveconcavelog g(x) for g concave and > 0
concave, nonincreasingconvexconcave√(1 − x²), the top half of a circle

A failure shows why the slope direction matters. h(u) = e−u is convex but decreasing, and g(x) = x² is convex. Their composition, the bell curve e−x², is not convex: at x = 0 it is 1, above the chord from −1 to 1, which sits at e−1 ≈ 0.368.

One move looks safe and is not: a plain minimum. min(x², (x − 2)²) is 0 at x = 0 and x = 2 but 1 at x = 1, above the chord at 0. Two bowls side by side make two valleys. Partial minimization is different: one jointly convex function, minimized over a convex set. CO4A 3-2 opens its minimization part by calling the minimum of convex functions convex; that sentence is wrong, though the formula after it is right. CO4A 3-2

Here is the toolkit on a real cost. A car's speed planner chooses accelerations a₁, …, aN, one every Δt seconds. A comfort cost penalizes acceleration and jerk, the change in acceleration per second, (ak+1 − ak)/Δt:

J(a) = Σ ak² + w Σ ((ak+1 − ak)/Δt)²

Each term is a square, which is convex, of an affine function of a (move 2), and the weights 1 and w are nonnegative (move 1). So J is convex for every w ≥ 0 and Δt > 0, with no Hessian in sight. Numbers, with N = 3, Δt = 1 and w = 1: plan A = (0, 2, 0) costs 4 + 8 = 12, plan B = (2, 0, 2) costs 8 + 8 = 16, and their average (1, 1, 1) costs 3 + 0 = 3, far below the average cost of 14. Blending two plans never costs more than blending their costs. That is the chord test again, and it is why a model predictive controller (Day 17) can find the single best plan reliably.

Going deeper (optional): two more rules and a catch

Perspective. If f is convex, its perspective g(x, t) = t·f(x/t), for t > 0, is convex as well. For example, f(x) = xTx gives g(x, t) = xTx/t, convex in x and t together. The logic runs from f to g; the examples in CO4A 3-2 state it the other way round. Boyd & Vandenberghe 2004 §3.2.6

Conjugate. The conjugate function f*(y) = supx (yTx − f(x)) is a supremum of functions that are affine in y, so by move 3 it is convex even when f is not. It is a standard tool in duality theory. Boyd & Vandenberghe 2004 §3.3.1

The catch in composition. The monotonicity of h must hold on all of ℝ once h is given the value +∞ outside its domain. h(u) = u² with domain u ≥ 0 increases on its domain, but its extension does not: it drops from +∞ to 0 at u = 0. With g(x) = x² − 1, h(g(x)) is defined only for |x| ≥ 1, which is not even a convex set. Boyd & Vandenberghe 2004 §3.2.4

6. Two looser cousins: quasiconvex and log-convex functions

Some useful functions are not bowls but still have only one valley. Count the 10-tonne trucks needed to move x tonnes: 0 for nothing, 1 for up to 10 tonnes, 2 for up to 20. The graph is a staircase, ⌈x/10⌉. It fails the chord test, since 5 tonnes needs 1 truck, above the chord's 0.5 between 0 and 10 tonnes. Yet it never goes down, so it never makes a second valley.

The idea that captures this is the sublevel set {x : f(x) ≤ α}, all the inputs that score at most α. A function is quasiconvex if every sublevel set is convex. In one variable that means the graph goes down and then up, or only one way, with no second dip. There is a chord-style test too, with the higher endpoint in place of the chord: CO4A 3-4-1 CO4A 3-4-2

f(θx + (1 − θ)y) ≤ max{f(x), f(y)}

Every convex function is quasiconvex, because its sublevel sets are convex. CO4A 3-1-3 The reverse fails. f(x) = √|x| has the sublevel sets [−α², α²], all intervals, so it is quasiconvex. It is not convex: between 0 and 4 the chord at x = 2 is at 1, while f(2) ≈ 1.414. But 1.414 ≤ max{f(0), f(4)} = 2, so the weaker test passes. Boyd & Vandenberghe 2004 §3.4.1

Weaker means fewer guarantees. A zero slope no longer marks a minimum: x³ only rises, so it is quasiconvex, and its slope at 0 is 0, but 0 is not a minimizer. For differentiable f, the correct first-order test is: if f(y) ≤ f(x), then ∇f(x)T(y − x) ≤ 0. Every point at least as good as x lies on the downhill side of the gradient. CO4A 3-4-3 garbles this statement, so follow Boyd and Vandenberghe here. Boyd & Vandenberghe 2004 §3.4.3

Two more warnings. A local minimum need not be global: at x = 5 tonnes nothing nearby needs fewer trucks, yet x = 0 needs none. Boyd & Vandenberghe 2004 §4.2.2 And sums can break quasiconvexity: x³ and −x each run one way, but x³ − x has the sublevel set {x : x³ − x ≤ 0} = (−∞, −1] ∪ [0, 1], two pieces.

The second cousin works on a log scale. A positive function f is log-concave if log f is concave, and log-convex if log f is convex. The bell curve e−x²/2 is the standard log-concave example: it is not concave everywhere (its tails bend up), but its log, −x²/2, is a dome. The Gaussian cumulative distribution function and det X on positive definite matrices are log-concave too. On the other side, 1/x on x > 0 is log-convex, since its log, −log x, is convex. CO4A 3-5 Boyd & Vandenberghe 2004 §3.5.1

Four facts are worth keeping. A log-convex f is convex, since f = elog f is a convex, nondecreasing function of the convex log f. Products of log-concave functions are log-concave, since their logs add. Sums of log-convex functions stay log-convex: log(f + g) is log-sum-exp applied to (log f, log g), which is convex and nondecreasing in each argument. (CO4A 3-5 argues this step with "the log of a convex function is convex", which is false.) Sums of log-concave functions need not stay log-concave: two bells at ±2, e−(x−2)²/2 + e−(x+2)²/2, have (log f)″(0) ≈ +3 > 0. Boyd & Vandenberghe 2004 §3.5.2

7. How to check convexity in practice

Faced with a new cost, work down this list and stop at the first step that answers. It is the recipe from the Boyd and Vandenberghe slides, cheapest step first. B&V slides 3.18

  1. Recognise it. Is it in the catalogue of section 4? Then it is convex.
  2. Build it. Can you write it as catalogue pieces joined by the five moves of section 5? Then it is convex, and you never needed a derivative.
  3. Differentiate it. For a function of one or two variables, compute f″ or the Hessian and check its sign or eigenvalues at every point of a convex domain.
  4. Slice it. Otherwise restrict to lines: g(t) = f(x + tv) must be convex in t for every point x and direction v.
  5. Attack it. If you suspect it is not convex, hunt for one bad chord, as the widget does, or one direction with a negative Hessian eigenvalue. One failure settles it. No number of passing samples proves convexity.

Steps 1 and 2 are automated in CVXPY, a Python modelling library, under the name disciplined convex programming (DCP). Every built-in function (an "atom", such as square, norm or log_sum_exp) carries its known curvature and monotonicity, and CVXPY applies the composition rule at every node of your expression (as of Oct 2026). CVXPY docs If the rules certify an expression, it is convex. If they cannot, CVXPY reports UNKNOWN, which may only mean the expression was written in an unlucky way: DCP is sufficient, not necessary. B&V slides 3.33

import cvxpy as cp
x = cp.Variable()
a = cp.Variable(3)                        # a 3-step acceleration plan

comfort = cp.sum_squares(a) + 4 * cp.sum_squares(cp.diff(a))  # w/Δt² = 4
print(comfort.curvature)                  # CONVEX
print(cp.log_sum_exp(a).curvature)        # CONVEX
print(cp.sqrt(1 + cp.square(x)).curvature)       # UNKNOWN, though convex
print(cp.norm(cp.hstack([1, x]), 2).curvature)   # CONVEX: same function
print(cp.minimum(cp.square(x), cp.square(x - 2)).curvature)  # UNKNOWN: truly not convex

The √(1 + x²) line is the textbook case. The function equals ‖(1, x)‖₂, a norm of an affine expression, which CVXPY certifies at once when it is written that way. Day 4 takes the next step and builds whole optimization problems from convex pieces.

Common misunderstandings

  • "One passing chord proves convexity." The rule covers all pairs. x³ passes from 0 to 2 (gap +3 at the midpoint) and fails from −2 to 0 (gap −3).
  • "The minimum of convex functions is convex." min(x², (x − 2)²) is 1 at x = 1, above the chord at 0. A maximum is safe; a minimum keeps convexity only as partial minimization of one jointly convex function.
  • "Strictly convex means f″ > 0." x⁴ is strictly convex with f″(0) = 0. Only the other direction holds: f″ > 0 on an interval implies strictly convex there.
  • "f″ > 0 wherever f is defined is enough." The domain must be convex too. 1/x² on x ≠ 0 has f″ = 6/x⁴ > 0, yet it is not convex: its domain has a hole at 0.
  • "Convex sublevel sets mean a convex function." That is quasiconvexity, which is weaker. √|x| has interval sublevel sets and fails the chord test.
  • "A convex function of a convex function is convex." Only if the outer one is nondecreasing. e−x² is a convex, decreasing function of the convex x², and it is not convex.

Check yourself

Q1. Which of these is convex on all of ℝ?

ex has f″ = ex > 0 everywhere. The others all bend down somewhere: x³ for x < 0, sin x on (0, π), and the bell e−x² for |x| < 0.707.

Q2. The first-order condition says that the tangent line of a convex function is…

The tangent is a global floor: f(y) ≥ f(x) + ∇f(x)T(y − x) for every y, not just nearby ones. With ∇f(x) = 0 this says f(y) ≥ f(x) for all y.

Q3. f(x) = x⁴ has f″(0) = 0. So f is…

f″ ≥ 0 everywhere gives convexity, and the chord lies strictly above x⁴ between any two different points. f″ > 0 is enough for strict convexity but not required; x⁴ is the standard example.

Q4. g(x) = x₁² + 4x₁x₂ + x₂² is…

The Hessian eigenvalues are 2 ± 4, so −2 and 6. Along (1, −1), g(t, −t) = −2t², a downward parabola. Positive coefficients and symmetry say nothing about the signs of the eigenvalues.

Q5. f₁ and f₂ are convex. Which of these can fail to be convex?

min(x², (x − 2)²) has two valleys and sits at 1, above the chord at 0 between them. Nonnegative sums, maxima and affine composition always keep convexity.

Q6. f(x) = √|x| is…

Every sublevel set {x : √|x| ≤ α} = [−α², α²] is an interval, so it is quasiconvex. Its chord from 0 to 4 is at 1 at x = 2, below f(2) ≈ 1.414, so it is not convex. It is not concave on ℝ either: the chord from −1 to 1 sits at 1, above f(0) = 0.

Recap: things to remember

  1. Convex means the chord between any two graph points lies on or above the graph; equivalently, the epigraph is a convex set. One bad chord disproves convexity.
  2. For differentiable f, the tangent is a global floor, f(y) ≥ f(x) + ∇f(x)T(y − x), so ∇f(x) = 0 means x is a global minimizer.
  3. For twice-differentiable f on a convex domain, convex ⇔ ∇2f(x) ⪰ 0 everywhere. Strongly convex (∇2f ⪰ mI, m > 0) ⇒ strictly convex ⇒ convex.
  4. Know the catalogue (norms, quadratics with P ⪰ 0, least squares, −log x, ex, max, log-sum-exp) and the safe moves (nonnegative sums, affine composition, maximum, partial minimization, composition with the right monotonicity). A plain minimum is not safe.
  5. Quasiconvex functions have convex sublevel sets and weaker guarantees; log-concave and log-convex functions are tested through log f. CVXPY's DCP rules automate the build-it check.
