Week 1 · Day 4

Convex problems

After today you can write a problem in standard form, explain why every local minimum of a convex problem is global, use the first-order optimality condition, and reshape problems with slack variables, epigraphs and other equivalent transformations.

About 60 min · Needs Day 3 · CO4A chapter 4

Today's big idea

A convex problem is a convex cost minimized over a convex set of allowed points. Such a problem has no false bottoms: if no small step improves a point, no big step does either. Much of the practical skill is rewriting a problem until its convexity is plain to see.

1. Writing a problem down: standard form

Every optimization problem says the same thing. Pick some numbers to make one number as small as possible, while obeying some rules. A delivery robot picks a route to make the travel time small without leaving the sidewalk.

Standard form is the agreed way to write this down, so that theorems and solvers can read it. CO4A 4-1

minimize f(x)
subject to gi(x) ≤ 0, i = 1, …, m
hj(x) = 0, j = 1, …, r

Here x ∈ ℝn is the optimization variable, the numbers you get to choose. f is the objective (CO4A also calls it the criterion), the number you want small. Each gi(x) ≤ 0 is an inequality constraint and each hj(x) = 0 is an equality constraint. All the rules are written as "something ≤ 0" or "something = 0", so a rule like x ≤ 3 becomes x − 3 ≤ 0.

A point that obeys every rule is a feasible point, and all of them together form the feasible set. The smallest objective value over the feasible set is the optimal value f*. A feasible point x* with f(x*) = f* is an optimal point, also called a solution or minimizer.

Two more names help. A feasible x with f(x) ≤ f* + ε is ε-suboptimal; solvers return such points, because they stop at a tolerance. An inequality with gi(x) = 0 is active at x: you are touching that fence. CO4A 4-1

The problem is a convex problem when f is convex, every gi is convex, and every hj is affine, so that all the equalities together read Ax = b. Why must equalities be affine? The rule h(x) = 0 is the same as two rules, h(x) ≤ 0 and −h(x) ≤ 0. Both are convex only when h is both convex and concave, which means affine. Tibshirani 2016 To maximize a concave function, minimize its negative instead.

Worked example: maximize 3x + 2y subject to x + y ≤ 4, x ≤ 3, x ≥ 0 and y ≥ 0. In standard form it reads: minimize −3x − 2y subject to x + y − 4 ≤ 0, x − 3 ≤ 0, −x ≤ 0 and −y ≤ 0. Linear functions are both convex and affine, so this is a convex problem. The feasible set is a four-sided region with corners (0, 0), (3, 0), (3, 1) and (0, 4), where 3x + 2y is 0, 9, 11 and 8. The best point is (3, 1), with maximum 11, so f* = −11 in the minimize form. There the rules x + y ≤ 4 and x ≤ 3 are active, and x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0 are not. (Day 5 explains why a corner always wins here.)

A driving example in one dimension: a lane-keeping planner chooses a lateral offset d, in metres from the lane centre. It would like d = 0.8 to give a cyclist room, but the lane edge allows at most d = 0.5. In standard form: minimize (d − 0.8)2 subject to d − 0.5 ≤ 0. The answer is d* = 0.5 with the rule active, and f* = 0.09. Keep this example in mind for section 3.

2. Why local means global

Imagine walking downhill in thick fog. You can only feel the slope under your feet, so you stop when every step goes up. In a single round valley you are now at the bottom. In the Alps you might be standing in a small hollow halfway up a mountain.

A feasible x is a local optimum if no feasible point within some distance R > 0 is better: f(x) ≤ f(y) for all feasible y with ‖y − x‖2 ≤ R. It is a global optimum if no feasible point anywhere is better. For a convex problem, every local optimum is a global optimum. Tibshirani 2016 Boyd & Vandenberghe 2004

The one-line reason: suppose some feasible y were better than a local optimum x. The straight segment from x to y stays feasible, because the feasible set is convex. Along it, f stays below the chord, because f is convex. So points on the segment just next to x are also better than x, and x was not a local optimum after all.

Worked example. The function f(x) = x4 − 3x2 + x is not convex. Its slope is zero at three points: x ≈ −1.301 (f ≈ −3.514, the global minimum), x ≈ 0.170 (a local maximum) and x ≈ 1.131 (f ≈ −1.070, a local minimum that is not global). Gradient descent from x = 2 with step 0.01 slides into the hollow at 1.131 and stops there. The convex function x2 + x has exactly one point of zero slope, x = −0.5, and that point is the global minimum.

Two more facts. First, the set of all optimal points is convex: if x and y are both optimal, every point between them is too. For example, f(x) = max(|x| − 1, 0) is flat on [−1, 1], and that whole interval is optimal. Second, if f is strictly convex (no flat stretches), there is at most one optimal point. CO4A 4-2

Going deeper (optional): the local-equals-global proof

Let x be locally optimal with radius R, and suppose a feasible y has f(y) < f(x). Then ‖y − x‖2 > R. Take z = (1 − θ)x + θy with θ = R / (2‖y − x‖2), a point on the segment at distance R/2 from x. Since the feasible set is convex, z is feasible. Since f is convex, f(z) ≤ (1 − θ)f(x) + θf(y) < f(x). That contradicts local optimality. The full version is in Boyd & Vandenberghe §4.2.2. Boyd & Vandenberghe 2004

3. The first-order optimality condition

Back to the lane-keeping planner. At d* = 0.5 the slope of the cost is f′(0.5) = 2(0.5 − 0.8) = −0.6, not zero. The cost would keep falling if d could grow, but the lane edge stops it. Every allowed move goes to some y ≤ 0.5, and the predicted change f′(d*)(y − d*) = −0.6(y − 0.5) is never negative. So every allowed move goes uphill, and d* is optimal.

The general rule is the first-order optimality condition. Take a convex problem with a differentiable f and feasible set C. Then x is optimal exactly when x ∈ C and CO4A 4-3

∇f(x)T(y − x) ≥ 0 for every y ∈ C

Read ∇f(x)T(y − x) as "the first-order change in f when you start moving from x toward y". The condition says no feasible direction goes downhill. Picture it: −∇f(x) is the steepest-downhill arrow, and at the optimum it points out of C. The line through x at right angles to ∇f(x) is a supporting hyperplane of C: it touches C at x, and all of C lies on its uphill side. Boyd & Vandenberghe 2004

With no constraints at all (C = ℝn), y − x can point anywhere, including along −∇f(x). Then the condition becomes the familiar ∇f(x) = 0. Example: f(x) = ½xTQx + bTx with Q = diag(2, 4) and b = (−2, −8). Setting ∇f(x) = Qx + b to zero gives x* = (1, 2). Tibshirani 2016

Now a two-dimensional example with constraints. Minimize f(x) = (x1 − 3)2 + (x2 − 2)2 over the triangle x1 ≥ 0, x2 ≥ 0, x1 + x2 ≤ 2. The level sets of f are circles around the target (3, 2), which lies outside the triangle. The best point is the triangle's closest point to the target, x* = (1.5, 0.5), with f* = 1.52 + 1.52 = 4.5.

Check the condition. The gradient is ∇f(x*) = (2(1.5 − 3), 2(0.5 − 2)) = (−3, −3). For any y in the triangle:

∇f(x*)T(y − x*) = −3(y1 + y2 − 2) ≥ 0

It is non-negative because y1 + y2 ≤ 2. At the corner y = (0, 0) it equals 6, and anywhere on the edge x1 + x2 = 2 it equals 0. Compare a point that is not optimal, x = (1, 1), where f = 5 and ∇f = (−4, −2). Toward y = (2, 0) the product is −4·1 − 2·(−1) = −2 < 0. That direction goes downhill: the point (1.2, 0.8) has f = 4.68 < 5.

Try it: drag the orange target and watch x* and the arrow −∇f(x*). The pink half-plane holds the points y with ∇f(x)T(y − x) < 0, which lie downhill to first order. Then pick "a candidate point x" and drag x around; the widget shows the corner that goes most downhill.

Notice that with the target at (3, 2), the best point is x* = (1.5, 0.5), with f* = 4.5 and ∇f(x*) = (−3, −3), which is not zero. The arrow −∇f = (3, 3) points straight out through the edge x1 + x2 = 2. The smallest value of ∇f(x*)T(y − x*) over the triangle is 0, so the pink downhill side does not enter the triangle.

Analogy

A ball rolls downhill until a fence stops it. The slope still pulls it toward the fence, and the fence pushes back just as hard. The first-order condition says the ball has nowhere left to roll.

If the only constraints are equalities Ax = b, the condition becomes ∇f(x) + ATu = 0 for some vector u. This is the Lagrange condition from calculus, and its numbers u return as dual variables on Day 9 and in the KKT conditions on Day 10. Tibshirani 2016

Here is the triangle problem in CVXPY, a Python modelling tool you will see all course:

import cvxpy as cp
x = cp.Variable(2)
f = cp.sum_squares(x - [3, 2])          # bowl centred on the target (3, 2)
rules = [x >= 0, cp.sum(x) <= 2]        # the triangle
prob = cp.Problem(cp.Minimize(f), rules)
prob.solve()
print(x.value, prob.value)              # about [1.5 0.5] and 4.5
print(rules[1].dual_value)              # about 3: how hard the edge pushes back

That last number, 3, is the fence's push. At x*, ∇f + 3·(1, 1) = (−3, −3) + (3, 3) = 0, so the slope and the push cancel.

4. Equivalent problems and slack variables

Equivalent problems are two problems where solving one quickly gives you a solution of the other. They can look very different, with different sizes or different smoothness. Boyd & Vandenberghe 2004 The rest of today is a toolbox of such rewrites, each used to make convexity visible or to fit what a solver accepts.

The simplest rewrite applies an increasing function to the objective. Minimizing ‖Ax − b‖2 and minimizing ‖Ax − b‖22 give the same x, because squaring a non-negative number keeps its order. Only the squared version is differentiable everywhere, which is why least squares uses it. CO4A 4-5

A slack variable turns an inequality into an equality by naming the leftover room. Think of an airline's 23 kg suitcase limit: the slack is how many kilograms you still have spare. In symbols: CO4A 4-7

gi(x) ≤ 0 ⇔ gi(x) + si = 0, si ≥ 0

Worked example: x + y ≤ 4 becomes x + y + s = 4 with s ≥ 0. At (3, 1), s = 0, so the rule is active. At (1, 1), s = 2: there are 2 units of room. In driving terms, a following-distance rule "gap ≥ 20 m" becomes 20 − gap + s = 0, and the slack s is the number of spare metres to the car ahead. Slacks are how linear programs reach their standard form on Day 5.

One warning. The new equality gi(x) + si = 0 is affine only if gi is affine. Add a slack to a curved rule such as x2 ≤ 1 and you get x2 + s = 1, a curved equality, and the problem stops being convex in standard form. CO4A 4-7

5. Epigraph form: move the objective into the rules

Think of the graph of f as a tent roof. Its epigraph is everything on or above the roof, as on Day 3. Finding the lowest point of the roof is the same as finding the lowest height t at which a point (x, t) still fits in the epigraph.

That gives the epigraph form of a problem. Add one new variable t and minimize it: Boyd & Vandenberghe 2004 Boyd slides

minimize t over (x, t)
subject to f(x) − t ≤ 0, gi(x) ≤ 0, Ax = b

The objective is now linear, and all the curvature has moved into the constraints. If f is convex, f(x) − t ≤ 0 is a convex rule, so the new problem is still convex.

Worked example: minimize max(2x + 1, 4 − x). The objective has a kink where the two lines cross, so it is not differentiable there. In epigraph form it becomes: minimize t subject to 2x + 1 ≤ t and 4 − x ≤ t. That is a linear program. The two lines meet where 2x + 1 = 4 − x, so x = 1 and t = 3. In planning, the same trick turns "make the worst of several errors small" into a linear program.

6. Substitutions: change of variables and removing equalities

Some problems are convex in disguise. A change of variables x = φ(z), with φ one-to-one and covering the feasible set, gives an equivalent problem in z that may be visibly convex. CO4A 4-5

The classic case is the geometric program (GP). A monomial is γx1a1⋯xnan with γ > 0 and positive x. A posynomial is a sum of monomials, each with its own γ and exponents. A GP minimizes a posynomial subject to posynomials ≤ 1 and monomials = 1. With zi = log xi, each monomial becomes eaTz + log γ, the exponential of an affine function. The log of a posynomial becomes a log-sum-exp, which is convex. Tibshirani 2016

Worked example: minimize x + y subject to xy = 1, with x, y > 0. As written it is not a convex problem, because xy = 1 is a curved equality. Put u = log x and v = log y. The problem becomes: minimize eu + ev subject to u + v = 0. Now the objective is convex and the rule is affine. Setting v = −u leaves eu + e−u, smallest at u = 0. So x = y = 1, with value 2.

A second substitution removes equality constraints. Find one point x0 with Ax0 = b and a matrix M whose columns span the null space of A. Then every solution of Ax = b is x = Mz + x0, and you can minimize over a free z instead. CO4A 4-6

Worked example: minimize x12 + x22 subject to x1 + x2 = 2. Take x0 = (2, 0) and M = (1, −1)T, so (x1, x2) = (2 + z, −z). Minimize (2 + z)2 + z2: the derivative 2(2 + z) + 2z is zero at z = −1. So x* = (1, 1) and f* = 2. In large problems this trick is often a poor idea in practice, because M can be costly to compute. Tibshirani 2016 CO4A adds that the new problem can lose sparsity.

7. Optimize in stages, or loosen the rules

Partial optimization means minimizing over some variables first, then over the rest. If f(x, y) is jointly convex and C is convex, then g(x) = min over y ∈ C of f(x, y) is convex in x. So the outer problem is still convex. CO4A 4-4

Worked example: minimize (x − 2)2 + (y − x)2 with y ∈ [0, 1]. For a fixed x, the best y is the point of [0, 1] closest to x. For x ≥ 1 that is y = 1, leaving (x − 2)2 + (x − 1)2, smallest at x = 1.5. For x ≤ 1 the cost is at least 1, which is worse. So the solution is (x, y) = (1.5, 1), with value 0.5.

CO4A's main example is the support vector machine. Its slack variables can be minimized out by hand, which leaves the hinge function a+ = max{0, a} in the objective. A training point whose margin is 0.6, short of the target 1, is charged 1 − 0.6 = 0.4. CO4A 4-4

A relaxation loosens the rules: you solve over a bigger set C̃ ⊇ C. With more choices you can only do as well or better, so the relaxed optimal value is a lower bound on the true one. CO4A 4-8 Example: minimize (x − 0.3)2 with x ∈ {0, 1}, which is not a convex set. The answer is x = 0 with value 0.09. Relax to x ∈ [0, 1] and you get x = 0.3 with value 0, a lower bound but not the same answer. Branch and bound on Day 15 (branch-and-bound card) is built on exactly such bounds. CO4A also relaxes a convex but non-affine equality h(x) = 0 to h(x) ≤ 0.

RewriteWhat you doStays convex whenToday's example
Monotone transformapply an increasing h to fh(f) is convex, e.g. squaring a norm‖Ax − b‖2 → ‖Ax − b‖22
Slack variableg(x) ≤ 0 → g(x) + s = 0, s ≥ 0g is affinex + y + s = 4
Epigraph formmin t s.t. f(x) ≤ tf is convexmax(2x + 1, 4 − x) → LP
Change of variablesx = φ(z), φ one-to-onethe new f and rules are convexGP with z = log x
Remove equalitiesx = Mz + x0always (affine map)(2 + z, −z) → (1, 1)
Partial optimizationmin over y firstf jointly convex, C convex(1.5, 1), value 0.5
Relaxationenlarge the feasible setgives a bound, not the same problem{0, 1} → [0, 1]

Explain it to a 10-year-old

Put a marble in a salad bowl. Wherever you drop it, it rolls to the same bottom, because a bowl has only one dip. Now put a wall across the bowl. The marble rolls until it hits the wall and stops there. It still cannot get stuck anywhere else, because there are no hidden dips. Convex problems are bowls with walls.

Common misunderstandings

  • "At the optimum the gradient is zero." Only when the optimum is unconstrained or inside the feasible set. In the widget's default, ∇f(x*) = (−3, −3). The correct test is ∇f(x*)T(y − x*) ≥ 0 for all feasible y.
  • "A convex feasible set and a convex objective make a convex problem." The rules themselves must be convex gi and affine hj. The rules x1/(1 + x22) ≤ 0 and (x1 + x2)2 = 0 describe a convex set but break this test; rewritten as x1 ≤ 0 and x1 + x2 = 0, they pass. Boyd & Vandenberghe 2004
  • "A slack variable always keeps the problem convex." Only for affine rules. For a curved g, g(x) + s = 0 is a curved equality.
  • "The relaxed answer is the answer." It is a lower bound. It matches only in special cases, such as PCA, where Tibshirani shows the relaxation is exact. Tibshirani 2016

Check yourself

Q1. Which of these is a convex problem in standard form?

Only the third has a convex objective, convex inequalities and an affine equality. The last one is tempting, because −log x is convex, but x3 = 8 is a non-affine equality, so it is not in convex standard form. The second maximizes a convex function, which is not a convex problem.

Q2. At the optimum x* of a convex problem with a differentiable f, the arrow −∇f(x*)…

If −∇f pointed into the feasible set, you could follow it and lower f. In the triangle example −∇f(x*) = (3, 3) points out through the active edge. It is zero only for an interior optimum, so "always zero" is wrong.

Q3. A solver on a convex problem stops at a point where no small feasible step lowers f. What can you conclude?

For convex problems, local optimality implies global optimality. Restarting from several points is the habit from non-convex problems such as x4 − 3x2 + x, where gradient descent from x = 2 stops at a local minimum.

Q4. Rewrite x + 2y ≤ 5 with a slack variable.

The slack is the room left: s = 5 − x − 2y ≥ 0. The second option means x + 2y ≥ 5, the opposite rule. The last also forces x + 2y ≥ 5, and it is a curved equality besides.

Q5. What is the epigraph form of "minimize max(2x + 1, 4 − x)"?

t must sit above both lines, so t ≥ max(2x + 1, 4 − x). The lowest such t is 3, at x = 1. The first option puts t below the lines, so t can go to −∞. The second bounds the sum, not the maximum.

Q6. In a minimization, you relax x ∈ {0, 1} to x ∈ [0, 1]. The relaxed optimal value is…

A bigger feasible set can only help a minimization. For (x − 0.3)2 the relaxed value is 0 and the true value is 0.09. They are equal only in special cases.

Recap: things to remember

  1. Standard form: minimize f(x) s.t. gi(x) ≤ 0, hj(x) = 0. It is convex when f and every gi are convex and every hj is affine.
  2. In a convex problem every local minimum is global, the solution set is convex, and strict convexity means at most one solution.
  3. x is optimal exactly when ∇f(x)T(y − x) ≥ 0 for all feasible y. Without constraints, that is ∇f(x) = 0.
  4. Slack variables, epigraph form, changes of variables, removing equalities and partial optimization give equivalent problems. A relaxation gives a lower bound.

Week 1 · Day 5

The problem zoo: LP → QP → SOCP → SDP

After today you can place a problem in the LP ⊂ QP ⊂ SOCP ⊂ SDP hierarchy and explain why that choice decides which solver you can use.

About 60 min · Needs Day 4 · CO4A chapter 5

Today's big idea

Convex problems come in nested families. Each family allows a richer kind of curvature, and each contains the one before it. Lower families can be handed to more solvers, including small ones built for just that form. So you place your problem in the lowest family that holds it.

1. Why sort problems into families?

When you ship a parcel, you pick the smallest container that fits: an envelope, a box, a padded box, or a climate-controlled crate. Everything fits in the crate, but the crate costs more and fewer carriers take it.

Convex problems are sorted the same way, by the kind of objective and constraints they use. CO4A orders the families like this, where ⊆ means "is a special case of": CO4A 5

LP ⊆ QP ⊆ QCQP ⊆ SOCP ⊆ SDP ⊆ conic

Why does the family matter? Modelling tools such as CVXPY rewrite your problem into a standard form, "e.g., LP, QP, SOCP, or SDP", and hand it to a solver built for that form. Boyd slides Fewer solvers handle each step up. In CVXPY's solver table, 31 solvers accept LPs, 25 accept QPs, 17 accept SOCPs and 9 accept SDPs (as of Oct 2026). CVXPY 2026

The rule of thumb follows: write your problem in the lowest family that holds it. That keeps the most solvers open to you, including the specialised ones built for simpler forms.

2. Linear programs: flat cost, flat walls

Tilt a flat tray with a marble on it. The marble rolls until it hits a wall, then slides along the wall into a corner. A linear program behaves the same way.

A linear program (LP) has an affine objective and affine constraints: CO4A 5-1

minimize cTx
subject to Gx ⪯ h, Ax = b

Here c is the cost vector, and Gx ⪯ h means each entry of Gx is at most the matching entry of h. The feasible set is a polyhedron, a region cut out by finitely many flat walls. Its corners are vertices.

The key fact: if an LP has a solution and its polyhedron has at least one corner, then some vertex is optimal. The one-line reason: the level sets cTx = k are parallel lines (or planes). Slide one as far downhill as the region allows. The last part of the region it touches is a vertex, or a whole edge in a tie.

Worked example, the classic diet problem. Tibshirani 2016 Food 1 costs $2 per unit and gives 3 g of protein and 1 mg of a vitamin. Food 2 costs $3 per unit and gives 1 g of protein and 3 mg of the vitamin. You need at least 6 g of protein and 6 mg of the vitamin.

minimize 2x1 + 3x2
s.t. 3x1 + x2 ≥ 6, x1 + 3x2 ≥ 6, x ⪰ 0

The region has three corners. At (0, 6) the cost is $18, at (6, 0) it is $12, and at (1.5, 1.5) it is $7.50. The optimum is 1.5 units of each food, where both nutrient rules are active.

Solvers often want one fixed layout, the standard form LP: minimize cTx subject to Ax = b and x ⪰ 0. You reach it with two tricks. Add a slack (Day 4) to each inequality, so Gx ⪯ h becomes Gx + s = h with s ⪰ 0. Split each free variable into two non-negative parts, x = x+ − x−. Boyd & Vandenberghe 2004 The simplex and interior-point methods (Day 12) work on this form.

Try it: the widget's polygon is x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0, x ≤ 3, x + y ≤ 4 and x + 2y ≤ 6. It maximizes cTx for the direction c = (cos θ, sin θ), which is the same as minimizing (−c)Tx. Slide θ and watch the best corner. Then switch to the QP mode and drag the target.

Notice that at θ = 30° the best corner is (3, 1), where cTx = 3.1. Slide θ past 45° and the optimum jumps to (2, 2); past 63.43° it jumps to (0, 3). Exactly at 45°, c is at right angles to the edge x + y = 4, and every point of that edge ties. The optimum jumps whenever c lines up with an edge's outward direction.

A hand check: maximize 3x + 2y over the same polygon. Its corners give 0, 9, 11, 10 and 6, so (3, 1) wins with 11. The direction (3, 2) has angle 33.7°, inside the 0° to 45° range where the widget picks (3, 1).

Analogy

An LP is a marble on a tilted tray: it always ends up in a corner. A QP is a marble in a round-bottomed bowl set on the tray: it settles at the bowl's lowest point, unless a wall gets in the way first. That is why LP solvers can hop from corner to corner, and QP solvers cannot.

3. Quadratic programs: a bowl on the tray

Keep the flat walls but make the cost curved. A quadratic program (QP) is CO4A 5-2

minimize ½xTPx + qTx
subject to Gx ⪯ h, Ax = b

The matrix P must be symmetric and positive semidefinite, written P ⪰ 0: uTPu ≥ 0 for every vector u, or equally, every eigenvalue of P is at least 0. That makes the cost a convex bowl. If P has a negative eigenvalue, the cost bends down in some direction and the problem is no longer convex. Tibshirani 2016 Setting P = 0 gives back an LP, so LP ⊆ QP.

The bowl changes where the optimum can sit. In the widget's QP mode the cost is ½‖x − p‖22, a round bowl centred on a target p. With p = (1, 1) the bowl's bottom is inside the polygon, so x* = (1, 1) and f* = 0. With p = (3.5, 2), the wall x + y ≤ 4 stops it at (2.75, 1.25), the middle of an edge, with f* = 0.5625. With p = (3, 3) it lands on the corner (2, 2), with f* = 1. So a QP optimum can sit inside, on an edge, or at a corner.

A driving example: smooth speed planning. A car is moving at 20 m/s, and a school zone 4 seconds ahead has a 10 m/s limit. The planner picks speeds v1, …, v4 at one-second steps. Harsh braking is uncomfortable, so it penalizes each squared speed change, which is the squared acceleration:

minimize (v1 − 20)2 + (v2 − v1)2
+ (v3 − v2)2 + (v4 − v3)2
subject to v4 ≤ 10

This is a QP: a sum of squares as the cost, one linear rule. The four speed changes must add up to at least −10 m/s, and squares punish big numbers, so the best plan splits the drop evenly. The answer is v = (17.5, 15, 12.5, 10), a steady 2.5 m/s² deceleration, with cost 4 × 2.52 = 25. Braking all at once, v = (20, 20, 20, 10), costs 102 = 100, four times as much. Real planners add speed tracking, jerk and many more steps, but the shape stays a QP. This is the heart of model predictive control on Day 17.

import cvxpy as cp
v = cp.Variable(4)                        # speeds at t = 1, 2, 3, 4 s
cost = cp.square(v[0] - 20) + cp.sum_squares(cp.diff(v))
prob = cp.Problem(cp.Minimize(cost), [v[3] <= 10, v >= 0])
prob.solve(solver=cp.OSQP)                # a QP solver is enough
print(v.value)                            # about [17.5 15. 12.5 10.]

Many familiar problems are QPs: least squares with linear constraints, the lasso, support vector machines, and Markowitz portfolios. Tibshirani 2016 OSQP, a solver built for exactly this form, is the subject of the OSQP paper card.

4. QCQP: curved walls

Now let the walls curve too. A robot vacuum must stay within 1 m of its dock; that rule is a disc, not a polygon. A QCQP (quadratically constrained quadratic program) allows convex quadratic rules: CO4A 5-3

minimize ½xTP0x + q0Tx + r0
s.t. ½xTPix + qiTx + ri ≤ 0, Ax = b

Every Pi must be positive semidefinite, so each rule describes an ellipse-shaped region (an ellipsoid in higher dimensions). Setting Pi = 0 in the rules gives back a QP, so QP ⊆ QCQP.

Worked example: minimize ‖x − (2, 2)‖22 subject to ‖x‖22 ≤ 1. The target (2, 2) lies outside the unit disc, so the answer pulls it straight back to the circle: x* = (2, 2)/‖(2, 2)‖2 = (0.7071, 0.7071). The cost there is 2 × (2 − 0.7071)2 = 3.343.

In practice a QCQP rarely gets its own solver. CVXPY's target forms are LP, QP, SOCP and SDP, so a convex QCQP is rewritten as an SOCP, the next family up. Boyd slides

5. Second-order cone programs: length limits

Picture an ice-cream cone standing on its tip. The higher you go, the wider it gets. That shape is the second-order cone, the set of points (x, t) with ‖x‖2 ≤ t. Some books call it the ice-cream cone.

A second-order cone program (SOCP) has a linear cost and rules of the form "a length must stay below a linear budget": CO4A 5-4 Boyd & Vandenberghe 2004

minimize fTx
s.t. ‖Aix + bi‖2 ≤ ciTx + di, Fx = g

Each rule says the point (Aix + bi, ciTx + di) lies inside a second-order cone. With Ai = 0 and bi = 0, a rule becomes an ordinary linear inequality, so LP ⊆ SOCP.

A driving example: the friction circle. A simple tyre model says the total horizontal acceleration a = (alon, alat) is limited by grip, ‖a‖2 ≤ μg. With friction μ = 0.8 and g = 9.81 m/s², the limit is 7.85 m/s². Braking at 6 m/s² while turning at 4 m/s² uses √(36 + 16) ≈ 7.2 m/s², which is allowed. A box rule |alon| ≤ 7.85, |alat| ≤ 7.85 is linear, but it permits the corner (7.85, 7.85), whose length is 11.1 m/s². That is about 41% more grip than the tyres have.

A second classic SOCP is the robust LP, an LP whose rules must hold for every value of an uncertain coefficient. Boyd & Vandenberghe 2004 Worked example: maximize x1 + x2 subject to aTx ≤ 2 for every a in the disc {(1, 1) + 0.5u : ‖u‖2 ≤ 1}, with x ⪰ 0.

The worst a turns (1, 1)Tx into (1, 1)Tx + 0.5‖x‖2, because uTx is largest when u points along x. So the rule becomes x1 + x2 + 0.5‖x‖2 ≤ 2, an SOC rule. Without uncertainty the best value of x1 + x2 is 2. With it, the best point is x1 = x2 = 0.7388, so x1 + x2 = 1.4776. Being safe for every a in the disc costs about 26%.

Why is a QCQP also an SOCP? A convex quadratic rule can always be rewritten as a length rule. The simplest case: ‖x‖22 ≤ 1 is the same set as ‖x‖2 ≤ 1. The general identity is in the box below. SOCPs also run rockets: powered-descent guidance for landing is solved as an SOCP after a convexification trick, as the lossless convexification paper card explains.

Going deeper (optional): turning a quadratic rule into a cone rule

For Q ⪰ 0, the rule ½xTQx ≤ t holds exactly when ‖(Q½x/√2, (1 − t)/2)‖2 ≤ (1 + t)/2. Square both sides to check: the left gives ½xTQx + (1 − t)2/4, the right gives (1 + t)2/4, and their difference is t − ½xTQx. Apply it to the objective with an epigraph variable t (Day 4) and to each quadratic rule, and any convex QCQP becomes an SOCP. Tibshirani 2016 CO4A 5-4 gives a longer route through eigendecompositions.

6. Semidefinite programs: matrices that never bend the wrong way

An LP asks every number in a list to be non-negative. A semidefinite program asks a whole symmetric matrix to be positive semidefinite: all its eigenvalues non-negative, so uTXu ≥ 0 in every direction u. Think of a bowl that curves up, or stays flat, in every direction and never curves down.

A linear matrix inequality (LMI) is a rule x1F1 + … + xnFn + G ⪯ 0, where the Fi and G are symmetric matrices and "⪯ 0" means negative semidefinite (all eigenvalues ≤ 0). A semidefinite program (SDP) is CO4A 5-5 Boyd & Vandenberghe 2004

minimize cTx
s.t. x1F1 + … + xnFn + G ⪯ 0, Ax = b

The standard form uses a matrix variable X: minimize tr(CX) subject to tr(AiX) = bi and X ⪰ 0, where tr is the trace, the sum of the diagonal. If every Fi and G is diagonal, the LMI is just n separate linear inequalities, one per diagonal entry. So LP ⊆ SDP.

Worked example: make the largest eigenvalue of a matrix as small as possible. Write matrices row by row, with rows separated by semicolons.

A(x) = [2 + x, 1; 1, −x]

The rule λmax(A(x)) ≤ t is the same as A(x) − tI ⪯ 0, an LMI in (x, t). So "minimize t subject to A(x) − tI ⪯ 0" is an SDP. Here the eigenvalues are 1 ± √(1 + (x + 1)2), so the largest is smallest at x = −1, with t* = 2. At x = 0 it would be 1 + √2 ≈ 2.414.

Every SOCP is also an SDP, through a matrix test called the Schur complement: Tibshirani 2016

‖x‖2 ≤ t ⇔ [tI, x; xT, t] ⪰ 0

Check it with x = (3, 4), whose length is 5. At t = 5 the block matrix has eigenvalues 0, 5 and 10: positive semidefinite, right on the boundary. At t = 4.9 they are −0.1, 4.9 and 9.9: not positive semidefinite, matching 5 > 4.9.

SDPs reach robotics too. Robot mapping (pose-graph SLAM) has an SDP relaxation that can certify a map is globally optimal; see the SE-Sync paper card.

7. Conic programs, and choosing a solver

All these families fit one template. A cone K is a set that stays inside itself when you scale by any α ≥ 0. The generalized inequality u ⪯K v means v − u lies in K. A conic program is CO4A 5-6

minimize cTx
s.t. Fx + g ⪯K 0, Ax = b

Choose K = ℝ+n, the non-negative numbers, and you get an LP. Choose a product of second-order cones and you get an SOCP. Choose the cone of positive semidefinite matrices and you get an SDP. Solvers such as SCS and Clarabel work in this form. They also accept an exponential cone, which handles log and exp terms like the geometric programs of Day 4. CVXPY 2026

To place a problem, read its pieces from the bottom of the ladder up, and stop at the first family that fits:

  1. Objective and every rule affine → LP.
  2. Convex quadratic objective (P ⪰ 0), affine rules → QP.
  3. Some rules convex quadratic → QCQP, solved as an SOCP.
  4. Rules like "‖Ax + b‖2 ≤ cTx + d", or worst cases over a ball → SOCP.
  5. Eigenvalues, matrix variables that must be ⪰ 0, matrix norms → SDP.

Here is what that choice means in practice. The table lists a few solvers from CVXPY's solver table, as of Oct 2026. CVXPY 2026

Solver (as of Oct 2026)LPQPSOCPSDPNotes
GLPK, GLOP✓–––LP only
OSQP✓✓––ships with CVXPY; built for QPs
ECOS✓✓✓–also the exponential cone
Clarabel, SCS✓✓✓✓ship with CVXPY; also exp and power cones
MOSEK✓✓✓✓commercial; installed separately
All 31 solvers in the table3125179count that accept each family

So the speed plan (a QP) can run on OSQP, the friction-circle plan (an SOCP) needs an SOCP solver such as ECOS or Clarabel, and the eigenvalue problem (an SDP) needs an SDP solver such as SCS, Clarabel or MOSEK. Writing a QP as an SDP would still give the right answer. It would just close the door on most of the table.

Explain it to a 10-year-old

Think of puzzles with harder and harder pieces. The easiest puzzles have only straight-edged pieces. Then come pieces with one curved side, then round pieces, then pieces that are whole shapes inside shapes. A person who can do the hardest puzzles can also do the easy ones, but it takes them longer. So you give each puzzle to the fastest person who can solve it.

Common misunderstandings

  • "A QP optimum is always at a corner." That is an LP property. In the widget's QP mode, p = (1, 1) gives an interior optimum and p = (3.5, 2) gives one in the middle of an edge, at (2.75, 1.25).
  • "An LP has exactly one solution." When c is at right angles to an edge, the whole edge ties. In the widget, θ = 45° makes every point from (3, 1) to (2, 2) optimal.
  • "Any ½xTPx + qTx is a QP." Only with P ⪰ 0. If P has a negative eigenvalue the problem is non-convex. Tibshirani 2016
  • "Send everything to an SDP solver, since SDP is the most general." You get the same answer, but only from far fewer solvers (9 of 31 in CVXPY's table, as of Oct 2026), and you give up the specialised ones.
  • "‖x‖2 ≥ t is an SOC rule too." Only ‖x‖2 ≤ t is. The set ‖x‖2 ≥ t is the outside of the cone, which is not convex; "stay at least 2 m from the obstacle" is such a rule, and Day 19 shows how to handle it.

Check yourself

Q1. An LP minimizes cTx (with c ≠ 0) over a bounded polygon. Where is the optimum?

Slide the level line cTx = k as far as you can; the last thing it touches is a corner or an edge. "Exactly one vertex" is tempting but fails in ties, such as θ = 45° in the widget.

Q2. Which family is the lowest that holds "minimize ‖Ax − b‖22 subject to x ⪰ 0"?

‖Ax − b‖22 = xTATAx − 2bTAx + bTb, a convex quadratic with P = 2ATA ⪰ 0, and the rules are linear. It is not an LP because the cost is curved. An SDP solver could solve it, but it is not the lowest family.

Q3. An LP rule aTx ≤ 2 must now hold for every a in a disc around (1, 1). What does the problem become?

The worst case over the disc adds a norm term: (1, 1)Tx + 0.5‖x‖2 ≤ 2. That is a second-order cone rule, so the robust LP is an SOCP. Nothing became quadratic in the cost, so it is not a QP.

Q4. In an SDP, every matrix Fi and G is diagonal. What is the problem really?

A diagonal matrix is ⪯ 0 exactly when each diagonal entry is ≤ 0, and each entry is affine in x. So the LMI splits into separate linear inequalities, and the problem is an LP.

Q5. Why place a problem in the lowest family that fits?

A problem has the same answer whichever family you write it in. What changes is which solvers you can use. SDP solvers can solve LPs, but far fewer of them exist.

Q6. The rule ‖(3, 4)‖2 ≤ t is written as the LMI [tI, x; xT, t] ⪰ 0 with x = (3, 4). What is the smallest t that satisfies it?

The Schur complement makes the LMI the same rule as ‖x‖2 ≤ t, and ‖(3, 4)‖2 = 5. At t = 5 the eigenvalues are 0, 5 and 10. 7 is the sum 3 + 4 (the ‖·‖1 length), and 25 is the squared length.

Recap: things to remember

  1. LP ⊆ QP ⊆ QCQP ⊆ SOCP ⊆ SDP ⊆ conic: each family is a special case of the next.
  2. LP: linear everything, optimum at a vertex or tied edge. QP: convex quadratic cost (P ⪰ 0), optimum can also sit inside or mid-edge.
  3. SOCP: "length ≤ linear budget" rules, such as the friction circle and robust LPs. SDP: a matrix must be positive semidefinite.
  4. Pick the lowest family that holds your problem; that decides how many solvers, and which fast ones, you can use.

Week 1 · Day 6

Gradient descent

After today you can run gradient descent, choose a step size (fixed, backtracking or exact line search), read its O(1/k) and linear convergence rates, and explain why stochastic gradient descent powers machine learning.

About 60 min · Needs Day 3 · CO4A chapter 6

Today's big idea

Gradient descent repeats one move: feel the slope, take a step downhill, feel again. Two numbers decide how well it works. One is the step size t, which you choose. The other is the condition number κ, which measures how stretched the bowl is. Choose t well and the method is simple, cheap and reliable. Choose it badly and it crawls, zig-zags or blows up.

1. The update: walk downhill

Picture yourself on a hillside in thick fog. You cannot see the valley, but you can feel which way the ground tilts under your feet. A sensible plan is to step in the steepest downhill direction, stop, feel the ground again, and repeat. That loop is the whole algorithm.

On Day 3 you met the gradient ∇f(x), the vector of slopes of f at x. It points in the direction where f rises fastest, so −∇f(x) points where f falls fastest. Gradient descent starts at a point x0 and repeats one line: CO4A 6-1

xk+1 = xk − t∇f(xk)

Here xk is the point after k steps. The number t > 0 is the step size; machine learning calls it the learning rate. Steps are long where the ground is steep and short where it is flat, because ∇f itself shrinks near the bottom. You stop when ‖∇f(xk)‖2 is tiny.

There is a second way to read the same rule. At x, gradient descent trusts the tangent plane of f, but it charges a fee for moving far from x. The next point minimizes that "tangent plane plus fee" model: Tibshirani 2016

x+ = argminy f(x) + ∇f(x)T(y − x) + ‖y − x‖22/(2t)

Set the derivative in y to zero and you get x+ = x − t∇f(x) again. A small t means a big fee, so the steps are cautious. A big t means you trust the tangent plane far away, which is risky because f curves.

Here is today's running example. Take f(x, y) = ½(x² + 10y²), a bowl ten times steeper in y than in x. Its gradient is ∇f = (x, 10y). From the start (10, 1) the gradient is (10, 10). With t = 0.1 the next point is (10 − 1, 1 − 1) = (9, 0). The steep y-direction is solved in one step. After that each step multiplies x by 0.9: 8.1, 7.29, 6.56, and so on. Boyd & Vandenberghe 2004

Explain it to a 10-year-old

You are blindfolded on a big slide and want to reach the bottom. You feel with your foot which way is down, take one step that way, and feel again. Big steps get you there faster, but if they are too big you jump right over the bottom and land higher up on the other side.

2. Fixed step size and the 2/L cliff

Think of a shower knob. Tiny turns take forever to warm the water. Big turns overshoot to scalding, then to freezing, and each swing can be worse than the last. A fixed step, the same t at every iteration, has the same two failure modes.

The safe range depends on how sharply the bowl can curve. A function is L-smooth (its gradient is L-Lipschitz) if the gradient never changes faster than L: CO4A 6-3-1

‖∇f(x) − ∇f(y)‖2 ≤ L‖x − y‖2

For a twice-differentiable f this means ∇2f(x) ⪯ LI: no direction curves more than L. So L is the steepest curvature of the bowl. Our example curves by 1 in x and by 10 in y, so L = 10.

Why does trouble start at t = 2/L? On our bowl the two coordinates update separately, each multiplied by its own factor:

xk+1 = (1 − t)·xk
yk+1 = (1 − 10t)·yk

A coordinate shrinks only if its factor lies strictly between −1 and 1. For y that means 0 < t < 2/10. In general, on a quadratic every curvature λ between the smallest and L gives a factor 1 − tλ, and all of them are safe exactly when 0 < t < 2/L. CO4A 6-2-1

The sign of the factor tells the story, as the figure shows. Between 0 and 1, the coordinate creeps toward 0 from one side. Between −1 and 0, it jumps across the valley floor and back, but each jump is shorter. Below −1, each jump is longer, and the iterates fly away. At t = 2/L exactly the factor is −1, and y flips between +1 and −1 forever.

Here are the real counts from (10, 1), stopping when f ≤ 10−6. The best fixed step sits in the middle of the safe window, not at its edge.

Step tx factory factorIterations to f ≤ 10⁻⁶
0.010.990.9882 (crawls)
0.050.950.5173
0.1 = 1/L0.9085
2/11 ≈ 0.1820.818−0.81845 (best fixed step)
0.190.81−0.974 (zig-zags)
0.2 = 2/L0.8−1never: f stalls at 5
0.210.79−1.1diverges: f > 10¹² at iteration 137

The best fixed step is t = 2/(m + L), where m is the smallest curvature (here m = 1). It balances the two coordinates so that both shrink by the same factor, (κ − 1)/(κ + 1) = 9/11 per step, where κ = L/m. CO4A 6-3-4 The catch: on a real problem you rarely know m or L. So the next section lets the algorithm find t by itself.

3. Let the algorithm choose t: backtracking and exact line search

Think of reversing into a parking spot. You start with a bold move. If you are about to hit the curb, you ease off and try a shorter one. Backtracking line search does exactly this at every iteration.

Fix two numbers, α and β. At each iteration let g = ∇f(x), start with t = 1, and shrink t ← βt as long as Tibshirani 2016

f(x − tg) > f(x) − α·t·‖g‖22

As soon as the inequality is false, you take the step x+ = x − tg. The inequality you are waiting for, f(x − tg) ≤ f(x) − αt‖g‖², is called the sufficient-decrease or Armijo condition.

What do α and β mean? The tangent line predicts that a step of length t lowers f by t‖g‖². That is too hopeful, because f curves upward. Boyd and Vandenberghe read α as the fraction of that predicted drop you insist on getting. With α = 0.3 you say "give me at least 30% of what the tangent line promised." β is how hard you cut t after a failure; β = 0.5 halves it. Boyd & Vandenberghe 2004

They take 0 < α < 0.5 and 0 < β < 1, and report typical values of α between 0.01 and 0.3 and β between 0.1 and 0.8. Conventions differ a little: Tibshirani's slides and CO4A also allow α = ½, and this lesson's example uses α = β = ½. CO4A 6-2-2

Here is that first step by hand. At (10, 1) we have f = 55, g = (10, 10) and ‖g‖² = 200. With α = ½ the test asks for f(x − tg) ≤ 55 − 100t.

  • t = 1: f = 405, but we need at most −45. Shrink.
  • t = 0.5: f = 92.5, but we need at most 5. Shrink.
  • t = 0.25: f = 39.4, but we need at most 30. Shrink.
  • t = 0.125: f = 38.6 ≤ 42.5. Accept, and move to x1 = (8.75, −0.25).

The very next step accepts t = 0.5, which is bigger than 2/L = 0.2, and nothing breaks. The test checks each step before it is taken, so an occasional bold step is safe. The full run needs 30 iterations plus 77 rejected trial points. It keeps the O(1/k) guarantee of Section 4, with t replaced by tmin = min{1, β/L}. CO4A 6-3-3

Exact line search goes one step further. Along the downhill ray, it jumps straight to the lowest point: CO4A 6-2-3

t = argmins ≥ 0 f(x − s∇f(x))

For a quadratic with Hessian H this has a formula, t = gTg / gTHg. From (10, 1) it gives t = 200/(100 + 1000) = 2/11 at every step. The iterates follow xk = 10(9/11)k and yk = (−9/11)k, so f drops by (9/11)² ≈ 0.669 per step and needs 45 iterations. This is Boyd and Vandenberghe's own example. Boyd & Vandenberghe 2004

Exact search matched the best fixed step here, but each step required solving a small optimization problem. For a general f that inner problem is expensive, so exact search is rarely worth it. Backtracking gets most of the benefit for a few extra function evaluations. Tibshirani 2016 The whole method fits in a few lines (see the gradient descent card):

def gradient_descent(f, grad, x, alpha=0.5, beta=0.5, tol=1e-6):
    while True:
        g = grad(x)
        if norm(g) <= tol:            # flat enough: stop
            return x
        t = 1.0
        while f(x - t*g) > f(x) - alpha*t*(g @ g):
            t = beta * t               # backtrack: shorter step
        x = x - t*g                    # the gradient step

Try it: start with the default (κ = 10, t = 1/L), then switch the rule to each option and watch the path and the bars. Next, slide κ up to 100 and see every rule slow down. Tap the plot to start somewhere else.

Notice: from (10, 1) at κ = 10, t = 1/L needs 85 iterations, the best fixed step 2/(1+L) and exact line search 45 each, and backtracking (α = β = ½) 30 plus 77 rejected trials. At 2/L, f stalls at 5. At 2.1/L it diverges at iteration 137. On the log chart every converging rule is close to a straight line.

4. How fast? O(1/k), linear rates and the condition number

There are two speed guarantees. A weak one holds for every smooth convex bowl. A strong one holds for bowls that curve upward in every direction.

The weak guarantee rests on a picture. If f is L-smooth, then at any point x a steep bowl of curvature L sits on top of f and touches it at x. That is the quadratic upper bound: CO4A 6-3-2

f(y) ≤ f(x) + ∇f(x)T(y − x) + (L/2)‖y − x‖22

With t ≤ 1/L the step goes downhill on that upper bowl, so f falls by at least (t/2)‖∇f(x)‖² at every step. Adding up these drops gives the theorem for convex, L-smooth f: CO4A 6-3-1

f(xk) − f* ≤ ‖x0 − x*‖22 / (2tk)

Here x* is a minimizer and f* = f(x*). The error falls like a constant over k, written O(1/k) and called a sublinear rate. To guarantee an error ε you need about 1/ε iterations, so one more correct digit costs ten times more steps.

On our bowl, t = 0.1 and ‖x0 − x*‖² = 101, so the bound is 505/k. Taken at face value it promises 10−6 only after 5.05 × 108 steps. The actual run needs 85. The bound covers the worst smooth convex function; our bowl is much kinder, because it is also strongly convex.

A function is strongly convex with parameter m > 0 if a shallow bowl of curvature m fits underneath it at every point: f(y) ≥ f(x) + ∇f(x)T(y − x) + (m/2)‖y − x‖22. For twice-differentiable f this is ∇2f ⪰ mI. Then every step removes a fixed share of the remaining error: CO4A 6-3-4

f(xk) − f* ≤ ck·(L/2)‖x0 − x*‖22, 0 < c < 1

This is linear convergence: on a log plot the error is a straight line. Reaching ε needs O(log(1/ε)) iterations, so each extra digit costs the same number of steps. For t = 1/L, CO4A's proof gives c = 1 − m/L. On our bowl c = 0.9, and the bound reaches 10−6 by iteration 191. The real error is 50·0.81k, which gets there at 85.

The condition number κ = L/m is the ratio of the steepest curvature to the flattest. It measures how stretched the bowl is. In a round bowl (κ = 1) the downhill arrow points straight at the bottom, and one step of t = 1/L lands on it. In a long narrow canyon the arrow points mostly at the nearest wall, not along the floor. So gradient descent bounces from wall to wall while it creeps along the floor. That bouncing is the zig-zag. Boyd & Vandenberghe 2004

The widget's κ slider shows the cost. From (10, 1), iterations to f ≤ 10−6:

κt = 1/Lt = 2/(1+L)Backtracking (½, ½)
1111
21392
10854530
50439227186
100882461327

The count grows roughly in proportion to κ, as Boyd and Vandenberghe's analysis predicts. Boyd & Vandenberghe 2004 Large κ often comes from badly scaled variables. Say a path planner's cost is ½(e² + 100θ²), with lateral error e in metres and heading error θ in radians. Its curvatures are 1 and 100, so κ = 100 even though nothing is wrong with the model. Measuring heading in a new unit, θ′ = 10θ, gives ½(e² + θ′²), a round bowl that one step solves. Day 11's Newton method does this kind of rescaling automatically, using the Hessian.

When should you stop? You cannot measure f − f* directly, but you can measure the gradient. For m-strongly convex f, ‖∇f(x)‖2 ≤ √(2mε) guarantees f(x) − f* ≤ ε. With m = 1 and ε = 10−6, stop once ‖∇f‖ ≤ 1.41 × 10−3. The catch is that you usually do not know m. Boyd & Vandenberghe slides

Analogy

A marble in a round salad bowl rolls straight to the middle. A marble dropped on the side of a long gutter first rolls across, overshoots up the other side, rolls back, and only slowly drifts along the gutter. Gradient descent in a bowl with large κ behaves like that marble in the gutter, except it has no momentum to smooth the trip. Adding momentum is the idea behind Day 8's acceleration.

Common misunderstandings

  • "A bigger step is always faster." Only up to the middle of the window. At κ = 10, t = 0.19 needs 74 iterations, t = 0.2 never settles and t = 0.21 blows up.
  • "Zig-zag means a bug." It is what gradient descent does in a stretched bowl. It is the condition number talking, not your code.
  • "Backtracking's t must stay below 1/L." It changes every step and can be larger: t = 0.5 is accepted on a bowl with L = 10, because each step is checked first.
  • "The O(1/k) bound predicts the iteration count." It is a worst-case promise. It says 505/k; the real run reached 10−6 in 85 steps.
  • "Exact line search beats κ." From (10, 1) it looks fast at κ = 50 (41 iterations) only because that start sits near the long axis. From the worst start (κ, 1) it needs 263 iterations at κ = 50 and 559 at κ = 100.

Going deeper (optional): why the error falls like 1/k

Write g = ∇f(x) and x+ = x − tg with t ≤ 1/L. Put y = x+ in the quadratic upper bound: f(x+) ≤ f(x) − t(1 − Lt/2)‖g‖² ≤ f(x) − (t/2)‖g‖². Convexity gives f(x) ≤ f* + gT(x − x*). Combine the two and complete the square:

f(x+) − f* ≤ (‖x − x*‖² − ‖x+ − x*‖²)/(2t)

Add this up over k steps. The right side telescopes to at most ‖x0 − x*‖²/(2t). Since f never goes up, the last error is at most the average, which gives the bound ‖x0 − x*‖²/(2tk). CO4A 6-3-1 writes out every line. Boyd and Vandenberghe (pp. 466–468) prove the linear rate, with c = 1 − m/L for exact search and an explicit c for backtracking.

5. Can we do better?

Picture a speed-limit sign for a whole family of methods. A first-order method learns about f only through gradients. Each new point lies in x0 plus the span of the gradients seen so far. Gradient descent is one such method, but there are cleverer ones.

Nesterov proved a lower bound for this whole family. For any k ≤ (n − 1)/2 and any start, there is an L-smooth convex function on ℝn where every first-order method has CO4A 6-3-6 Tibshirani 2016

f(xk) − f* ≥ 3L‖x0 − x*‖22 / (32(k + 1)2)

So no first-order method can beat a rate of 1/k² on the worst functions. Gradient descent only guarantees 1/k, which leaves a gap. Put in our numbers, L = 10 and ‖x0 − x*‖² = 101. At k = 10 the unavoidable error is 0.78, while gradient descent's guarantee is 50.5. The lower bound is about hard functions in many dimensions, not about our 2-D bowl.

The gap is real. Accelerated gradient methods reach O(1/k²), that is O(1/√ε) iterations. For ε = 10−6 that is on the order of a thousand steps instead of a million. That is Day 8 (see the FISTA card). Two other limits of plain gradient descent point to other days. It needs a gradient, so kinks like |x| need Day 7's subgradients. And it ignores curvature, which Day 11's Newton method uses.

6. Gradient boosting: gradient descent on predictions

Picture a line of tutors. Each one looks only at the mistakes the earlier tutors left behind and tries to fix those. Boosting builds simple models one after another, each fitting what the current team still gets wrong. Bagging, by contrast, trains many models independently on resampled data and averages them. CO4A 6-4

Boosting is gradient descent in disguise. Treat the vector of predictions u = (u1, …, un) on the n training points as the variable, with total loss Σi L(yi, ui). A gradient step on u would move along di = −∂L(yi, ui)/∂ui. But the model must also predict new points, so you fit a small tree Tk to d by least squares and step along the tree instead: Tibshirani 2016

u(k) = u(k−1) + αk·Tk

Here αk is the boosting step size (not the backtracking α). The final model is a weighted sum of trees, which is what gradient boosting is. Take two points with labels y = (3, 5), a first guess u(0) = (4, 4), and squared loss ½(y − u)². Then d = y − u = (−1, 1), which is just the residuals. A one-split tree that separates the two points matches d exactly. With α = 1 you get u(1) = (3, 5), a perfect fit. For squared loss, "fit the residuals" and "follow the negative gradient" are the same move. Other losses, such as the logistic loss, only change d.

7. Stochastic gradient descent: why machine learning runs on it

Imagine asking for directions. You could survey the whole town before every step, or you could ask one random passer-by. One answer is noisy, but you get a thousand of them for the price of one survey.

Most learning objectives are sums with one term per training example: f(x) = Σi=1..m fi(x). A batch method such as plain gradient descent needs all m gradients for every step. Stochastic gradient descent (SGD) uses just one: Tibshirani 2016 CO4A 6-5

xk+1 = xk − tk∇fik(xk)

The index ik follows the cyclic rule (1, 2, …, m, 1, 2, …) or the randomized rule (uniform at random), and the random one is more common. In cost, m stochastic steps equal about one batch step. When there are 500 million examples, that difference decides whether training is possible at all. The rule of thumb is that SGD thrives far from the optimum and struggles close to it. Tibshirani 2016 (SG)

Why does it struggle near the end? Near x* the individual gradients ∇fi disagree, even though their sum is zero. With a fixed step each one keeps kicking the iterate, so it hovers in a cloud around x*. The theory matches: a fixed step only promises to get within a band around f* whose width grows with t. Steps that shrink, with Σtk = ∞ but Σtk² < ∞ (for example tk = 1/k), close the band. These are called diminishing step sizes or step-size decay. Tibshirani 2016 (SG)

A tiny example shows both behaviours. Let f(x) = Σ ½(x − ai)² with a = (1, 2, 3, 6), so x* = 3, the mean. Batch gradient descent with t = 0.25 from 0 lands on 3 in one step. Cyclic SGD with a fixed t = 0.25 visits 0.25, 0.69, 1.27, 2.45 in its first pass. After 200 passes it is still circling: 2.94, 2.70, 2.78, 3.58. With tk = 1/k, SGD computes a running mean (1, 1.5, 2, 3) and lands on 3 after one pass.

In practice you use a minibatch: average the gradients of b random examples per step. Averaging cuts the noise, and a GPU computes the b gradients in parallel. One epoch is one pass over the data, so each epoch takes m/b steps. Adam is a stochastic gradient method that also adapts a separate step size for each coordinate. Kingma & Ba 2014 As of Oct 2026 it is a common choice for training neural networks. See the SGD card for a summary.

Try it: compare the blue full-gradient path with the orange SGD scribble. Then switch to b = 10, and then to the decaying step. Watch how low the orange band sits at the end, and when blue passes it.

Notice (defaults: b = 1, fixed t = 0.1): after one epoch full GD has taken a single step and still has f − f* = 0.84. In the same work SGD took 1,000 cheap steps and is already in its noise band; at that instant it happens to dip to 6.6×10⁻⁵. It never leaves the band, which has a median of 8.5×10⁻³ in the last epoch. GD keeps falling in a straight line, passes the band at epoch 32 and ends at 5.6×10⁻⁴. With b = 10 or the decaying step, the band drops below 10⁻³.

Check yourself

Q1. On f = ½(x² + 10y²) with a fixed step, which t makes gradient descent diverge?

L = 10, so the cliff is at 2/L = 0.2. With t = 0.21 the y-coordinate is multiplied by 1 − 10·0.21 = −1.1 each step, so it grows. t = 0.19 looks risky but its factor is −0.9, so it still converges (in 74 iterations).

Q2. In backtracking line search, when do you shrink t ← βt?

You shrink until the new point gives at least the fraction α of the drop the tangent line predicts. "Smaller than f(x)" is too weak a test, and backtracking never needs to know L. It happily accepts t = 0.5 when L = 10.

Q3. You raise the condition number κ from 10 to 100 and keep the best fixed step 2/(1+L). What happens?

The best fixed step still shrinks each coordinate by (κ − 1)/(κ + 1) per step. That factor creeps toward 1 as κ grows, so the count grows about tenfold. Choosing t well cannot undo a stretched bowl; rescaling or Newton's method can.

Q4. What does strong convexity add to the O(1/k) guarantee of gradient descent?

A bowl that curves up at least m everywhere means each step removes a fixed share of the error, ck with c = 1 − m/L for t = 1/L. One step from anywhere happens only when κ = 1. O(1/k²) is the accelerated rate of Day 8, a different improvement.

Q5. For L-smooth convex functions, what is the best worst-case rate any first-order method can guarantee?

Nesterov's lower bound, 3L‖x₀ − x*‖²/(32(k+1)²), says no gradient-only method beats 1/k² on the hardest functions, and accelerated methods reach it. Gradient descent's 1/k is short of that limit. Exponential rates need strong convexity.

Q6. SGD with a fixed step t on f(x) = Σ ½(x − ai)² typically…

Near x* the single-example gradients disagree, so each one kicks the iterate. With a = (1, 2, 3, 6) and t = 0.25 the iterate still circles 3 after 200 passes. A decaying step such as 1/k closes in. It does not diverge, because each kick is small.

Recap: things to remember

  1. Gradient descent repeats xk+1 = xk − t∇f(xk): trust the tangent plane, but not too far.
  2. A fixed step must satisfy 0 < t < 2/L. The best fixed step is 2/(m + L), and t = 1/L is the safe default.
  3. Backtracking (shrink t until f drops by at least α·t·‖∇f‖²) chooses t automatically and is the usual choice. Exact line search is rarely worth its cost.
  4. Smooth convex f gives O(1/k). Strong convexity gives a linear rate, whose speed is set by κ = L/m. Large κ means zig-zag, and 1/k² is the limit that acceleration reaches.
  5. SGD and minibatches trade exact gradients for cheap, noisy ones. They are fast far from the optimum, and near it they need a decaying step.

Week 1 · Day 7

Subgradients

After today you can handle functions with kinks such as |x|, max and the L1 norm, compute subgradients, use the optimality rule 0 ∈ ∂f(x), and run the subgradient method with a sensible step-size rule.

About 60 min · Needs Day 6 · CO4A chapters 7 and 8

Today's big idea

Gradient descent needs a slope, but |x|, max and the L1 norm have corners where no single slope exists. At a corner there is a whole fan of slopes whose lines stay under the graph, and each one is a subgradient. A point is a minimum exactly when the flat slope 0 is in the fan. You can run gradient descent with any slope from the fan, as long as the steps shrink and you remember the best point so far.

1. Why kinks need a new tool

Many objectives worth minimizing have corners. The absolute value |x| has one at 0. The L1 norm ‖x‖1 = |x1| + … + |xn| has one wherever a coordinate is 0. A maximum of several functions has one wherever two of them tie.

These corners are not an accident. A path planner that cares about the worst of several obstacle clearances is working with a maximum. A lane-line fit that should shrug off one bad GPS fix uses absolute errors, because a squared error lets a single outlier dominate. A model that should use only a few of many sensors adds an L1 penalty, and Day 8 builds a fast solver for exactly that.

On Day 6 every function was smooth. For a smooth convex function, the tangent line at any point never rises above the graph Tibshirani 2016:

f(y) ≥ f(x) + ∇f(x)T(y − x) for all y

Check it on f(x) = x² at x = 1. The tangent is 1 + 2(y − 1) = 2y − 1. The gap is y² − (2y − 1) = (y − 1)², which is never negative. So the tangent stays under the bowl everywhere.

Now look at the tip of a V. Coming from the left the slope is −1, coming from the right it is +1, so there is no single tangent. But many lines still pass through the tip and stay under the V. That is today's whole idea: keep the "line under the graph" property, and drop the demand that the line be unique.

2. Subgradients: every line that fits under the graph

The right-hand picture above is the definition. Each line in the fan touches the V at its tip and never rises above it. The slope of any such line is called a subgradient.

In symbols: a vector g is a subgradient of f at x if the line (or plane) with slope g through the point (x, f(x)) stays under the graph everywhere CO4A 7-1:

f(y) ≥ f(x) + gT(y − x) for all y

It is the tangent inequality from Section 1, with ∇f(x) replaced by g. A kink is a point where f is continuous but has no derivative, like the tip of the V.

Try it on f(x) = |x| at x = 0. With g = 0.5 the line is 0.5y, and |y| ≥ 0.5y for every y, so 0.5 is a subgradient. With g = 1.2 the line at y = 1 gives 1.2, but |1| = 1. The line pokes above the graph, so 1.2 fails. Any g from −1 to 1 works.

Three facts make subgradients usable. A convex function has at least one subgradient at every point inside its domain. Where a convex f is differentiable, its only subgradient is ∇f(x), so nothing changes for smooth functions. A nonconvex function may have none at all, because no line fits under a dip CO4A 7-2.

Here are the subgradients you will use most often Tibshirani 2016:

FunctionAway from the kinkAt the kink
|x|sign(x)any g in [−1, 1] at x = 0
‖x‖2x / ‖x‖2any g with ‖g‖2 ≤ 1 at x = 0
‖x‖1sign(xi) in each coordinateany value in [−1, 1] in each coordinate where xi = 0
max{f1, f2}∇ of the larger pieceany point on the segment between ∇f1 and ∇f2 where they tie

Try it: the widget draws the fan at a point x₀. Drag "Your slope g" to 1.2 and watch the line turn red where it rises above f. Then switch to function (c) and look at the last tile. Move x₀ off the kink to see the fan collapse to one slope.

Notice: at the kink x₀ = 0 of |x|, the fan fills every slope from −1 to 1. The default line g = 0.5 sits inside the fan and stays under the V. And because 0 is in ∂f(0) = [−1, 1], the widget reports that x₀ = 0 is a minimizer.

Analogy

Balance a ruler on the bottom of a V-shaped valley. You can tilt it quite a lot and it still touches the bottom without cutting into either wall. Every tilt that works is a subgradient. On a smooth, round valley floor the ruler has only one resting angle: the tangent.

3. The subdifferential, and the rules for building it

Collect every subgradient at x into one set. That set is the subdifferential ∂f(x), the whole fan of allowed slopes CO4A 7-2:

∂f(x) = { g : f(y) ≥ f(x) + gT(y − x) for all y }

The set is always closed and convex, so in one dimension it is an interval. For convex f it is never empty. It shrinks to the single point {∇f(x)} exactly where f is differentiable.

Take f(x) = max(1 − x, 2x − 2). The two pieces cross at x = 1, where f = 0. The left piece has slope −1 and the right piece has slope 2, so ∂f(1) = [−1, 2]. At x = 0 only 1 − x is active, so ∂f(0) = {−1}: one slope, as at any smooth point.

You rarely check the definition by hand. As with derivatives, a few rules build ∂f from simple pieces CO4A 7-2-2:

  • Scaling: ∂(af) = a·∂f for a > 0.
  • Sum: ∂(f1 + f2) = ∂f1 + ∂f2. Add every member of one set to every member of the other.
  • Affine inside: if h(x) = f(Ax + b), then ∂h(x) = AT∂f(Ax + b).
  • Maximum: for f = maxi fi, ∂f(x) is the convex hull of the subgradients of the active pieces, meaning all weighted averages of them.

The L1 norm is a sum of |xi| terms, so its subgradient is built one coordinate at a time. At x = (2, 0, −1) the first and third coordinates are fixed at sign(2) = 1 and sign(−1) = −1. The middle one is free in [−1, 1]. So ∂‖x‖1 = {(1, s, −1) : s ∈ [−1, 1]}. That makes (1, 0.3, −1) a subgradient and (1, 1.5, −1) not one.

The sum rule also explains flat-bottomed valleys. Take f(x) = |x| + |x − 2|. At x = 1 both terms are smooth, and ∂f(1) = {1} + {−1} = {0}. At x = 0, ∂f(0) = [−1, 1] + {−1} = [−2, 0], which also contains 0. In fact every x in [0, 2] has 0 in its fan, and f = 2 on that whole stretch.

Constraints fit into the same language. The indicator function IC of a set C is 0 on C and +∞ outside it. Adding IC to an objective is the same as demanding x ∈ C, because any point outside costs infinity.

Picture standing with your back against a wall. You can push in any direction that does not point back into the room. That set of pushes is the normal cone, and it is exactly the subdifferential of the indicator at a point x of C CO4A 7-2-1:

∂IC(x) = NC(x) = { g : gT(y − x) ≤ 0 for all y ∈ C }

Take C = [0, 1] on the number line. At x = 0.5, inside, no push is allowed except g = 0, so NC(0.5) = {0}. At the right end any push to the right is fine: NC(1) = [0, ∞). At the left end, NC(0) = (−∞, 0].

One more function you will meet is the distance to a convex set, dist(x, C) = ‖x − PC(x)‖2. Here the projection PC(x) is the point of C closest to x. Outside C the distance is smooth, and its gradient is the unit arrow pointing away from the nearest point CO4A 7-3-5:

∇dist(x, C) = (x − PC(x)) / ‖x − PC(x)‖2

Take C = the unit disk and x = (3, 4). The nearest point is PC(x) = (0.6, 0.8), the distance is 4, and the gradient is (0.6, 0.8). The formula needs x outside C, where the distance is positive. CO4A does not say so, but the slides do Tibshirani 2016.

4. The optimality rule: 0 ∈ ∂f(x*)

At a minimum you cannot go lower in any direction. In the picture, the flat line through (x*, f(x*)) fits under the whole graph. That is the same as saying slope 0 is a subgradient. This is the subgradient optimality condition CO4A 7-3-1:

f(x*) = minx f(x) ⇔ 0 ∈ ∂f(x*)

The proof is one line. Put g = 0 into the definition and you get f(y) ≥ f(x*) for all y, which is what "minimum" means. The rule holds for any function. Convexity is what makes ∂f easy to compute, and so makes the rule easy to use.

For max(1 − x, 2x − 2), ∂f(1) = [−1, 2] contains 0, so x* = 1 and f* = 0. Now take max(0.5x, 2x − 1.5). It also has a kink at x = 1, with ∂f(1) = [0.5, 2]. Zero is not in that interval, so this kink is not a minimum. Both slopes are positive, so moving left lowers f. This is function (c) in the widget above.

Constraints work the same way. To minimize a smooth f over C, minimize f + IC. The sum rule turns 0 ∈ ∂(f + IC) into a simple test: the downhill direction must point out of C CO4A 7-3-2.

−∇f(x*) ∈ NC(x*)

Example: minimize (x − 2)² over C = [0, 1]. At x = 1 the gradient is 2(1 − 2) = −2, so −∇f = 2. That lies in NC(1) = [0, ∞). The ball wants to roll right, the wall at 1 stops it, and x* = 1. Day 10 grows this rule into the KKT conditions.

The rule's most famous use is the lasso: least squares plus an L1 penalty.

minimize ½‖y − Xβ‖22 + λ‖β‖1

Here X is the data matrix (one column per feature), y holds the measurements, β holds the coefficients, and λ > 0 sets how hard the penalty pushes. Write Xi for column i. Applying 0 ∈ ∂f one coordinate at a time gives two cases CO4A 7-3-3:

XiT(y − Xβ) = λ·sign(βi) if βi ≠ 0
|XiT(y − Xβ)| ≤ λ if βi = 0

Read XiT(y − Xβ) as the pull the data exert on coefficient i. A coefficient stays at exactly zero while that pull is at most λ, like a block held by static friction. Only a pull stronger than λ gets it moving. This is why the lasso keeps a few features and sets the rest to zero.

With X = I the conditions solve in closed form. Each βi is yi moved toward 0 by λ, and set to 0 if |yi| ≤ λ. This map is soft-thresholding Sλ CO4A 7-3-4:

Sλ(y) = y − λ if y > λ
Sλ(y) = 0 if |y| ≤ λ
Sλ(y) = y + λ if y < −λ

Take y = (3, 0.4, −1.5) and λ = 1, so S1(y) = (2, 0, −0.5). Check coordinate 1: 3 − 2 = 1 = λ·(+1). Coordinate 2: |0.4 − 0| = 0.4 ≤ 1. Coordinate 3: −1.5 − (−0.5) = −1 = λ·(−1). All three conditions hold. Day 8 turns soft-thresholding into a fast solver for any X.

5. The subgradient method

Now the algorithm. Take gradient descent and replace the gradient by any subgradient. That is the whole subgradient method CO4A 8-1:

xk+1 = xk − tkgk, gk ∈ ∂f(xk)

Here tk > 0 is the step size at step k. Any member of the fan will do, so you never have to compute the whole set.

There is one catch. A negative subgradient need not point downhill. Near a kink a step can jump to the far side and raise f. So this is not a descent method, and you keep the best point found so far. Its value is fbest:

fbest(k) = min{ f(x0), f(x1), …, f(xk) }

Think of walking down a faceted rock in fog. Each step follows the slope of the face under your feet. Sometimes you step over a ridge onto a face that tilts the other way.

A tiny example shows the catch. Take f(x) = |x|, start at x0 = 1, and use a fixed step t = 0.3. While x > 0 the subgradient is 1, so the iterates are 0.7, 0.4, 0.1. The next step jumps past 0 to −0.2, where the subgradient is −1. Then it goes back to 0.1, then −0.2 again, forever. The best value stays at fbest = 0.1.

In code the method is a few lines. The only additions to gradient descent are the subgradient and the bookkeeping for the best point.

import numpy as np

def subgradient_method(f, subgrad, x0, step, iters=1000):
    x = np.array(x0, float)
    best_x, best_f = x.copy(), f(x)
    for k in range(1, iters + 1):
        g = subgrad(x)                    # any member of ∂f(x)
        x = x - step(k, x, g) * g
        if f(x) < best_f:                 # not a descent method,
            best_x, best_f = x.copy(), f(x)   # so keep the best point
    return best_x, best_f

f  = lambda x: abs(x[0]) + 2 * abs(x[1])
sg = lambda x: np.array([np.sign(x[0]), 2 * np.sign(x[1])])
print(subgradient_method(f, sg, [2, -1.5], lambda k, x, g: 1 / k)[1])  # ≈ 1.0e-3

Using np.sign(0) = 0 at a kink is fine, because 0 is in [−1, 1]. The subgradient method card collects the update, the rates and the pitfalls in one place.

6. Step sizes, and how fast it can go

The step-size rule decides everything. Unlike on Day 6, the steps are fixed before the run starts. No line search is used CO4A 8-1-1.

  • Fixed step: tk = t for every k.
  • Diminishing steps: tk → 0 with Σtk = ∞ and Σtk² < ∞. The standard example is tk = 1/k.

Why those two sums? Σtk = ∞ means the steps add up to enough distance to reach any point. Σtk² < ∞ means the bouncing around the minimum shrinks to nothing. For tk = 1/k, 1 + 1/2 + 1/3 + … grows without bound, while 1 + 1/4 + 1/9 + … = π²/6 ≈ 1.645.

The guarantees assume f is convex with Lipschitz constant G: |f(x) − f(y)| ≤ G‖x − y‖2. In words, f never changes faster than G per unit of distance. Then every subgradient has length at most G CO4A 8-1-3.

One master bound covers every rule. Let R = ‖x0 − x*‖2 be the distance from the start to a minimizer. After k steps the basic inequality says CO4A 8-1-2:

fbest(k) − f* ≤ (R² + G²Σti²) / (2Σti)

With a fixed t the bound becomes R²/(2kt) + G²t/2. The first term dies away, but the second does not. So the method can stall up to about G²t/2 above f*. With diminishing steps both sums grow, their ratio goes to 0, and fbest → f*.

How many steps for accuracy ε? Choose t = ε/G², and the bound drops below ε once k ≥ R²G²/ε². With R = G = 1 and ε = 0.01 that is 10,000 iterations CO4A 8-1-4. Gradient descent on an L-smooth function needs O(1/ε) iterations, roughly 100 here up to constants. That gap, O(1/ε²) against O(1/ε), is the price of kinks.

If you happen to know the optimal value f*, there is a smarter step. The Polyak step picks the t that makes the one-step bound on the distance to x* as small as possible CO4A 8-1-6:

tk = (f(xk) − f*) / ‖gk‖2²

Example: f(x) = |x1| + 2|x2| at x0 = (2, −1.5), where f* = 0. Here f = 5, g = (1, −2) and ‖g‖² = 5, so t = 1. The step lands at (1, 0.5), where f = 2. In the worst case the Polyak step is still O(1/ε²); it just uses information the other rules lack.

RuleStep tkLong runNeeds
Fixedtstalls, up to about G²t/2 above f*nothing
Diminishingfor example 1/kfbest → f*, slowlynothing
Polyak(f(xk) − f*)/‖gk‖²fbest → f*the value f*

Try it: the widget runs all three rules on f = |x1| + 2|x2| from (2, −1.5), where G = √5 ≈ 2.236. Switch the fixed step to 0.5 and to 0.01. A bigger step stalls higher, and a smaller one starts slower.

Notice: the fixed step t = 0.1 stalls at fbest = 0.2 from about k = 20 on, under its ceiling G²t/2 = 0.25. The rule tk = 1/k keeps improving and reaches about 1.0e−3 at k = 1000. The Polyak step is below 1e−10 by k = 50, but that comes from this sharp test function, which grows linearly away from its minimum. It is not the general rate.

Going deeper (optional): where the basic inequality comes from

Expand one step: ‖xk+1 − x*‖² = ‖xk − x*‖² − 2tkgkT(xk − x*) + tk²‖gk‖². The subgradient inequality at xk, used with y = x*, gives gkT(xk − x*) ≥ f(xk) − f*. So each step obeys ‖xk+1 − x*‖² ≤ ‖xk − x*‖² − 2tk(f(xk) − f*) + tk²G². Add these up from the first step to the last. The distances telescope, the final distance is at least 0, and each f(xi) − f* is at least fbest − f*. Rearranging gives the bound. CO4A 8-1-2 writes it out in full, with a few typos; the slides are cleaner Tibshirani 2016.

The slow rate is not a weakness of this particular method. Nesterov showed that for any k ≤ n − 1, some G-Lipschitz convex function forces f(xk) − f* ≥ RG/(2(1 + √(k + 1))) for every method that only combines past subgradients. With R = G = 1 and k = 99 that floor is 1/22 ≈ 0.045. So O(1/ε²) cannot be beaten in this class Tibshirani 2016. The way out is to use more structure, which is Day 8's topic CO4A 8-3.

7. Constraints: project after each step

Often x must stay in a set C: a box of actuator limits, the nonnegative orthant, a ball. The projected subgradient method takes the usual step, then snaps back to the nearest point of C CO4A 8-1-8:

xk+1 = PC(xk − tkgk)

It keeps the same guarantees, provided the projection is cheap. For C = ℝ2+, the nonnegative quadrant, a raw step that lands at (1, −2) projects to (1, 0): just clip the negative entry to 0. Clipping also projects onto a box, such as limits on steering angle and acceleration.

Easy sets to project onto include {x : Ax = b}, affine images {Ax + b}, the nonnegative orthant, L1, L2 and L∞ balls, and simple cones. A general polyhedron {x : Ax ≤ b} is hard: projecting onto it is itself a quadratic program Tibshirani 2016.

A neat special case finds a point in the intersection of convex sets C1, …, Cm. Minimize f(x) = maxi dist(x, Ci). If the sets meet, f* = 0, so the Polyak step is available. Working it out, each Polyak step simply projects onto the farthest set. For two sets this is alternating projections CO4A 8-1-7. CO4A's closing sentence says "closest"; that is a typo, and the slides say farthest Tibshirani 2016.

Here are real numbers. Let C1 be the line x2 = 0 and C2 the disk of radius 1.5 centred at (3, 1). Start at (0, 3). C1 is 3 away and C2 is 2.106 away, so project onto C1: (0, 0). Then C2 is farther, so project onto it: (1.577, 0.526). Then back onto C1: (1.577, 0). The worst distance falls 1.662, 0.526, 0.239, 0.138, 0.083, … toward the meeting point (≈ 1.882, 0).

Going deeper (optional): stochastic subgradients

Many objectives are sums, f = f1 + … + fm, one term per data point. The stochastic subgradient method uses a subgradient of just one term per step, picked in a fixed cycle or at random CO4A 8-2-1. Picking at random needs about m times fewer iterations than cycling in the worst-case bounds, in expectation CO4A 8-2-3. In practice it gets close fast and then struggles near the optimum, while the full-batch method is slow but steady CO4A 8-2-4. It is the nonsmooth cousin of SGD on the SGD card.

Explain it to a 10-year-old

Put a stick under a smooth hill so it touches at one spot. There is only one way to hold it without poking into the hill. Now put the stick at the pointy bottom of a V. You can rock it back and forth and it still just touches the bottom. Each of those angles is a subgradient. If you can hold the stick perfectly flat, you are at the lowest spot.

Common misunderstandings

  • "The subgradient method always goes downhill." It does not. A step can jump past a kink and raise f, as the step from 0.1 to −0.2 does on |x|. Always track fbest.
  • "A kink is always a minimum." max(0.5x, 2x − 1.5) has a kink at 1 with ∂f(1) = [0.5, 2]. Zero is not in it, and moving left lowers f.
  • "∂|x| at 0 is one number." It is the whole interval [−1, 1]. Any member is a valid subgradient, so code that uses sign(0) = 0 is fine.
  • "A fixed step gets there if you wait long enough." It stalls up to about G²t/2 above f*. In the widget, t = 0.1 stops at 0.2.
  • "The distance gradient works everywhere." The formula (x − PC(x))/dist(x, C) needs x outside C. Inside C, dist = 0 and the formula divides by zero.

Check yourself

Q1. Which number is a subgradient of f(x) = |x| at x = 0?

0.5 works because |y| ≥ 0.5y for every y. Any value in [−1, 1] works. 1.5 and −2 fail: their lines rise above the V on one side. "No slope" confuses the gradient, which does not exist at 0, with subgradients, which do.

Q2. For f(x) = max(1 − x, 2x − 2), what is ∂f(1)?

Both pieces are active at x = 1, with slopes −1 and 2. The max rule takes the convex hull, which is the whole interval [−1, 2], not only its two ends. It contains 0, which is why x = 1 is the minimizer, but the set is far bigger than {0}.

Q3. Which vector is a subgradient of ‖x‖1 at x = (2, 0, −1)?

Nonzero coordinates must equal their sign (1 and −1). The zero coordinate may be anything in [−1, 1], so 0.3 is fine. (1, 1.5, −1) breaks the [−1, 1] limit, (1, 0, 1) has the wrong sign in the third coordinate, and (2, 0, −1) is x itself, not its signs.

Q4. Why does the subgradient method keep track of fbest?

The method is not a descent method. Near a kink a step can overshoot and raise f, so the last iterate may not be the best one. Steps shrink rather than grow, subgradients are usually not unique, and the Polyak step needs f*, not fbest.

Q5. You run a fixed step t = 0.1 on a convex f with Lipschitz constant G = √5. What long-run ceiling on fbest − f* does the theory give?

The ceiling is G²t/2 = 5 × 0.1 / 2 = 0.25. A fixed step does not converge to f* in general; only diminishing steps do. In the widget the actual stall level is 0.2, under the ceiling.

Q6. What is the Polyak step at x = (2, −1.5) for f = |x1| + 2|x2|, where f* = 0?

f(x) = 2 + 3 = 5 and g = (1, −2), so ‖g‖² = 5 and t = (5 − 0)/5 = 1. The value 5 forgets to divide by ‖g‖², 0.2 divides the wrong way, and 2.236 is ‖g‖ rather than ‖g‖².

Recap: things to remember

  1. g is a subgradient of f at x if f(y) ≥ f(x) + gT(y − x) for all y. The set of all of them, ∂f(x), is the fan of slopes. At smooth points it is just {∇f(x)}.
  2. Build ∂f with rules: scaling, sums, affine maps, and the convex hull for a max. ∂|x| at 0 is [−1, 1], and the indicator of C gives the normal cone.
  3. x* is a minimizer exactly when 0 ∈ ∂f(x*). For the lasso this says a coefficient stays at 0 while its pull is at most λ, and with X = I it gives soft-thresholding.
  4. The subgradient method is xk+1 = xk − tkgk. It is not a descent method, so keep fbest. Fixed steps stall near G²t/2; diminishing steps such as 1/k converge.
  5. Its rate is O(1/ε²) iterations, far slower than gradient descent, and no subgradient-only method can do better in the worst case. With constraints, project after each step.
