Week 2 · Day 8

Proximal gradient & acceleration

After today you can solve the lasso with ISTA's soft-thresholding step, explain how FISTA's momentum turns O(1/k) into O(1/k²), and recognise projected gradient as a special case.

About 60 min · Needs Day 7 · CO4A chapter 9

Today's big idea

Split the objective into a smooth part g and a simple kinky part h. Take an ordinary gradient step on g, then settle h exactly with a "prox" step. For the lasso the prox is soft-thresholding, and the method, ISTA, runs at gradient-descent speed O(1/k) instead of the subgradient method's O(1/√k). Adding momentum gives FISTA, which improves the rate to O(1/k²).

1. Smooth plus simple: composite objectives

Yesterday's subgradient method treats the whole objective as kinky, and it pays for that with O(1/ε²) iterations. But most kinky objectives are kinky only in a simple, known way. The lasso is a smooth least-squares fit plus a penalty λ‖β‖1, whose kinks all sit where some coordinate is 0.

A composite objective is a sum of two such parts CO4A 9-1:

f(x) = g(x) + h(x)

Here g is convex and differentiable, and h is convex, possibly not differentiable, but simple. The lasso splits as g(β) = ½‖y − Xβ‖2² and h(β) = λ‖β‖1.

A courier drives the highway to the right block, then walks the last bit on foot. Nobody tries to drive through the pedestrian zone. Today's method works the same way: a gradient step handles the smooth part, and a short exact "walk" handles the kinks.

Sparse sensor selection is a lasso. Say a perception stack has 40 candidate input channels, such as radar range bins or lidar features. You want a linear model that uses only the few that matter. The L1 penalty drives useless weights to exactly 0, so the pattern of zeros tells you which channels to keep. The widget in Section 7 solves a small version: 20 measurements, 40 correlated channels, and only 3 that truly matter.

2. Gradient descent as "jump to the bottom of a simple model"

Here is a new way to see a gradient step. At the current point x, replace f by a simple model: its tangent plane plus a round bowl. Then jump to the bottom of the bowl Tibshirani 2016.

x+ = argminz f(x) + ∇f(x)T(z − x) + (1/2t)‖z − x‖2²

The bowl term (1/2t)‖z − x‖² has Hessian (1/t)I. It pretends the curvature is 1/t in every direction. CO4A writes (1/2t)I here, but the ½ already sits in the bowl term, so the Hessian is (1/t)I. Setting the derivative in z to zero gives ∇f(x) + (z − x)/t = 0, so z = x − t∇f(x). That is exactly the Day 6 step.

A number check: f(x) = x², x = 1, t = 0.25. The model is 1 + 2(z − 1) + 2(z − 1)². Its bottom is at z = 1 − 0.25·2 = 0.5, the same point a gradient step reaches.

Now the key move. Use the simple model only for g, and keep h exactly as it is:

x+ = argminz g(x) + ∇g(x)T(z − x)
+ (1/2t)‖z − x‖² + h(z)

Completing the square tidies this up CO4A 9-1:

x+ = argminz (1/2t)‖z − (x − t∇g(x))‖² + h(z)

Read it as two moves. First take a gradient step on g. Then look for the point that stays close to where that step landed while keeping h small.

3. The proximal operator

That second move has a name. The proximal operator of h with step t is CO4A 9-1:

proxt(x) = argminz (1/2t)‖x − z‖2² + h(z)

It is a compromise. The first term says "stay near x", the second says "make h small", and a larger t gives h more say. Three examples show the range:

  • h = 0: nothing to fix, so proxt(x) = x.
  • h = IC, the indicator from Day 7: stay as close to x as possible while staying in C. That is the projection PC(x).
  • h = λ‖x‖1: soft-thresholding at level λt, the subject of Section 4.

Proximal gradient descent repeats the two moves CO4A 9-1:

xk+1 = proxt(xk − t∇g(xk))

The prox depends only on h, not on g. So g can be as messy as you like, as long as you can compute its gradient. When h's prox is cheap, each iteration costs about as much as a gradient step Tibshirani 2016.

It helps to write the update as xk+1 = xk − tGt(xk), where the generalized gradient is

Gt(x) = (x − proxt(x − t∇g(x))) / t

When h = 0 it is just ∇g. In general it plays the gradient's role: Gt(x) = 0 exactly when x minimizes f.

4. ISTA: proximal gradient for the lasso

For h = λ‖β‖1 the prox splits into one tiny problem per coordinate. Each is solved by Day 7's soft-thresholding, at level λt instead of λ:

[Sλt(β)]i = βi − λt if βi > λt
[Sλt(β)]i = 0 if −λt ≤ βi ≤ λt
[Sλt(β)]i = βi + λt if βi < −λt

CO4A drops the minus sign in the middle case and writes λt ≤ βi ≤ λt. The band is symmetric: −λt ≤ βi ≤ λt Tibshirani 2016.

Think of a flat tax of λt on every coefficient's size. Big coefficients pay it and survive, a little smaller. Anything smaller than the tax is wiped out to exactly zero.

The gradient of g(β) = ½‖y − Xβ‖² is −XT(y − Xβ). Put the gradient step and the prox together and you get ISTA, the iterative soft-thresholding algorithm CO4A 9-1 Beck & Teboulle 2009:

β+ = Sλt(β + tXT(y − Xβ))

Try one step on a lasso with a single coefficient: g(β) = ½(4 − 2β)² and λ = 2. Here g′(β) = −2(4 − 2β) and L = 4, so take t = 1/4. Start at β = 0.

  • Gradient step: 0 − 0.25·(−8) = 2.
  • Prox: S0.5(2) = 1.5, since λt = 2 × 0.25 = 0.5.
  • Check Day 7's rule: g′(1.5) = −2(4 − 3) = −2, and −2 + λ·sign(1.5) = 0. So β = 1.5 is optimal.

It lands in one step only because, in one dimension with t = 1/L, the model of g is exact. In many dimensions ISTA needs many steps. Here is one prox with λt = 1: a gradient step that lands at (3, 0.4, −1.5) is soft-thresholded to (2, 0, −0.5). The middle coefficient falls inside the band and is zeroed.

Try it: drag λ and watch the flat band widen. Then drag the input y through the band and watch the output stick at 0.

Notice: at λ = 1 the input y = 2 comes out as S(2) = 1. Every input in the shaded band [−1, 1], such as 0.5, comes out as exactly 0, and −2 comes out as −1. Outside the band the curve has slope 1, shifted toward 0 by λ.

The whole solver fits in a dozen lines. The same loop gives FISTA (Section 7) when the momentum weight is switched on.

import numpy as np

def soft(z, a):                         # prox of a·‖·‖₁
    return np.sign(z) * np.maximum(np.abs(z) - a, 0)

def lasso(X, y, lam, iters=1000, fista=True):
    t = 1 / np.linalg.norm(X, 2) ** 2   # t = 1/L, L = λmax(XᵀX)
    b = b_old = np.zeros(X.shape[1])
    for k in range(1, iters + 1):
        w = (k - 2) / (k + 1) if fista else 0.0
        v = b + w * (b - b_old)          # momentum (FISTA only)
        b_old = b
        b = soft(v + t * X.T @ (y - X @ v), lam * t)
    return b

The ISTA card and the FISTA card summarize both methods.

5. How fast is ISTA, and how to pick t

The rate matches gradient descent. Assume g has a Lipschitz gradient with constant L, also called L-smooth: ‖∇g(x) − ∇g(y)‖2 ≤ L‖x − y‖2. For the lasso, L is the largest eigenvalue of XTX. With a fixed step t ≤ 1/L CO4A 9-2:

f(xk) − f* ≤ ‖x0 − x*‖2² / (2tk)

That is O(1/k) error, or O(1/ε) iterations, against O(1/ε²) for the subgradient method. Take ‖x0 − x*‖² = 1 and t = 1. Reaching ε = 10⁻⁴ needs k ≥ 1/(2·10⁻⁴) = 5,000 iterations by this bound. The subgradient bound with R = G = 1 would ask for R²G²/ε² = 10⁸.

Two cautions. The count is iterations, not work. Each iteration costs one prox, which is cheap for soft-thresholding and expensive when it needs a matrix factorization (Section 6). Also, ISTA's objective never goes up: it is a descent method Beck & Teboulle 2009.

You rarely know L. Backtracking line search works much as on Day 6. Start each iteration at t = 1 and shrink t ← βt, with 0 < β < 1, until the smooth part's quadratic upper model holds at the new point CO4A 9-2:

g(x − tGt(x)) ≤ g(x) − t∇g(x)TGt(x)
+ (t/2)‖Gt(x)‖²

Only g is tested, never h. The rate becomes ‖x0 − x*‖²/(2tmink) with tmin = min{1, β/L}. Every trial step costs one prox call.

On the seeded lasso from Section 7, computed offline with β = 0.5, 200 backtracking iterations used 1,319 prox calls, about 6.6 per iteration. They accepted steps as large as 0.25, where 1/L = 0.00395, and reached an error of 1.8×10⁻⁴. Fixed-step ISTA was at 9.1×10⁻² after 200 iterations and at 4.9×10⁻⁴ after 1,319. So here the bigger steps were worth their extra prox calls.

6. Special cases: one method, many names

Proximal gradient is also called generalized gradient descent, because familiar methods fall out of it when you choose g or h CO4A 9-4:

  • h = 0: the prox is the identity, and you get plain gradient descent.
  • h = IC: the prox is the projection, and you get projected gradient descent, x+ = PC(x − t∇g(x)).
  • g = 0: you get the proximal minimization algorithm, x+ = proxt(x). It beats the subgradient method, but only when the prox has a closed form.

A projected-gradient example with numbers: minimize (x − 3)² over C = [0, 1], with L = 2 and t = 0.25, from x = 0. The gradient step goes to 0 − 0.25·(−6) = 1.5, and the projection brings it back to PC(1.5) = 1. From x = 1 the gradient step goes to 1 − 0.25·(−4) = 2, which projects back to 1 again. The point has stopped moving, and a point the step leaves unchanged is the optimum.

Robots use projected gradient all the time. If the variables are steering and acceleration commands with hard limits, C is a box and PC just clips each command to its range. Box limits on inputs come back in Day 17's model predictive control.

One heavier example shows why the cost of a prox matters. In matrix completion you see some entries of a matrix Y, such as a few ratings, and want a low-rank B that matches them. The trace norm ‖B‖tr, the sum of the singular values, is the L1 norm of the singular values. It is a convex stand-in for rank CO4A 9-3.

Its prox soft-thresholds the singular values. Singular values (5, 2, 0.5) with λt = 1 become (4, 1, 0), and the rank drops from 3 to 2. With t = 1 the method is called Soft-Impute: fill the missing entries with your current guess, then shrink the singular values. Each step needs a singular value decomposition (SVD), which is far more work than a soft-threshold.

7. Acceleration: FISTA

ISTA forgets its past. Each step starts from where it stands, so along a long, gently sloping valley it inches forward. Momentum fixes that: before each step, keep going a little in the direction you were already moving.

Think of pushing a swing. Small pushes timed with the motion build speed, because each push adds to the motion already there.

FISTA (fast ISTA) adds one line to ISTA. Set x−1 = x0. Then for k = 1, 2, … CO4A 9-5-1:

v = xk−1 + ((k − 2)/(k + 1))(xk−1 − xk−2)
xk = proxt(v − t∇g(v))

The momentum weight (k − 2)/(k + 1) starts small and creeps toward 1. It is 0 at k = 2, 0.25 at k = 3, 0.727 at k = 10 and 0.970 at k = 100. At k = 1 it is −0.5, which does no harm because x0 − x−1 = 0.

This is the form CO4A and the CMU slides use. Beck and Teboulle's original paper builds the weight from a sequence tk, which there is a momentum counter, not a step size Beck & Teboulle 2009. Start with t1 = 1 and set

tk+1 = (1 + √(1 + 4tk²)) / 2, weight = (tk − 1)/tk+1

Both forms carry the same guarantee. On the widget's example they differ only slightly: at k = 100 the error is 6.2×10⁻⁴ with CO4A's weights and 5.6×10⁻⁴ with Beck and Teboulle's.

With t ≤ 1/L, FISTA guarantees CO4A 9-5-2:

f(xk) − f* ≤ 2‖x0 − x*‖2² / (t(k + 1)²)

That is O(1/k²) error, or O(1/√ε) iterations. With ‖x0 − x*‖² = 1 and t = 1, ε = 10⁻⁴ needs (k + 1)² ≥ 20,000, so k = 141, against 5,000 for ISTA. In the worst case over smooth convex problems, no method that only uses gradients can do better.

Why does looking back help? On a valley floor, consecutive steps point the same way, so the momentum adds up and the effective step grows. Across a valley, steps alternate in direction, and the momentum mostly cancels.

FISTA is not a descent method. Momentum can carry it past the bottom, so f rises for a while. These bumps are called Nesterov ripples CO4A 9-5-1. In the widget's example, FISTA's objective rose on 430 of its first 1,000 steps, the first time at k = 35. ISTA never rose. If you need a curve that only goes down, report the best value so far.

Try it: the chart runs ISTA and FISTA on the seeded lasso (20 measurements, 40 correlated channels, λ = 1, t = 1/L with L = 253.1). Switch the FISTA weights between the two forms, and press "Show bounds" to draw both guarantees.

Notice: on this example, at k = 100 ISTA is still 0.465 above f* while FISTA is at 6.2e−4, about 750 times closer. To get within 10⁻³ of f*, ISTA needs 1,146 iterations and FISTA needs 98.

ISTAFISTA
Step taken fromxk−1v = xk−1 + wk(xk−1 − xk−2)
Guarantee, t ≤ 1/L‖x0 − x*‖²/(2tk)2‖x0 − x*‖²/(t(k + 1)²)
Bound: iterations for ε = 10⁻⁴ (‖x0 − x*‖² = 1, t = 1)5,000141
Widget example: iterations to 10⁻³1,14698
Objective each stepnever goes upcan go up (ripples)
Memoryone pointtwo points

Acceleration is not always worth it CO4A 9-5-4. A warm start begins a solve from the answer to a nearby problem. Along a path of λ values, λ1 > λ2 > …, each solve starts so close to its answer that plain ISTA often does just as well. In matrix completion, backtracking costs several SVDs per step, and the extrapolated point v need not be low rank, which makes each SVD slower.

Prox steps return later. Day 13's ADMM is built from prox steps on each part of a split problem, and Day 14 shows coordinate descent, another fast lasso solver.

Going deeper (optional): where the rates come from

CO4A states the O(1/k) theorem without proof. A full proof is Theorem 3.1 of Beck and Teboulle: one lemma bounds the progress of a single prox-gradient step, and the bounds telescope. Their version reads F(xk) − F* ≤ αL‖x0 − x*‖²/(2k), with α = 1 for a constant step. Their loss is ‖Ax − b‖² without the ½, so their L is twice ours Beck & Teboulle 2009.

The O(1/k²) proof (their Lemmas 4.1 to 4.3 and Theorem 4.4) rests on two facts about the momentum sequence: tk² = tk+1² − tk+1, and tk ≥ (k + 1)/2. The second makes the error shrink like 1/tk², which is at most 4/(k + 1)². The rate is a worst case. A particular lasso can converge much faster, sometimes almost linearly. The widget's example uses correlated columns and a small λ, so the gap between O(1/k) and O(1/k²) is visible.

Explain it to a 10-year-old

You are tidying a messy room with one rule: every toy pays a one-coin tax, and toys worth less than one coin go in the bin. Each round, you first move things toward where they belong, then apply the tax. The little junk disappears for good, and only the toys that matter are left. FISTA is the same, except you keep walking in the direction you were already going, so you finish much sooner.

Common misunderstandings

  • "Proximal gradient is the subgradient method with a new name." It handles h exactly through the prox, which is why it gets O(1/k) instead of O(1/√k).
  • "ISTA thresholds at λ." It thresholds at λt. The zero band is −λt ≤ βi ≤ λt, with a minus sign on the left.
  • "FISTA's objective falls every step." Ripples are normal. In the widget's example it rose on 430 of 1,000 steps. Report the best value, or use a monotone variant.
  • "Only iterations count." One prox can be an SVD, and backtracking multiplied the prox calls by about 6.6 on the widget's example.
  • "Acceleration always helps." With warm starts, or when each prox is costly, it can be neutral or worse.

Check yourself

Q1. For h = λ‖x‖1 and step size t, what is proxt?

The prox minimizes (1/2t)‖x − z‖² + λ‖z‖1. Multiplying by t shows the penalty is λt, so each coordinate shrinks by λt. Thresholding at λ forgets the step size. Hard-thresholding keeps large entries unshrunk, which is not what the L1 penalty does. Projection onto an L1 ball is the prox of an indicator, not of the norm.

Q2. One ISTA step for g(β) = ½(4 − 2β)², λ = 2 and t = 0.25, starting from β = 0, lands at:

The gradient step goes to 2. Soft-thresholding at λt = 0.5 gives 1.5. Stopping at 2 skips the prox step. 1.75 thresholds at 0.25 instead of λt. 0 would mean the whole value sat inside the band.

Q3. Using the guarantees with ‖x0 − x*‖² = 1, t = 1 and ε = 10⁻⁴, how many iterations do ISTA and FISTA need?

ISTA: 1/(2k) ≤ 10⁻⁴ gives k = 5,000. FISTA: 2/(k + 1)² ≤ 10⁻⁴ gives (k + 1)² ≥ 20,000, so k = 141. The 10,000 / 100 pair drops the constants 2 in both bounds, and the swapped pair has the faster method backwards.

Q4. When does proximal gradient become projected gradient descent?

The prox of an indicator is the projection, so the update becomes PC(x − t∇g(x)). h = 0 gives plain gradient descent, and g = 0 gives the proximal minimization algorithm. A squared norm is smooth and adds shrinkage, not a constraint.

Q5. In a FISTA run the objective went up at step 35. What is the most likely reason?

Nesterov ripples are normal. In the widget's example, FISTA rose for the first time at k = 35 with t = 1/L exactly, so the step size is not to blame. Check the best value so far, not each step.

Q6. Backtracking in proximal gradient checks its sufficient-decrease condition on:

The test compares g at the new point with g's quadratic upper model, because only g was replaced by a model. h is handled exactly by the prox, so it needs no test. Fixed steps are allowed, but they are not required.

Recap: things to remember

  1. For f = g + h with g smooth and h simple, take xk+1 = proxt(xk − t∇g(xk)): a gradient step on g, then a prox step for h.
  2. The prox of λ‖·‖1 is soft-thresholding at λt. For the lasso this gives ISTA, β+ = Sλt(β + tXT(y − Xβ)), and its zeros come from the band −λt ≤ βi ≤ λt.
  3. With t ≤ 1/L, ISTA's error is at most ‖x0 − x*‖²/(2tk), the gradient-descent rate. Backtracking tests only g.
  4. h = IC gives projected gradient, h = 0 gives gradient descent, and g = 0 gives proximal minimization.
  5. FISTA adds momentum, (k − 2)/(k + 1) in CO4A's form or tk in Beck and Teboulle's. The rate becomes O(1/k²), but the objective can ripple upward.

Week 2 · Day 9

Duality

After today you can build the Lagrangian and the dual function, use weak duality to get a lower bound on the best value, and tell when strong duality holds (Slater's condition).

About 60 min · Needs Day 4 · CO4A chapters 10 and 11

Today's big idea

Every minimization problem has a twin, its dual, whose job is to find the best guaranteed floor under the answer. You build the floor by putting a price on each rule instead of forbidding violations. Every price gives a valid floor. For convex problems with a little room to spare, the best price gives a floor that touches the answer exactly.

1. A referee who proves "you can't do better"

Picture a factory that must ship at least 2 tons of product. Plant X makes it for $1 a ton and plant Y for $3 a ton. Write x and y for the tons each plant makes. The cheapest plan solves this linear program (LP):

minimize x + 3y
s.t. x + y ≥ 2, x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0

Here the answer is obvious: use only the cheap plant, (x, y) = (2, 0), for a cost of 2. With 10,000 variables nothing is obvious. A solver hands you a plan and says it is the best. How could anyone check that claim without trying every plan?

Bring in a referee. She never looks at plans. She only combines the rules that every plan must obey. Take the rule x + y ≥ 2 once and the rule y ≥ 0 twice, and add them: (x + y) + 2y ≥ 2 + 0, which reads x + 3y ≥ 2. The left side is exactly the cost. So no plan can cost less than 2, and the plan (2, 0) is the best one. CO4A 10-01

That is duality in miniature. A floor that matches a plan you hold is a certificate: a short proof of optimality that anyone can check with a few additions. The referee's weights (1, 0 and 2 for the three rules) are the certificate.

Now make the trick systematic. Give each rule a weight: u1 for x + y ≥ 2, u2 for x ≥ 0, and u3 for y ≥ 0. Each weight must be ≥ 0, because multiplying an inequality by a negative number flips it. Adding the weighted rules gives

(u1 + u2)x + (u1 + u3)y ≥ 2u1

If the left side equals the cost, that is u1 + u2 = 1 and u1 + u3 = 3, then 2u1 is a floor under every plan. The referee wants the highest floor, so she solves a problem of her own: CO4A 10-01

maximize 2u1
s.t. u1 + u2 = 1, u1 + u3 = 3, u ≥ 0

Because u2 and u3 cannot be negative, these constraints say u1 ≤ 1 and u1 ≤ 3. The best choice is u1 = 1, with floor 2: exactly the cost of the best plan. The referee's problem is the dual problem. The original one is the primal problem.

The weight u1 also has a price tag. Raise the demand from 2 tons to 2.1 tons, and the cheapest plan costs 2.1 instead of 2. Each extra ton of demand costs u1 = 1 dollar. A multiplier is the price of its rule: what one more unit of tightening would cost you. Boyd & Vandenberghe 2004 Hold on to that reading. It is the story behind everything below.

Explain it to a 10-year-old

Your teacher says: "This maze takes at least 12 steps." She proves it without walking it. The exit is 12 squares away, and every step moves you one square. That is a floor. If you then find a 12-step path, the floor proves your path is the best one possible. Duality is a machine for building floors like that, for any problem.

2. Every LP has a twin

The referee's recipe works for any LP. Take the form "pay as little as possible while meeting every requirement":

primal: minimize cTx
s.t. Ax ≥ b, x ≥ 0

Here x ∈ ℝn lists the amounts, c lists their unit costs, and each row of Ax ≥ b is one requirement. Give each row a weight, and collect the weights in a vector u ≥ 0. Every feasible x then obeys uTAx ≥ uTb. If also ATu ≤ c entry by entry, then x ≥ 0 gives cTx ≥ (ATu)Tx = uTAx ≥ bTu. The best floor of this kind is the dual:

dual: maximize bTu
s.t. ATu ≤ c, u ≥ 0

The factory is the case c = (1, 3), A = [1 1] and b = 2. Its dual is "maximize 2u1 s.t. u1 ≤ 1, u1 ≤ 3, u1 ≥ 0". In Section 1 the extra weights u2 and u3 did the same job: u1 + u2 = 1 with u2 ≥ 0 just says u1 ≤ 1. Tibshirani 2016

Notice the swap. Each primal requirement becomes one dual variable, and each primal variable becomes one dual constraint. The costs c and the requirements b trade places. The table collects the sign rules. CO4A 10-02

In the primal (minimize)In the dual (maximize)
a requirement aiTx ≥ bia variable ui ≥ 0
a requirement aiTx = bia variable ui of any sign
a variable xj ≥ 0a constraint (ATu)j ≤ cj
a variable xj of any signa constraint (ATu)j = cj
the right-hand sides bthe objective bTu
the costs cthe right-hand sides of the constraints

A "≤" requirement is multiplied by −1 first. Why may an equality's weight have any sign? You can scale an equation by a negative number without breaking it: a = b also gives −a = −b. CO4A 10-02 states the same rules for the form "Ax = b, Gx ≤ h". Watch the letters on that page: it uses u for the equalities and v for the inequalities, the reverse of chapter 11 and of this lesson.

A dual you can see: max flow and min cut

Picture water pipes running from a source s to a sink t, each pipe with a capacity. The max flow is the most water per second you can push from s to t. A cut splits the nodes into two groups, one holding s and the other holding t. Its capacity is the total capacity of the pipes that run from the s group to the t group. The min cut is the cut with the smallest capacity.

Every drop of water must cross every cut, so any cut's capacity is a ceiling on the flow. The primal here is a maximum, so the referee's job flips. Her certificate now says "you can't push more than this".

Max flow is an LP. Its variables are the flows fij in the pipes, with 0 ≤ fij ≤ cij on each pipe (CO4A prints < here; it should be ≤) and "flow in = flow out" at every node except s and t. Its dual turns out to be the LP relaxation of min cut: the same problem with the 0-or-1 labels "which side is this node on" allowed to take fractional values. So max flow ≤ relaxed min cut ≤ min cut, and the max-flow min-cut theorem says all three are equal. CO4A 10-03 Tibshirani 2016

The figure shows a small case. The best flow sends 4 units. The cut that separates {s, a} from {b, t} crosses three pipes with capacities 2, 1 and 1, so it also totals 4. The other cuts are larger: {s} alone gives 5, {s, b} gives 7 and {s, a, b} gives 5. A flow of 4 and a cut of 4 certify each other, just as the factory plan and the referee's floor did.

3. Prices instead of walls: the Lagrangian

For an LP the referee can combine rules by hand. Curved problems need a recipe that always works. Here it is: turn each hard rule into a price. Instead of a wall that forbids breaking a rule, charge a fine of u for each unit of violation, and pay a rebate of u for each unit of room to spare.

First the letters, because the books disagree. This lesson follows CO4A chapter 11 and Tibshirani's slides.

ItemThis lesson (CO4A ch. 11)Boyd & Vandenberghe
Cost (objective)f(x)f0(x)
Inequality ruleshi(x) ≤ 0fi(x) ≤ 0
Equality rulesℓj(x) = 0hi(x) = 0
Their multipliersui ≥ 0 and vjλi ≥ 0 and νi
Dual functiong(u, v)g(λ, ν)

So in Boyd & Vandenberghe the letter h means an equality, while here it means an inequality. Day 4 followed CO4A chapter 4 and wrote the rules as gi(x) ≤ 0 and hj(x) = 0. Today the letter g belongs to the dual function, so the inequalities become hi and the equalities ℓj. Day 10 keeps hi and ℓj but names the multipliers λ and ν, as CO4A chapter 12 does.

Day 4's standard form, in today's letters, is

minimize f(x)
s.t. hi(x) ≤ 0, i = 1, …, m
ℓj(x) = 0, j = 1, …, r

Write p* for its best value. The Lagrangian adds every rule to the cost, each with its own price:

L(x, u, v) = f(x) + Σi uihi(x) + Σj vjℓj(x)

The prices ui ≥ 0 and vj (any sign) are the Lagrange multipliers, also called dual variables. There is one for each rule, just like the referee's weights. CO4A 11-1

One fact makes everything work: on the feasible set, L never exceeds f. If x obeys the rules, each hi(x) ≤ 0, so uihi(x) ≤ 0. That term is a rebate, or nothing. Each ℓj(x) = 0, so the v terms vanish. CO4A 11-1

L(x, u, v) ≤ f(x)
for every feasible x and every u ≥ 0

A worked example. Take min x2 s.t. x ≥ 1, whose answer is x* = 1 with p* = 1. In "≤ 0" form the rule is h(x) = 1 − x ≤ 0, so

L(x, u) = x2 + u(1 − x)

At the feasible point x = 1.5 with price u = 1, L = 2.25 + (1 − 1.5) = 1.75. That is below f(1.5) = 2.25: the point has 0.5 units of room and earns a rebate of 0.5. At the infeasible point x = 0.5, L = 0.25 + 0.5 = 0.75. That point breaks the rule by 0.5 and pays a fine of 0.5.

Analogy: an emissions cap versus a carbon price

A regulator can impose a hard cap: "emit at most 100 tons". Or it can set a price: pay u for each ton above 100, and earn u in credits for each ton below. Under the price, a firm may break the cap whenever that is cheaper for it. So its cheapest priced cost, g(u), can never be above its cheapest cost under the hard cap, p*. The regulator's dual problem is to find the price that makes the firm's best priced cost as high as possible. When strong duality holds, the right price makes the firm's own cheapest choice land right on the cap. You can watch this in the x2 example: at u = 2 the lowest point of L is x = 1, exactly on the rule.

4. The dual function g(u, v), and why it is always concave

Now set x free. Fix the prices, ignore the rules, and find the lowest point of L over all x. That lowest value is the Lagrange dual function:

g(u, v) = min over all x of L(x, u, v)

(Strictly, "min" should be "inf", the greatest lower bound, because the lowest value may never be reached.) Why is g a floor? Freedom plus a fair fine can only make things cheaper. Formally, let x* be the best feasible point. Then g(u, v) ≤ L(x*, u, v) ≤ f(x*) = p*. The first step holds because g takes the minimum over all x. The second holds because x* is feasible. CO4A 11-2

Back to min x2 s.t. x ≥ 1. For a fixed u, L(x, u) = x2 + u(1 − x) is a bowl in x. Its slope 2x − u is zero at x = u/2. Plug that in:

g(u) = u2/4 + u(1 − u/2) = u − u2/4

Price uLowest point of L, x = u/2Does it obey x ≥ 1?Floor g(u)
00no0
10.5no0.75
21yes (on the boundary)1
31.5yes0.75
42yes0

Every floor is at most p* = 1, as promised. Look at u = 1: the lowest point x = 0.5 breaks the rule. That is fine, because g(u) is a floor, not a plan. The best price, u = 2, gives a floor of exactly 1.

The value of g can also be −∞, which is a useless floor. This happens all the time in LPs. For the factory, L = x + 3y + u1(2 − x − y) − u2x − u3y. Collect terms:

L = (1 − u1 − u2)x + (3 − u1 − u3)y + 2u1

This is linear in x and y. Unless both brackets are zero, x or y can run off and make L as negative as you like. So g = 2u1 when u1 + u2 = 1 and u1 + u3 = 3, and −∞ otherwise. The general recipe has rebuilt the referee's LP from Section 1. CO4A 10-04 Prices with u ≥ 0 and g(u, v) > −∞ are called dual feasible.

Now the surprising part. Fix one x and watch L(x, u) = f(x) + u·h(x) as the price u changes. It is a straight line in u that starts at height f(x) with slope h(x). Each x gives one line, and g(u) is the lowest line at each u: their lower envelope. The figure draws five of these lines for our example.

The lowest of many straight lines always bends down, never up. It is a concave function: a cap shape, the negative of a convex function. Check it with numbers. Halfway between u = 0 and u = 2, the chord sits at (0 + 1)/2 = 0.5, while g(1) = 0.75 sits above it. Nothing in this argument used the shape of f or h. So g is concave for every problem, however nonconvex the primal is. CO4A 11-3

The dual problem asks for the best floor. Write d* for its best value:

d* = maximize g(u, v) s.t. u ≥ 0

Maximizing a concave function over the convex set u ≥ 0 is a convex problem, because maximizing a concave g is the same as minimizing the convex −g. So the dual is always a convex problem, even when the primal is not. There is one catch. Each value of g needs a minimization over x, and that can be hard when f is nonconvex. CO4A 11-3

5. Weak duality, strong duality, and Slater's condition

Back to the referee. Her best floor can never pass the true answer. This is weak duality: CO4A 11-3

d* ≤ p* (always)

The proof is the one line from Section 4: every g(u, v) is at most p*, so the best one is too. It holds for every problem, convex or not. The difference p* − d* ≥ 0 is the optimal duality gap. When it is zero we have strong duality, p* = d*: the referee's best floor touches the answer.

In the x2 example, d* = g(2) = 1 = p*, so there is no gap. The best price u* = 2 also carries the meaning from Section 1. Tighten the rule to x ≥ 1.1, and the best cost rises from 1 to 1.21. That is an increase of 0.21, close to u* × 0.1 = 0.2. The multiplier is the price of the rule. Boyd & Vandenberghe 2004

When is the gap zero? The standard test is Slater's condition. Suppose the problem is convex: f and every hi are convex, and every ℓj is affine. Suppose also that some point is strictly feasible: hi(x) < 0 for every i, and ℓj(x) = 0 for every j. Then p* = d*. Affine inequalities may even hold with equality; only the curved rules need room to spare. CO4A 11-4 Tibshirani 2016

In words: a convex problem with a little wiggle room inside every curved rule has no gap. For x2 with x ≥ 1, the point x = 2 has h(2) = 1 − 2 = −1 < 0. Slater holds, and the gap is indeed zero.

An LP has only affine rules, so for LPs feasibility is enough. Strong duality holds whenever the primal or the dual is feasible, and it fails only if both are infeasible. Tibshirani 2016 That is why the max flow equals the relaxed min cut in Section 2.

Without convexity, a real gap can open. Take f(x) = x4 − 50x2 + 100x s.t. x ≥ −4.5. The cost has two valleys, near x = −5.4 and x = 4.4. The rule cuts off the deeper one, so the best feasible point sits on the boundary: p* = f(−4.5) = −1052.4375. CO4A 11-3

The Lagrangian is L = x4 − 50x2 + (100 − u)x − 4.5u. The best price is u = 100. It cancels the linear term and leaves two equal valleys at x = ±5, so g(100) = 625 − 1250 − 450 = −1075. No other price does better, so d* = −1075 and the gap is 22.5625. Note that strict feasibility holds here: x = 0 is strictly inside the rule. What fails is convexity. CO4A 11-3

The gap is also useful while a solver runs. For any feasible x and any dual-feasible (u, v), the duality gap is f(x) − g(u, v). Since g(u, v) ≤ p* ≤ f(x), it bounds how far x is from the best value: CO4A 11-5

f(x) − p* ≤ f(x) − g(u, v)

For example, x = 1.2 costs f = 1.44, and the price u = 1.5 gives g = 1.5 − 0.5625 = 0.9375. The gap is 0.5025, so x is at most 0.5025 above the best value. (The truth is 0.44.) A gap of zero proves that both are optimal. Solvers stop once the gap falls below a tolerance ε, because then f(x) − p* ≤ ε is guaranteed. CO4A 11-5

Try it: drag the price u and watch the dashed priced cost L(x, u) tilt. Its lowest point, the orange dot, gives the floor g(u), the purple dot below. Then switch to the nonconvex quartic and hunt for the best price.

Notice: at the default price u = 1 the floor is g(1) = 0.75, a gap of 0.25, and L's lowest point x = 0.5 breaks the rule x ≥ 1. The purple curve stays under p* = 1 everywhere and touches it only at u = 2 (Slater holds: x = 2 is strictly feasible). On the quartic, the best floor is −1075 at u = 100, where L has two lowest points, x = −5 and x = 5. That floor stops 22.56 short of p* = −1052.44.

Common misunderstandings

  • "Weak duality needs a convex problem." It does not. d* ≤ p* holds for every problem, and the quartic shows it. Convexity matters only for strong duality.
  • "The multipliers can take any sign." Only the equality ones can. An inequality price must be u ≥ 0. With u < 0 a feasible point would pay a positive amount, L could exceed f, and the floor would break.
  • "Convex means no gap." Usually, but not always. You also need a condition such as Slater's. A convex example with a gap of 1 is in the box below.
  • "g(u) is the cost of some plan." It is a floor, not a plan. The x that minimizes L may break the rules: at u = 1 in the x2 example it is x = 0.5, which violates x ≥ 1.
  • "The quartic has a gap because Slater fails." x = 0 is strictly feasible. The gap comes from nonconvexity, since Slater's condition first needs a convex problem.
  • "h means the same thing in every book." In CO4A and Tibshirani, hi(x) ≤ 0 are the inequalities. In Boyd & Vandenberghe, hi(x) = 0 are the equalities. Check the letters before you copy a formula.

Going deeper (optional): why Slater closes the gap, and a convex problem with a gap

The proof uses a separating hyperplane. Collect every pair (rule value, cost) that some x can reach, together with everything above and to the right of it. For a convex problem this set is convex. So a hyperplane separates it from the points (0, t) with t < p*, which no x can reach. The tilt of that hyperplane gives the best price. The strictly feasible point stops the hyperplane from standing vertical, which would mean an infinite price. Boyd & Vandenberghe give the full argument in §5.3.2; CO4A does not prove it. Boyd & Vandenberghe 2004

Convexity alone is not enough. Boyd & Vandenberghe's exercise 5.21 minimizes e−x s.t. x2/y ≤ 0, over y > 0. The rule forces x = 0, so p* = 1. No point is strictly feasible, and the dual function is g(u) = 0 for every u ≥ 0: send x to infinity with y = x3, and both terms of L shrink to 0. So d* = 0, and the gap is 1. Boyd & Vandenberghe 2004

6. Worked example: the dual of a least-squares problem

A small robot has two thrusters. Thruster 1 pushes with force x1. Thruster 2 sits on a lever, so its force x2 counts double. Together they must deliver a push of exactly 5, so x1 + 2x2 = 5. Energy grows with the square of each force, so we want the least total effort:

minimize x12 + x22
s.t. x1 + 2x2 = 5

This asks for the shortest solution of a linear equation, a least-squares problem with a constraint. In matrix form it is min ‖x‖22 s.t. Ax = b, with A = [1 2] and b = 5. There is one equality, so there is one multiplier v, of any sign.

Step 1, the Lagrangian:

L(x, v) = x12 + x22 + v(x1 + 2x2 − 5)

Step 2, minimize over x. L is a bowl in x. Its gradient is (2x1 + v, 2x2 + 2v), which is zero at x1 = −v/2 and x2 = −v.

Step 3, plug back in. Then x12 + x22 = 1.25v2 and x1 + 2x2 − 5 = −2.5v − 5, so

g(v) = 1.25v2 + v(−2.5v − 5)
= −1.25v2 − 5v

This is a downward parabola, concave as promised. Any v gives a floor. For example, v = −1 gives g = −1.25 + 5 = 3.75.

Step 4, maximize. The slope −2.5v − 5 is zero at v* = −2, so d* = g(−2) = −5 + 10 = 5.

Step 5, compare. Put v* = −2 into Step 2 to get x = (1, 2). It obeys 1 + 2·2 = 5, and its effort is 1 + 4 = 5 = d*. The gap is zero, as Slater predicts: the problem is convex and its only rule is affine.

Two things to notice. The multiplier v* = −2 is negative, which is allowed for an equality. And the dual's answer handed back the primal's answer through Step 2. Day 10 turns that into a rule.

The same five steps work for any A and b. The lowest point of L is x = −ATv/2, and

g(v) = −¼ vTAATv − bTv

Boyd & Vandenberghe work this exact problem in chapter 5, and CO4A 11-2 runs the same steps on quadratic programs. Boyd & Vandenberghe 2004 CO4A 11-2 The few lines of Python below check every number.

import numpy as np
A = np.array([[1.0, 2.0]]); b = np.array([5.0])      # x1 + 2*x2 = 5
AAt = A @ A.T
x_star = A.T @ np.linalg.solve(AAt, b)               # least-norm solution
g = lambda v: -0.25 * v @ AAt @ v - b @ v            # dual function
v_star = -2 * np.linalg.solve(AAt, b)                # where g peaks
print(x_star, x_star @ x_star)                       # [1. 2.] 5.0
print(v_star, g(v_star), g(np.array([-1.0])))        # [-2.] 5.0 3.75
print(-A.T @ v_star / 2)                             # [1. 2.]: primal from dual

Going deeper (optional): the dual of a general QP

Take min ½xTQx + cTx s.t. Ax = b, x ≥ 0, with Q ≻ 0. The rule x ≥ 0 reads −x ≤ 0 and gets prices u ≥ 0, so L = ½xTQx + cTx − uTx + vT(Ax − b). Its gradient is zero when Qx + c − u + ATv = 0, that is, x = −Q−1w with w = c − u + ATv. Plugging in gives

g(u, v) = −½ wTQ−1w − bTv

CO4A 11-2 prints the zero-gradient condition as Qx − (c − u + ATv) = 0. That is a sign slip, but its final g is right. When Q ⪰ 0 is singular, g = −½ wTQ+w − bTv if w lies in the range of Q, and −∞ otherwise. Here Q+ is the pseudo-inverse. The formula (QTQ)−1QT that the page gives for Q+ does not exist for a singular Q. CO4A 11-2 Tibshirani 2016

7. Where duality goes next

Today's ideas carry much of the rest of the course. Three later days use them directly.

  • Day 10, KKT conditions. When the gap is zero, the best x* and the best prices u* are locked together by four conditions you can check. You have already met one. In the x2 example, u* = 2 is positive and the rule is tight at x* = 1. A rule with room to spare would get a price of zero.
  • Day 13, dual methods. Instead of solving the primal, climb the concave hill g. In our example the slope of g is g′(u) = 1 − u/2. That equals h(x̂) = 1 − x̂ at L's lowest point x̂ = u/2. So "raise the price while the rule is broken, lower it while there is room" walks uphill on g. That is dual ascent (dual ascent card), and ADMM grows from it (ADMM card).
  • Day 19, collision avoidance. A self-driving car must keep a safe distance from every obstacle. The distance between two convex shapes is itself a minimization, which is awkward to place inside a planner's constraints. OBCA writes that distance as a dual problem instead. By weak duality, any dual-feasible prices certify "the distance is at least this much". So the planner carries the prices as extra variables and asks the certified floor to exceed the safe distance. Strong duality means nothing is lost. See the OBCA paper.

Check yourself

Q1. For min x + 3y s.t. x + y ≥ 2, x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0, the referee puts weights (u1, u2, u3) = (1, 0, 2) on the three rules. What floor does that prove?

Adding 1·(x + y ≥ 2) + 0·(x ≥ 0) + 2·(y ≥ 0) gives x + 3y ≥ 2. The left side is the cost, so the floor is 2u1 = 2. Only the first rule has a nonzero right side, so the weights on x ≥ 0 and y ≥ 0 add nothing to the floor. That is why 6 and 4 are wrong.

Q2. For min x2 s.t. x ≥ 1, what is the dual function value g(1)?

g(u) = u − u2/4, so g(1) = 1 − 0.25 = 0.75. The number 0.5 is where L(x, 1) has its lowest point (x = 0.5), not the floor itself. The value 1 is p*, which the floor reaches only at u = 2.

Q3. Weak duality, d* ≤ p*, holds…

The one-line proof, g(u, v) ≤ L(x*, u, v) ≤ f(x*), uses only that x* is feasible and u ≥ 0. Convexity and Slater's condition are what you need for strong duality (d* = p*), not for weak duality.

Q4. The quartic problem min x4 − 50x2 + 100x s.t. x ≥ −4.5 is nonconvex. Its dual problem, maximize g(u) s.t. u ≥ 0, is…

For each fixed x, L(x, u) is a straight line in u, and g is their lower envelope. So g is concave for any problem, and maximizing it over u ≥ 0 is a convex problem. The two lowest points at u = 100 only mean that g has a kink there.

Q5. For min x2 s.t. x ≥ 1, the point x = 1.2 and the price u = 1.5 give f = 1.44 and g = 0.9375, a gap of 0.5025. What does that tell you?

Because g ≤ p* ≤ f(x), the gap is an upper bound on how far x is from the best, not the exact distance. Here the true distance is 1.44 − 1 = 0.44. Only a gap of zero would prove that x and u are both optimal.

Q6. Which fact proves strong duality for min x2 s.t. x ≥ 1?

That is Slater's condition: a convex problem with a strictly feasible point. Concavity of g proves nothing about the gap, because g is concave for every problem. The quartic also has a concave g, and its gap is 22.56.

Recap: things to remember

  1. A dual variable is a price on a rule. Prices turn rules into floors, through weighted sums in an LP or the Lagrangian L = f + Σuihi + Σvjℓj in general. Inequality prices must be ≥ 0; equality prices may have any sign.
  2. The dual function g(u, v) = min over x of L is a floor under p* for every u ≥ 0. It is always concave, so the dual problem is always convex.
  3. Weak duality, d* ≤ p*, holds for every problem. Strong duality, d* = p*, holds for convex problems with a strictly feasible point (Slater) and for every feasible LP.
  4. A feasible x and dual-feasible (u, v) bound the error: f(x) − p* ≤ f(x) − g(u, v). A zero gap certifies that both are optimal.
  5. Numbers to keep: min x2 s.t. x ≥ 1 has g(u) = u − u2/4, u* = 2 and p* = d* = 1. The quartic has p* = −1052.44 and d* = −1075, a gap of 22.56.

Week 2 · Day 10

KKT conditions

After today you can write down and check the four KKT conditions, use them to solve problems by hand (equality-constrained QP, water-filling, SVM), and use conjugate functions and dual norms to write duals quickly.

About 60 min · Needs Day 9 · CO4A chapters 12 and 13

Today's big idea

At the best point of a constrained problem, the forces balance. The objective pulls downhill, each constraint you touch pushes back with a force λ ≥ 0, and constraints you don't touch push with zero force. Writing that balance down gives four checks, the KKT conditions. For a convex problem, passing all four proves you have the optimum.

1. Four checks at the bottom of the bowl

Picture a marble in a round bowl, with a straight fence across part of it. If the lowest point of the bowl is on the allowed side, the marble rolls there and the fence does nothing. If the lowest point is behind the fence, the marble ends up pressed against it. It stays put because the fence pushes back exactly as hard as the slope pulls.

Three facts hide in that picture. A fence can push but never pull. A fence the marble is not touching pushes with zero force. And at rest, the pull and all the pushes add up to zero. Add "the marble is on the allowed side", and you have the whole of today's lesson.

Now with numbers. Minimize f(x) = (x1 − 2)2 + (x2 − 1)2, a round bowl with its lowest point at (2, 1). Add one fence: x1 + x2 ≤ 2. The bowl's bottom breaks this rule, since 2 + 1 = 3, so the answer must lie on the fence line x1 + x2 = 2. The figure shows three versions of the problem.

Now the general version. A constrained problem asks to minimize f(x) subject to hi(x) ≤ 0 for i = 1, …, m and lj(x) = 0 for j = 1, …, r. As on Day 9, each inequality gets a multiplier and each equality gets a multiplier. Day 9 called them ui and vj, like CO4A's chapter 11 and the CMU slides. From today we switch to the more common names λi and νj. The Lagrangian is

L(x, λ, ν) = f(x) + Σ λihi(x) + Σ νjlj(x)

Think of λi as the force of fence i. The gradient ∇hi(x) points straight out of the allowed region, at right angles to the fence. A constraint with hi(x) = 0 is an active constraint: the marble touches that fence.

The KKT conditions are four checks on a candidate (x, λ, ν). They are named after Karush, who wrote them in a 1939 master's thesis, and Kuhn and Tucker, who published them in 1951. CO4A 12

CheckFormulaPlain meaning
1. Stationarity∇f(x) + Σ λi∇hi(x) + Σ νj∇lj(x) = 0the pull and the pushes cancel
2. Primal feasibilityhi(x) ≤ 0 and lj(x) = 0the marble is on the allowed side
3. Dual feasibilityλi ≥ 0fences push, never pull
4. Complementary slacknessλi · hi(x) = 0 for every ian untouched fence pushes with zero force

Read stationarity as −∇f = Σ λi∇hi + Σ νj∇lj. The left side is the downhill direction. The right side mixes the outward normals of the walls you touch, with weights λi ≥ 0. So at the optimum, every downhill direction leads straight through a wall. If f or hi has kinks, use the subgradients of Day 7 in place of gradients. CO4A 12-01

Check the middle panel. Here h(x) = x1 + x2 − 2, so ∇h = (1, 1), and ∇f(x) = (2(x1 − 2), 2(x2 − 1)). Try x⋆ = (1.5, 0.5) with λ = 1. (The star ⋆ marks an optimum; the plain * is saved for section 7.)

  • Stationarity: ∇f(x⋆) + λ∇h = (−1, −1) + (1, 1) = (0, 0). ✓
  • Primal feasibility: 1.5 + 0.5 − 2 = 0 ≤ 0. ✓
  • Dual feasibility: λ = 1 ≥ 0. ✓
  • Complementary slackness: λ · h = 1 · 0 = 0. ✓

The cost is f(x⋆) = 0.5. Day 9's dual function here is g(λ) = λ − λ2/2, which peaks at λ = 1 with value 0.5: the duality gap is zero. In the corner panel, ∇f(1.8, 0.2) = (−0.4, −1.6), and the wall normals (1, 1) and (0, 1) cancel it with λ1 = 0.4 and λ2 = 1.2. Both walls are doing work.

To find λ by hand, guess which constraints are active, solve stationarity with those constraints as equalities, and check the signs. Here the guess "active" gives x1 = 2 − λ/2 and x2 = 1 − λ/2, and x1 + x2 = 2 forces λ = 1. Had λ come out negative, the guess would be wrong, and that fence should be released.

The multiplier is also a price. Move the fence out by a small amount ε, and the best cost drops by about λε: with x1 + x2 ≤ 2.01 the optimum falls from 0.5 to 0.49005. Boyd & Vandenberghe 2004 For a car planner that keeps a margin from the lane edge, λ is the cost saved per centimetre of extra room.

2. When the checks are enough, and when they are required

Two different questions. If a point passes all four checks, is it optimal? That asks whether KKT is sufficient. If a point is optimal, does it pass? That asks whether KKT is necessary.

Sufficient, for convex problems. Suppose f and every hi are convex and every lj is affine (flat, like a line or plane). Then any (x, λ, ν) that passes all four checks is optimal, with zero duality gap. The one-line reason: stationarity says x minimizes the convex function L(·, λ, ν), so g(λ, ν) = L(x, λ, ν). Slackness and feasibility make that equal to f(x). A feasible point whose cost equals a lower bound cannot be beaten. CO4A 12-01 Boyd & Vandenberghe 2004

Necessary, when strong duality holds. Strong duality means the primal and dual optimal values are equal. Then every optimal x⋆, paired with any dual optimal (λ⋆, ν⋆), passes the four checks. Day 9 gave an easy test for strong duality, Slater's condition: the problem is convex and some point is strictly feasible, with every hi(x) < 0. CO4A 12-01

Put together: for a convex problem that meets Slater's condition, "x is optimal" and "x passes KKT with some λ, ν" mean the same thing. So solving by hand means writing down the four checks and solving them.

ProblemKKT sufficient?KKT necessary?
Convex, Slater holdsyesyes
Convex, Slater failsyesnot guaranteed
Not convexno: a KKT point can be a saddle or a maximumonly under extra conditions (Day 16)

Solvers use the same checks, but a computer never hits zero exactly. So it measures how far each check is from holding. These are the KKT residuals, such as the size of the stationarity left side or the amount of constraint violation. For convex problems, small residuals mean "nearly optimal".

The duality gap f(x) − g(λ, ν) is a second certificate, since it is never smaller than the true error f(x) − f⋆. CO4A 13-01 In our example, the feasible guess x = (1, 1) has f = 1, and λ = 0.5 gives g = 0.375. The gap promises an error of at most 0.625; the true error is 0.5.

This is how a model predictive controller (MPC) decides that it is done. A car's MPC solves a fresh quadratic program many times a second (Day 17). The OSQP solver stops when its primal residual ‖Ax − z‖∞ and dual residual ‖Px + q + ATy‖∞ both drop below a tolerance: 10−3, absolute and relative, by default as of Oct 2026. OSQP docs OSQP settings Its iterates meet complementary slackness by construction, so these two residuals are the KKT checks still open. The OSQP paper and the ADMM card show how it gets there. Interior-point solvers (Day 12) instead aim at a relaxed KKT system with λihi(x) = −1/t and tighten it as t grows. Boyd & Vandenberghe 2004

Going deeper (optional): why every optimum passes KKT under strong duality

Let x⋆ be primal optimal and (λ⋆, ν⋆) dual optimal, with f(x⋆) = g(λ⋆, ν⋆). Then

f(x⋆) = g(λ⋆, ν⋆) = minx L(x, λ⋆, ν⋆)
≤ L(x⋆, λ⋆, ν⋆) ≤ f(x⋆)

The last step holds because λ⋆i ≥ 0, hi(x⋆) ≤ 0 and lj(x⋆) = 0. Both ends are equal, so both inequalities are equalities. The first one says x⋆ minimizes L(·, λ⋆, ν⋆), which is stationarity. The second says Σ λ⋆ihi(x⋆) = 0. Every term in that sum is ≤ 0, so every term is 0, which is complementary slackness. CO4A 12-01 CMU 10-725 2016

3. Only equality constraints: KKT is one linear system

Now replace the fences with rails: the point must stay on a line or a flat plane. With no inequalities, checks 3 and 4 have nothing to say. Two remain: the pull is balanced by the rails, and the point is on the rails. For a quadratic cost both are linear equations, so the whole problem is one linear solve.

The simplest picture: find the point on the line x1 + x2 = 1 closest to the origin. Your eye says (0.5, 0.5), where the line meets the direction from the origin at a right angle. KKT gets there mechanically.

The general problem is to minimize ½xTPx + qTx + r subject to Ax = b, with P ⪰ 0. Stationarity reads Px + q + ATν = 0 and feasibility reads Ax = b. Stacked, they form one square system: CO4A 12-02 Boyd & Vandenberghe 2004

P x + ATν = −q
A x = b

[ P AT ; A 0 ] [ x ; ν ] = [ −q ; b ]

Numbers: minimize ½(x12 + x22) subject to x1 + x2 = 1. Here P is the 2×2 identity, q = 0, A = [1 1] and b = 1. The three equations are x1 + ν = 0, x2 + ν = 0 and x1 + x2 = 1. So x⋆ = (0.5, 0.5) and ν⋆ = −0.5. The multiplier is negative, and that is fine. A rail can push either way, so only inequality multipliers carry a sign.

import numpy as np
P = np.eye(2); q = np.zeros(2)
A = np.array([[1.0, 1.0]]); b = np.array([1.0])
K = np.block([[P, A.T], [A, np.zeros((1, 1))]])   # the KKT matrix
sol = np.linalg.solve(K, np.concatenate([-q, b]))
x, nu = sol[:2], sol[2:]
print(x, nu)                                       # [0.5 0.5] [-0.5]

Two links forward. On Day 11, Newton's method for equality-constrained problems solves this same system at every step, with P = ∇2f(x) and q = ∇f(x). CO4A 12-02 And a linear MPC with a quadratic cost, whose only constraints are the vehicle's linear dynamics, is exactly this kind of problem. One linear solve gives the whole plan. Add a steering limit or a lane bound and you get inequalities, which is why the solvers on Day 17 have to iterate.

4. Water-filling: pour the power into the quiet channels

A radio has four channels, each with its own noise level αi, and a fixed power budget P to split across them. Quiet channels turn power into data well, but every channel has diminishing returns. How should you split it?

Draw each channel as a vessel whose floor sits at height αi. Pour the whole budget in as water and let it settle. The water finds one common level, so quiet channels (low floors) get deep water and noisy ones get little or none. The depth in vessel i is its power xi. KKT says this picture gives the exact optimum.

The problem is Boyd and Vandenberghe's Example 5.2: CO4A 12-03 Boyd & Vandenberghe 2004

min −Σ log(αi + xi)
s.t. x ≥ 0, x1 + … + xn = P

Give λi to the constraint −xi ≤ 0 and ν to the budget. The four checks become

−1/(αi + xi) − λi + ν = 0
λixi = 0, λi ≥ 0, xi ≥ 0, Σ xi = P

Split into two cases. If channel i gets power (xi > 0), slackness forces λi = 0, so αi + xi = 1/ν: its water reaches the level 1/ν. If it gets none (xi = 0), then λi = ν − 1/αi ≥ 0, which means αi ≥ 1/ν: its floor is above the level. One formula covers both cases:

xi = max{0, 1/ν − αi}

Only one number is still unknown, the water level 1/ν. The budget fixes it through Σ max{0, 1/ν − αi} = P. The left side rises steadily with the level, so exactly one level works. This is water-filling. CO4A 12-03

Numbers: α = (0.1, 0.4, 0.6, 1.2) and P = 1. Guess that three channels are wet and write L = 1/ν. Then (L − 0.1) + (L − 0.4) + (L − 0.6) = 1, so 3L = 2.1 and L = 0.7. The guess holds up: the third floor (0.6) is below 0.7 and the fourth (1.2) is above. So x = (0.6, 0.3, 0.1, 0) and ν = 1/0.7 ≈ 1.4286.

The dry channel's multiplier is λ4 = ν − 1/α4 = 1.4286 − 0.8333 ≈ 0.595. Read it as a price again. Force a small amount of power ε into channel 4, taking it from the wet channels, and Σ log(αi + xi) drops by about 0.595ε. At the optimum Σ log(αi + xi) = −0.888, against −1.272 for an equal split of 0.25 each.

Try it: drag the budget and watch the channels switch on one by one. Then drag the level by hand. The formula keeps stationarity, dual feasibility and slackness at zero for any level, so only the budget residual moves. "Match budget" snaps it back.

Notice that at budget 1 the level is 0.700 (ν = 1.4286), the powers are 0.600, 0.300, 0.100 and 0, and the dry channel 4 has λ4 = 0.595. All four KKT residuals read 0.0000. The channels switch on at budgets 0, 0.30, 0.70 and 2.50, as the level reaches each floor.

Explain it to a 10-year-old

Think of a fish tank whose floor has four steps of different heights. You pour in one jug of water. The water's surface is flat, so the low steps end up under deep water and the high steps under shallow water. A step that sticks out above the surface stays dry. That is the best way to split radio power between quiet and noisy channels: deep water means lots of power.

5. SVM: the points that hold the line

A support vector machine separates two classes of points with the widest possible street. Only the points on the edge of the street, or inside it, matter. Delete a point that sits comfortably on its own side, and the street does not move. Complementary slackness is the reason.

The soft-margin SVM picks a direction β, an offset β0, and a slack ξi for each point, which measures how far point i intrudes into the street: CO4A 12-04

min ½‖β‖22 + C Σ ξi
s.t. yi(xiTβ + β0) ≥ 1 − ξi, ξi ≥ 0

Here xi is a data point, yi = ±1 is its class, and C > 0 is the cost of an intrusion. Give the multiplier wi to the margin constraint and vi to ξi ≥ 0. Stationarity gives

β = Σ wiyixi, Σ wiyi = 0, wi = C − vi

Since vi ≥ 0, every wi lies between 0 and C. Complementary slackness, wi(1 − ξi − yi(xiTβ + β0)) = 0 and viξi = 0, then sorts the points into three groups:

  • Clear of the street (margin yi(xiTβ + β0) > 1): the constraint is slack, so wi = 0, and the point drops out of β.
  • On the edge (ξi = 0 and margin exactly 1): wi can be anywhere from 0 to C.
  • Inside the street or on the wrong side (ξi > 0): then vi = 0, so wi = C.

The points with wi > 0 are the support points, also called support vectors. They alone build β.

Numbers, in one dimension with C = 1: x = −1 (class −1), and x = 1 and x = 3 (class +1). The solution is β = 1 and β0 = 0, with no intrusions, and w = (0.5, 0.5, 0). Check stationarity: β = 0.5·(−1)·(−1) + 0.5·1·1 + 0·1·3 = 1, and Σ wiyi = −0.5 + 0.5 + 0 = 0. The point at 3 has margin 3 > 1, so slackness forces its w to 0. The primal cost ½β2 = 0.5 equals the dual value, so the gap is zero.

6. Budget or price: constrained and penalty forms

You can keep a model simple with a budget ("total size at most t") or with a price ("pay λ per unit of size"). A traveller told "spend at most $200" and one fined for every dollar spent can make the same choices, if the fine is set right. KKT says which price matches which budget.

(C) min f(x) s.t. h(x) ≤ t
(L) min f(x) + λ h(x)

The second line is the Lagrange form, also called the penalized form. Going from (C) to (L): if (C) has a strictly feasible point, its KKT multiplier λ⋆ makes x⋆ a solution of (L). The reason is that the stationarity check of (C) is, word for word, the optimality condition of (L). Going back: a solution x⋆ of (L) solves (C) with t = h(x⋆). So as t and λ sweep their ranges, both forms trace out much the same family of solutions. CO4A 12-05 CMU 10-725 2016

Numbers, with a one-dimensional lasso and data y = 3. The penalty form min ½(3 − β)2 + 1·|β| gives β = 2: shrink 3 toward zero by λ = 1, the soft-thresholding of Day 8. The budget form min ½(3 − β)2 s.t. |β| ≤ 2 also gives β = 2. Its stationarity check at β = 2 reads −(3 − 2) + λ·1 = 0, so its multiplier is λ = 1, the same price.

One more KKT fact, about the lasso min ½‖y − Xβ‖22 + λ‖β‖1 with n data points and p features. When p > n it could in principle have many solutions, but KKT shows that they all share the fitted values Xβ̂ and, for λ > 0, the value ‖β̂‖1. If the entries of X come from a continuous distribution, the solution is unique with probability 1. It also has at most min{n, p} nonzeros, even when p is far larger than n. CO4A 12-06 So a lasso fit on 50 samples of continuous data picks one answer that uses at most 50 features.

Going deeper (optional): why the lasso answer is unique

The lasso's KKT condition is XT(y − Xβ̂) = λs, where si = sign(β̂i) if β̂i ≠ 0 and si ∈ [−1, 1] otherwise. So every feature's correlation with the residual is at most λ in size, and the features in use sit exactly at ±λ. The equicorrelation set E = {i : |XiT(y − Xβ̂)| = λ} is the same for every solution, because the fit is. If the columns of XE are linearly independent, the KKT equations on E have one answer:

β̂E = (XETXE)−1(XETy − λsE)

with β̂ = 0 off E. Continuous data puts the columns in "general position", which makes them independent with probability 1. CO4A 12-06 prints (XETXET)−1 here; the second transpose is a typo. CO4A 12-06 CMU 10-725 2016

7. Writing duals fast: dual norms and conjugates

CO4A chapter 13 collects tools that turn "derive the dual" from a page of algebra into a lookup. Two ideas do most of the work. CO4A 13

Dual norms. How big can zTx get if x must stay inside the unit ball of some norm? Picture a line at right angles to z, sliding outward until it last touches the ball. The point it last touches is the best x.

That largest value is the dual norm of z:

‖z‖* = max { zTx : ‖x‖ ≤ 1 }

So |zTx| ≤ ‖x‖ · ‖z‖* for every x and z, a general form of the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality. The pairs to know are ℓ1 ↔ ℓ∞, ℓ2 ↔ ℓ2, and ℓp ↔ ℓq with 1/p + 1/q = 1. For matrices, the trace norm (sum of singular values) pairs with the operator norm (largest singular value). The dual of the dual is the original norm. CO4A 13-03 Boyd & Vandenberghe 2004

With z = (3, −4), the diamond's best corner (0, −1) gives 4 = ‖z‖∞. The square's best corner (1, −1) gives 3 + 4 = 7 = ‖z‖1. The circle's best point z/5 gives 5 = ‖z‖2.

A robotics use: suppose a car's position error w is only known to satisfy |wi| ≤ 0.2 m in each coordinate. Then w can add at most 0.2‖c‖1 to cT(x + w), since ℓ1 is the dual of the box's ℓ∞. So a robust planner enforces cTx ≤ d − 0.2‖c‖1 in place of cTx ≤ d.

Conjugate functions. Picture selling x units at price y each, when making them costs f(x). Your best profit at price y is the conjugate of f. On a graph, yx is a line through the origin with slope y. The best profit is the biggest vertical gap between that line and the curve, and it sits where the curve's slope equals y.

In symbols, the conjugate of f is

f*(y) = maxx [ yTx − f(x) ]

f* is always convex, even when f is not, because it is a maximum of functions that are linear in y. Fenchel's inequality, f(x) + f*(y) ≥ xTy, holds for every x and y, with equality when y is a slope (subgradient) of f at x. If f is closed and convex, then f** = f. CO4A 13-04 Boyd & Vandenberghe 2004

Numbers with f(x) = x²: the gap yx − x² peaks at x = y/2, so f*(y) = y²/4. Fenchel at x = 1 and y = 2 gives 1 + 1 = 2 = xy, an equality because 2 is the slope of x² at 1. At y = 3 it gives 1 + 2.25 = 3.25 ≥ 3.

The indicator function IC is 0 on a set C and +∞ off it, which turns a constraint into a function. Its conjugate is the support function of C, max over x ∈ C of yTx. Four conjugates cover most needs:

f(x)f*(y)Why
x2y2/4best x = y/2
½xTQx, Q ≻ 0½yTQ−1ybest x = Q−1y
‖x‖ (any norm)0 if ‖y‖* ≤ 1, else +∞the indicator of the dual-norm ball
IC(x)maxx∈C yTxthe support function of C

For the quadratic, yTx − ½xTQx is strictly concave in x, and its maximizer is x = Q−1y. CO4A 13-04 copies a slip from the CMU slide and says "concave in y". CO4A 13-04 CMU 10-725 2016

The shifting trick. For min f(x) + g(Ax), name z = Ax and give that constraint a multiplier u. Minimizing the Lagrangian over x and over z separately produces two conjugates: CO4A 13-04-03

dual: maxu −f*(ATu) − g*(−u)

With A = I, this splits min f(x) + g(x). When g is a norm, the table turns g*(−u) into the constraint ‖u‖* ≤ 1. CO4A 13-04-02 After solving the dual, you can read off x⋆ as the minimizer of L(x, u⋆), when that minimizer is unique. CO4A 13-02

The lasso shows the trick at work. Write z = Xβ in min ½‖y − z‖22 + λ‖β‖1. Minimizing over z gives z − y + u = 0, so z = y − u. (CO4A 13-04-01 and the CMU slide print "z − y + β = 0"; it should be u.) Minimizing over β leaves the constraint ‖XTu‖∞ ≤ λ, because ℓ∞ is the dual of ℓ1. The dual is CO4A 13-04-01

max ½(‖y‖22 − ‖y − u‖22)
s.t. ‖XTu‖∞ ≤ λ

It finds the point of the region {u : ‖XTu‖∞ ≤ λ} closest to y, and that point is the lasso's residual: Xβ⋆ = y − u⋆. With X = 1, y = 3 and λ = 1, the region is |u| ≤ 1, so u⋆ = 1, which is indeed 3 − 2. The dual value ½(9 − 4) = 2.5 matches the primal ½·12 + 1·2 = 2.5.

One subtlety: rewriting that dual as min ‖y − u‖22 keeps the solution u⋆ = 1 but changes the optimal value to 4. A rewritten dual keeps its solution, not necessarily its value. CO4A 13-06

Analogy

A Lagrange multiplier is a price tag on a rule. Complementary slackness says a rule you are not even close to breaking costs nothing. A conjugate f*(y) is a price list: for each price y, the best profit a seller with cost curve f can make. Duality swaps "what should I do?" for "what is each rule worth?", and for convex problems that meet Slater's condition the two answers agree.

Going deeper (optional): dual cones and the double dual

The dual cone of a cone K is K* = {y : yTx ≥ 0 for all x ∈ K}: every vector that makes a non-obtuse angle with all of K. The nonnegative orthant ℝn+ and the cone of PSD matrices are their own dual cones. For min f(x) s.t. Ax ∈ K, the dual is max −f*(ATu) s.t. u ∈ K*. CO4A 13-05 If f and the hi are closed and convex and the lj are affine, the dual of the dual is the primal again. CO4A 13-06

Common misunderstandings

  • "KKT holds, so I have the minimum, whatever the problem." Only for convex problems. Minimize −x2 on −1 ≤ x ≤ 1: the point x = 0 passes all four checks with λ = 0, yet it is the worst point. The minima are at ±1.
  • "Every minimum satisfies KKT." Only when strong duality holds. Minimize x subject to x2 ≤ 0. The only feasible point, x = 0, is optimal, but stationarity needs 1 + 2λ·0 = 0, which no λ satisfies. Slater fails, since no x has x2 < 0.
  • "Equality multipliers must be ≥ 0." Only inequality multipliers carry a sign. In section 3, ν⋆ = −0.5.
  • "Complementary slackness means exactly one of λi and hi(x) is zero." Both can be zero. Put the fence at x1 + x2 ≤ 3: the bowl's bottom (2, 1) just touches it, so h = 0, and λ = 0 because ∇f = 0 there.
  • "The conjugate is a kind of inverse function, and needs f convex." It is a maximum over lines. It is defined for any f and is always convex.

Check yourself

Q1. At a KKT point, constraint i has hi(x) = −0.3. What must λi be?

Answer 3. Complementary slackness needs λi · (−0.3) = 0, so λi = 0: an untouched fence pushes with zero force. "Any value ≥ 0" is dual feasibility alone and forgets slackness.

Q2. Water-filling with noise α = (0.1, 0.4, 0.6, 1.2) and budget P = 1. What is the water level 1/ν?

Answer 1. Three channels are wet: 3L − 1.1 = 1 gives L = 0.7, and 0.6 < 0.7 < 1.2 confirms the guess. 0.825 assumes all four are wet, but then channel 4 would get 0.825 − 1.2 < 0. A level of 0.6 uses only 0.7 of the budget.

Q3. For a convex problem that satisfies Slater's condition, the KKT conditions are…

Answer 4. Convexity makes KKT sufficient. Slater gives strong duality, which makes KKT necessary. Without Slater you keep sufficiency but can lose necessity.

Q4. In a soft-margin SVM, a training point lies strictly outside the street: yi(xiTβ + β0) > 1. What is its multiplier wi?

Answer 2. Its margin constraint is slack, so complementary slackness forces wi = 0, and the point is not a support point. wi = C belongs to points inside the street or on the wrong side, and a multiplier can never be negative.

Q5. What is the dual norm of the ℓ1 norm?

Answer 4. Over the ℓ1 diamond, zTx is largest at a corner on an axis, which picks out the largest |zi|: that is ‖z‖∞. ℓ2 is its own dual; the trace norm pairs with the operator norm.

Q6. What is the conjugate f*(y) of f(x) = x2?

Answer 2. yx − x2 peaks at x = y/2 with value y2/2 − y2/4 = y2/4. y2/2 is the conjugate of ½x2, and 2y is the derivative of x2, not its conjugate.

Recap: things to remember

  1. KKT is four checks: stationarity (the pull is balanced by the normals of the walls you touch), primal feasibility, dual feasibility (λ ≥ 0), and complementary slackness (λihi(x) = 0).
  2. For convex problems KKT is sufficient. With Slater's condition it is also necessary. Without convexity a KKT point is only a candidate.
  3. To solve by hand, guess the active constraints, solve, and check the signs. An equality-constrained QP is one linear system. Water-filling gives xi = max(0, 1/ν − αi). In an SVM, only the points with wi > 0 matter.
  4. Multipliers are prices: λ tells how much the optimum improves per unit of loosening. Solvers such as OSQP stop when the KKT residuals are small.
  5. The dual norm is ‖z‖* = max zTx over the unit ball (ℓ1 ↔ ℓ∞, ℓ2 ↔ ℓ2). The conjugate is f*(y) = max yTx − f(x). With them, min f(x) + g(Ax) has the dual max −f*(ATu) − g*(−u).
