Week 2 · Day 11

Newton & quasi-Newton

After today you can explain Newton's method as "minimise the local quadratic model", see why it converges quadratically near the optimum, and choose between gradient descent, Newton, BFGS and L-BFGS by iterations and cost per step.

About 60 min · Needs Day 6 · CO4A chapters 14, 18 and 19

Today's big idea

Newton's method fits a bowl to the function where you stand and jumps to the bowl's bottom. Near the answer the bowl fits so well that the correct digits double every step. The price is the bowl: an n × n matrix that costs O(n³) to solve with. Quasi-Newton methods learn the bowl from gradient changes instead, for O(n²) (BFGS) or O(mn) (L-BFGS) per step.

1. The Newton step: jump to the bottom of a fitted bowl

Gradient descent from Day 6 is like walking downhill in fog: you feel the slope under your feet and take a stride of a set length. Newton's method also feels how the slope is changing, the curvature. Slope plus curvature is enough to fit a bowl to the ground around you, and Newton jumps to the bowl's lowest point.

Start in one dimension. At the current point xk, measure the slope f′(xk) and the curvature f″(xk). The parabola with the same height, slope and curvature is the local quadratic model q(x):

q(x) = f(xk) + f′(xk)(x − xk) + ½f″(xk)(x − xk)2

The bottom of this bowl is where q′(x) = 0. Solving that one linear equation gives the 1-D Newton update:

xk+1 = xk − f′(xk) / f″(xk)

A worked example: f(x) = log(ex + e−x), whose minimum is at 0. At xk = 1 the slope is 0.76 and the curvature is 0.42, so the jump goes to 1 − 0.76/0.42 = −0.81. That overshoots 0 a little. Repeat the recipe and the points go 0.41, −0.047, 0.00007, closing in very fast. Boyd & Vandenberghe 2004

In n dimensions the slope becomes the gradient ∇f(x) and the curvature becomes the Hessian ∇2f(x), the n × n matrix of second derivatives. The quadratic model of f around x is

f(y) ≈ f(x) + ∇f(x)T(y − x) + ½(y − x)T∇2f(x)(y − x)

Setting the model's gradient to zero gives the Newton step v, the jump to the bottom of the bowl. CO4A 14-01

∇2f(x) v = −∇f(x), x+ = x + v

Written with an inverse, v = −(∇2f(x))−1∇f(x). In code you never form the inverse: you solve the linear system, usually by Cholesky factorisation.

Gradient descent is the same recipe with a lazier bowl: (1/t)I in place of ∇2f, a round bowl whose bottom is x − t∇f(x). Newton's bowl has the right shape, long where the valley is long and steep where it is steep. So gradient descent zig-zags across a narrow valley while Newton heads straight in. CO4A 14-01-01

The cleanest example is a quadratic, f = ½(10x12 + x22) from (1, 1). Its quadratic model is the function itself, so one Newton step lands exactly on (0, 0). Gradient descent needs 106 steps with t = 0.1 to bring f below 10−10, and 62 with the best fixed step, t = 2/11.

A second view: minimising f means solving ∇f(x) = 0, and Newton's method began as a root finder. To solve F(x) = 0, replace F by its tangent and solve that: x+ = x − F′(x)−1F(x). With F = ∇f, F′ is the Hessian, so this is the same step. CMU 10-725 2016 CO4A 14-02-01

2. Damped Newton: shorten the jump when the bowl is a poor guide

The bowl is fitted at one point. Near that point it matches f well; far away it can be a poor guide, and a full jump can land somewhere worse than where you started.

The function from section 1 shows this. Its full Newton step is x+ = x − ½sinh(2x). From x0 = 1.1 the points go −1.13, 1.23, −1.70, 5.71, −23,000, each jump overshooting more. Always taking the full step t = 1 is called pure Newton, and here it diverges from every |x0| > 1.0887. Boyd & Vandenberghe 2004

The fix keeps the direction and shortens the jump. Damped Newton picks the step length t by backtracking line search, as on Day 6: try t = 1, and while the drop in f is not "enough", shrink t.

t = 1; while f(x + tv) > f(x) + αt∇f(x)Tv: t = βt

Here α ∈ (0, ½] and β ∈ (0, 1). "Enough" means f falls by at least a fraction α of what the slope along v promises. CO4A 14-04 Boyd and Vandenberghe suggest a small α such as 0.01 and β around 0.5. Boyd & Vandenberghe 2004

Back to x0 = 1.1, now with α = 0.1 and β = 0.7. The first step is shortened once, to t = 0.7, and lands at −0.46. Then every full step passes the test: 0.068, −0.00021, 6·10−12. Four steps, only one damped.

That pattern is general. Near the optimum the full step t = 1 always passes the test (for α < ½), so damped Newton turns into pure Newton by itself and keeps the fast finish. CO4A 14-05

3. The Newton decrement: a built-in progress meter

Before Newton jumps, it already knows how deep its bowl is below the current point. That depth forecasts how much f will drop, and it is almost free once v is computed. The Newton decrement λ(x) measures it:

λ(x)2 = ∇f(x)T (∇2f(x))−1 ∇f(x) = −∇f(x)Tv

It has three readings. CO4A 14-03

  • f(x) minus the bottom of the bowl equals λ2/2. This is the predicted drop.
  • The slope of f along the Newton step is ∇f(x)Tv = −λ2. That is the term the backtracking test uses.
  • λ is the length of the step v measured with the Hessian as the ruler: λ2 = vT∇2f(x)v.

The first reading gives a stopping rule. You cannot compute f(x) − p⋆ during a run, because the optimal value p⋆ is unknown, but you can compute λ2/2. Stop when it falls below a tolerance ε. Put together, this is Boyd and Vandenberghe's Algorithm 9.5. Boyd & Vandenberghe 2004

given a start x, tolerance eps, alpha in (0, 0.5], beta in (0, 1)
repeat:
    g = grad f(x);  H = hess f(x)
    v = solve(H, -g)                  # Newton step (Cholesky)
    lam2 = -g @ v                     # Newton decrement squared
    if lam2 / 2 <= eps: stop          # stopping rule
    t = 1
    while f(x + t*v) > f(x) - alpha*t*lam2:
        t = beta * t                  # backtracking
    x = x + t*v

How good is the forecast? On the widget's function (section 5), λ2/2 goes 4.45, 0.86, 0.14, 4.7·10−3, 5.6·10−6, 7.9·10−12, against true errors f − p⋆ of 6.60, 1.17, 0.157, 4.8·10−3, 5.6·10−6, 7.9·10−12. Rough at the start, almost exact at the end, which is where a stopping rule needs it.

4. Why it finishes so fast: two phases

Near the answer, Newton's next error is roughly the square of its current error. Square 10−3 and you get 10−6. Square that and you get 10−12. The number of correct digits doubles every step. This is quadratic convergence.

Compare linear convergence, where the error shrinks by a fixed factor each step. Gradient descent on the widget's function shrinks it by about 0.42 per step, one digit every two or three steps. Boyd & Vandenberghe 2004

In symbols, near a minimiser x⋆ there is a constant K with

‖x+ − x⋆‖ ≤ K ‖x − x⋆‖2

The one-line reason: the bowl gets the height, slope and curvature right, so it misses only through the change in curvature, and that miss shrinks like the distance squared. CO4A 14-02-03

This fast finish is local. Far from x⋆, Newton is in the damped phase: backtracking shortens some steps, and the theory promises only a fixed drop γ in f per step. Once the gradient is small enough, it enters the quadratic phase, takes t = 1 every time and never leaves. Counting both phases bounds the total number of steps: CO4A 14-05

iterations ≤ (f(x0) − p⋆)/γ + log2 log2(ε0/ε)

The second term is tiny: six quadratic-phase steps shrink the error bound by 2−64 ≈ 5·10−20. In practice that means some damped steps, then five or six full steps to machine precision. Boyd & Vandenberghe 2004

On the widget's function every Newton step is a full step, and the log10 error goes 0.82, 0.07, −0.80, −2.32, −5.25, −11.10: the last three exponents roughly double. The widget's "log of that sum" option shows both phases, with three shortened steps (t = 0.058, 0.49, 0.49) before the full steps.

Going deeper (optional): the constants, and self-concordance

The classic proof assumes f is m-strongly convex, ∇f is L-Lipschitz and ∇2f is M-Lipschitz. With η = min{1, 3(1 − 2α)}m2/M, the damped phase lasts while ‖∇f(x)‖2 ≥ η and cuts f by at least γ = αβη2m/L2 per step. (CO4A 14-05 prints β2; its own proof gives β.) CO4A 14-05

Nobody knows m, L and M in practice. For a self-concordant function (|f‴| ≤ 2f″3/2 along every line) the bound becomes C(α, β)(f(x0) − p⋆) + log log(1/ε), with no problem constants. The log barrier is self-concordant, which Day 12 relies on. CO4A 14-06 CO4A 14-06-02

5. Units don't matter: affine invariance

Draw the same hillside on two maps, one in metres and one with the north–south axis in kilometres. Newton walks the same path on the ground, in the same number of steps, on both maps. Gradient descent does not: its bowl is round in the map's units, so stretching one axis changes its direction and its step count.

The reason in plain words: Newton's bowl is fitted to the function itself. Stretch the map and the bowl stretches with it, so its bottom stays at the same spot on the ground. This is affine invariance: an invertible linear change of coordinates leaves Newton's path unchanged.

In symbols, let x = Au with A invertible, and minimise g(u) = f(Au). The chain rule gives

∇g(u) = AT∇f(x), ∇2g(u) = AT∇2f(x) A

So Newton's step in the new units is Δu = −A−1(∇2f)−1∇f, and AΔu is exactly the old Newton step. The gradient step in the new units maps back to

AΔu = −t AAT∇f(x)

That is a different direction unless AAT is a multiple of I. (CO4A 14-02-02 writes the product as A∇f(x)AT, the wrong order.) The Newton decrement is unchanged too, so the stopping rule ignores units as well. CO4A 14-02-02 Boyd & Vandenberghe 2004

The numbers make the point. On Boyd and Vandenberghe's test function (their eq. 9.20, used in the widget below), start at (−1, 1) and measure y in new units, y = s·u. Newton needs 5 steps for every s. Gradient descent needs 29 at s = 1, 53 at s = 0.2, 150 at s = 0.1, 596 at s = 5 and 2,345 at s = 10.

A car's planner mixes metres, radians and metres per second. Gradient descent needs someone to pick good scalings; Newton-type methods are far less sensitive, one reason robotics solvers lean on them.

Try it: read the step counts. Pick "Log of that sum" to see Newton's damped first steps, set "Rescale y by s" to 10, or tap the plot to move the start. (BFGS, the third path, comes in section 7.)

Notice: from (−1, 1), gradient descent needs 29 steps to reach an error of 10−10, BFGS 7 and Newton 5. Newton's error falls 6.6, 1.2, 0.16, 4.8·10−3, 5.6·10−6, 7.9·10−12, all with full steps, while gradient descent zig-zags across the valley.

6. The price of a Newton step

Newton buys few iterations with expensive ones. Each step needs the Hessian (n2 entries) and a linear solve with it. A dense Cholesky solve costs about n3/3 multiply-adds, so a step is O(n3). Gradient descent needs O(n) per step beyond the gradient. CO4A 14-07

With 8-byte numbers, at n = 1,000 the Hessian takes 8 MB and a solve about 3.3·108 operations, a fraction of a second. At n = 106 it would take 8 TB. Measured in seconds, Newton's lead shrinks, and for huge n it vanishes. CMU 10-725 2016

Structure rescues Newton. If the Hessian is banded or sparse, a step can cost O(n). CO4A 14-08 Trajectory problems are the standard case: each time step couples only to its neighbours, so the Hessian is block-banded and the cost grows linearly with the horizon. That is how model predictive control (Day 17) and trajectory optimisation (Day 18) afford Newton-type steps.

Equality-constrained Newton, briefly: to minimise f(x) subject to Ax = b, minimise the bowl while staying on the plane Ax = b. The step v and a multiplier estimate w solve the KKT system from Day 10:

∇2f(x) v + ATw = −∇f(x)
A v = −(Ax − b)

Example: minimise ½(10x12 + x22) subject to x1 + x2 = 1 from (0.5, 0.5). The model is exact, so one step lands on the answer (1/11, 10/11) ≈ (0.091, 0.909), with w = −10/11, the optimal multiplier ν⋆. CO4A 14-08

Where Newton runs in practice: interior-point solvers (Day 12) take Newton steps on a smoothed KKT system. IPOPT, an open-source interior-point solver for nonlinear programs, uses exact second derivatives by default (as of Oct 2026) IPOPT docs and is a common back end for robot trajectory optimisation and nonlinear MPC (Day 16). SLAM and other least-squares problems use Newton's cousins Gauss–Newton and Levenberg–Marquardt (LM card). See also the Newton card.

7. Quasi-Newton: learn the curvature from the gradients

Quasi-Newton methods skip the Hessian and measure curvature from gradients they already have. After each step, compare the gradient before and after. The change per unit of step is a curvature reading, and it costs nothing extra.

Analogy

You can estimate a car's acceleration without an accelerometer. Read the speedometer twice, a second apart, and divide the change in speed by the time. Here the gradient plays the speedometer and the Hessian plays the acceleration.

In n dimensions, call the step s = x+ − x and the change in gradient y = ∇f(x+) − ∇f(x). The new curvature estimate B+ must explain the change you just saw. That requirement is the secant equation: CO4A 18-01

B+s = y, with sTy > 0

The second part is the curvature condition: along the step the slope went up, which a positive definite B+ needs. Strictly convex f gives it for free; otherwise the Wolfe conditions in the line search enforce it.

One vector equation cannot pin down a whole matrix, so each quasi-Newton method picks, in its own sense, the B+ closest to the old B. Three updates matter. CMU 10-725 2016

  • SR1 (symmetric rank one): B+ = B + uuT/(uTs) with u = y − Bs. Simplest, but it can lose positive definiteness, and the denominator can be near zero. CO4A 18-02
  • DFP (Davidon–Fletcher–Powell): a rank-2 update of the inverse estimate H = B−1 that stays positive definite when sTy > 0. CO4A 18-03
  • BFGS (Broyden–Fletcher–Goldfarb–Shanno): DFP with the roles of B and H swapped. It stays positive definite, recovers from bad early estimates better than DFP, and is the standard. CO4A 18-04

BFGS is usually written for the inverse estimate H, so the step is a matrix–vector product, −H∇f, with no linear solve. With ρ = 1/(yTs):

H+ = (I − ρsyT) H (I − ρysT) + ρssT

Both the update and the step cost O(n2), and the start can be H = I, so no Hessian is ever computed. The idea goes back to William Davidon, whose mid-1950s computer runs kept crashing before they finished, so he needed a method that converged faster. CO4A 18

A worked example: f = ½xTQx with Q = diag(10, 1), B = H = I and step s = (1, 1), so y = Qs = (10, 1) and sTy = 11 > 0. SR1 recovers the exact Hessian diag(10, 1) in one update. BFGS gives H+ ≈ [[0.107, −0.074], [−0.074, 1.744]]: it satisfies H+y = s, stays positive definite (eigenvalues 0.104 and 1.747), and its corner 0.107 is already near the true 0.1.

The payoff is superlinear convergence: the ratio between successive errors goes to zero, slower than quadratic but far faster than linear. In the widget, BFGS's first step is exactly gradient descent's, because it starts from H = I; after that it learns the curvature and finishes in 7 steps to Newton's 5. A rough rule of thumb from the slides: n quasi-Newton steps do the work of one Newton step. CO4A 14-09 CO4A 18-06

BFGS still stores an n × n matrix, 8 TB at n = 106. L-BFGS (limited-memory BFGS) keeps only the last m pairs (s, y), typically m = 3 to 20, and rebuilds H∇f from them with two loops of dot products, never forming a matrix. Memory is 2mn numbers (160 MB for m = 10, n = 106) and the work about 4mn multiplications per step. Chen 2025 (UW CS726) CO4A 18-07

# L-BFGS direction p = -H g from the last m pairs (s[i], y[i])
q = -g
for i in newest ... oldest:          # i = k-1 down to max(k-m, 0)
    a[i] = (s[i] @ q) / (y[i] @ s[i])
    q = q - a[i] * y[i]
p = gamma * q                        # gamma = s@y / y@y of the newest pair
for i in oldest ... newest:          # i = max(k-m, 0) up to k-1
    b = (y[i] @ p) / (y[i] @ s[i])
    p = p + (a[i] - b) * s[i]
return p                             # about 4mn multiplications

CO4A's figure of this recursion, copied from the slides, prints min(k − m, 0) where max(k − m, 0) is meant. The price of the diet is a weaker guarantee, only linear convergence in general, yet L-BFGS is the default for large smooth problems. As of Oct 2026, SciPy's minimize uses BFGS when unconstrained and L-BFGS-B with bounds, SciPy 1.18 docs scikit-learn's logistic regression defaults to lbfgs, scikit-learn 1.9 docs and IPOPT's limited-memory option keeps 6 pairs. IPOPT docs See the BFGS card.

MethodNeedsMemoryWork per step (dense)Near the answerPick it when
Gradient descentgradientO(n)O(n)linearn is huge and modest accuracy is enough
Newtongradient and HessianO(n2)O(n3), or O(n) if bandedquadraticn is up to a few thousand, or the Hessian is sparse, and you want high accuracy
BFGSgradientO(n2)O(n2)superlinearn is moderate and the Hessian is unavailable or too costly
L-BFGS (m pairs)gradientO(mn)O(mn), about 4mnlinear guaranteed, often fastn is large (millions) and f is smooth

Sources: CO4A 14-07, the CMU slides and Chen's UW notes. BFGS's O(n2) is standard arithmetic, not stated in those sources.

Going deeper (optional): proximal Newton

For f = g + h with g smooth and h nonsmooth (say λ‖x‖1), proximal gradient (Day 8) fits the round bowl (1/t)I to g. Proximal Newton fits H = ∇2g instead: v = argmin ∇gTv + ½vTHv + h(x + v), then x+ = x + tv. This is a scaled proximal map, a prox in the H-norm; h = 0 gives Newton and H = I/t gives proximal gradient. CO4A 19-01-02

It is quadratic near the answer, but each step is a lasso-like subproblem, so it pays off only with a fast inner solver such as coordinate descent (Day 14), as in glmnet and QUIC. CO4A 19-03 CO4A 19-05 CMU 10-725 2016

Explain it to a 10-year-old

You are blindfolded on a skateboard in a bowl-shaped park and want to stop at the bottom. One friend only says which way is downhill, so you roll a bit and ask again. A second friend also says how the ground curves, so you roll straight to the bottom: that is Newton. A third friend remembers how the slope changed after each roll and learns the shape as you go: that is BFGS.

Common misunderstandings

  • "Newton always converges because it uses more information." Pure Newton on log(ex + e−x) diverges from x0 = 1.1. You need the line search (damped Newton).
  • "Quadratic convergence happens from the start." It is local. Far from the answer you are in the damped phase, where the guarantee is only a fixed drop per step.
  • "Fewer iterations means faster." A dense Newton step costs O(n3), a gradient step O(n). In seconds Newton's lead shrinks, and at n = 106 a dense step is impossible.
  • "BFGS needs the Hessian to start." H = I is a fine start. The curvature is learned from gradient changes.
  • "L-BFGS is just as good as BFGS." It trades BFGS's superlinear guarantee for O(mn) memory: usually a good trade for large n, but a trade.

Check yourself

Q1. You run pure Newton on a strictly convex quadratic f(x) = ½xTQx + cTx in ℝn. How many steps does it need to reach the exact minimum?

One step. The quadratic model of a quadratic is the function itself, so the bowl's bottom is the true minimum. "n steps" is the answer for conjugate gradients in exact arithmetic, and the condition number matters for gradient descent, not for Newton.

Q2. What does one Newton step cost with a dense n × n Hessian?

O(n3), for the Cholesky solve (about n3/3 operations). O(n2) is a dense BFGS step, which needs only a matrix–vector product, and O(mn) is L-BFGS. A banded Hessian can bring Newton down to O(n).

Q3. B+ is the new estimate of the Hessian, s = x+ − x and y = ∇f(x+) − ∇f(x). Which equation must B+ satisfy?

The secant equation B+s = y: curvature times step must equal the change in gradient. The tempting B+y = s is the version for the inverse estimate H = B−1, not for B. And sTy must be positive, not zero, to keep B+ positive definite.

Q4. You run pure Newton (always t = 1) on f(x) = log(ex + e−x) from x0 = 1.1. What happens?

It diverges: −1.13, 1.23, −1.70, 5.71, −23,000. Each full jump overshoots the minimum at 0 by more than the last. Damped Newton with backtracking fixes it, converging in four steps.

Q5. In the widget, Newton needs 5 steps. You rescale y by s = 10. How many steps does Newton need now?

Still 5, along the same path. Newton's method is affine invariant: its bowl stretches with the coordinates. 2,345 is gradient descent's count at s = 10.

Q6. You must minimise a smooth function of n = 106 variables. Gradients are cheap and no Hessian is available. Which method fits best?

L-BFGS: it needs only gradients and stores 2mn numbers, about 160 MB. BFGS also needs only gradients, but its n × n matrix would take 8 TB, and so would a dense Hessian for Newton.

Recap: things to remember

  1. Newton fits a quadratic bowl at x and jumps to its bottom: solve ∇2f(x)v = −∇f(x). Gradient descent is the same idea with a round bowl (1/t)I.
  2. Use damped Newton: backtracking from t = 1. Stop when the Newton decrement's forecast λ2/2 falls below ε.
  3. Convergence has two phases, damped and then quadratic. In the quadratic phase the correct digits double each step, so a few full steps reach machine precision.
  4. Newton is affine invariant (units don't matter); gradient descent is not. In the widget a y-rescale moves gradient descent from 29 to 2,345 steps and leaves Newton at 5.
  5. Cost per step: Newton O(n3), BFGS O(n2), L-BFGS O(mn) with m = 3–20. Quasi-Newton methods learn curvature from the secant equation B+s = y.

Week 2 · Day 12

Interior-point methods

After today you can explain how a log barrier turns inequality constraints into a smooth penalty, follow the central path to the optimum, and see why interior-point solvers finish in a few tens of Newton steps almost regardless of problem size.

About 60 min · Needs Days 10 and 11 · CO4A chapters 15, 16 and 17

Today's big idea

Replace every hard wall by a smooth penalty that rises to infinity as you approach it, then minimize cost plus penalty with Newton's method. Weaken the penalty step by step, and the minimizers slide along a smooth curve, the central path, to the true optimum. Every point on that curve comes with a certificate: its cost is at most m/t above the best possible.

1. Inequalities are walls: soften them with a log barrier

Picture a robot vacuum heading for the dirtiest spot in a room. If the spot is in the middle, the walls do not matter. If it is in a corner, two walls decide the answer. You do not know in advance which walls you will end up touching.

That is the hard part of every problem with "≤" rules hi(x) ≤ 0. A rule that holds with equality at the answer is active, and the set of active rules is the active set. With m rules there are many possible active sets, and trying them one by one gets slow. CO4A 15-1-1

One exact trick moves the rules into the cost. The indicator function IC(x) is 0 when x is in the feasible set C and +∞ outside it. Minimizing f(x) + IC(x) is the same problem as before. But IC is a cliff: flat, then infinitely high. Newton's method (Day 11) learns from slope and curvature, and a cliff has neither.

The fix is a smooth wall that starts rising before you reach it. For one rule x ≤ b, use the penalty −log(b − x). The gap b − x is the slack, the room you have left. The penalty is 0 at slack 1. It is 2.30 at slack 0.1, 4.61 at slack 0.01 and 6.91 at slack 0.001. Every 10× step closer adds 2.30, and at slack 0 the penalty is infinite.

For general rules hi(x) ≤ 0, the slack is −hi(x), and the log barrier puts one such wall on every rule: CO4A 15-1-2

φ(x) = −Σi log(−hi(x))

φ is defined only where every hi(x) < 0. Such points are strictly feasible: they keep some room from every wall. If every hi is convex, so is φ, and it is smooth there.

To imitate the cliff, scale the wall by 1/t. The barrier parameter t > 0 sets how sharp the wall is. With t = 2, the penalty at slack 0.01 drops from 4.61 to 2.30, yet the wall itself stays infinite. So a larger t hugs the indicator more closely.

Newton also needs the slope. For a linear rule aiTx ≤ bi, write the slack as si = bi − aiTx. The chain rule gives: CO4A 15-1-3

∇φ(x) = Σi ai / si
∇2φ(x) = Σi aiaiT / si2

Read each term −ai/si as a push away from wall i with strength 1/slack. At slack 1 the push is 1, and at slack 0.01 it is 100. Boyd and Vandenberghe call this a force field. Boyd & Vandenberghe 2004, §11.2

The point where all the pushes cancel minimizes φ by itself. It is the analytic center, the point that is farthest from all the walls in this log sense. Worked example: the pentagon x1 ≥ 0, x2 ≥ 0, x1 ≤ 3, x2 ≤ 3, x1 + x2 ≤ 4. At (1, 1) the five slacks are 1, 1, 2, 2 and 2, and the pushes add up to zero. So (1, 1) is the analytic center. This pentagon is today's running example.

Analogy: an electric fence

The indicator is an invisible fence that you only notice when you hit it. The log barrier is a fence that buzzes from a few steps away, louder the closer you get. You stay inside without ever touching it. Raising t shrinks the buzz zone, so you can walk closer to the fence before it bothers you.

2. The barrier problem and the central path

Put a ball on a table with springy walls, and tilt the table toward one corner. A gentle tilt leaves the ball near the middle. A steep tilt rolls it close to the low corner, but the springs keep it off the walls. The tilt is t, and the ball's resting place is x*(t).

In symbols, multiply the cost by t and add the barrier. The barrier problem is: CO4A 15-1-2

minimize t·f(x) + φ(x)
subject to Ax = b

It has the same minimizer as f + (1/t)·φ, and no inequality rules are left, so Newton's method (Day 11) can solve it. Call its minimizer x*(t).

As t grows from 0 to ∞, x*(t) traces a smooth curve called the central path. Small t means "mostly stay away from the walls", so the path starts near the analytic center. Large t means "mostly care about cost", so the path ends at the optimum x*. CO4A 15-2

The smallest example: minimize x subject to x ≥ 0. The barrier problem is minimize t·x − log x. Setting the slope t − 1/x to zero gives x*(t) = 1/t. So t = 1 gives 1, t = 10 gives 0.1, and t = 100 gives 0.01. The true answer is 0, and the error is exactly 1/t.

Now the pentagon. Minimize cTx with c = (−1, −2), that is, push up and to the right, with x2 counting twice. The optimum is the corner (1, 3), with cost p* = −7. Setting the gradient of t·cTx + φ(x) to zero gives the centering condition:

t·c + Σi ai / si = 0

In words: at x*(t), the pull of the cost, −t·c, balances the total push of the walls. Newton's method gives these points (m = 5 rules; section 3 explains the last column):

tx*(t)cost cTx*(t)true error cTx*(t) − p*bound m/t
0.1(1.0429, 1.1321)−3.30713.69350
1(1.1384, 2.1161)−5.37051.6295
10(1.0062, 2.8985)−6.80320.1970.5
100(1.0001, 2.9900)−6.98000.0200.05

The path bends. x1 first rises to about 1.14, then returns to 1 as the top wall and the diagonal wall close in. In the widget below, the cost line through x*(t) just touches the barrier level curve there, because the two gradients balance. CO4A 15-2

Try it: drag the slider from t = 0.01 to t = 1000, or press the t buttons. The orange dots are the Newton iterates of the last move. A warm start from the previous t usually needs only a few steps.

Notice: at the default t = 1, x*(t) = (1.1384, 2.1161), reached in 6 Newton steps from the analytic center (1, 1). The primal cost −5.3705 minus the dual value −10.3705 is exactly 5 = m/t. Press t = 10 and t = 100: the point moves to (1.0062, 2.8985) and (1.0001, 2.9900), and the guaranteed gap falls to 0.5 and 0.05. The dot never touches a wall.

3. The duality gap m/t: a certificate for free

A delivery app says "at most 5 minutes away". You do not know the exact arrival time, but you have a guaranteed bound. Each central point gives the same kind of promise about cost: you are at most m/t above the best value, even though you do not know that value.

Where does it come from? Day 9 showed that any dual feasible point gives a lower bound on p*, and a central point hands you one. The barrier problem's optimality condition is t∇f(x) + ∇φ(x) + ATw = 0, where w is the multiplier of Ax = b. Set: CO4A 15-3-1

ui(t) = −1 / (t·hi(x*(t))), v(t) = w / t

Each ui is positive, because hi < 0. For an LP it is simply ui = 1/(t·si). Divide the centering condition by t, and it becomes ∇f + Σ ui∇hi + ATv = 0. That is the stationarity condition of Day 10, so x*(t) minimizes the Lagrangian at (u, v), and (u, v) is dual feasible.

Compare the whole list with the KKT conditions. Only one line really changes: complementary slackness becomes "uihi = −1/t" instead of "= 0". These are the perturbed KKT conditions. As t → ∞ they turn back into KKT.

ConditionKKT (Day 10)Central path at t
Stationarity∇f + Σ ui∇hi + ATv = 0the same
Primal feasibilityhi(x) ≤ 0, Ax = bhi(x) < 0, Ax = b
Dual feasibilityui ≥ 0ui > 0
Complementary slacknessuihi(x) = 0uihi(x) = −1/t

Now the gap. The dual function at (u, v) is the Lagrangian at x*(t). In it, each product uihi equals −1/t, and the term vT(Ax − b) is zero. Adding the m products gives: CO4A 15-3-2

f(x*(t)) − g(u, v) = m / t
so f(x*(t)) − p* ≤ m / t

The duality gap, primal value minus dual value, is exactly m/t, where m is the number of inequality rules. Weak duality says g(u, v) ≤ p*, which turns the gap into a bound on the true error.

Check it on the pentagon at t = 1. The slacks at x*(1) give u = (0.8784, 0.4726, 0.5372, 1.1313, 1.3413). This LP's dual value is −bTu = −10.3705, and the primal value is −5.3705. The gap is exactly 5.0000 = 5/1. The true error is only 1.63, so the bound is safe but not tight.

The multipliers also tell you which walls matter. As t → ∞, u approaches (0, 0, 0, 1, 1), the true KKT multipliers u*. They are nonzero only for x2 ≤ 3 and x1 + x2 ≤ 4, the two walls that meet at (1, 3). Check: ATu* + c = (1, 2) + (−1, −2) = 0. In the 1-D example, u(t) = 1/(t·x*(t)) = 1 for every t, which is already the true multiplier.

This also gives a stopping rule. To be within ε of optimal, stop once m/t ≤ ε, that is, once t ≥ m/ε. For the pentagon with ε = 10−6, you need t ≥ 5 × 106.

4. The barrier method: raise t, then re-center with Newton

If t ≥ m/ε is all we need, why not set t = 5 × 106 at once? CO4A calls this barrier method v.0, and it is a bad idea. With a huge t, the barrier problem is badly conditioned: its valley is a steep, narrow canyon pressed against the walls. Newton's method started far away needs many small damped steps to get in. CO4A 15-4

Climb stairs instead. Each riser multiplies t by a factor μ > 1, which divides the guaranteed gap by μ. Each tread is a short Newton run that starts from the previous center. That start is already close to the new center, so Newton is in its fast, quadratic zone (Day 11).

Each re-centering is a centering step. Raising t is an outer iteration, and each Newton step inside a centering is an inner iteration. The factor μ is the update factor. In pseudocode: CMU 10-725 2016

given strictly feasible x, t := t0 > 0, mu > 1, eps > 0
repeat
    # centering (inner loop): Newton's method on t*f + phi,
    # subject to Ax = b, started from the current x
    x := argmin  t*f(x) + phi(x)
    if m / t <= eps: stop          # certificate from section 3
    t := mu * t                    # outer iteration

The number of outer iterations is known in advance. After k raises the guaranteed gap is m/(μkt(0)), so you need this many raises, plus the first centering: CO4A 15-5

⌈ log(m / (t(0)ε)) / log μ ⌉

For the pentagon with t(0) = 1 and ε = 10−6, log(5 × 106) = 15.4. With μ = 2 that is ⌈22.2⌉ = 23 raises, so 24 centerings. With μ = 10 there are 8 centerings, and with μ = 50 or μ = 150 there are 5.

So how should you pick μ? A small μ gives many outer iterations, but each needs only 1–3 Newton steps, because the new center is close. A large μ gives few outer iterations, each needing more Newton steps. The totals hardly change. Boyd and Vandenberghe found the total nearly flat for μ from about 3 to 200, and suggest 10 ≤ μ ≤ 100. Boyd & Vandenberghe 2004, p. 573

On the pentagon (start (1, 1), t(0) = 1, ε = 10−6), μ = 2 takes 35 Newton steps in total, μ = 10 takes 39, μ = 50 takes 30 and μ = 150 takes 27. With μ = 2, the centerings take 5, 3, 2, 2, 2, 2, 2 steps and then 1 step each. Centering need not be exact either; practical codes stop each Newton run early (CO4A's barrier method v.2). CO4A 15-6

Try it: read each staircase as the gap m/t against total Newton steps. Then switch to a random LP with m = 100 rules: the problem is 20 times larger, but the totals grow far less.

Notice: on the default pentagon, μ = 2, 10, 50 and 150 need 35, 39, 30 and 27 Newton steps (24, 8, 5 and 5 centerings), and primal-dual reaches η ≤ 10−8 in 13 steps. With m = 100, the barrier totals are 73, 58, 45 and 41, and primal-dual needs 21.

5. Phase I: finding a point strictly inside

The barrier method must start strictly inside every wall, because φ is undefined anywhere else. Often you have no such point. A driving planner may start from a guess that cuts into an obstacle margin. Is there any trajectory that obeys every rule?

Ask a different question whose start is easy: how far must every rule be loosened before my guess obeys it? Add one extra variable s and solve the phase I problem: CO4A 15-7

minimize s over (x, s)
subject to hi(x) ≤ s, Ax = b

Any x with Ax = b, together with any s larger than maxi hi(x), is strictly feasible for this problem. So the barrier method can start on it right away.

Then read the sign of the optimal s*. If s* < 0, every rule holds with room to spare: a strictly feasible start. If s* > 0, no point obeys all the rules, so the problem is infeasible. In practice you stop phase I as soon as s drops below 0.

Pentagon example: start from the bad guess x = (5, 5). The rule values aiTx − bi are (−5, −5, 2, 2, 6), so s(0) = 7 is strictly feasible for phase I. The phase I optimum is s* = −4/3 at x = (4/3, 4/3). There the slacks of x1 ≥ 0, x2 ≥ 0 and x1 + x2 ≤ 4 all equal 4/3. Since s* < 0, a strictly feasible start exists.

A variant gives each rule its own slack: minimize 1Ts subject to hi(x) ≤ si, s ≥ 0 and Ax = b. When the problem is infeasible, the nonzero si point to the rules that cannot be met, for example a speed limit that clashes with an arrival deadline. That makes it a good debugging tool. CMU 10-725 2016

Modern solvers rarely run a separate phase I. Primal-dual methods (next section) can start from infeasible points. MOSEK's interior-point optimizer solves a homogeneous self-dual model, which returns either a solution or a certificate that none exists. Clarabel also uses a homogeneous embedding. MOSEK docs Clarabel docs

6. Duality revisited, and the primal-dual method

CO4A's chapter 16 looks at an LP from both sides at once. Take an LP in standard form and its dual: CO4A 16-1 CMU 10-725 2016

primal: minimize cTx
s.t. Ax = b, x ≥ 0
dual: maximize bTy
s.t. ATy + s = c, s ≥ 0

Here s is the dual slack. The KKT conditions are Ax = b, ATy + s = c, x ≥ 0, s ≥ 0 and xisi = 0 for every i. The central path relaxes only the last condition, to xisi = τ with τ = 1/t > 0. CO4A 16-2

This view separates two families of LP methods. The simplex method keeps the equations and xisi = 0 true at every step, and fights for x, s ≥ 0. It walks from corner to corner: on the pentagon, from (0, 0) to (0, 3) and then to (1, 3). Interior-point methods keep x, s > 0 true and drive xisi toward 0. They cut through the middle.

The symmetry goes further. The dual of the LP barrier problem is the barrier problem of the dual LP. Semidefinite programs (Day 5) follow the same pattern. The primal "minimize tr(CX) s.t. tr(AiX) = bi, X ⪰ 0" has the dual "maximize bTy s.t. Σ yiAi ⪯ C". The barrier is −log det X, and the central path is XS = τI. CO4A 16-3 CO4A 17-5

Now the method. The barrier method walks to each station on the central path before heading for the next one. The primal-dual interior-point method cuts the corner: it never re-centers fully, and aims each step at a moving target on the path. CO4A 17-2

Treat the perturbed KKT conditions as equations r(x, u, v) = 0 in the primal x and the duals u and v together. Each of the three blocks is a residual: how much one group of conditions is violated. CO4A 17-2-1

rdual = ∇f(x) + Σ ui∇hi(x) + ATv
rcent,i = uihi(x) + τ
rprim = Ax − b

Day 11's Newton method also solves equations: linearize r around the current point, solve one linear system for the step (Δx, Δu, Δv), and move. The primal-dual method takes one such step, lowers τ, and repeats. There is one loop instead of two.

The iterates need not be feasible: Ax = b and dual feasibility hold only in the limit. So the m/t certificate does not apply directly. Instead the method tracks the surrogate duality gap: CO4A 17-2-2

η = −h(x)Tu = Σi uisi

It equals the true duality gap once rdual = 0 and rprim = 0. Each iteration sets τ = σ·η/m with σ = 1/μ, a fraction of the current average uisi. A careful line search keeps the iterates interior. It caps the step so that u stays positive, starts at 0.99 of that cap, halves until h(x) < 0, and halves again until the residual has shrunk enough. CO4A 17-2-3

Pentagon numbers. Start at x = (1, 1) with ui = 1/si = (1, 1, 0.5, 0.5, 0.5), so η = 5. The dual residual ATu + c has length 2.24, so this u is not dual feasible: an infeasible start. With μ = 10, η goes 5 → 2.31 → 1.64 → 0.75 → 0.40 → 0.22 → 0.020 → 0.0022, and from then on it shrinks about 9× per step. After 13 iterations, η ≤ 10−8 and ‖rdual‖ ≤ 10−8, with x = (1, 3) and u = (0, 0, 0, 1, 1). The barrier method needed 27–39 Newton steps for less accuracy.

Barrier methodPrimal-dual method
Loopsouter (raise t) and inner (Newton)one: one Newton step per iteration
Variables updatedx only (u is read off at the end)x, u and v together
Feasibilitystrictly feasible start (phase I)only u > 0 and h(x) < 0 are kept
Gap measurem/t, exact on the central pathsurrogate gap η
Typical speedgoodusually faster, especially at high accuracy

Going deeper (optional): reading CO4A chapters 15–17 alongside

A few slips in the CO4A pages are worth knowing about. In 15-3-1, the rescaled stationarity line carries an extra t in front of ATv; with v = w/t it should read ∇f + Σ ui∇hi + ATv = 0. In 16-1, the boxed LP dual constraint reads ATy + s = 0; it should be ATy + s = c, as in the derivation and the CMU slides. In 16-3, the SDP dual and the barrier SDP dual are written as "minimize"; both are maximizations. In 17-4, the small Boyd–Vandenberghe test LP is described as having 100 equality constraints; in the book it is an inequality-form LP with 100 inequalities and 50 variables. Finally, 15-1-1 says interior-point methods need "20~30" Newton steps without a source; use Boyd and Vandenberghe p. 575 and p. 615 instead (section 7). Boyd & Vandenberghe 2004, p. 571

7. Why a few tens of Newton steps, and who uses interior-point methods

A Newton step is expensive, because it solves a linear system. A gradient step (Day 6) costs about one matrix–vector product. Interior-point methods bet on a few expensive steps; first-order methods such as ADMM (Day 13) bet on many cheap ones.

How few is "a few"? Boyd and Vandenberghe solved 2,000 random standard-form LPs, with m from 10 to 1,000 equality constraints and n = 2m variables, using μ = 100. Cutting the duality gap by a factor of 104 took on average about 21 Newton steps at the small end and 27 at the large end, with a standard deviation near 2. Their summary: the count grows very slowly with size and is almost always around a few tens. Boyd & Vandenberghe 2004, p. 575

The primal-dual method does even better. In the same chapter, it reached a gap of 10−8 in 15 to 35 iterations as the size grew, roughly like log m. On their small inequality-form LP (100 rules, 50 variables), the residual fell to zero, up to rounding, in 24 iterations. Boyd & Vandenberghe 2004, pp. 613–615

Our own quick check agrees: 5 random LPs per size, m rules, m/2 variables, and absolute targets (10−6 for barrier, 10−8 for primal-dual). The size grew 100×; the step count grew less than 2×.

rules m201005002000
barrier, μ = 5034–3940–4952–5956–61
primal-dual, μ = 1013–1820–2427–3033–40

The worst-case theory is far more pessimistic. With a self-concordant barrier and μ = 1 + 1/√m, the provable bound grows like √m·log(1/ε) Newton steps. For one small LP in the book, that bound is about 8,000 steps, while practice needs a few tens. Nobody runs the theory's tiny μ. Boyd & Vandenberghe 2004, p. 590

Going deeper (optional): the formal barrier method

A self-concordant barrier with parameter ν is a barrier whose curvature changes in a controlled way; the log barrier of m linear rules has ν = m. Measure the distance to the current center by the Newton decrement λt(x) from Day 11. CO4A 15-8 shows: if λt(x) ≤ 1/9 and you raise t by a factor of at most 1 + 1/(8√ν), a single Newton step brings λ back below 1/9. So one Newton step per centering is enough, and about √ν·log(ν/(t(0)ε)) steps reach accuracy ε. The full analysis is in Boyd and Vandenberghe §11.5. CO4A 15-8

What does grow with size is the cost of each step: a dense Newton system in n variables costs about n3 operations. So real solvers exploit sparsity, and MPC solvers (Day 17) exploit the stage-by-stage structure of their Newton systems along the time horizon.

Which solvers use interior-point methods? Here are five common ones, described from their own documentation (as of Oct 2026). Day 21 compares solvers in practice.

SolverProblemsMethod
MOSEKlinear and conic problems (LP, SOCP, SDP)homogeneous self-dual interior-point MOSEK docs
ClarabelLP, QP, SOCP, SDP, exponential and power conesinterior point with a homogeneous embedding Clarabel docs
ECOSSOCP, in small library-free C for embedded useinterior point Domahidi et al. 2013
IPOPTgeneral nonlinear programs (finds a local solution)interior-point line-search filter method Ipopt docs
HPIPMQPs with optimal-control structure, for MPCinterior point; used by acados HPIPM acados docs

IPOPT carries the barrier idea beyond convexity, to the nonlinear problems of Day 16. For contrast, OSQP, a popular QP solver for MPC, is not an interior-point method; it uses ADMM (Day 13, OSQP paper). The algorithm cards summarize both methods of today: barrier card and primal-dual card.

A short history. Dantzig's simplex method (1940s) is fast in practice, but Klee and Minty (1972) built LPs on which it takes about 2n steps. Khachiyan's ellipsoid method (1979) was polynomial but slow. Karmarkar's interior-point method (1984) was polynomial and practical. Modern LP solvers offer both simplex and interior-point methods. CO4A 17-3 CMU 10-725 2016

In CVXPY you never write the barrier yourself. You state the problem and pick an interior-point solver:

import cvxpy as cp, numpy as np
A = np.array([[-1, 0], [0, -1], [1, 0], [0, 1], [1, 1]])
b = np.array([0, 0, 3, 3, 4])
x = cp.Variable(2)
rules = [A @ x <= b]
prob = cp.Problem(cp.Minimize(-x[0] - 2 * x[1]), rules)
prob.solve(solver=cp.CLARABEL)    # an interior-point solver
print(prob.value, x.value)        # about -7 and [1, 3]
print(rules[0].dual_value)        # about [0, 0, 0, 1, 1]
print(prob.solver_stats.num_iters)  # interior-point iterations

Explain it to a 10-year-old

You want to stand as close as you can to a cookie jar in the corner of a room, but the walls are "lava". At first you play it safe and stand in the middle. Then someone says the lava is cooling, so you take a few careful steps toward the jar. They say it again, and you take a few more steps. You end up right next to the cookies, and you never touched a wall.

Common misunderstandings

  • "The barrier method moves along the boundary." It stays strictly inside and reaches the boundary only in the limit t → ∞. In the widget, x*(100) = (1.0001, 2.9900) is still 0.01 below the top wall.
  • "Just set t huge from the start." That is barrier method v.0. The barrier problem becomes badly conditioned, and Newton needs many damped steps. Raise t gradually and warm-start.
  • "m/t is the error." It is an upper bound. On the pentagon at t = 10, the true error is 0.197, while the bound is 0.5.
  • "The number of Newton steps is constant." It grows slowly, roughly like log m in the book's tests, and the cost of each step grows with size.
  • "Primal-dual iterates are feasible." Only u > 0 and h(x) < 0 are kept. Ax = b and dual feasibility are reached only in the limit; the pentagon run starts with a dual residual of 2.24.

Check yourself

Q1. An LP has 5 inequality rules. On the central path at t = 10, the duality gap is…

On the central path the gap is exactly m/t = 5/10 = 0.5. The value 0.05 is the gap at t = 100, and 50 is the gap at t = 0.1. The true error at t = 10 is smaller still, 0.197 on the pentagon.

Q2. Why not start the barrier method with t = m/ε right away?

The answer would be correct, within ε, but finding it is slow: the valley is a narrow canyon against the walls. The barrier φ does not depend on t at all, so it stays defined.

Q3. How do the perturbed KKT conditions differ from the KKT conditions?

Stationarity and Ax = b are unchanged. Only uihi = 0 is relaxed to −1/t, with hi < 0 and ui > 0. Adding the m products gives the gap m/t.

Q4. Phase I returns s* = −4/3. What does this mean?

s* < 0 means hi(x) ≤ −4/3 < 0 for every rule at the phase I solution. Phase I only measures feasibility; it says nothing about the original cost. Infeasibility would show up as s* > 0.

Q5. What is a key difference between the primal-dual method and the barrier method?

Primal-dual applies Newton's method to the perturbed KKT equations in all variables at once, one step per iteration, with no inner loop. It keeps only u > 0 and h(x) < 0. On the pentagon it needs 13 steps; the barrier method needs 27–39.

Q6. In Boyd and Vandenberghe's test, the LPs grew 100× in size. The average number of Newton steps went from about…

The count grew from about 21 to 27 (book p. 575): slowly, but not exactly constant. Each step does get more expensive as the problem grows.

Recap: things to remember

  1. The log barrier φ(x) = −Σ log(−hi(x)) replaces each wall by a smooth penalty that pushes with strength 1/slack. It is defined only at strictly feasible points.
  2. The barrier problem minimizes t·f + φ. Its minimizers x*(t) form the central path, from the analytic center (small t) to the optimum (t → ∞).
  3. On the central path, ui = −1/(t·hi) is dual feasible and the duality gap is exactly m/t: a free stopping rule.
  4. The barrier method re-centers with Newton, stops when m/t ≤ ε, and otherwise sets t ← μt, with μ between about 10 and 100. Phase I finds a strictly feasible start or proves there is none.
  5. The primal-dual method takes one Newton step on the perturbed KKT equations per iteration, may start infeasible, and tracks the surrogate gap η. Both methods finish in a few tens of Newton steps almost regardless of size.

Week 2 · Day 13

Splitting: dual methods & ADMM

After today you can solve a problem through its dual with dual ascent, add an augmented Lagrangian to make it robust, and run ADMM, the split-and-coordinate method behind solvers such as OSQP, while reading its primal and dual residuals.

About 60 min · Needs Days 9 and 10 · CO4A chapters 20 and 21

Today's big idea

Many big problems are easy pieces tied together by a few shared rules. Put a price on breaking each shared rule, let every piece solve its own small problem at that price, and adjust the price until the pieces agree. ADMM is the robust version of this recipe: it adds a spring that pulls the pieces toward agreement, and it lets them take turns.

1. Solve through the dual: set a price, not a rule

Two delivery robots share a charging station with 4 kWh left. Robot A would like 4 kWh and robot B would like 2, so together they want 6. The station could solve one joint problem for both of them. Instead it posts a price per kWh and lets each robot decide for itself.

On Day 9 a dual variable was the price of breaking a rule. Today the price becomes a control knob. Take the problem: minimize f(x) subject to Ax = b, where x ∈ ℝn and A is a matrix. Attach a price vector u to the rule, one entry per row of A. (This chapter of CO4A calls the equality price u; Day 9 wrote v.) CO4A 20-1

L(x, u) = f(x) + uT(Ax − b)
g(u) = minx L(x, u)

The dual function g(u) is the lowest priced cost when x may roam with no rules. Day 9 showed it is a lower bound on the optimum. Today's new fact is about its slope. Let x(u) be the x that minimizes L(x, u). Then the gradient of g at u is the constraint residual Ax(u) − b, how far the rule is from holding. The one-line reason: L is linear in u, with slope Ax − b.

So you improve a price by stepping along the residual. This is dual (sub)gradient ascent: CO4A 20-1

x(k) ∈ argminx L(x, u(k−1))
u(k) = u(k−1) + t(Ax(k) − b)

Here k counts iterations and t > 0 is the step size. Too much demand (Ax > b) raises the price, and too little lowers it. If f is strictly convex, x(u) is unique, g is differentiable, and this is plain gradient ascent on g. Otherwise Ax − b is only a subgradient, as on Day 7.

Worked example. The robots' total cost is f(x) = ½(x1 − 4)2 + ½(x2 − 2)2, and the rule is x1 + x2 = 4. At price u, robot A minimizes ½(x1 − 4)2 + u·x1, so it picks x1 = 4 − u. Robot B picks x2 = 2 − u. Start at u = 0 with t = 0.25:

Step kRobots pick (x1, x2)Residual x1 + x2 − 4New price u
1(4, 2)+20.5
2(3.5, 1.5)+10.75
3(3.25, 1.25)+0.50.875
4(3.125, 1.125)+0.250.9375

The price climbs toward u* = 1, where the robots pick x* = (3, 1) and use exactly 4 kWh. The gap to u* halves at every step. Both robots cut back by the same price, but robot A, which wanted more, still gets more.

The step needs care. With t = 1 the price jumps 0, 2, 0, 2, … and never settles. Here any 0 < t < 1 converges. In general, suppose f is strongly convex with parameter d, meaning it curves upward at least like (d/2)‖x‖22. Then the dual is smooth, and dual ascent converges like gradient descent. The box below has the details. CO4A 20-1-1

Going deeper (optional): why the dual's slope is the residual

Fix a price u and let x(u) minimize L(x, u). For any other price v, g(v) ≤ L(x(u), v) = g(u) + (v − u)T(Ax(u) − b). So Ax(u) − b is a supergradient of the concave function g at u: a subgradient (Day 7), turned upside down for maximizing. CMU 10-725 2016

Now the speed. If f is d-strongly convex, then ∇f* is (1/d)-Lipschitz, where f*(y) = maxx yTx − f(x) is the conjugate. So ∇g is (‖A‖22/d)-Lipschitz. With a fixed step of at most d/‖A‖22, dual gradient ascent needs O(1/ε) iterations to get within ε, or O(log(1/ε)) if ∇f is also Lipschitz. CO4A writes the step as t = d, which is safe only when ‖A‖2 ≤ 1. In the robot example d = 1 and ‖A‖22 = 2, so the safe step is 0.5, and t = 1 is exactly where the price starts to bounce. CO4A 20-1-1

2. Dual decomposition: broadcast a price, gather the usage

Notice what the station did not do. It never looked at the robots' cost functions. It posted one number, each robot solved its own tiny problem, and the station added up the answers. That pattern scales to thousands of pieces.

It works whenever the cost is a sum of separate pieces, f(x) = f1(x1) + … + fB(xB), and the shared rule is linear, A1x1 + … + ABxB = b. For a fixed price the Lagrangian splits into B separate terms. So the x-step splits into B independent problems. This is dual decomposition: CO4A 20-2-1

xi(k) ∈ argmin fi(xi) + (u(k−1))TAixi
u(k) = u(k−1) + t(Σi Aixi(k) − b)

CO4A calls the two halves broadcast and gather. Broadcast sends the current price to every worker, which can be a separate machine or robot. Gather collects their usage Aixi, and one sum updates the price. Only prices and totals travel, and no worker sees another's cost.

Shared resources are usually limits, not exact amounts: Σi Aixi ≤ b. Then the price must stay non-negative, and the update clips it at zero: CO4A 20-2-2

u(k) = (u(k−1) + t(Σi Aixi(k) − b))+

Here (v)+ = max(v, 0), entry by entry. Now the price story is complete: raise the price of an over-used resource, lower it when there is spare capacity, and never go below zero. Example: give the station 8 kWh instead of 4. At u = 0 the robots ask for 6. The update gives (0 + 0.25(6 − 8))+ = 0, so the price stays at zero. A resource with room to spare is free, which is complementary slackness from Day 10.

3. The augmented Lagrangian: add a spring toward the rule

Dual ascent is fragile in two ways. You saw the first: the step size must suit the problem, or the price bounces. The second is worse. If f is not strictly convex, the x-step can fail outright. Take f(x) = x with the rule x = 1. For any price u ≠ −1, L(x, u) = x + u(x − 1) is a sloped straight line in x, with no minimum.

The fix is to add a spring. The augmented Lagrangian adds a quadratic penalty on the residual: CO4A 20-3

Lρ(x, u) = f(x) + uT(Ax − b) + (ρ/2)‖Ax − b‖22

The penalty parameter ρ > 0 sets how stiff the spring is. The new term is zero at every feasible point, so the solution does not change. But now the x-step always has a minimum. In the example, x + u(x − 1) + (ρ/2)(x − 1)2 is a parabola for every u.

The method of multipliers is dual ascent on Lρ, with the step size set to ρ: CO4A 20-3

x(k) = argminx Lρ(x, u(k−1))
u(k) = u(k−1) + ρ(Ax(k) − b)

Why a step of exactly ρ? The x-step's optimality condition reads 0 ∈ ∂f(x(k)) + AT(u(k−1) + ρ(Ax(k) − b)). The bracket is exactly the new price u(k). So each new pair (x(k), u(k)) meets the stationarity condition from Day 10, and only feasibility is left to fix.

Worked example: the robots again, with ρ = 1. The x-step now gives a total use of (14 − 2u)/3. From u = 0 the total is 4.667, the residual 0.667, and the new price 0.667. Then the price goes 0.889, 0.963, 0.988. The gap to u* = 1 shrinks by a factor 1/(1 + 2ρ) = 1/3 per step, and by 1/21 for ρ = 10. Any ρ > 0 converges here, and nothing bounces. In the f(x) = x example with ρ = 1, the first step gives x = 0 and u = −1, and the second lands on x = 1.

The spring has a cost of its own. Expand (ρ/2)(x1 + x2 − 4)2 and you find a cross term ρx1x2. Robot A's best choice now depends on robot B's, so the x-step no longer splits. The method of multipliers converges far more reliably, but it gives up dual decomposition. CO4A 20-3 CMU 10-725 2016 The dual ascent and method of multipliers card sums up both.

4. ADMM: take turns instead of deciding together

Can we keep the spring and still split the work? Yes, if the pieces take turns. That is the idea behind the alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM). It works on problems with two blocks of variables, each with its own cost, tied by a linear rule: CO4A 20-4-1

minimize f(x) + g(z)
subject to Ax + Bz = c

(Here g names the second cost, not the dual function.) The lasso from Day 8 fits this shape once you make a copy. It minimizes ½‖y − Xβ‖22 + λ‖β‖1 for data X, y and a weight λ > 0. Call the copy α, set f(β) = ½‖y − Xβ‖22 and g(α) = λ‖α‖1, and require β − α = 0. Each piece alone is easy: f is least squares, and g is handled by soft-thresholding. CO4A 21-3

The augmented Lagrangian of the two-block problem is

Lρ(x, z, u) = f(x) + g(z)
+ uT(Ax + Bz − c) + (ρ/2)‖Ax + Bz − c‖22

The method of multipliers would minimize it over x and z together. ADMM minimizes over x, then over z using the new x, then updates the price: CO4A 20-4-1

x(k) = argminx Lρ(x, z(k−1), u(k−1))
z(k) = argminz Lρ(x(k), z, u(k−1))
u(k) = u(k−1) + ρ(Ax(k) + Bz(k) − c)

One pass of x and then z replaces the joint minimization. The x-step sees only f and the spring, and the z-step only g and the spring. So the work splits again, while the spring keeps the robustness.

The formulas get shorter with the scaled dual w = u/ρ. Completing the square folds the price term into the spring: CO4A 20-4-3

x ← argminx f(x) + (ρ/2)‖Ax + Bz − c + w‖22
z ← argminz g(z) + (ρ/2)‖Ax + Bz − c + w‖22
w ← w + (Ax + Bz − c)

Now w is simply the running sum of all residuals so far. It works like the integral term of a PI controller: a disagreement that lasts keeps pushing harder until it is gone.

When the rule is x = z (A = I, B = −I, c = 0), each step is a proximal operator. Recall from Day 8 that proxf,λ(v) = argminx f(x) + ‖x − v‖22/(2λ): "move toward v, but keep f small". CO4A 21-2

x ← proxf,1/ρ(z − w)
z ← proxg,1/ρ(x + w)
w ← w + x − z

For the lasso this reads: ridge regression, then soft-threshold, then add the disagreement. Soft-thresholding St shrinks each entry toward 0 by t, and sets it to 0 if its size is at most t. CO4A 21-3

β ← (XTX + ρI)−1(XTy + ρ(α − w))
α ← Sλ/ρ(β + w)
w ← w + β − α

Worked example with a single number. Minimize ½(β − 3)2 + |β|, whose answer is β* = S1(3) = 2. Take ρ = 1 and start at β = α = w = 0, so the β-step is β = (3 + α − w)/2. Step 1: β = 1.5, α = S1(1.5) = 0.5, and w = 1. Step 2: β = 1.25 and α = S1(2.25) = 1.25, so w stays at 1. After that β = α = 1.625, 1.8125, 1.906, …, and step 8 reaches 1.988. The gap to 2 halves each step. The price u = ρw = 1 is the slope of |β| at the answer, just as KKT predicts.

The same three lines in Python, with the stopping rule from the next section:

import numpy as np
from scipy.linalg import cho_factor, cho_solve

def admm_lasso(X, y, lam, rho=1.0, tol=1e-4, max_iter=2000):
    p = X.shape[1]
    F = cho_factor(X.T @ X + rho * np.eye(p))   # factor once
    Xty, alpha, w = X.T @ y, np.zeros(p), np.zeros(p)
    for k in range(1, max_iter + 1):
        beta = cho_solve(F, Xty + rho * (alpha - w))          # ridge step
        old, v = alpha, beta + w
        alpha = np.sign(v) * np.maximum(np.abs(v) - lam / rho, 0)  # soft-threshold
        w = w + beta - alpha                                   # add the disagreement
        r = np.linalg.norm(beta - alpha)                       # primal residual
        s = rho * np.linalg.norm(alpha - old)                  # dual residual
        if r <= tol and s <= tol:
            return alpha, k
    return alpha, max_iter
MethodPrice updateSplits the work?Needs
Dual ascentu + t(Ax − b)Yes, if f is a sum of piecesstrictly convex f and a well-chosen step t
Method of multipliersu + ρ(Ax − b)No: the spring couples the piecesconvex f; any ρ > 0
ADMMu + ρ(Ax + Bz − c)Yes: separate x- and z-stepsconvex f and g; any ρ > 0, but ρ sets the speed

Analogy

Two specialists edit one report. One polishes the wording (f), and the other enforces the style guide (g). They take turns on a shared draft, each changing only their own part. A referee keeps a running tally of where their versions still differ (w) and tells the next editor to lean that way. ρ is how loudly the referee speaks.

5. When to stop: two residuals, two questions

ADMM's stopping rule asks two questions. Do the two copies agree yet? And have they stopped moving, so that the prices have settled? Each question has its own number: Boyd et al. 2011

r(k) = Ax(k) + Bz(k) − c
s(k) = ρATB(z(k) − z(k−1))

The primal residual r measures how badly the rule is broken; for the lasso it is β − α. The dual residual s measures how much z moved in this step, times ρ; for the lasso its size is ρ‖α(k) − α(k−1)‖2. After the z-step, z's own optimality condition holds exactly, and x's is off by s. So when both are small, every KKT condition nearly holds, and f + g is near the optimal value p*. Boyd et al. 2011

Look back at the scalar example. At step 2, β = α = 1.25, so r = 0. Yet the answer is 2, not 1.25. The dual residual gives it away: s = 1 × |1.25 − 0.5| = 0.75. Stop on r alone and you would quit far too early.

Boyd et al. stop when ‖r‖2 ≤ εpri and ‖s‖2 ≤ εdual. Each tolerance mixes an absolute and a relative part:

εpri = √p·εabs + εrel·max{‖Ax‖, ‖Bz‖, ‖c‖}
εdual = √n·εabs + εrel·‖ATu‖

Here p is the length of r and n the length of x, and εrel = 10−3 or 10−4 is typical. The widget below uses a simpler rule: both norms at most 10−4. Boyd et al. 2011

Does ADMM always get there? The guarantee is broad. Suppose f and g are closed, proper and convex, and the plain Lagrangian has a saddle point. Then for every ρ > 0 the residual goes to 0, f + g goes to p*, and the price goes to an optimal u*. A and B need not have full rank. CO4A 20-4-2

Speed is another matter. Boyd et al. report that ADMM often reaches "modest accuracy" "within a few tens of iterations", but can be very slow to reach high accuracy. Boyd et al. 2011 In the widget's lasso at ρ = 0.1, the tolerances 10−3, 10−4 and 10−6 take 81, 130 and 229 iterations. Each extra digit costs about 50 more iterations, the pattern of a first-order method like gradient descent on Day 6. If you need many digits, an interior-point method (Day 12) is usually the better fit.

Going deeper (optional): why ADMM converges

Boyd et al. prove convergence with a Lyapunov function, a quantity that falls at every step: V = (1/ρ)‖u − u*‖22 + ρ‖B(z − z*)‖22 (their Appendix A). They also bound the objective error by the residuals, f + g − p* ≤ −uTr + (x − x*)Ts, which is why small residuals mean a small error. ADMM is a special case of Douglas–Rachford splitting, itself a proximal point method (§3.5). Faster, linear rates need extra assumptions such as strong convexity; CO4A 20-5 lists the papers. A common speed-up is over-relaxation, which pushes each step further by a factor between 1.5 and 1.8 (§3.4.3). Boyd et al. 2011 CO4A 20-5

6. Choosing ρ, and letting it adapt

Think of ρ as how loudly the referee shouts "agree!". Shout too softly, and each copy chases its own cost while agreement comes slowly, so r stays large. Shout too loudly, and the copies agree at once but barely move toward the optimum, so s stays large. CO4A puts it this way: a large ρ puts too little weight on minimizing f + g, and a small ρ too little on feasibility. CO4A 21-3 CMU 10-725 2016

The widget's lasso shows both patterns. At ρ = 0.1 the first three steps give ‖r‖ = 2.568, 1.597, 0.581 and ‖s‖ = 0.000, 0.110, 0.129, so r is on top. At ρ = 10 they give ‖r‖ = 0.065, 0.002, 0.003 and ‖s‖ = 2.946, 2.637, 2.304. Now s is on top, and it is still 0.92 at step 10.

Since the two residuals pull ρ in opposite directions, a simple rule can balance them. Residual balancing raises ρ when r is much larger than s, and lowers it in the opposite case: Boyd et al. 2011

if ‖r‖ > μ‖s‖: ρ ← τρ and w ← w/τ
if ‖s‖ > μ‖r‖: ρ ← ρ/τ and w ← τw

Typical values are μ = 10 and τ = 2. Rescaling w keeps the real price u = ρw unchanged. If the x-step reuses a factorization, it must be refactored whenever ρ changes. One caution: the convergence proof assumes a fixed ρ, so it covers adaptive ρ only if ρ eventually stops changing. Boyd et al. 2011

Try it: the widget runs scaled ADMM on a seeded lasso with 30 data points and 10 features (λ = 0.2516). The answer is β* ≈ (1.825, −1.336, 0, 0, 0.925, 0, …, 0), which recovers the three true features 1, 2 and 5. Slide ρ, or tap a preset, and watch which residual stays on top. Then switch on adaptive ρ and try the ends of the slider, 0.01 and 100.

Notice that at the default ρ = 1 both residuals fall below 10−4 after 16 iterations. The lower chart is a U: 130 iterations at ρ = 0.1 and 123 at ρ = 10, about 8× more, and over 1,000 at the two ends of the slider. With adaptive ρ the purple line is nearly flat: 18, 17 and 19 iterations from starts of 0.1, 1 and 10, and 16 to 25 from any start.

7. ADMM at work: lasso, consensus, projections, and OSQP

The lasso at scale. The β-step solves with the same matrix XTX + ρI every time, and that matrix is always invertible. So you factor it once, with a Cholesky factorization costing O(p3) for p features. After that each iteration costs only O(p2). CO4A 21-3 Boyd et al. report a lasso with 1,500 examples and 5,000 features, also with one factorization up front. With ρ = 1 it met the stopping rule in 15 iterations, and the whole solve took about 1.5 s, of which about 1 s was the first factorization. Boyd et al. 2011 The group lasso, which zeroes whole groups of features at once, swaps in group soft-thresholding, Rt(v) = (1 − t/‖v‖2)+v. CO4A 21-3

Consensus: many machines, one answer. Suppose the cost is a sum f1(x) + … + fN(x), and each fi lives on a different machine, for example because each holds part of the data. Give machine i its own copy xi, and require every copy to equal one shared value x̄. This is consensus ADMM: CO4A 21-5

xi ← argmin fi(xi) + (ρ/2)‖xi − x̄ + wi‖22
x̄ ← average of the xi
wi ← wi + xi − x̄

The xi-steps run in parallel, as in dual decomposition, but each has a spring, as in the method of multipliers. (Strictly, the z-step averages xi + wi. The wi start at zero and always sum to zero, so this is a plain average.)

Worked example: three machines hold the numbers a = 1, 2 and 6, with fi(x) = (x − ai)2 and ρ = 1. The shared value goes 2.0, 2.667, 2.889, 2.963, 2.988, 2.996, toward the mean 3, which is the true minimizer. The primal residual shrinks by about 2/3 per step: 2.49, 1.66, 1.11, 0.74, 0.49, 0.33. The prices wi approach (−4, −2, 6). Each one records how hard, and in which direction, that machine's data pulls away from the shared answer.

Alternating projections. To find a point in the overlap of two convex sets C and D, minimize IC(x) + ID(z) subject to x = z. The indicator function IC is 0 on C and +∞ off it, so its prox step is the projection PC, the closest point of C: CO4A 20-4-4 CMU 10-725 2016

x ← PC(z − w), z ← PD(x + w)
w ← w + x − z

Without w this would be the classical back-and-forth between the two sets. Boyd et al. note that the ADMM version is like Dykstra's alternating projections, which is far more efficient than the classical method. Boyd et al. 2011

More splits. Robust PCA writes a video as a low-rank background L plus a sparse foreground S. ADMM alternates singular-value soft-thresholding for L with entrywise soft-thresholding for S. CO4A 21-4 And how you split matters. For a 2-D fused lasso on an image, splitting into row and column problems that are each solved exactly converges much faster than the generic split, at a similar cost per cycle. CO4A 21-6

OSQP and model predictive control. OSQP is a free solver for quadratic programs: minimize ½xTPx + qTx subject to l ≤ Ax ≤ u, with P ⪰ 0. (Here l and u are bounds, not prices.) It runs ADMM on a split chosen so that the x-step's linear system has the same matrix at almost every iteration. OSQP factors that matrix once. After that, each iteration is cheap vector work plus clipping into the box [l, u]. It is the lasso's factor-once trick, applied to any convex QP. Stellato 2020

That suits model predictive control (Day 17). There a controller solves a QP of the same shape at every control step, and only the measured state changes. OSQP can warm-start from the last solution and reuse its factorization. In the paper's MPC benchmark with a 10-step horizon, this cut the solve time from 7 ms to 2 ms with 20 states, and from 67 ms to 22 ms with 80 states. The iteration counts barely changed, so the saving came from reusing the factorization. Stellato 2020 The OSQP paper page and the ADMM card have more.

The trade-offs are ADMM's own. On the paper's 1,400 test QPs at low accuracy (10−3), OSQP was the fastest solver overall and failed on none. It is still a first-order method, though. On hard, badly scaled problems GUROBI was faster, and the authors call the choice of ρ "still an open research question". The paper's defaults adapt ρ during the solve and over-relax with a factor of 1.6. The current default starting ρ is 0.1 (as of Oct 2026). Stellato 2020 OSQP docs

Going deeper (optional): fixes if you read CO4A alongside

  • 20-04-04 (alternating projection): the objective should read IC(x) + ID(z), and the dual update w ← w + x − z, as in the CMU slides and Boyd et al.
  • 20-04-02: the residual is Ax + Bz − c, and the objective is f(x(k)) + g(z(k)).
  • 21-03 (lasso): the costs are O(p3) for the factorization and O(p2) per iteration, where p is the number of features.
  • 21-03 (group lasso): group soft-thresholding is Rt(x) = (1 − t/‖x‖2)+x; the t is missing.

Explain it to a 10-year-old

Two friends draw one picture. Mia is good at shapes and Leo is good at colours. They take turns: Mia fixes the shapes, then Leo colours Mia's new drawing. After each turn they write down where their two versions still don't match. A mismatch that stays on the list gets an extra star, and the next person works harder to fix it. Soon the two versions match, and the picture is good at both shapes and colours.

Common misunderstandings

  • "ADMM's x- and z-steps can run at the same time." The z-step must use the new x. Updating both from the old values is a different, Jacobi-style method without ADMM's guarantee. (In consensus ADMM the many xi-steps do run in parallel with each other; the averaging waits for all of them.)
  • "A tiny primal residual means you are done." In the scalar example r = 0 at step 2, with β = α = 1.25, but the answer is 2. The dual residual, 0.75, showed that α was still moving. Check both.
  • "A bigger ρ is stricter, so it is better." In the widget, ρ = 10 takes 123 iterations and ρ = 1 takes 16. Too large a ρ makes the copies agree early and then crawl.
  • "ADMM is fast, so it is fast to high accuracy." It is quick to modest accuracy and slow after that: 81, 130 and 229 iterations for 10−3, 10−4 and 10−6 at ρ = 0.1.
  • "u and w are the same price." u = ρw. If you change ρ in the scaled form, rescale w, or you silently change the price.

Check yourself

Q1. In dual ascent, what is the gradient of the dual function g at the price u?

g(u) = L(x(u), u), and L is linear in u with slope Ax − b. So the price rises exactly where demand exceeds supply. ∇f(x(u)) is tempting, but at the minimizer it equals −ATu, which tells you about x, not about how to change the price.

Q2. Why can dual decomposition run on many machines at once?

With f = Σfi(xi) and Ax = ΣAixi, L splits into Σ[fi(xi) + uTAixi] − uTb. The penalty option is backwards: (ρ/2)‖Ax − b‖2 is what couples the blocks in the method of multipliers. The constraint does not disappear either; the price update still enforces it.

Q3. In the method of multipliers, why is the price step exactly ρ?

The x-step's optimality reads 0 ∈ ∂f(x) + AT(u + ρ(Ax − b)), and the bracket is the new u. Only feasibility is left to fix. It does not make x feasible at once: in the robot example the total use after step 1 was 4.667, not 4.

Q4. What does ADMM give up, compared with the method of multipliers, to get splitting back?

ADMM keeps Lρ and its dual step ρ. It only replaces "minimize over x and z together" with one pass of x and then z. Dropping the penalty instead would give back plain dual decomposition, with its fragile step size.

Q5. In a run, ‖r‖ is already 0.002 but ‖s‖ is still 2.6 and falling slowly. What is the most likely cause?

A large ρ forces the copies to agree at once, so r is tiny, while z and the prices keep crawling. These are the widget's ρ = 10 numbers: ‖r‖ = 0.002 and ‖s‖ = 2.637 at step 2, and 123 iterations in all. A small ρ gives the opposite pattern, with r on top.

Q6. Which description of ADMM's convergence matches practice and the Boyd et al. monograph?

ADMM behaves like a first-order method: each extra digit costs about as much as the last. At ρ = 0.1 the widget needs 81, 130 and 229 iterations for 10−3, 10−4 and 10−6. It converges for every ρ > 0; ρ only changes the speed.

Recap: things to remember

  1. Dual ascent: for a fixed price, minimize the Lagrangian, then move the price along the residual Ax − b. It needs a strictly convex f and a careful step.
  2. If f is a sum of pieces, the x-step splits into independent problems: broadcast the price, gather the usage. That is dual decomposition.
  3. The augmented Lagrangian adds (ρ/2)‖Ax − b‖2. The method of multipliers uses step ρ and converges for any ρ, but loses the splitting.
  4. ADMM: an x-step, a z-step that uses the new x, then w ← w + residual. Stop when both the primal residual r and the dual residual s are small.
  5. ρ trades r against s, and residual balancing adapts it. ADMM reaches modest accuracy fast and high accuracy slowly. OSQP uses it to solve the QPs of MPC.
