Week 2 · Day 14

Frank–Wolfe & coordinate descent

After today you can minimize over a constraint set without projecting by using Frank–Wolfe's linear-minimization step, and decide when updating one coordinate at a time (coordinate descent) is the fastest way to solve problems like the lasso.

About 60 min · Needs Days 6 and 8 · CO4A chapters 22 and 23

Today's big idea

Two cheap tricks replace an expensive step. Frank–Wolfe never projects: it asks which corner of the allowed set is best for a straight-line guess of the cost, and leans toward it. Coordinate descent never takes a full gradient step: it fixes every variable but one and solves that one exactly. Each trick is fast when the problem has the right shape, and today is about recognising that shape.

1. When the fence is the hard part

Recall projected gradient from Day 8. You take a step downhill, and if you land outside the allowed set C, you snap back to the nearest allowed point. Picture a dog on a walk that runs past the park fence and is pulled back to the closest spot inside.

For a box or a ball the snap is one line of code: clip each entry, or rescale the vector. For many other sets the snap is an optimization problem of its own. The projection of a point y onto C is

PC(y) = argminx ∈ C ‖x − y‖22

That is a quadratic problem over C. Frank–Wolfe asks an easier question instead: which point of C is best for a linear cost gTs? A linear cost over a polytope is always smallest at a corner, as you saw for linear programs on Day 5. So the answer is "the corner furthest in the direction −g". CO4A 22-02

Here is a case where the gap in cost is large. Recommender systems fill in a ratings matrix by asking it to be low-rank. A common convex way to ask is a ball in the nuclear norm, the sum of a matrix's singular values. Projecting onto that ball needs a full singular value decomposition (SVD). The linear question needs only the top singular vector pair, which a few rounds of the power method find. CO4A 22-02 Jaggi 2013

A projection-free method is one that never projects onto C. The oldest one is due to Marguerite Frank and Philip Wolfe (1956). It is also called the conditional gradient method. CO4A 22

Analogy

You are inside a fenced park and want to get as close as possible to an ice-cream van parked outside. You may not climb the fence. From where you stand, you can see which corner post is nearest the van. Walk part of the way toward that post, look again, and repeat. You never leave the park, and you never need to work out the closest point of the fence exactly.

2. The Frank–Wolfe step: lean toward the best corner

Stand at the current point x. Near x, the cost f looks like its tangent plane. Ask: "if f really were this plane, where in C would I go?" The answer is a corner s. The plane is only a guess, so you move only part of the way toward s.

In symbols, the Frank–Wolfe method repeats two lines. CO4A 22-02 Jaggi 2013

sk ∈ argmins ∈ C ∇f(xk)Ts
xk+1 = (1 − γk) xk + γk sk
γk = 2/(k + 2), k = 0, 1, 2, …

The first line is the linear minimization oracle (LMO): a routine that returns the best point of C for the linear cost ∇f(xk)Ts. The second line blends the old point with that corner. The weight γk runs 1, 2/3, 1/2, 2/5, …, so later steps are more cautious. This default, the 2/(k+2) step, needs no tuning.

Why does x stay feasible? Because xk+1 lies on the segment between two points of C, and a convex set contains every such segment (Day 2). No projection is ever needed. A note if you read CO4A: it writes the step as 2/(k + 1) with k starting at 1. That is the same sequence 1, 2/3, 1/2, … with the count shifted by one. CMU 10-725 2016

Worked example. Let C be the triangle with corners (0, 0), (1, 0) and (0, 1), and let f(x) = ‖x − p‖22 with p = (0.9, 0.5). The point p lies outside C, so the best point is the closest point of C to p: x* = (0.7, 0.3), with f* = 0.22 + 0.22 = 0.08.

Start at x0 = (0, 0). The gradient is ∇f = 2(x − p) = (−1.8, −1.0). The oracle scores each corner: (0, 0) gives 0, (1, 0) gives −1.8 and (0, 1) gives −1.0. The lowest is (1, 0). With γ0 = 1 you jump all the way, so x1 = (1, 0).

At x1 the gradient is (0.2, −1.0), so now the corner (0, 1) wins with −1.0. With γ1 = 2/3, x2 = ⅓(1, 0) + ⅔(0, 1) = (0.333, 0.667). The next points are (0.667, 0.333), (0.8, 0.2), (0.533, 0.467) and (0.667, 0.333). The iterates zig-zag between the two corners of the edge that holds x*, closing in on (0.7, 0.3).

import numpy as np
V = np.array([[0, 0], [1, 0], [0, 1]])   # corners of C
p = np.array([0.9, 0.5])                 # f(x) = ||x - p||^2
x = np.zeros(2)
for k in range(10):
    g = 2 * (x - p)                      # gradient
    s = V[np.argmin(V @ g)]              # LMO: the best corner
    x = x + 2 / (k + 2) * (s - x)        # lean toward it
g = 2 * (x - p); s = V[np.argmin(V @ g)]
print(x, g @ (x - s))                    # [0.727 0.273] and its gap 0.079

That is the whole method: no step size to tune and no projection to code. The price, as you will see, is speed.

3. Cheap oracles, sparse answers

For a linear cost, the best point of a polytope is a corner, so the oracle only compares corners. For the common sets you do not even need a list of corners. One pass over the gradient tells you which corner wins.

Here are the oracles you will meet most. In each row, g = ∇f(x) and t is the radius of the set. CO4A 22-02 Jaggi 2013

Set CIts corners (atoms)Oracle answer sCost
Probability simplex: s ≥ 0, Σsi = 1e1, …, enei with i = argminj gjO(n)
ℓ1 ball: ‖s‖1 ≤ t±t·eii = argmaxj |gj|, s = −t·sign(gi)·eiO(n)
ℓ∞ ball (box): ‖s‖∞ ≤ tevery sign pattern ±tsi = −t·sign(gi) for each iO(n)
ℓp ball, 1/p + 1/q = 1(a curved boundary)si ∝ −sign(gi)·|gi|q−1, scaled so ‖s‖p = tO(n)
Nuclear-norm ball: ‖S‖* ≤ trank-one matricesS = −t·u1v1T, the top singular pair of ga few power steps

Worked example. Take g = (0.3, −2, 1) and t = 1. On the ℓ1 ball the largest |gj| is 2, at j = 2, so s = −sign(−2)·e2 = (0, 1, 0), with gTs = −2. On the box, s = −sign(g) = (−1, 1, −1), with gTs = −3.3. On the simplex the smallest entry is −2, so s = e2 = (0, 1, 0) again. The widget's triangle works the same way, with (0, 0) as one more corner.

A sanity check for the ℓp row: with p = q = 2 it gives s = −t·g/‖g‖2. On the round ball, the best point for a linear cost is straight downhill, at the edge. For g = (0.3, −2, 1), ‖g‖2 = 2.256 and s = (−0.133, 0.887, −0.443).

Reading CO4A alongside? Three fixes

  • ℓ1 oracle. CO4A 22-02 picks argmaxi ∇if without the absolute value. You need argmaxi |∇if|: a steep negative slope is as useful as a steep positive one, and the sign is applied afterwards.
  • ℓp oracle. CO4A 22-02 and the CMU slides write the exponent as p/q with ‖s‖q = t. Use Jaggi's version in the table: exponent q − 1, scaled so ‖s‖p = t. Jaggi 2013
  • Gap inequality. The proof in CO4A 22-03 writes g(x) ≤ f(x) − f*. It must be ≥, as section 4 explains and as 22-02 states correctly. The same proof's "(k − 1/k + 1)" should read (k − 1)/(k + 1).

Now a bonus. Each step mixes in exactly one corner, so after k steps from a corner, x is a blend of at most k + 1 corners. The corners are called atoms: the building blocks whose convex hull is C. A point made of only a few atoms is a sparse iterate. On the ℓ1 ball, starting from x0 = 0, that means at most k nonzero entries after k steps. On the nuclear-norm ball it means rank at most k.

A lasso example from Day 13's 30 × 10 data, written as a constraint ‖β‖1 ≤ 4.0856 (the ℓ1 norm of the lasso answer). Frank–Wolfe touches only coordinates 1, 2 and 5. It has 1 nonzero for k = 1 to 3, 2 at k = 5, and 3 from k = 10 on. The error f − f* is 2.2 × 10−1 at k = 10, 1.2 × 10−3 at k = 100 and 3.4 × 10−5 at k = 1000. The iterates are sparse and each step is cheap, but high accuracy is slow to arrive.

A robotics reading of the same idea: suppose a planner blends a library of precomputed motion primitives, with weights on the simplex. The oracle picks the single primitive that best fits the current gradient. Started from one primitive, after 5 steps the plan mixes at most 6, which is easy to inspect and to execute.

This trade between sparsity and accuracy is the best possible. Jaggi shows that for f = ‖x‖22 on the simplex, any point with at most k nonzeros has error at least 1/k − 1/n. So about 1/ε atoms are unavoidable for accuracy ε. Jaggi 2013

4. A free certificate, and the O(1/k) rate

A convex function lies above every tangent plane (Day 3). So the tangent plane at x, pushed to its lowest point over C, is a floor under f*. And the oracle has already found that lowest point: it is s.

Write that floor down. Convexity gives f* ≥ f(x) + ∇f(x)T(s − x). Rearranged, it says the Frank–Wolfe duality gap is an upper bound on how far you are from optimal: CO4A 22-02 CMU 10-725 2016

g(x) = ∇f(x)T(x − s) ≥ f(x) − f*

You get g(x) for free, because the oracle already computed s. So you can stop the moment g(x) ≤ ε, without knowing f*. The name "duality gap" comes from a Fenchel dual of the problem; you do not need that view to use it.

Check it on the triangle. At x0 = (0, 0) with s = (1, 0), g = (−1.8, −1.0)T(−1, 0) = 1.8. The true error is f(x0) − f* = 1.06 − 0.08 = 0.98, which is indeed below 1.8. At k = 10 the error is 1.5 × 10−3 and the gap is 7.9 × 10−2. At k = 100 they are 1.3 × 10−4 and 1.0 × 10−2. The gap does not fall every step, but it never drops below the error.

How fast does the error fall? With γk = 2/(k + 2), for k ≥ 1: CO4A 22-03 Jaggi 2013

f(xk) − f* ≤ 2Cf / (k + 2)
Cf ≤ L · diam(C)2

Here Cf is the curvature constant, which CO4A calls M. It measures how far f bends away from its tangent planes over C. L is the Lipschitz constant of ∇f from Day 6, and the diameter diam(C) is the largest distance between two points of C. The one-line reason: each step lowers f by at least γ times the gap, minus a bending penalty of (γ2/2)Cf. Since the gap is at least the error, the error shrinks like 1/k.

On the triangle, f = ‖x − p‖2 has L = 2, and the longest distance in C is from (1, 0) to (0, 1), so diam2 = 2. Hence Cf ≤ 4 and the bound reads 8/(k + 2): 0.67 at k = 10, 0.078 at k = 100 and 0.008 at k = 1000. The actual errors, 1.5 × 10−3, 1.3 × 10−4 and 1.8 × 10−8, are far smaller. The bound is a worst case.

O(1/k) is the same rate as gradient descent on a smooth problem, and slower than FISTA's O(1/k2) from Day 8. In the worst case, each extra correct digit costs ten times as many steps. Frank–Wolfe has one more nice property, affine invariance: stretching or skewing the coordinates does not change its iterates, and Cf does not change either. CMU 10-725 2016

Going deeper (optional): the O(1/k) proof in three lines

The definition of Cf gives f(xk+1) ≤ f(xk) − γkg(xk) + (γk2/2)Cf. Write hk = f(xk) − f* and use g ≥ h: hk+1 ≤ (1 − γk)hk + (γk2/2)Cf. With γk = 2/(k + 2) and the guess hk ≤ 2Cf/(k + 2), the right side is 2Cf(k + 1)/(k + 2)2 ≤ 2Cf/(k + 3), because (k + 1)(k + 3) ≤ (k + 2)2. That is the induction step. Jaggi also shows that the smallest gap seen in the first k steps falls like O(1/k) too. Jaggi 2013 CO4A 22-03

Try it: in mode A, slide k and watch the path bounce between the corners (1, 0) and (0, 1). The orange ring marks the corner the oracle picks next. In the chart, compare the gap (orange) with the true error (pink). Switch p to the inside preset, then try exact line search on both presets. Tap the plot to move p anywhere.

Notice that after k = 10 steps with γ = 2/(k+2), the error f − f* is 1.5e−3 while the gap g(x) is 7.9e−2. The gap sits above the error, as promised, and you computed it without knowing x*. The worst-case bound 8/(k+2) = 0.667 is far looser than both.

The zig-zag is the method's weak spot. When x* lies on an edge, the oracle keeps pointing at the edge's two corners, and the path bounces between them. With exact line search (γ chosen to minimize f along the segment to s) on the edge preset, f − f* is 3.1 × 10−3 at k = 100 and 3.4 × 10−4 at k = 1000: exactly 1/k behaviour. Here the plain 2/(k+2) step does better (1.3 × 10−4 at k = 100). That is a property of this example, not a rule.

When x* is inside the triangle, line search is fast: f − f* = 2.9 × 10−6 at k = 10, and it hits the limit of floating-point arithmetic before k = 100. Two standard fixes target the zig-zag. Fully corrective Frank–Wolfe re-optimizes over all atoms found so far. An away step moves weight away from the worst atom currently in use. With away steps, Lacoste-Julien and Jaggi (2013) prove linear convergence for strongly convex f over a polytope. CO4A 22-04

5. Coordinate descent: one knob at a time

Think of an old shower with separate hot and cold taps. You turn the hot tap until the water is as good as it gets, then the cold tap, then the hot one again. Each turn is easy because you only move one knob. That is coordinate descent.

Coordinate descent (CD) minimizes f over one coordinate at a time, keeping the others fixed. The cyclic version sweeps through i = 1, …, n and repeats: CO4A 23-01

xi ← argminxi f(x1, …, xi, …, xn)
for i = 1, 2, …, n, then repeat

One sweep over all n coordinates is a cycle. Each update uses the newest values of the other coordinates. This one-at-a-time scheme is called Gauss–Seidel, and it matters: updating every coordinate at once from the old values (the Jacobi scheme) need not converge. You can also visit coordinates at random, or greedily pick the one with the largest gradient entry (the Gauss–Southwell rule). Blocks of coordinates work too. CMU 10-725 2016

Does it find the true minimum? For a smooth convex f, yes. Stop at a point where no single coordinate can improve, a coordinatewise minimum. There every partial derivative is zero, so the whole gradient is zero, and on Day 4 you saw that ∇f = 0 means a global minimum.

Worked example: a tilted bowl, f(x) = ½(x12 + 2c·x1x2 + x22) with a coupling c between 0 and 1. Setting ∂f/∂x1 = x1 + c·x2 to zero gives the exact update x1 = −c·x2. Likewise x2 = −c·x1. From (2, 1.5) with c = 0.9 the path is (−1.35, 1.5), (−1.35, 1.215), (−1.0935, 1.215), … an axis-aligned staircase. Each cycle multiplies the coordinates by c2 = 0.81.

Coupling c00.50.80.90.950.99
CD cycles to f ≤ 10−10192652102479
GD steps, t = 1/L125801673331554

At c = 0 the bowl is round and aligned with the axes, so one cycle solves it. As c grows the bowl tilts and stretches, and both methods slow down. CD stays about three times faster here. Is that a fair race? Yes, because one CD cycle costs about one gradient. Each coordinate update reads one row of the problem, and a cycle reads every row once.

For least squares, ½‖y − Xβ‖22 with n data rows and p features, the update for feature i is βi ← βi + XiTr / ‖Xi‖22, where Xi is column i and r = y − Xβ is the residual. The residual trick keeps r up to date after each change, at a cost of O(n). So a full cycle costs O(np), the same as one gradient step. CO4A 23-02

Try it: here is the same widget in mode B. Slide the coupling c and watch the orange staircase and the blue gradient-descent path. Tap the plot to start somewhere else.

Notice that at coupling c = 0.9, coordinate descent needs 52 cycles to reach f ≤ 10⁻¹⁰, while gradient descent with step 1/L needs 167 steps, about 3.2 times as many for the same work per step. Slide c to 0 and both finish in one move.

6. Where coordinate descent gets stuck

Now add a kink that runs diagonally. Take f(x) = |x1 − x2| + 0.1(x12 + x22). It is convex, and its minimum is at (0, 0) with f = 0. Start CD at (2, 1), where f = 1.5.

Fix x2 = 1 and minimize |x1 − 1| + 0.1x12. At x1 = 1 the slope jumps from −1 + 0.2 = −0.8 to +1 + 0.2 = 1.2, so zero slope sits inside the jump, and x1 = 1 is the minimizer. Then fix x1 = 1 and minimize over x2: the same sum gives x2 = 1. CD is stuck at (1, 1), with f = 0.2.

Is (1, 1) special? No. Every point (a, a) with |a| ≤ 5 is a coordinatewise minimum, so CD stops wherever it first lands on the diagonal. The direction downhill points along the diagonal, and both axis moves go uphill. A smooth convex function cannot do this, because at a smooth point "no axis move helps" already means "no move helps".

Analogy

A taxi may only drive north–south or east–west. It is looking for the lowest point of a V-shaped valley that runs diagonally across the city grid. Once it reaches the valley floor, every street leads uphill, even though the valley keeps sloping down along its length.

So when is a kink harmless? When it runs along the axes. The safe shape is a smooth part plus a separable function, a sum of one-variable pieces: CO4A 23-01

f(x) = g(x) + Σi hi(xi)

Here g is smooth and convex, and each hi is convex but may have kinks. Then a coordinatewise minimum is a global minimum. The one-line reason: every kink of Σhi(xi) lies along a coordinate direction, so single-coordinate moves can "see" it. The lasso penalty λ‖β‖1 = λΣ|βi| is separable. So are box constraints li ≤ xi ≤ ui, written as indicator functions.

Tseng (2001) turned this into a convergence theorem for cyclic CD. Assume f has this form and is continuous on the closed and bounded set {x : f(x) ≤ f(x0)}, and that its minimum is attained. Then every limit point of cyclic CD is a minimizer. CO4A states the result without these conditions; the CMU slides give them. CMU 10-725 2016

What breaks it is a nonsmooth term that ties coordinates together. Examples are |x1 − x2| above, the fused lasso Σ|βi+1 − βi|, and total variation in images. The support vector machine dual has a coupling constraint αTy = 0, which is why its classic solver, SMO, updates two coordinates at a time and needs its own analysis. CMU 10-725 2016 In the widget, mode C shows a separable kink that CD handles, and mode D shows the diagonal kink that stops it.

Going deeper (optional): why separable kinks are safe

Let x be a coordinatewise minimum of g + Σhi. For each i, the one-variable problem in xi is solved, so −∇ig(x) ∈ ∂hi(xi) (a subgradient condition from Day 7). For any y, convexity gives f(y) − f(x) ≥ ∇g(x)T(y − x) + Σ[hi(yi) − hi(xi)]. Regroup it as Σi[∇ig(x)(yi − xi) + hi(yi) − hi(xi)]. Each bracket is ≥ 0 by the subgradient condition, so f(y) ≥ f(x). The regrouping needs h to split by coordinate; |x1 − x2| cannot be split, and the proof fails. CO4A 23-01

7. The lasso, one coordinate at a time

The lasso, min ½‖y − Xβ‖22 + λ‖β‖1, is the poster child for CD. Its penalty is separable, so Tseng's theorem applies. And the one-coordinate problem has a closed-form answer: do least squares on feature i alone, then shrink the result toward zero.

βi ← Sλ/‖Xi‖²( XiTr−i / ‖Xi‖22 )
r−i = y − X−iβ−i

Here r−i is the residual with feature i left out, and St(z) = sign(z)·max(|z| − t, 0) is soft-thresholding from Day 8. It shrinks z toward 0 by t, and sets it to exactly 0 if |z| ≤ t. That is how the lasso produces exact zeros. CO4A 23-03

Worked example in 2-D: f = ½(x12 + 1.6x1x2 + x22) − x1 − 0.2x2 + 0.1(|x1| + |x2|). The two updates are x1 = S0.1(1 − 0.8x2) and x2 = S0.1(0.2 − 0.8x1). Start at (−1, 2). Cycle 1 gives x1 = S(−0.6) = −0.5, then x2 = S(0.6) = 0.5. Cycle 2 gives (0.5, −0.1).

After 10 cycles the point is (1.7958, −1.1366), and the limit is x* = (11/6, −7/6) ≈ (1.8333, −1.1667), with f* = −0.65. Check it with the optimality condition: the smooth part's gradient at x* is (−0.1, 0.1), exactly −λ·sign(x*) = −0.1·(1, −1). CD reaches f − f* ≤ 10−10 in 27 cycles. On Day 13's 30 × 10 lasso, cyclic CD reaches f − f* ≤ 10−8 in 5 full sweeps, with the same β* as ADMM.

import numpy as np
def lasso_cd(X, y, lam, cycles=100):
    n, p = X.shape
    beta = np.zeros(p)
    r = y.copy()                        # residual y - X beta
    sq = (X ** 2).sum(axis=0)           # ||X_i||^2 for each column
    for _ in range(cycles):
        for i in range(p):
            r += X[:, i] * beta[i]      # leave feature i out: r_{-i}
            z = X[:, i] @ r / sq[i]     # least squares on feature i
            beta[i] = np.sign(z) * max(abs(z) - lam / sq[i], 0)
            r -= X[:, i] * beta[i]      # put it back, O(n)
    return beta

Real lasso solvers wrap this loop in a pathwise scheme, popularized by Friedman, Hastie and Tibshirani's glmnet. Friedman 2010 You rarely want one λ; you want a whole path of them. Start at the λ where β = 0 is optimal, then step down a grid λ1 > λ2 > …. Each solve begins from the previous answer, a warm start, so it needs only a few cycles. CO4A 23-04

Inside each solve, the active set trick saves more. Run a few cycles, then cycle only over the nonzero coordinates until they settle. Finally check the optimality condition |XiT(y − Xβ)| ≤ λ for every zero coordinate, and add back any that break it. "Strong rules" (Tibshirani and colleagues, 2012) screen out likely-zero features even before that. Tibshirani 2012 CO4A 23-04

Why is this so fast in practice? Each update is a closed form with no step size to tune. Each costs O(n) thanks to the residual trick. Most coordinates are zero and stay zero, so they are skipped. And warm starts mean each λ needs few cycles. On CO4A's regression and lasso examples, CD beats gradient descent, accelerated gradient and proximal gradient. CO4A 23-02 CO4A 23-03

The theory is less complete than the practice. For smooth problems, randomized and cyclic CD both have O(1/k) error, and linear convergence under strong convexity (Nesterov 2010; Beck and Tetruashvili 2013, as summarized by CO4A). Greedy selection can beat random selection. CO4A 23

So which tool when? Frank–Wolfe suits a cheap oracle with a costly projection, when modest accuracy is enough. CD suits a smooth loss plus a separable penalty or box. If a nonsmooth term couples the variables, or you need high accuracy, reach for proximal methods, ADMM (Day 13) or interior-point methods (Day 12).

Explain it to a 10-year-old

Frank–Wolfe: you are inside a fenced playground and want the spot nearest the ice-cream van outside. You look for the corner nearest the van and walk a little way toward it. Then you look again. You never climb the fence.

Coordinate descent is an Etch A Sketch. One knob moves left and right, the other up and down. Turn one knob until the line is as low as it goes, then the other. That works in a round bowl. It fails in a ditch that runs from corner to corner, because no single knob can follow the ditch.

Common misunderstandings

  • "Frank–Wolfe is projected gradient with a different step." It never takes a gradient step. It moves toward a corner chosen by a linear problem, and the gradient only decides which corner.
  • "Frank–Wolfe reaches high accuracy quickly." O(1/k) means about ten times more steps per extra digit, and it zig-zags when x* sits on an edge or face. On Day 13's lasso it needed 1000 steps to reach 3.4 × 10−5.
  • "The gap is a lower bound on the error." It is an upper bound: g(x) ≥ f(x) − f*. CO4A 22-03 prints the inequality the wrong way round.
  • "Exact line search always beats the 2/(k+2) step." Not on the edge preset: 3.1 × 10−3 versus 1.3 × 10−4 at k = 100. Which wins depends on the problem.
  • "Coordinate descent works on any convex function." A nonsmooth term that couples coordinates can stop it, as at (1, 1) for |x1 − x2| + 0.1‖x‖2.
  • "Compare one coordinate update with one gradient step." Compare a full cycle with one gradient step; for least squares both cost O(np).
  • "Updating all coordinates at once from the old values is coordinate descent." That is the Jacobi scheme, and it need not converge. Use each new value immediately.

Check yourself

Q1. What does each Frank–Wolfe iteration need to compute?

Frank–Wolfe calls a linear minimization oracle and then blends x with its answer. A projection, which is the same thing as the prox of the indicator of C, is exactly what it avoids.

Q2. ∇f(x) = (0.5, −3, 2) and C is the ℓ1 ball of radius 1. What does the oracle return?

The largest |entry| is 3, at position 2, and s = −sign(−3)·e2 = (0, 1, 0), which gives ∇fTs = −3. (0, −1, 0) forgets the minus sign and gives +3. (−1, 1, −1) is the box answer, and the scaled gradient is the round-ball answer.

Q3. A Frank–Wolfe run reports the gap g(x) = 0.004. What do you know?

Convexity puts f* above the tangent plane's lowest value over C, so the gap bounds the error from above. CO4A 22-03 prints this inequality the wrong way round. On the triangle at k = 10, the error is 1.5e−3 and the gap is 7.9e−2.

Q4. You run 10 Frank–Wolfe steps on an ℓ1 ball in ℝ1000, starting from x0 = 0. At most how many entries of x10 are nonzero?

Each step blends in one corner ±t·ei, which adds at most one new nonzero. Ten steps give at most 10. "1" would be true only if the oracle kept picking the same coordinate.

Q5. Cyclic coordinate descent on f = |x1 − x2| + 0.1‖x‖2, started at (2, 1), ends at…

The x1-update lands on the diagonal kink at (1, 1), where f = 0.2. From there both axis moves go uphill, though a diagonal move to (0.5, 0.5) gives f = 0.05. The function is convex, which is why (0, 0) is tempting, but its kink couples the coordinates.

Q6. For which problem do Tseng's conditions guarantee that cyclic coordinate descent finds a minimizer?

The lasso is smooth plus separable: λΣ|βi| splits by coordinate. The other three couple coordinates through a nonsmooth term or a constraint. The SVM dual is why SMO updates two coordinates at a time.

Recap: things to remember

  1. Frank–Wolfe swaps projection for a linear minimization oracle: s = argmins∈C ∇f(x)Ts, then x ← (1 − γ)x + γs with γ = 2/(k + 2). It stays feasible with no projection.
  2. The oracles are cheap: the best ei on the simplex, one signed coordinate with the largest |∇if| on the ℓ1 ball, −t·sign(∇f) on the box, the top singular pair on the nuclear-norm ball. The iterates are sparse or low-rank.
  3. The gap ∇f(x)T(x − s) ≥ f(x) − f* comes free as a stopping test, and the error is at most 2Cf/(k + 2): an O(1/k) method that zig-zags when x* is on an edge.
  4. Coordinate descent solves for one coordinate at a time. It finds a global minimum when f is smooth plus separable, and can get stuck when a kink couples coordinates.
  5. For the lasso, each update is a soft-threshold, and a full cycle costs about one gradient. With warm starts and active sets (glmnet), CD is often the fastest lasso solver.

Week 3 · Day 15

Mixed-integer programs

After today you can model yes/no decisions with binary variables and big-M constraints, explain why integer problems are hard, and solve small ones with LP relaxations, branch and bound and cutting planes.

About 60 min · Needs Days 5 and 9 · CO4A chapters 24 and 25

Today's big idea

Some decisions are switches, not dials: take the parcel or leave it, pass the obstacle on the left or on the right. Forbid fractions and the problem stops being convex, but a convex problem still hides inside it. Drop the "whole numbers only" rule and you get a relaxation whose value bounds the answer. Branch and bound and cutting planes use those bounds to find the true optimum, and to prove it, without trying every combination.

1. Switches, not dimmers

So far every variable was a dimmer that could sit anywhere, such as 0.3 or 0.71. Many real decisions are light switches instead. A robot takes a parcel or leaves it; a car passes an obstacle on the left or on the right.

An integer program (IP) is an optimization problem in which some variables must be whole numbers. CO4A writes it as a convex problem plus one extra rule: CO4A 24-1

minimize f(x)
subject to x ∈ C, xj ∈ ℤ for j ∈ J

Here f is a convex function, C is a convex set, ℤ is the set of integers, and J lists the variables that must be integers. If J holds every variable, the problem is a pure integer program. If J holds only some, it is a mixed-integer program (MIP). A binary variable is an integer limited to 0 or 1: a yes/no switch.

The names follow the convex part, using the zoo from Day 5. A linear objective over a polyhedron gives a MILP (mixed-integer LP). A convex quadratic objective gives a MIQP. With a general convex f and C it is a mixed-integer convex program.

Our running example is a delivery robot that can carry 11 kg. Four parcels are waiting, each with a fee and a weight.

ParcelPaysWeight$ per kg
A$604 kg15
B$309 kg3.33
C$155 kg3
D$107 kg1.43

Let xA = 1 mean "take A" and xA = 0 mean "leave it", and the same for B, C and D. Choosing items to maximize value under a weight limit is the knapsack problem: CO4A 24-2

maximize 60xA + 30xB + 15xC + 10xD
subject to 4xA + 9xB + 5xC + 7xD ≤ 11
x ∈ {0, 1}4

There are only 24 = 16 ways to choose, so we can check them all. The best is A + C: $75 for 9 kg. Next come A + D ($70, 11 kg) and A alone ($60). With 50 parcels there would be 250 ≈ 1015 choices, and checking them all is no longer an option.

Combinatorial optimization, picking the best subset from a finite set of options, is full of binary IPs like this one. CO4A's examples include assignment, facility location, K-medoids clustering and best subset selection. CO4A 24-2

2. Why not just round the LP?

The obvious shortcut: forget the switch rule, solve the easy problem, then round. Replacing "x is 0 or 1" with 0 ≤ x ≤ 1 gives the LP relaxation. It is a plain LP from Day 5, so it solves fast.

For a knapsack the LP has a simple answer. Fill the bag in order of dollars per kilogram, and cut the first item that does not fit. A earns $15/kg, so take all of it: 4 kg, leaving 7 kg. B is next at $3.33/kg but weighs 9 kg, so take 7/9 of it. The bag is now full.

x = (1, 7/9, 0, 0)
value = 60 + 30 · 7/9 = 250/3 ≈ 83.33

Now round. Rounding B up packs 13 kg, which breaks the 11 kg limit. Rounding B down leaves A alone, worth $60. The true optimum is $75, and it uses C, an item the LP did not touch at all. Figure 1 shows the four packings side by side.

The distance between the relaxation's optimum and the integer optimum is the integrality gap. Here it is 83.33 − 75 = 8.33, or 11.1% of the answer. CO4A lists three ways rounding goes wrong: integer-feasible points can be hard to find, the relaxed optimum can sit far from the integer one, and the rounded point can be poor. CO4A 24-3

Is there a clever trick that always works? Almost certainly not. Integer programming is NP-hard in general, so no known method solves every instance in time that grows only polynomially with its size. CO4A 24-3 The methods below are exact, but on bad instances they can still take exponential time.

3. Modelling yes/no decisions with binaries

Binaries become powerful when wired into other constraints. Think of a binary as the lock on a gate: locked, the rule holds; open, the rule is switched off.

Counting and linking. Σ zi ≤ k means "at most k of these", and Σ zi = 1 means "exactly one". "Serve customer i from depot j only if depot j is open" becomes xij ≤ yj, where yj = 1 means open, as in CO4A's facility-location model. CO4A 24-2

Fixed costs. Renting a van costs $50 a day, whether you ship one parcel or a hundred, plus $3 per parcel. Let y = 1 if you rent the van, and let x be the number of parcels (at most 100):

cost = 50y + 3x, x ≤ 100y

If y = 0, then x must be 0. If y = 1, up to 100 parcels can go. Shipping 20 parcels costs 50 + 60 = $110.

A big-M constraint uses a binary to switch a whole inequality on or off. To make the rule g(x) ≤ 0 switchable, write

g(x) ≤ M · b, b ∈ {0, 1}

With b = 0 it reads g(x) ≤ 0: the rule is on. With b = 1 it reads g(x) ≤ M. For that to be harmless, M must be at least the largest value g can take on the region you care about. Example: x lies in [0, 10] and the rule is x ≤ 2, so g(x) = x − 2. Its largest value is 10 − 2 = 8, so M = 8 is the smallest valid choice, and the switchable rule is x ≤ 2 + 8b.

Logical OR. The constraints of a convex problem are joined by AND. To demand "x ≤ 2 OR x ≥ 4", give each side its own switch and insist that at least one stays on:

x ≤ 2 + 8b1, x ≥ 4 − 4b2
b1 + b2 ≤ 1

The second M is 4, because 4 − x is at most 4 on [0, 10]. Check x = 5: set b2 = 0 and b1 = 1, and every row holds. Check x = 3: both rules fail, so b1 = b2 = 1, which breaks the last row, and x = 3 is excluded. The allowed set [0, 2] ∪ [4, 10] is not convex; the binaries let a convex solver handle it anyway.

Many solvers also accept an indicator constraint, "if z = 1 then g(x) ≤ 0", and handle it without a hand-picked M. It is the safer choice when M is hard to bound.

You wantWrite it asExample
At most k of nΣ zi ≤ kbest subset: at most k features
Use only what is openxij ≤ yjdepot j serves customers only if open
A fixed cost50y + 3x, x ≤ 100ypay $50 for the van only if used
Switch a rule offg(x) ≤ M · bx ≤ 2 + 8b on [0, 10]
Either-orone switch per side, Σ b ≤ sides − 1x ≤ 2 or x ≥ 4
Not bothxA + xB ≤ 1A and B together are too heavy

4. Bounds from both sides

A convex problem tells you it is solved through a local test, such as the KKT conditions of Day 10. An integer program has no such test, so CO4A squeezes instead: guaranteed limits from one side, real solutions from the other, until they meet. CO4A 24-3

Picture a negotiation. The best offer so far is a price you can actually get; the walk-away limit is a price nobody will beat. When they meet, the deal is done. For our maximization problem:

  • a floor: the value of the incumbent, the best integer-feasible solution found so far. Any real packing gives one; rounding down gave $60.
  • a ceiling: a bound (or dual bound), a guaranteed limit on how good any solution can be. The LP relaxation gave $83.33.

Why is the LP value a ceiling you can trust? A relaxation is an easier problem whose feasible set contains the original one and whose objective is never worse on the original points. CO4A 24-4 Every packing is also a feasible point of the LP, so the LP's best is at least as good as the best packing. CO4A states it for minimization, where the relaxation gives a lower bound:

X ⊆ Y and g(x) ≤ f(x) for x ∈ X
⇒ minx∈Y g(x) ≤ minx∈X f(x)

For a maximization problem, flip it: the relaxation gives an upper bound. The difference between ceiling and floor is the optimality gap (MIP gap). Solvers report it as they run and stop when it falls below a tolerance you choose; a gap of zero means proven optimal. In our example the gap starts at 83.33 − 60 = 23.33. Figure 2 shows how the search in section 5 closes it.

This is Day 9's idea in new clothes. There, every dual-feasible point gave a lower bound on a minimization problem. Here, Lagrangian relaxation does the same: move a hard constraint into the objective with a price u ≥ 0 per unit. CO4A 24-4

For the knapsack, rent the robot's capacity at u dollars per kilogram. You collect 11u for all 11 kg, and each parcel is worth taking only if its fee vi beats its rent u · wi, where wi is its weight:

L(u) = 11u + Σi max(0, vi − u · wi)

The one-line reason it is a ceiling: for any packing that fits, the unused capacity 11 − Σ wixi is ≥ 0, so adding u times it can only raise the value. Try a few prices: L(0) = 115, L(3) = 84, L(10/3) = 83.33, L(4) = 88. The lowest ceiling is at u = 10/3, which is B's dollars per kilogram, and it equals the LP bound. For a single knapsack row the two always agree.

5. Branch and bound

Rounding failed, but the LP did point at B, the item it could not decide on. So split on B: one branch says "take B" (xB = 1), the other "skip B" (xB = 0). Every packing lands in exactly one branch, so the best packing is the better of the two branch optima.

Each branch is a smaller knapsack with its own LP ceiling. The key move: if a branch's ceiling is no better than a packing you already hold, nothing inside it can win, so discard the whole branch unopened.

Picture hunting for the cheapest flight. You already hold a $400 ticket. If the most optimistic fare through Tokyo is $450, you never look at a single Tokyo route.

Branch and bound (B&B) repeats this move. Each piece is a node in a tree. CO4A writes the splitting rule for minimization over a set X cut into pieces X1, …, Xk: CO4A 24-5

minx∈X f(x) = mini ( minx∈Xi f(x) )

Pruning (or fathoming) discards a node for good, in one of three ways:

  • its relaxation is infeasible, so the node holds no points;
  • its relaxation's solution is already integer, so record it as a candidate incumbent;
  • its bound is no better than the incumbent (for our maximization, bound ≤ incumbent).

Otherwise, branch on a fractional variable and add the two children to the list of open nodes. Here is the whole search on the robot's parcels:

  1. Root: x = (1, 7/9, 0, 0), bound $83.33. B is fractional, so split on B.
  2. B = 1 fills 9 kg and leaves 2 kg, so half of A fits: x = (1/2, 1, 0, 0), bound $60. B = 0 takes A, then C (9 kg in all), then 2/7 of D: x = (1, 0, 1, 2/7), bound 545/7 ≈ $77.86.
  3. Open the more promising node, B = 0, and split on D. D = 1 gives x = (1, 0, 0, 1), $70, integer: the first incumbent. D = 0 gives x = (1, 0, 1, 0), $75, integer: the new incumbent.
  4. Only B = 1 is left. Its bound $60 ≤ $75, so prune it. Nothing is open, so $75 is proven optimal.

That took 5 LP solves instead of 16 packings. The tree itself is the proof: every branch was either solved or shown unable to beat $75.

Which open node comes next? CO4A leaves this open; two standard rules are worth knowing. Best-bound search always opens the node with the highest ceiling. It tends to solve the fewest nodes but can keep many open at once. Depth-first search keeps diving down one branch before backing up. It finds feasible points early and uses little memory, but a dive into a poor branch wastes work.

On our parcels, depth-first search that tries "take" first dives into B = 1. With no incumbent yet, nothing can be pruned, so it digs four levels deep, meets three infeasible nodes (13, 14 and 16 kg), and finds B alone, worth $30. Then it backs up to B = 0 and finds $70 and $75. Total: 11 LP solves instead of 5. See the branch-and-bound card for the general algorithm.

Try it: the widget opens on the finished best-bound search. Press Reset, then Step to open one node at a time, and read the log below the tree. Then switch to "Depth-first, take first" and watch the dive.

Notice that the root bound is $83.33, and best-bound proves $75 (A + C) optimal with 5 LP solves, pruning B = 1 because $60 ≤ $75. Switch to depth-first, take first: it needs 11 LP solves (3 infeasible), and its best-so-far goes $30 → $70 → $75.

The same best-bound search in plain Python, where lp is the greedy fill from section 2:

import heapq
v, w, W = [60, 30, 15, 10], [4, 9, 5, 7], 11      # items sorted by $ per kg

def lp(fix):                                       # LP bound with some items fixed to 0 or 1
    cap = W - sum(w[i] for i in fix if fix[i])
    if cap < 0: return None, None                  # infeasible: too heavy already
    x = [fix.get(i, 0) for i in range(4)]
    for i in (i for i in range(4) if i not in fix):
        x[i] = min(1, cap / w[i]); cap -= x[i] * w[i]   # greedy fill, one item may be cut
    return sum(a * b for a, b in zip(v, x)), x

best, solves = 0, 1
bound, x = lp({}); heap = [(-bound, 0, {}, x)]     # best-bound: largest bound first
while heap:
    nb, _, fix, x = heapq.heappop(heap)
    if -nb <= best: continue                       # prune: cannot beat the incumbent
    j = next(i for i in range(4) if 0 < x[i] < 1)  # the fractional item
    for f in (1, 0):                               # take it, then skip it
        b, xc = lp({**fix, j: f}); solves += 1
        if b is None: continue
        if all(t in (0, 1) for t in xc): best = max(best, b)
        else: heapq.heappush(heap, (-b, solves, {**fix, j: f}, xc))
print(best, solves)                                # 75 5

6. Cutting planes and branch and cut

Branching splits the region in two; a cutting plane shaves it instead. Picture whittling a block of wood toward the shape hidden inside, the integer points. Each cut slices off a corner that contains none of them.

The ideal finished shape is the convex hull of the integer points: the smallest convex set that contains them all. With a linear objective, the LP over the convex hull has the same optimum as the integer program, because an LP's optimum sits at a corner and every corner of the hull is an integer point. CO4A 25-1-1 The catch is that the hull can need exponentially many inequalities, so nobody writes it down in full.

Instead, add inequalities one at a time. A valid inequality is one that every integer-feasible point satisfies. It is a cutting plane (or cut) if the current fractional LP solution x(k) violates it: CO4A 25-1-2

valid: πTx ≤ π0 for every integer-feasible x
cut: valid, and πTx(k) > π0

The loop: solve the LP; if the answer is integer, stop; otherwise add a cut and solve again.

The robot's parcels give the easiest cuts. A cover cut says that if a set of items is too heavy for the bag, you cannot take all of them. A and B weigh 13 kg > 11 kg, so

xA + xB ≤ 1

Every packing obeys it, but the LP point (1, 7/9, 0, 0) has xA + xB = 1.78, so it is cut off. The new LP optimum is (1, 0, 1, 2/7), worth $77.86. C and D weigh 12 kg > 11 kg, so xC + xD ≤ 1 is valid too. With both cuts the LP optimum is (1, 0, 1, 0), worth $75. That point is integer, so it is optimal, with no branching at all. In the widget, pick one cut and best-bound needs 3 LP solves; pick both and it needs 1.

Cover cuts only work on knapsack rows. In 1958 Gomory found a recipe for any integer program with integer data. CO4A 25-1 It rests on one fact: if a ≤ b and a is an integer, then a ≤ ⌊b⌋, where ⌊b⌋ means b rounded down. CO4A 25-1-3

A tiny example. Maximize x2 subject to 3x1 + 2x2 ≤ 6 and −3x1 + 2x2 ≤ 0, with x1, x2 ≥ 0 and integer. The LP region is the triangle in Figure 3, and the LP optimum is its top corner (1, 1.5), with value 1.5.

Add slack variables s1 = 6 − 3x1 − 2x2 and s2 = 3x1 − 2x2, both ≥ 0. All the data are integers, so s1 and s2 are integers at every integer point. The simplex method's final row for x2 reads

x2 + ¼s1 + ¼s2 = 3/2

Keep only the fractional part of each number: 0 for x2's coefficient 1, and ½ for the right side 3/2. Since x2 is an integer, the remaining terms must make up at least that ½:

¼s1 + ¼s2 ≥ ½, that is, s1 + s2 ≥ 2

Since s1 + s2 = 6 − 4x2, the cut is 6 − 4x2 ≥ 2, or x2 ≤ 1. The new LP value is 1, and the integer point (1, 1) reaches it, so (1, 1) is optimal. In general, a Gomory cut comes from any tableau row Σ ajxj = a0 with fractional a0 and integer xj ≥ 0: CO4A 25-1-3

Σj (aj − ⌊aj⌋) xj ≥ a0 − ⌊a0⌋

Real solvers do both moves. Branch and cut is branch and bound with cuts added at the nodes: solve the relaxation; stop if it is infeasible or integer; otherwise either add a cut and solve again, or branch. CO4A 25-1-4 CO4A names Gurobi, CPLEX and FICO as examples.

The history, as CO4A reports it: Dantzig, Fulkerson and Johnson used cuts on the travelling salesman problem in 1954, and Gomory gave a general method in 1958. For about 30 years cuts were thought impractical. Around 1990 they were combined with branch and bound, and branch and cut became the core of commercial solvers. CO4A 25-1 CO4A also reports that from 1990 to 2016 MIP solving got more than 500,000 times faster from algorithms and more than 500,000 times faster from hardware, about 2.5 × 1011 combined. CO4A 25-1-4

So: hard in theory, often fine in practice. The worst case still grows exponentially with the number of integer variables. Yet branch and cut solves many practical models in seconds to minutes, as the footstep planner below shows. For modellers, a tight relaxation (small M, good cuts) often matters more than a faster computer.

7. Integers at work: statistics and robots

CO4A's chapter 25 ends with two statistics examples. Best subset selection asks for the best regression model that uses only k of p features. Give each coefficient βi a switch zi, so that zi = 0 forces βi = 0: CO4A 25-2-1

minimize ½‖y − Xβ‖22
subject to |βi| ≤ Mizi, Σ zi ≤ k
z ∈ {0, 1}p

Here y holds n measurements, X is the n × p data, and Mi comes from preprocessing. CO4A's tip for this MIQP is a warm start: start the solver from a good solution, found by cheap gradient steps that keep only the k largest coefficients. In CO4A's figures (n = 350, p = 64, k = 6) the good solution appears early, most of the time goes into proving it optimal, and warm starts beat cold starts. CO4A 25-2-1

The second example fits a line that ignores outliers by minimizing the q-th smallest absolute residual. CO4A says it tolerates about 50% outliers but is NP-hard; binaries choose which residuals sit below a threshold. (The page is titled "least mean squares", but it covers least median, or quantile, of squares.) CO4A 25-2-2

Which side of the obstacle? A point robot drives in the square [0, 10] × [0, 10] (in metres). A box obstacle covers [2, 4] × [1, 3]. Being outside the box means: left of x = 2, OR right of x = 4, OR below y = 1, OR above y = 3. That set is not convex, so give each side a binary, with b = 1 meaning "this side is switched off":

x ≤ 2 + M b1, x ≥ 4 − M b2
y ≤ 1 + M b3, y ≥ 3 − M b4
b1 + b2 + b3 + b4 ≤ 3

The last row keeps at least one side on. How big must M be? A switched-off row must still hold everywhere in the square. Row 1 needs x − 2 ≤ M, and x − 2 is at most 10 − 2 = 8. The other rows need 4 − 0 = 4, 10 − 1 = 9 and 3 − 0 = 3. One shared M must cover the largest, so the smallest valid shared M is 9 (M = 10 also works).

Check the point (5, 2): switch on row 2 (b2 = 0, and x ≥ 4 holds) and switch the rest off. Allowed. Check the obstacle's center (3, 2): every row fails when switched on, so all four b's must be 1, and their sum 4 breaks the last row. Excluded.

Now the warning. In the LP relaxation each b may be fractional. With M = 10 and b = (0.1, 0.1, 0.1, 0.1), the rows read x ≤ 3, x ≥ 3, y ≤ 2 and y ≥ 2, so the center (3, 2) is allowed, and the sum 0.4 ≤ 3 is fine. The relaxation drives straight through the obstacle. With M = 1000, b = 0.001 each is enough. A bigger M gives a weaker relaxation and worse bounds, so use the smallest valid M.

For a trajectory, repeat the four rows for every time step and obstacle, a pattern Deits and Tedrake credit to Richards and colleagues' UAV planners. Deits & Tedrake 2014 With 20 time steps and 3 obstacles that is 4 × 20 × 3 = 240 binaries.

Footstep planning. Deits and Tedrake turn the question around (see the footstep paper). Instead of one binary per obstacle side, they first compute R convex patches of safe, flat ground, using the IRIS method from the IRIS paper. Then a binary Hr,j says "footstep j lies in region r": Deits & Tedrake 2014

Hr,j = 1 ⇒ Arfj ≤ br
Σr Hr,j = 1 for each step j

Here fj is the position of footstep j, and Arf ≤ br describes region r. Once every H is fixed, the rest of the problem is convex. A reachability rule keeps each step inside two discs placed relative to the previous foot, which is a convex quadratic constraint. Turning enters through sin and cos, replaced by piecewise-linear pieces that more binaries choose, built so the robot never overestimates its reach. Because of the quadratic constraints, the authors call the problem a MIQCQP: a mixed-integer program with a quadratic objective and quadratic constraints. Deits & Tedrake 2014

With Gurobi on an Intel i7 2.9 GHz laptop, typical plans with 10–20 footsteps and 10 safe regions took from a few seconds to one minute, and a few steps took well under a second. Every plan shown was within 0.1% of the global optimum, as reported by Gurobi. The limits are honest ones: a person had to seed the safe regions, and only the foot positions are checked for collisions, not the swing between them. Deits & Tedrake 2014 Day 19 returns to obstacles and convex pieces, and the GCS paper builds formulations whose relaxations are much tighter.

Analogy

Packing a suitcase. You take the camera or you don't; you can't pack 7/9 of it (binary). A quick estimate that pretends you could pack fractions tells you the best you could hope for (relaxation). If a whole family of plans, say "everything with the big boots", cannot beat the bag you already packed, you stop considering it (pruning). And noticing "the boots and the tripod never fit together" removes nonsense plans before you even start (a cut).

Explain it to a 10-year-old

Your backpack holds 11 kg of toys, and each toy has a fun score. First you cheat and pretend you can saw a toy in half. That tells you the most fun you could ever get. Then you ask: "Do I take the heavy toy or not?" For each answer you cheat again to see the best you could get. If one answer can't beat a backpack you already packed, you never think about it again.

Common misunderstandings

  • "Round the LP solution and call it optimal." B = 7/9 rounds to a 13 kg packing that does not fit, or to A alone at $60. The optimum is $75.
  • "Pick M really big, to be safe." A huge M makes the relaxation weak: with M = 10 the obstacle's center is LP-feasible at b = 0.1 each, and with M = 1000 at b = 0.001. It also hurts the numerics. Use the smallest M that is valid on bounded variables, or an indicator constraint.
  • "The relaxation is always a lower bound." Only for minimization. For a maximization like the knapsack it is an upper bound.
  • "Branch and bound tries every combination." Here it solved 5 LPs instead of checking 16 packings, because the bounds did the pruning. The worst case is still exponential.
  • "A cut may throw away integer solutions." A valid cut removes only fractional points. Every packing still obeys xA + xB ≤ 1.

Going deeper (optional): why each step is exact

Branching. The children xj = 0 and xj = 1 split the parent's integer points into two groups with nothing lost, so the better child optimum is the parent optimum (CO4A 24-5's identity). Fractional points in between are dropped, which is the point.

Lagrangian bounds. For any feasible x and u ≥ 0 the price term uT(Ax − b) is ≤ 0, so the relaxed value bounds the true one. L(u) is a pointwise minimum of affine functions of u, so it is concave (in CO4A's minimization form) and can be maximized with subgradient steps from Day 7. CO4A 24-4

Gomory cuts. Split each coefficient into its integer part and its fractional part fj ∈ [0, 1). At an integer point the integer parts give an integer, so Σ fjxj differs from f0 by a whole number. It is also ≥ 0, so it is at least f0. Making a pure cutting-plane method finish in finitely many steps needs extra rules, which we skip.

The convex hull. If the data A and b are rational, the convex hull of the integer points of {x : Ax ≤ b} is a polyhedron, but it can need exponentially many inequalities. CO4A 25-1-1 Other cut families (Chvátal, split, lift-and-project) are named in CO4A 25-1-3.

Check yourself

Q1. The LP relaxation of the robot knapsack is worth $83.33. What does that tell you?

Every packing is a feasible point of the LP, so the LP's value is a ceiling for this maximization problem. No packing reaches it here: the best is $75, and the LP point itself uses 7/9 of B.

Q2. Node "B = 1" has bound $60, and the incumbent is $75. What happens to the node?

The bound is the best any packing with B can earn. Since $60 ≤ $75, branching on A would only waste LP solves. $60 is a bound, not a packing, so it cannot be an incumbent.

Q3. Why did depth-first search (take first) need 11 LP solves when best-bound needed 5?

Depth-first does prune by bound, but there was nothing to compare against until it found $30 at the bottom of the B = 1 branch. Best-bound opened B = 0 first, found $75, and pruned B = 1 at once.

Q4. On x ∈ [0, 10] you write the switchable rule x ≤ 2 + M·b. What is the smallest valid M?

With b = 1 the row must hold for every x in [0, 10], so 2 + M ≥ 10, giving M ≥ 8. M = 10 also works but is weaker, and 1000 makes the relaxation much weaker.

Q5. Why does a very large M hurt, even though it is still valid?

The integer problem is unchanged, so its optimum is the same. But tiny fractional b values now switch rules almost fully off: with M = 1000, b = 0.001 lets the relaxed robot drive through the obstacle's center.

Q6. What is a cutting plane?

A cut must be valid (keeps every integer point) and must slice off the current LP solution. xA + xB ≤ 1 is one: every packing obeys it, but (1, 7/9, 0, 0) does not.

Recap: things to remember

  1. A mixed-integer program is a convex problem plus "some variables are whole numbers". Binaries model yes/no choices, counts, links, fixed costs and OR.
  2. Big-M switches a rule off with b = 1. Choose the smallest M that is valid on the bounded region; bigger M means a weaker relaxation.
  3. Dropping integrality gives a relaxation and a bound (upper for max, lower for min). Rounding its answer can be infeasible or poor: $60 versus $75.
  4. Branch and bound splits on a fractional variable and prunes nodes that are infeasible, integer, or bounded below the incumbent. Best-bound took 5 LPs here; depth-first took 11.
  5. Cuts shave fractional corners without losing integer points. Branch and cut combines both, and it is how modern solvers, and planners like Deits and Tedrake's footstep MIQCQP, work.
