Week 3 · Day 16

When it isn't convex: nonlinear optimization

After today you can tell local from global minima and saddle points, read the KKT conditions for nonlinear programs, and explain how SQP, Gauss–Newton and Levenberg–Marquardt solve the nonconvex problems that robots actually face.

About 70 min · Needs Days 10 and 11 · No CO4A chapter (this day is new)

Today's big idea

Most robot problems are not convex. Rotations, camera projections and vehicle dynamics bend the landscape into many valleys. Local solvers still work well, but they only promise the floor of a nearby valley, and the starting point decides which one. The best nonconvex solvers are built from convex pieces: each step solves a convex model, and a convex relaxation can sometimes prove that the answer is global.

1. Many valleys: local minima, saddles and the starting point

On Day 1 a convex function was a single bowl. Walk downhill from anywhere and you reach the one bottom. A nonconvex function is a mountain range. Walking downhill takes you to the floor of whichever valley you started above.

Two words make this precise. A point x* is a local minimum if no feasible point near it is lower: f(x*) ≤ f(x) for every feasible x close to x*. It is a global minimum if no feasible point anywhere is lower. In a convex problem every local minimum is global (Day 4). Without convexity that promise is gone.

A stationary point is a point where the gradient is zero, ∇f(x) = 0. Every unconstrained minimum of a smooth function is stationary, but so is every hilltop and every mountain pass. To tell them apart you look at the Hessian ∇2f, the matrix of second derivatives, which measures how the surface curves.

∇f(x*) = 0 and ∇2f(x*) ≻ 0 ⇒ x* is a strict local minimum

The symbol ≻ 0 means positive definite: the function curves upward in every direction. At any local minimum the Hessian is at least ⪰ 0, so it never curves down. A saddle point is a stationary point that curves up in some directions and down in others, like a mountain pass. The standard example is g(x, y) = x2 − y2 at the origin: ∇g(0, 0) = 0, and the Hessian is diag(2, −2), so the surface rises along x and falls along y.

Now a number. Day 1's bumpy curve, a "double well" (there called g), is f(x) = x4 − 4x2 + x. It has three stationary points on [−2, 2], where f′(x) = 4x3 − 8x + 1 = 0:

xf(x)f″(x)What it is
−1.4730−5.444218.04 > 0global minimum
0.12600.0627−7.81 < 0local maximum (a hilltop)
1.3470−2.618613.77 > 0local minimum, not global

A solver that stops at x ≈ 1.347 passes every local test, yet its answer is 2.83 above the best one.

The set of starts that a method sends to the same minimum is that minimum's basin of attraction. Run gradient descent (Day 6, step 0.02, 2,000 steps) from the nine starts −2, −1.5, …, 2. The five starts at or below 0 reach the global minimum. The four starts at 0.5 and above get stuck at 1.347. The hilltop at x ≈ 0.126 is the border between the two basins.

The cheapest fix is multi-start: run a local solver from many starting points and keep the best result. The starts can be random or on a grid, and they run in parallel.

x̂ = best of local_solve(x₀(k)), k = 1 … K

On the double well, 5 of the 9 grid starts land in the right basin, so the grid finds the global minimum. But multi-start gives no certificate: more starts only raise the odds. Boyd and Vandenberghe put the trade simply. Local methods are fast but say little about how far from global they ended. Global methods can certify the answer, at a worst-case cost that grows exponentially. Boyd & Vandenberghe 2004 §1.4

Analogy

A hiker in thick fog has only a slope sensor. She can always walk downhill, and she can tell when the ground is flat and rises on every side. That proves "I'm at a low point nearby". It can never prove "this is the lowest point in the country". Sending several hikers from different places, and comparing altimeters at the end, is multi-start.

2. Constraints: the KKT conditions for nonlinear programs

A nonlinear program (NLP) is an optimization problem whose objective or constraints are nonlinear, and possibly nonconvex. We use Day 10's notation, writing its lj as ℓj so it is not mistaken for a 1:

minimize f(x)
subject to hi(x) ≤ 0, ℓj(x) = 0

Recall Day 10's picture: a ball rests against some walls. Its downhill pull is exactly cancelled by the push of the walls it touches. A wall can only push, never pull, and a wall it is not touching pushes with zero force.

The formula says the same thing. The Lagrangian is L(x, λ, ν) = f(x) + Σ λihi(x) + Σ νjℓj(x). Each Lagrange multiplier λi or νj is the force (or price) of one constraint. An inequality that holds with equality at x is an active constraint: it is a wall you are touching.

∇f(x) + Σ λi∇hi(x) + Σ νj∇ℓj(x) = 0
hi(x) ≤ 0, ℓj(x) = 0, λi ≥ 0, λihi(x) = 0

These are the same four KKT conditions as on Day 10. Two things change when the problem is not convex. Wikipedia: KKT

First, KKT is necessary only under a constraint qualification. A constraint qualification is a regularity condition on the constraints. The common one is LICQ (linear independence constraint qualification): the gradients of the active constraints at x* are linearly independent. If LICQ holds at a local minimum, the KKT conditions hold there, with unique multipliers.

Here is what goes wrong without one. Minimize x subject to x2 ≤ 0. The only feasible point is x = 0, so it is optimal. But ∇h(0) = 2·0 = 0, so LICQ fails, and stationarity would need 1 + λ·0 = 0, which is impossible. The optimum is not a KKT point. The wall exists, but it has no direction to push in.

Second, KKT is no longer sufficient. On Day 10, any KKT point of a convex problem was optimal. Now KKT points include maxima and saddles, so you also check curvature. In plain words: stand at the KKT point and look along every direction that keeps the active constraints satisfied, to first order. If the Lagrangian curves upward along all of them, you are at a strict local minimum. This is the second-order sufficient condition:

sT∇2xxL(x*, λ, ν) s > 0 for every such direction s ≠ 0

A worked example shows both points. Minimize x₁ + x₂ on the circle x₁2 + x₂2 = 2, so ℓ(x) = x₁2 + x₂2 − 2. The gradient ∇ℓ = (2x₁, 2x₂) is never zero on the circle, so LICQ holds everywhere. Stationarity reads 1 + 2νx₁ = 0 and 1 + 2νx₂ = 0, so x₁ = x₂ = −1/(2ν). Putting that on the circle gives ν = ±½.

KKT pointνf∇2xxL = 2νIVerdict
(−1, −1)½−2I, curves upminimum
(1, 1)−½2−I, curves downmaximum

A note on sources. The nonlinear-programming theory in Sections 2 and 3 is standard textbook material, taken here from the Wikipedia articles on KKT and SQP and from Boyd and Vandenberghe. No page of Nocedal and Wright's Numerical Optimization, the usual reference, was opened while writing this lesson.

3. SQP: solve a QP at every step

Picture driving a winding road in the dark. You fit a parabola to the stretch your headlights show, drive to its best point, and fit again. Sequential quadratic programming (SQP) does this with a problem. At the current guess xk it builds a QP (Day 5): a quadratic model of the Lagrangian and straight-line models of the constraints. It solves the QP for a step d, moves, and repeats. Wikipedia: SQP

minimize over d: ∇f(xk)Td + ½ dT∇2xxL(xk) d
subject to ℓ(xk) + ∇ℓ(xk)Td = 0
h(xk) + ∇h(xk)Td ≤ 0

With only equality constraints, the QP's own KKT conditions are one linear system. That system is exactly Newton's method (Day 11) applied to the KKT equations of the original problem. This is why SQP converges fast once it is close. ν⁺ is the new multiplier estimate:

∇2xxL · d + ∇ℓ · ν⁺ = −∇f
∇ℓTd = −ℓ(xk)

Run it on the circle from x₀ = (−1.5, −0.5) with ν₀ = 1. This start is off the circle: ℓ(x₀) = 2.25 + 0.25 − 2 = 0.5. Here ∇ℓ(x₀) = (−3, −1) and ∇2xxL = 2ν₀I = 2I. The system becomes 2d₁ − 3ν⁺ = −1, 2d₂ − ν⁺ = −1 and −3d₁ − d₂ = −0.5. Its solution is d = (0.25, −0.25) with ν⁺ = 0.5, so x₁ = (−1.25, −0.75).

kxkνkconstraint error ℓ(xk)
0(−1.5, −0.5)10.5
1(−1.25, −0.75)0.50.125
2(−1.0368, −1.0221)0.48530.119
3(−1.00024, −1.00066)0.49941.8×10⁻³
4(−1.000000, −1.000000)0.50004.9×10⁻⁷
5(−1.000000, −1.000000)0.50001.8×10⁻¹³

From step 3 on, the error roughly squares each step (10⁻³, 10⁻⁷, 10⁻¹³): Newton speed. The figure above draws this path on the right.

Real SQP solvers add safety gear. On a nonconvex problem ∇2xxL can curve down, which makes the QP nonconvex. Solvers then regularize the matrix, or replace it by a BFGS approximation kept positive definite (BFGS card). A merit function or a filter judges whether a step made progress on both the objective and the constraint violation. A line search or trust region decides how far to go. Codes that implement SQP include SciPy's SLSQP, SNOPT, KNITRO and acados. Wikipedia: SQP See also the SQP card.

The robotics payoff: nonlinear vehicle dynamics in a model predictive controller do not stop you from using the QP machinery of Day 17. SQP turns the nonlinear problem into a sequence of QPs of that kind.

4. Interior points for nonconvex problems: IPOPT

Recall Day 12. A barrier method replaces each inequality hi(x) ≤ 0 by a log penalty that shoots to infinity at the wall. It then shrinks the barrier weight μ step by step, following the central path from deep inside the feasible set toward the boundary.

minimize f(x) − μ Σ log(−hi(x)) s.t. ℓ(x) = 0
then let μ → 0

This is Day 12's t·f(x) + φ(x) divided by t, with μ = 1/t, so shrinking μ is the same as growing t.

Nothing in that recipe needs convexity. The open-source solver IPOPT applies it to general NLPs of the form "minimize f(x) subject to gL ≤ g(x) ≤ gU and xL ≤ x ≤ xU". Its home page calls it an "interior point line search filter method that aims to find a local solution". The functions may be nonconvex but must be twice continuously differentiable. Ipopt docs This makes IPOPT an interior-point method for NLPs. Compare the barrier card and the primal–dual card.

What changes without convexity? Each Newton step uses the Hessian of the Lagrangian. If that Hessian curves down somewhere, which convexity rules out, the step may head for a maximum or a saddle. IPOPT therefore needs a sparse linear solver that reports the matrix's inertia, meaning how many positive and negative eigenvalues it has. MA27, MA57, MUMPS and PARDISO can do this. Ipopt docs The solver uses that count to spot bad curvature and correct it before stepping. The answer is still a local solution, so IPOPT also needs a sensible start.

SQPInterior point (IPOPT)
Each step solvesa QP modela Newton system for the barrier problem
Inequalitieslinearized; the QP picks which are activea log barrier keeps x strictly inside
Progress testmerit function or filterfilter line search
Resulta local solutiona local solution

5. Nonlinear least squares and Gauss–Newton

Most robot estimation is fitting: choose parameters so that predictions match measurements. In pose-graph SLAM you choose robot poses so that odometry and loop closures agree. In bundle adjustment you refine camera poses and 3-D points so that their projections land on the measured pixels. In calibration you choose camera intrinsics, lidar-to-camera mounting or IMU biases. All of these are the same problem, and rotations sit inside the residuals, which makes them nonconvex.

The common form is nonlinear least squares. Each residual ri(x) is a prediction minus a measurement. The Jacobian J = ∂r/∂x stacks the residual gradients as rows. Global minimization is intractable in general, so solvers settle for a local minimum. Ceres Solver docs

minimize F(x) = ½ Σ ri(x)2 = ½‖r(x)‖22

Gauss–Newton pretends every residual is linear near the current x: r(x + δ) ≈ r(x) + Jδ. Then F becomes a convex quadratic in δ, an ordinary linear least-squares problem. Its solution comes from the normal equations:

(JTJ) δ = −JTr, then x ← x + δ

Compare Newton (Day 11). The gradient of F is JTr, and its Hessian is JTJ + Σ ri∇2ri. Gauss–Newton drops the second term. It never needs second derivatives, and JTJ ⪰ 0 always. The dropped term is small when the residuals are small, so near a good fit the method is fast: quadratic convergence if the fit is exact, linear otherwise. Wikipedia: Gauss–Newton

Now real numbers. Nine measurements were taken at t = 0, 0.5, …, 4: y = 4.86, 4.05, 3.08, 2.57, 2.17, 2.02, 1.47, 0.96, 0.91 (made as 5e−0.4t plus a little noise). Fit the model y = a·ebt. The residual is ri = a·ebti − yi, and row i of J is [ebti, a·tiebti].

Start at (a, b) = (1, 0). Every prediction is 1, so F = 16.82. The rows of J are [1, ti], which gives JTJ = [[9, 18], [18, 51]] and JTr = (−13.09, −11.76). Solving gives δ = (3.377, −0.961), so the new point is (4.377, −0.961) with F = 7.09. One step cut the cost by more than half.

Keep going and something odd happens: F goes 16.8 → 7.09 → 62.9 → 6.16 → 0.359 → 0.0773 → 0.0761. Step 2 made the fit nearly 9 times worse. The linear model was trusted too far, where the exponential bends hard. The method recovers and converges in 6 steps to a = 4.86548, b = −0.40969, with F = 0.07607 (RMS residual 0.13). From the start (1, −3) it is worse: the first step jumps to b ≈ 31.9, where e31.9·4 is astronomically large, and F ≈ 7.5×10¹¹¹. Ceres's documentation warns that the plain iteration may not converge. Ceres Solver docs

6. Levenberg–Marquardt: Gauss–Newton on a leash

Think of walking a dog. When it walks nicely you give it a long leash. After it bolts into the road you shorten the leash. Levenberg–Marquardt (LM) puts Gauss–Newton on a leash by adding a penalty on the step length.

(JTJ + λI) δ = −JTr

The damping parameter λ is the leash. With λ = 0 you get the Gauss–Newton step. With a large λ the equation becomes δ ≈ −JTr / λ, a short step straight downhill, as in gradient descent (Day 6). Any λ > 0 gives a direction that goes downhill. Madsen et al. 2004 (This λ is LM's traditional name. It has nothing to do with the multipliers of Section 2.)

Here are the first steps from (1, 0) for four values of λ:

λstep δ = (Δa, Δb)step lengthnew F
0 (Gauss–Newton)(3.377, −0.961)3.517.09
1(2.393, −0.602)2.475.94
10(0.703, −0.015)0.709.84
100(0.109, 0.065)0.1314.86

As λ grows, the step shrinks and turns toward steepest descent. Here λ = 1 beats plain Gauss–Newton (5.94 against 7.09), and λ = 100 barely moves.

A fixed λ is a poor compromise, so LM adjusts it as it goes. The simplest rule, used in the widget below: try the step. If F drops, accept it and divide λ by 10. If not, reject it and multiply λ by 10. Careful solvers instead compare the actual decrease with the decrease the linear model predicted. That ratio is the gain ratio ρ:

ρ = [F(x) − F(x + δ)] / [M(0) − M(δ)], M(δ) = ½‖r + Jδ‖2

ρ near 1 means the model was right (loosen the leash); a small or negative ρ means it was wrong (tighten it). Marquardt's rule doubles λ when ρ < 0.25 and divides it by 3 when ρ > 0.75. Madsen et al. 2004 Seen this way, LM is a trust region method in disguise: a large λ means a small region where you trust the model. Ceres writes it with an explicit radius that it doubles or halves. It also scales the penalty with D = √diag(JTJ), so the units of a and b do not matter. Ceres Solver docs

Adaptive LM pays off on our data. From (1, 0) with λ₀ = 1, F goes 16.8 → 5.94 → 2.53 → 0.144 → 0.0762 → 0.0761: 5 steps, every one downhill. From (1, −3), where Gauss–Newton blew up, it converges in 6 iterations with one rejected step. A fixed leash is slow if it is short: λ = 10 needs 54 steps, and λ = 100 has still not converged after 200 (F = 0.0885).

lam = 1.0
for k in range(200):
    r, J = residuals(x), jacobian(x)
    d = solve(J.T @ J + lam * I, -J.T @ r)
    if F(x + d) < F(x):          # model was good enough
        x, lam = x + d, lam / 10  # accept, loosen the leash
    else:
        lam = lam * 10            # reject, tighten the leash
    if converged(x): break

Robot-scale problems run the same loop with a huge, sparse J. In bundle adjustment JTJ splits into camera and point blocks, and Ceres uses the Schur complement trick: it eliminates the points, solves a much smaller system for the cameras, then recovers the points. Ceres Solver docs See the Gauss–Newton and LM card.

Try it: with the defaults (Gauss–Newton from (1, 0)), press Step six times and watch the curve and the cost. Then pick "LM, adaptive λ" and do the same. Finally choose the start (1, −3) and compare the two methods again.

Notice: by default (Gauss–Newton from (1, 0)) the log reads 16.8 → 7.09 → 62.9 → 6.16 → 0.359 → 0.0773 → 0.0761. The cost jumps up at step 2, and the run still converges in 6 steps, ending at a = 4.8655, b = −0.4097. Switch to adaptive LM and it takes 5 steps, all downhill. From (1, −3), Gauss–Newton diverges at step 1, while adaptive LM converges in 6 (5 accepted, 1 rejected).

7. Where convexity still helps

You cannot flatten the mountains, but convex tools still give you a good place to start, a reliable map of the valley floor around you, and sometimes an altimeter that proves nothing is lower. Boyd and Vandenberghe list the same roles: convex starting points, convex heuristics, and bounds from relaxations and duality. Boyd & Vandenberghe 2004 §1.4

1. Good starting points. Take logs of the model: ln y = ln a + bt. This is linear in (ln a, b), so fitting it is ordinary least squares, a convex problem with a closed-form answer. It gives a = 4.9644, b = −0.4247 and F = 0.0851. One Gauss–Newton step from there reaches 0.07607, against 6 steps and a scary detour from (1, 0). Try the "log-linear fit" start in the widget. SLAM solvers also start from a carefully built guess: the Gauss–Newton baseline in the SE-Sync paper uses the "chordal initialization". SE-Sync, arXiv v2

2. Convex subproblems. SQP solves a QP at each step, and Gauss–Newton solves a linear least-squares problem. Sequential convex programming (SCP) generalizes the idea. At x(k) it replaces the problem by a convex approximation and solves it inside a trust region:

T(k) = { x : |xi − xi(k)| ≤ ρi }

In the Stanford EE364b version, a step is accepted if the true decrease is at least 10% of the predicted one. Then ρ grows by a factor 1.1; otherwise it halves. The same slides note that this kind of method, for least squares, is often called Gauss–Newton, and some variants Levenberg–Marquardt. Stanford EE364b Day 18 builds trajectory optimization on SCP (SCP card).

3. Lower bounds. The Lagrange dual of any problem, convex or not, is a convex problem whose value is a lower bound (Day 9). EE364b runs SCP from 10 starts on a nonconvex QP with 20 variables. The runs end between about −60 and −50, and the dual bound is about −66.5. So the best run is provably within about 6.5 (roughly 10%) of the true optimum. (These values are read off the slides' plot, so they are approximate.) Multi-start alone never gives such a guarantee. Stanford EE364b

4. Certifiable SLAM. Pose-graph SLAM looks for rotations Ri and translations ti that best explain noisy relative measurements R̃ij and t̃ij, each with a weight κij or τij. The maximum-likelihood problem is:

minimize Σ κij‖Rj − RiR̃ij‖F2 + τij‖tj − ti − Rit̃ij‖2
over ti ∈ ℝd, Ri ∈ SO(d)

The set of rotations SO(d) is not convex, so the problem is not either, and Gauss–Newton is the de facto standard solver for it. SE-Sync eliminates the translations and solves an SDP relaxation instead: minimize tr(Q̃Z) subject to Z ⪰ 0 with every diagonal block of Z equal to the identity. Every true set of rotations is feasible, so the SDP value is a lower bound. Below a noise threshold the relaxation is an exact relaxation: its solution gives the global optimum. You can also check this after solving, which makes SE-Sync a certifiably correct algorithm. SE-Sync, arXiv v2

DatasetPosesGauss–NewtonSE-SyncSpeed-up
garage1,66117.81 s5.33 s3.3×
cubicle5,750136.86 s13.08 s10.5×
rim10,195575.42 s36.66 s15.7×

On all six benchmarks in the paper's Table 1, both methods reached the same objective value, but only SE-Sync came with a proof: its certified suboptimality was at most 5.6×10⁻¹¹. In simulations the relaxation stayed exact up to about 15° RMS rotation noise, roughly 10 times typical sensor noise. The limits are real: the model assumes no outliers, and it covers pose graphs only, not bundle adjustment. SE-Sync, arXiv v2 Read the SE-Sync paper review.

Explain it to a 10-year-old

You are looking for the lowest spot in a bumpy playground at night. Your flashlight only shows the ground at your feet. You can always walk downhill until you stop in a dip, but it might be a small dip and not the deepest one. So friends start in different places, and you compare. Gauss–Newton guesses the shape of the ground and jumps to the bottom of the guess. Levenberg–Marquardt takes smaller jumps after a guess turns out wrong.

Common misunderstandings

  • "The solver converged, so it found the best answer." Converged means a stationary or KKT point. On the circle, (1, 1) passes the KKT test and is the maximum. The double well's x ≈ 1.347 is a local minimum 2.83 above the global one.
  • "Gauss–Newton always goes downhill." On the widget's data, F jumps from 7.09 to 62.9 at step 2, and from (1, −3) the method diverges. Use LM, a trust region or a line search.
  • "Crank λ up to be safe." Damping trades speed for caution: a fixed λ = 100 had not converged after 200 iterations, while adaptive LM needed 5.
  • "Every optimum satisfies KKT." Only under a constraint qualification. For minimize x subject to x2 ≤ 0, the optimum x = 0 is not a KKT point.
  • "Nonconvex means convex tools are useless." Convex starting points, convex subproblems (SQP, SCP, each Gauss–Newton step) and SDP relaxations such as SE-Sync's are the standard toolkit.

Going deeper (optional): the fine print

Second-order conditions. Precisely, sᵀ∇2xxL s ≥ 0 is necessary and > 0 is sufficient for s in the "critical cone". These are directions tangent to the equality constraints and to the active inequalities with positive multipliers. Degenerate cases need higher-order terms. Wikipedia: KKT

Other constraint qualifications. Weaker ones than LICQ, such as MFCQ, also make KKT necessary. Slater's condition (Day 10) plays this role for convex problems.

SQP's speed. Near a solution where LICQ and the second-order condition hold, the Newton-on-KKT view gives quadratic convergence. With BFGS Hessians it is superlinear.

The IPOPT facts come from its home page. How it corrects bad curvature is in the Wächter–Biegler paper the home page cites, which was not opened, just as no Nocedal and Wright page was.

Check yourself

Q1. A solver reports ∇f(x) = 0 on a nonconvex function. What can you conclude?

Zero gradient only means flat. The double well's hilltop at x ≈ 0.126 and the saddle of x² − y² both have ∇f = 0. You need the Hessian to say more, and even a local minimum need not be global.

Q2. Minimize x₁ + x₂ subject to x₁² + x₂² = 2. Which KKT point is the minimum?

Both (−1, −1) and (1, 1) are KKT points, which is exactly the trap. The second-order check separates them: ∇²L = 2νI is I at (−1, −1) (minimum, f = −2) and −I at (1, 1) (maximum, f = 2). The point (0, √2) fails stationarity.

Q3. What does SQP solve at each iteration?

SQP replaces the problem near xk by a QP and steps to its solution. With equality constraints only, this is Newton's method on the KKT equations, which is why the circle example's constraint error went 10⁻³ → 10⁻⁷ → 10⁻¹³.

Q4. Gauss–Newton approximates the Hessian of F = ½‖r(x)‖² by …

The exact Hessian is JᵀJ + Σ rᵢ∇²rᵢ. Gauss–Newton keeps only JᵀJ, which needs no second derivatives and is always ⪰ 0. JJᵀ has the wrong size: it is m × m (residuals), not n × n (parameters).

Q5. In adaptive LM, a trial step makes F larger (the gain ratio ρ is negative). What should happen?

A negative ρ means the linear model promised a decrease that did not happen. So LM stays put and tightens the leash: a larger λ gives a shorter step, closer to steepest descent. From (1, −3) the widget's adaptive LM rejects one step this way and still converges in 6 iterations.

Q6. What does SE-Sync's certificate tell you when it succeeds?

If the rounded solution attains the SDP's lower bound, nothing can be better, so it is the global optimum. The relaxation is exact only below a noise threshold. Above it, SE-Sync still returns an estimate and a bound, but no certificate.

Recap: things to remember

  1. Without convexity, zero gradient means a minimum, a maximum or a saddle. Local solvers find a nearby valley, and the start decides which one. Multi-start raises the odds but proves nothing.
  2. NLP KKT conditions are necessary only under a constraint qualification such as LICQ, and they are not sufficient. Check that the Lagrangian curves up along the constraints.
  3. SQP solves a QP model at every step (Newton on KKT). IPOPT applies Day 12's barrier idea to nonconvex problems and returns a local solution.
  4. Gauss–Newton solves (JᵀJ)δ = −Jᵀr and can overshoot or diverge. LM adds λI as a leash: it rejects bad steps, raises λ, and lowers it again when the model behaves.
  5. Convexity still helps through convex starting points, convex subproblems (SQP, SCP) and relaxations that can certify a global answer (SE-Sync).

Sources

  1. Convex Optimization, §1.4 (local and global optimization, the role of convex methods), S. Boyd and L. Vandenberghe, Cambridge University Press 2004 (accessed 2026-10-26).
  2. Sequential Convex Programming (lecture slides), Stanford EE364b (accessed 2026-10-26).
  3. Ipopt documentation, home page, COIN-OR (accessed 2026-10-26).
  4. Solving Non-linear Least Squares (documentation source), Ceres Solver, GitHub master branch (accessed 2026-10-26).
  5. Methods for Non-Linear Least Squares Problems, 2nd ed., K. Madsen, H. B. Nielsen and O. Tingleff, DTU IMM 2004 (accessed 2026-10-26).
  6. Karush–Kuhn–Tucker conditions, Wikipedia (accessed 2026-10-26).
  7. Sequential quadratic programming, Wikipedia (accessed 2026-10-26).
  8. Gauss–Newton algorithm, Wikipedia (accessed 2026-10-26).
  9. SE-Sync: A Certifiably Correct Algorithm for Synchronization over the Special Euclidean Group (arXiv v2), D. M. Rosen, L. Carlone, A. S. Bandeira and J. J. Leonard, 2017; journal version in IJRR 2019 (accessed 2026-10-26).
  10. All worked numbers (double well, circle SQP, curve fit, LM runs) were recomputed in Node.js for this lesson on 2026-10-26. The NLP theory is standard and rests on sources 1, 6 and 7. Nocedal and Wright's Numerical Optimization was not opened.

Week 3 · Day 17

Model predictive control as a QP

After today you can write a vehicle MPC problem as a quadratic program, explain the receding-horizon loop, and reason about horizon length, weights, constraints and warm starts in a real-time controller.

About 60 min · Needs Days 5, 10 and 12 · No CO4A chapter (this day is new)

Today's big idea

Model predictive control steers by optimising. Ten times a second the car plans its next two seconds, applies only the first input, measures where it is, and plans again. With a linear model, a quadratic cost and linear limits, each plan is a convex QP like those of Day 5, solvable in milliseconds because every tick's problem is almost the same.

1. Plan, act a little, re-plan

Picture driving on a dark road. Your headlights show the next stretch. You plan a path through what you can see, but you only turn the wheel for this instant. A moment later the beams reach further, and you adjust.

That is model predictive control (MPC): control by repeatedly solving a short optimal-control problem and applying only its first input. The plan looks N steps ahead. N is the horizon, covering N·dt seconds for a time step dt. The window slides forward one step every tick, so this is a receding horizon.

One tick solves the problem below. xk is the predicted state k steps ahead, uk the input, xr the target and x̄ the state measured right now. OSQP docs: MPC

minimize Σk (xk − xr)TQ(xk − xr) + ukTRuk

subject to xk+1 = Axk + Buk, x0 = x̄

umin ≤ uk ≤ umax, xmin ≤ xk ≤ xmax

The weight matrices Q and R price being off target and using input. The term inside the sum is the stage cost, paid at every step. Many formulations add a terminal cost, an extra penalty with its own weight QN on the last predicted state. Then: apply u0*, wait one tick, measure x̄, solve again.

In numbers: in the widget below, a car wants the lane 3.5 m to its left. At t = 0 its 2-second plan is u = 2.00, 2.00, 1.93, 1.54, 1.20, … m/s², and only the first 2.00 is used. At t = 0.5 s the fresh plan starts with 1.17. At t = 1.5 s it starts with −0.29, already braking the sideways motion. Feedback comes from re-solving, not from following the old plan.

Analogy

A chess player thinks five moves ahead but plays only one. After the opponent replies, the old plan is thrown away and a new one is worked out from the new position. Looking ahead makes the move good; re-planning makes the player hard to surprise.

2. The car, sideways: a double integrator

Think of a shopping cart on ice. Push it sideways and its sideways speed changes. That speed, in turn, changes where it is. With no friction, nothing else happens.

That chain is a double integrator: the input is an acceleration, which integrates once to a velocity and again to a position. In a lane change at constant forward speed, the car's lateral error y behaves almost exactly like this. Lateral error is the sideways distance from a reference line, here the start-lane centre. The input u is lateral acceleration in m/s², and v is lateral speed.

A computer holds u constant during each tick of length dt. This is a zero-order hold, and with it the one-tick update is exact:

yk+1 = yk + dt·vk + ½dt²·uk

vk+1 = vk + dt·uk

So x = (y, v), A = [[1, dt], [0, 1]] and B = [½dt², dt]T. With dt = 0.1 s, B = [0.005, 0.1]T. From rest, one tick at u = 2 m/s² gives y1 = 0.010 m and v1 = 0.20 m/s. Pushing at the full 2 m/s² and then braking at the full 2 m/s², a 3.5 m move from rest to rest takes 2·√(3.5/2) ≈ 2.65 s. The widget's MPC takes 4.4 s, because it also pays for effort.

What does this mean at the steering wheel? The kinematic bicycle model treats the car as one front and one rear wheel and ignores tyre forces. On a straight road and for small angles it gives u ≈ (V²/L)·δ, with forward speed V, wheelbase L and road-wheel angle δ. At V = 25 m/s and L = 2.7 m, |u| ≤ 2 m/s² means |δ| ≤ 0.0086 rad, about 0.5°. These numbers (25 m/s, 2.7 m, 2 m/s², 3.5 m lanes) are illustrative, not comfort or road-design standards.

Going deeper (optional): where the double integrator comes from

Track a path of curvature κ with lateral error ey and heading error eψ. For small angles the kinematic bicycle gives ėy ≈ V·eψ and ėψ ≈ (V/L)·δ − V·κ. Differentiate the first and substitute the second:

ëy ≈ (V²/L)·δ − V²·κ

At constant V this is a double integrator with input u = (V²/L)·δ − V²·κ, a standard small-angle derivation written for this lesson. Kong et al. compared kinematic and dynamic bicycle models on experimental data. Their abstract argues that kinematic-model MPC costs less computation and works at low speed, where tyre models become singular. Kong 2015

3. What the controller wants: cost and constraints

Give the planner three wishes: be in the target lane, arrive without still drifting sideways, and push gently. They conflict, because arriving fast needs hard pushes, so weights decide the trade. The widget's cost has target yref = 3.5 m and weights qy, qv and r:

J = Σk=1…N [qy(yk − yref)² + qvvk²]

+ Σk=0…N−1 r·uk²

Each term squares something linear in the inputs, so J is a convex quadratic. With all weights at 1, being 1 m off the lane costs as much as moving sideways at 1 m/s, or pushing at 1 m/s² for one tick. The widget uses no terminal cost.

Constraints are the hard rules. The three common kinds are all linear, so the problem stays a QP:

  • Input bounds |uk| ≤ umax limit how hard the car may push (here 2 m/s²).
  • Rate bounds |uk − uk−1| ≤ Δmax limit how fast the push may change; u−1 is last tick's input. With an illustrative Δmax = 0.3 m/s² per tick, ramping from 0 to 2 m/s² takes at least 7 ticks.
  • State bounds xmin ≤ xk ≤ xmax keep the car on the road, −1.75 m ≤ yk ≤ 5.25 m for our two lanes, or cap its lateral speed.

When each variable has its own lower and upper limit and nothing more, that is a box constraint. A variable sitting on its bound is in saturation. The widget keeps only the input box, which a few lines of browser code can solve exactly.

Try it: press Play to watch the car re-plan every tick; the orange dots are its current plan. Then try N = 5, qv = 0 or r = 0.1, and watch the arrival time, the overshoot and the solver iterations. Reset restores the defaults.

Notice: at the defaults (N = 20, qy = qv = r = 1, umax = 2 m/s²) the car reaches the target lane at 4.4 s, about 110 m of road at 25 m/s, and overshoots by only 2.6 cm. Its peak |u| is 2.00 m/s², on the bound for the first 3 ticks. Of each 20-input plan, only the first input is applied.

The sliders teach three lessons. First, a short horizon is not "more aggressive". At N = 5 (0.5 s of look-ahead) the car is timid: it peaks at 0.40 m/s² and reaches the lane only at 9.3 s. Within half a second a push buys a few centimetres but costs effort at once. Arrival takes 5.6 s at N = 10, 4.7 s at 15, 4.4 s at 20 and 4.3 s at 30 or 40, so past about 20 steps a longer horizon buys little.

Second, the speed weight qv makes the car brake its sideways motion before it arrives. With qv = 0 and N = 5 the car overshoots by 2.91 m, nearly a full lane, and has not settled after 15 s. With N = 20 the overshoot shrinks to 0.32 m, because the planner sees it coming. Third, the bound shapes the motion. At umax = 4 it never touches (peak 2.70 m/s², still 4.4 s); at 0.5 the car saturates for 20 ticks and arrives at 5.5 s.

4. Two ways to hand the QP to a solver

Picture a spreadsheet with one row per time step, each row depending only on the row above. You can keep every row as an unknown and add rules linking neighbours. Or, as with dominoes, you can note that the pushes decide every row, and write each row directly in terms of the pushes.

The first is the sparse formulation: states and inputs are all variables, and the dynamics are equality constraints. The second is the condensed formulation: eliminate the states and keep a small, dense QP in the inputs only.

OSQP, the ADMM solver from Day 13, takes QPs in the form below. Its own names for the constraint matrix and the upper bound, A and u, clash with ours, so here they are C and h. Stellato 2020

minimize ½zTPz + qTz

subject to l ≤ Cz ≤ h

For MPC, z = (x0, …, xN, u0, …, uN−1), and P holds Q, QN and R in diagonal blocks. The rows of C encode x0 = x̄ (with l = h = x̄), the dynamics xk+1 − Axk − Buk = 0 (with l = h = 0), and the bounds (an identity block, with l and h holding the limits). OSQP docs: MPC

Between ticks only x̄ changes, and it appears only in l and h. P and C never change, so one matrix factorization from start-up serves every tick. This is factorization caching, and it is why the sparse form suits OSQP. OSQP factors with a sparse direct solver, and the staircase has only a few nonzeros per row however long the horizon. For our car (nx = 2, nu = 1) the sparse QP has nx(N+1) + nu·N variables and nx(N+1) equality rows: 17 and 12 at N = 5, 62 and 42 at N = 20, 122 and 82 at N = 40. Stellato 2020, App. A.3

The condensed form writes the stacked states X = (x1, …, xN) in terms of the inputs U = (u0, …, uN−1):

X = Φx̄ + ΓU

Φ stacks A, A², …, AN. Γ is lower-triangular, because input j moves state k > j through Ak−1−jB. Substituting into J leaves a QP in U alone, where Q̄ and R̄ repeat Q and R down the diagonal:

J(U) = ½UTHU + fTU + const

H = 2(ΓTQ̄Γ + R̄)

f = 2ΓTQ̄(Φx̄ − Xref)

Only f changes each tick. Input bounds stay a box on U, but state bounds become xmin ≤ Φx̄ + ΓU ≤ xmax, with dense rows. At N = 20 that is 20 variables and a dense 20 × 20 H, which is what the widget solves.

Which wins? Condensing has quadratic complexity in the horizon length. Verschueren 2021, §2.7 Interior-point solvers that keep the stage structure (FORCES, HPMPC, HPIPM) avoid this. Liniger et al. report FORCES solve times growing linearly with the horizon, which let them use 40 steps. Liniger 2015 As a rough guide, condensing suits short horizons with few inputs, and the sparse form suits long ones. Partial condensing sits between: it condenses blocks of stages into a shorter, denser horizon. acados' chain-of-masses benchmark used a partially condensed horizon of 5. Verschueren 2021, Table 3

In practice a modelling tool such as CVXPY builds the sparse form and hands it to OSQP. This sketch is the widget's problem at its defaults:

import cvxpy as cp, numpy as np
dt, N, u_max, y_ref = 0.1, 20, 2.0, 3.5
A = np.array([[1, dt], [0, 1]]); B = np.array([0.5*dt**2, dt])
x, u = cp.Variable((2, N+1)), cp.Variable(N)   # states (y, v), inputs
x0 = cp.Parameter(2)                           # measured state: changes every tick
cost, cons = 0, [x[:, 0] == x0]
for k in range(N):
    cons += [x[:, k+1] == A @ x[:, k] + B * u[k], cp.abs(u[k]) <= u_max]
    cost += cp.square(x[0, k+1] - y_ref) + cp.square(x[1, k+1]) + cp.square(u[k])
mpc = cp.Problem(cp.Minimize(cost), cons)
x0.value = np.zeros(2)                         # every tick: measure, solve, apply u[0]
mpc.solve(solver=cp.OSQP, warm_start=True)
print(u.value[:4].round(2))                    # about [2. 2. 1.93 1.54]

5. A two-step example you can check by hand

Suppose your first push is capped. The car moves less than planned, so a good planner pushes a little harder on the next step. Clipping the unconstrained answer never does this, because it changes one input without telling the others.

Take the smallest case: N = 2, dt = 1 s for round numbers, qy = 1, qv = 0, r = 1, target 3.5 m, start at rest. Then y1 = 0.5u0 and y2 = 1.5u0 + 0.5u1, so:

J = (0.5u0 − 3.5)² + (1.5u0 + 0.5u1 − 3.5)²

+ u0² + u1²

H = [[7, 1.5], [1.5, 2.5]], f = (−14, −3.5)

H has eigenvalues 2.05 and 7.45, so J is a strictly convex bowl. The limit |u0|, |u1| ≤ 1.5 is a square box.

  • No limits. Solving HU = −f gives U = (1.951, 0.230) and J = 10.44, but u0 breaks the limit.
  • Clip it. U = (1.5, 0.230) and J = 11.15: feasible, not optimal.
  • Solve the QP. With u0 at 1.5, J is a parabola in u1 with its minimum at 0.5, so U = (1.5, 0.5) and J = 11.06.

The true answer raises the second input from 0.23 to 0.5, the "make up for it" move. It predicts y1 = 0.75 m and y2 = 2.50 m.

To confirm it, check the KKT conditions of Day 10. At (1.5, 0.5) the gradient HU + f is (−2.75, 0). The free input u1 has zero gradient. The saturated u0 has a negative gradient: the cost wants it larger, but it sits on its upper bound with multiplier λ = 2.75 ≥ 0, the price of the fence. At the clipped point the gradient is (−3.16, −0.68), and the free u1 still has a nonzero gradient, so KKT fails. With 20 or 40 coupled inputs and state bounds there is no clipping shortcut, which is why MPC needs a real QP solver.

6. How solvers find the plan

The simplest method that respects a box walks downhill, and stops at the fence when a step would cross it. That is projected gradient: a gradient step, then projection onto the feasible set, which for a box just clips each entry. It is the proximal gradient of Day 8 with the box as the constraint.

U ← clip(U − (HU + f)/L, −umax, umax)

L = λmax(H) is the steepest curvature, which makes 1/L a safe step. In the two-step example L = 7.454. From U = 0 one step lands at (1.88, 0.47), clipped to (1.5, 0.47), already close to (1.5, 0.5). The widget runs this rule every tick.

The number of steps depends on the condition number κ = λmax/λmin, the ratio of steepest to flattest curvature (Day 6). At the widget defaults L = 8.14 and λmin ≈ 2.0, so κ ≈ 4 and the first solve takes 33 iterations. With r = 0.1, κ ≈ 31 and it takes 213. Why? The last planned input acts for one tick at the very end and barely moves the car. In that direction only its own r·u² term curves the cost, so λmin ≈ 2r. At N = 40, L rises to 58 and κ to about 29, and the first solve takes 203 iterations.

OSQP uses ADMM, the Day 13 splitting method that alternates simple sub-steps (ADMM card, OSQP paper). Each iteration solves one linear system with a fixed matrix, clips its estimate of Cz into [l, h], and updates the multipliers. The matrix is factored once, and after that no iteration divides. Stellato 2020 OSQP also detects infeasible problems and returns a certificate, which matters when a state bound can no longer be met. As of Oct 2026 its documented defaults are ρ = 0.1, σ = 10⁻⁶, α = 1.6, εabs = εrel = 10⁻³, at most 4,000 iterations, warm starting on and polishing off. OSQP docs 2026

Interior-point methods (Day 12, primal-dual card) take Newton steps on smoothed KKT conditions and need a few tens of iterations almost regardless of size. Boyd & Vandenberghe 2004 Each iteration factors a new matrix, but in MPC that matrix is banded in time. FORCES, HPMPC and HPIPM exploit this, so the work grows only linearly with N. Verschueren 2021 Their weak spot is that interior-point methods are not easily warm started. Stellato 2020

All of them stop on KKT residuals, not on looks. OSQP checks the primal residual ‖Cz − w‖∞, which asks whether the constraints hold (w is its clipped estimate of Cz). It also checks the dual residual ‖Pz + q + CTy‖∞, which asks whether the multipliers y balance the gradient. Both must fall below εabs plus εrel times the size of the terms. Stellato 2020, §3.4 Liniger et al. stopped FORCES at residuals of 10⁻⁵ and a duality gap of 10⁻⁴. Liniger 2015 The widget stops when no input moves more than 10⁻⁵, which is a KKT test too: a projected-gradient step leaves U unchanged exactly at a KKT point. From (1.5, 0.5) the step pushes u0 to 1.87, the clip returns it to 1.5, and u1 stays put.

7. Real time: warm starts, real-time iteration, honest timings

Consecutive MPC problems are nearly identical, so the last plan shifted by one step is a good first guess. It is like re-planning a road trip after an hour of driving: you drop the first hour of the old plan instead of starting over. A warm start starts the solver from the previous solution. The usual shift repeats the last input:

Ustart = (u1*, u2*, …, uN−1*, uN−1*)

In the widget, over the first 8 s (80 ticks), warm starting cuts iterations from 1,821 to 1,392 at N = 20 (24%) and from 9,365 to 3,365 at N = 40 (64%). At N = 5 it saves nothing (401 against 390), because each solve is only a handful of iterations. OSQP warm starts its primal and dual iterates together. In the OSQP paper's MPC tests (20 to 80 states, horizon 10), warm start plus caching made solves 2.6 to 4 times faster: 7 ms became 2 ms at 20 states. Yet at 40 to 80 states the iterations barely moved (32 to 31.75 at 80), so the gain came mainly from reusing the factorization. Stellato 2020, Table 7

Real cars are not double integrators. Large steering angles break the small-angle model, and near the grip limit the tyres matter. The dynamics xk+1 = f(xk, uk) are then nonlinear, and each problem is a nonconvex NLP (Day 16). Fast controllers linearise around the shifted previous plan (x̂k, ûk) and solve one QP:

xk+1 ≈ f(x̂k, ûk) + Ak(xk − x̂k)

+ Bk(uk − ûk)

acados calls this the real-time iteration (RTI): one SQP-type iteration, so one QP, per sample (SQP card). Verschueren 2021, §2.8 Liniger et al.'s contouring controller raced 1:43-scale cars this way. Every 20 ms it linearised a bicycle model with tyre forces around the shifted last trajectory, "the basic version of the real-time iterations". Liniger 2015 Day 18 turns this loop into sequential convex programming.

QuestionLinear MPC (today)Nonlinear MPC (preview of Day 18)
Modelxk+1 = Axk + Buk, fixed A and Bxk+1 = f(xk, uk), e.g. a bicycle model with tyres
Each tick solvesone convex QP, to tolerancea nonconvex NLP, often just one QP of it (RTI)
What you getthe best plan for the modelan improvement around the last plan
Fitslane keeping and lane changes at steady speedracing, large steering angles, the grip limit

Fast enough means finished before the next tick, every tick. OSQP, FORCES and acados offer code generation: they emit problem-specific C code for the embedded target. OSQP's generated code needs no dynamic memory, no libraries and no divisions. OSQP docs: codegen Below are published timings. They are different problems on different hardware, so read each row alone and do not rank them.

SolverProblemHardwareTimeSource
OSQP (ADMM)linear MPC, 20 states, 10 inputs, horizon 10Intel Xeon E5-2650 server, one thread7 ms cold, 2 ms with warm start and cachingStellato 2020, Table 7
acados (RTI + HPIPM)chain of 5 masses, N = 40not stated with the tablemedian 1.05 ms per iteration (max 2.23); ACADO 1.97, IPOPT 59.84Verschueren 2021, Table 5
acados (RTI + HPIPM)engine boost-pressure NMPC, N = 20, 50 ms tickdSPACE MicroAutoBox II, 900 MHz PowerPC, 16 MBmax under 10 ms, about 3× slower than a 2.5 GHz Core i7Verschueren 2021, §5.3
FORCES (Liniger, tracking MPC)N = 14, 132 variables, 20 ms tickARM A9 (Exynos 4412), 1.7 GHzQP mean 5.10 ms, max 7.56 msLiniger 2015, Table II
FORCES (Liniger, contouring MPC)N = 40, 570 variables, 20 ms tickARM Cortex-A15 (Exynos 5410), 1.6 GHzQP mean 15.03 ms, max 21.16 msLiniger 2015, Table III
This page's widget (projected gradient)lane change, N = 20, 20 inputsyour browser17.4 iterations per tick on average warm, 22.8 cold (first 8 s)computed here

Two lessons hide in the table. The worst case matters more than the mean. Liniger's contouring controller averaged 15 ms against a 20 ms tick but peaked at 21 ms, and it missed the deadline in 4.4% of samples, "(soft) real-time" in the authors' words. It still lapped faster: 8.9 to 9.2 s, against 9.5 to 9.8 s for the tracking controller. Liniger 2015 And a laptop is not a car computer: acados' engine controller ran about 3 times slower on the 900 MHz automotive box than on a 2.5 GHz Core i7. Verschueren 2021, §5.3

Explain it to a 10-year-old

Walk across a playground towards a friend. You think "ten steps that way", but you only take one. Then you look again, because a ball might have rolled in front of you, and you think of ten new steps. A self-driving car does this ten times a second. Its computer picks the steps by finding the cheapest plan that obeys rules like "don't turn too hard".

Common misunderstandings

  • "The car follows its plan." Only u0 is applied; the rest is a forecast, re-optimised next tick.
  • "Clip the unconstrained solution and you have the constrained one." In the two-step example clipping gives J = 11.15; the true optimum (1.5, 0.5) gives 11.06. Clipping ignores how the inputs are coupled.
  • "A shorter horizon is more aggressive." At N = 5 the car is timid (peak 0.40 m/s², 9.3 s to the lane). Without a speed weight, N = 5 overshoots by 2.91 m instead. Short horizons are myopic, not bold.
  • "This solver takes 2 ms." A timing means nothing without the problem size and hardware. OSQP's 2 ms on a Xeon with 20 states and Liniger's 15 ms on a phone-class ARM chip with N = 40 cannot be compared.
  • "Warm starting always cuts iterations." In the widget it saves 24% at N = 20 and nothing at N = 5. In OSQP's MPC runs with 40 to 80 states, iterations barely changed; the speed-up came from factorization caching.

Check yourself

Q1. In receding-horizon MPC, what is sent to the actuator at each tick?

Only u0* is applied; then the state is measured and the problem is solved again. Running the whole plan open loop throws away the feedback that makes MPC robust.

Q2. The lateral double integrator has nx = 2 and nu = 1. With N = 20, how many decision variables does the condensed QP have?

Condensing eliminates the states and keeps only the inputs: N·nu = 20. 62 is the sparse count, nx(N+1) + nu·N, and 42 is the number of sparse equality rows.

Q3. In the sparse OSQP formulation, what changes between two consecutive MPC solves?

x̄ enters only the bounds of the initial-state rows. P and the constraint matrix stay fixed, so their factorization is computed once and reused: factorization caching.

Q4. Two-step example: the unconstrained optimum is (1.95, 0.23) and the limit is |u| ≤ 1.5. What is the constrained optimum?

With u0 stuck at 1.5, the second input should push harder to make up: J = 11.06 at (1.5, 0.5) against 11.15 for the clipped point. The gradient (−2.75, 0) with multiplier 2.75 ≥ 0 confirms KKT.

Q5. Lowering the effort weight r from 1 to 0.1 makes the widget's first solve take 213 iterations instead of 33. Why?

λmin(H) ≈ 2r, because the last input barely moves the car. Smaller r flattens the valley, κ rises, and gradient steps crawl. The cost stays convex and the box is unchanged.

Q6. Liniger et al.'s contouring MPC (N = 40) ran on a 1.6 GHz ARM Cortex-A15 with a 20 ms tick. What did its QP take?

Mean 15.03 ms, max 21.16 ms; the controller missed the deadline in 4.4% of samples. The last option is the tempting one: the mean fits the tick, but the worst case did not.

Recap: things to remember

  1. MPC plans N steps, applies the first input, measures, and plans again. Feedback comes from re-solving.
  2. A linear model, a quadratic cost and linear bounds make each tick a convex QP. The lateral double integrator has A = [[1, dt], [0, 1]] and B = [½dt², dt]T.
  3. The sparse form suits OSQP: only l and h change, so one factorization serves every tick. The condensed form is small and dense, and its input bounds stay a box.
  4. Clipping is not optimal; KKT residuals define "solved". Conditioning, set by r and N, decides how many first-order iterations you need.
  5. Real time means the worst case on the target hardware. Warm starts, factorization caching, code generation and RTI are the standard tools.

Week 3 · Day 18

Trajectory optimization & SCP

After today you can turn a motion-planning problem into a finite optimisation by direct transcription, solve nonconvex trajectory problems with sequential convex programming (linearise, add a trust region, solve, repeat), and explain how lossless convexification makes rocket landing an exact convex problem.

About 60 min · Needs Days 16 and 17 · No CO4A chapter (new material)

Today's big idea

Planning a whole motion is a big nonconvex problem, because obstacles leave holes in the free space and the dynamics are curved. Sequential convex programming does not fight that head-on. It replaces the hard parts with convex stand-ins that are only trusted near the current guess, solves that convex problem fast, and repeats. In a few special cases, such as rocket landing, a clever reformulation is exactly convex, and one solve gives the true best answer.

1. Trajectory optimisation: MPC with a long horizon

Think of parallel parking. A good driver does not pick only the next steering angle. They picture the whole manoeuvre (back up, turn in, straighten out) and then follow it. A computer can plan the same way.

Trajectory optimisation chooses a whole time-indexed path of states and inputs at once: where the vehicle is at each moment, and what the controls do. On Day 17, MPC solved a short-horizon QP with a linear model. Trajectory optimisation is the same idea stretched out: a long horizon, often the whole manoeuvre, and the real nonlinear dynamics. A common split is that a trajectory optimiser plans the manoeuvre and a fast MPC loop tracks it.

There is a catch: a path holds infinitely many numbers, and a solver needs a finite list. Direct transcription fixes this, like planning a hike by pushing pins into a map. Chop time into K steps of length dt. Make the state xk and the input uk at every node an unknown. Then require each pin to be reachable from the previous one. Malyuta 2022

Written out, the finite problem is:

minimise Σk ℓ(xk, uk)
s.t. xk+1 − F(xk, uk) = 0
g(xk, uk) ≤ 0, x0 = xstart, xK = xgoal

Here ℓ is the running cost (fuel, effort or time), F is the one-step model, and g collects the path rules, such as speed limits and obstacles. Each equation "next state minus predicted next state = 0" is a defect constraint.

F needs a rule for integrating the dynamics ẋ = f(x, u) across one step. Collocation is the family of such rules: describe the path between two nodes by a simple polynomial, and require it to obey the dynamics at chosen points. The simplest is the trapezoidal rule. The change over a step equals the average of the slopes at its two ends:

xk+1 − xk = (dt/2)·[f(xk, uk) + f(xk+1, uk)]

Here the input is held constant over the step (zero-order hold). GuSTO's experiments use exactly this rule with 30 to 40 nodes. Bonalli 2019

A worked example: a cart on a rail with position p and velocity v, so ṗ = v and v̇ = u. Start at rest, push with u = 2 m/s², and take dt = 0.1 s. Velocity: v1 = 0 + 0.05·(2 + 2) = 0.2 m/s. Position: p1 = 0 + 0.05·(0 + 0.2) = 0.010 m. The exact answer is ½·2·0.1² = 0.010 m: the trapezoid is exact here because velocity grows linearly. With 20 steps the problem has 21 × 2 states plus 20 inputs, which is 62 unknowns, tied together by 40 defect equations.

For a car, the kinematic bicycle model is ẋ = v cos θ, ẏ = v sin θ, θ̇ = (v/L) tan δ. Here θ is the heading, L the wheelbase and δ the steering angle. Those sines and cosines end up inside F, and that is where the trouble starts.

2. Why trajectory problems are not convex

Day 4 gave the test: a convex problem needs a convex feasible set, so every equality constraint must be affine. Trajectory problems usually break this in three ways. Malyuta 2022

Obstacles. Take a round obstacle with centre c = (5, 0.5) and radius r = 2. The points (2.5, 0.5) and (7.5, 0.5) are both 2.5 m from the centre, so both are free. Their midpoint is the centre itself. The free space has a hole, and a set with a hole is not convex.

Nonlinear dynamics. A defect constraint with sin θ inside describes a curved surface, not a flat one. Curved equality sets fail the midpoint test too. The points (1, 0) and (−1, 0) both satisfy ‖p‖ = 1, but their midpoint (0, 0) does not.

Nonconvex input limits. A rocket engine cannot throttle below a minimum thrust. With limits 4972 N ≤ ‖T‖ ≤ 13260 N, the thrusts (8000, 0) N and (−8000, 0) N are both allowed. Their midpoint is zero thrust, which is not. Blackmore 2010

Source of nonconvexityRobot exampleToday's fix
Obstacles (state constraints)A car must stay outside a parked truckSCP: replace the obstacle by a halfspace, re-drawn every iteration
Nonlinear dynamicsBicycle model, quadrotor attitudeSCP: linearise around the last trajectory, inside a trust region
Nonconvex input limitsMinimum engine thrustLossless convexification: an exact convex reformulation

Day 16 handed such problems to general nonlinear solvers such as SQP. Today keeps a convex solver at the core instead, and there are two routes. Route one is lossless convexification, a reformulation that is exactly convex: rare, but one solve gives the global optimum. Route two is sequential convex programming: approximate, solve, repeat. Malyuta 2022

3. The SCP loop: linearise, fence, trust region, slack

Sequential convex programming (SCP) builds a convex model of the problem around the current guess, solves that model, moves to its answer, and repeats. The current guess is the reference trajectory, written with a bar: x̄, p̄. Four ingredients make the loop work. See the SCP card for the one-page version.

Ingredient 1: linearise the dynamics. A curve looks straight if you zoom in far enough. So near the reference, replace the one-step model by its tangent:

F(x, u) ≈ F(x̄, ū) + A(x − x̄) + B(u − ū)

A and B are the Jacobians of F at the reference, the same idea as Newton's method on Day 11. The defect constraints become linear equalities, which are convex. A quick check: around θ̄ = 0.5, sin θ ≈ 0.479 + 0.878(θ − 0.5). At θ = 0.6 that gives 0.567 against the true 0.565. At θ = 1.5 it gives 1.357 against 0.997, badly wrong. The model is only good near the reference.

Ingredient 2: turn the obstacle into a fence. Picture walking around a round pond. Instead of tracking the curved shore, you stand behind a straight fence placed at the point of the shore closest to you. The far side of a straight fence is a halfspace, and halfspaces are convex.

In symbols, the rule "waypoint pi stays outside the disk" is ‖pi − c‖ ≥ r. At the reference waypoint p̄i, take the unit vector pointing from the centre to it, and keep the waypoint on the far side of the tangent line:

ni = (p̄i − c) / ‖p̄i − c‖
niT(pi − c) ≥ r

Why is this safe? For any unit vector, nT(p − c) ≤ ‖p − c‖, so every point that obeys the fence is at least r from the centre. The fence is an inner (conservative) approximation: a convex set that sits inside the true free space. Worked example: c = (5, 0.5), r = 2, and the guess p̄ = (5, 0) is inside the obstacle, 0.5 m below the centre. Then n = (0, −1), the fence reads −(y − 0.5) ≥ 2, and so y ≤ −1.5. The fence is 1.5 m below the guess.

Ingredient 3: a trust region. When you cross thin ice, you only step where you have tapped with your stick. The linear model and the fence are only trustworthy near the reference, so each iteration may move each point at most Δ:

‖pi − p̄i‖ ≤ Δ

This trust region also prevents artificial unboundedness: a linearised cost can slope downhill forever, so without a limit the subproblem runs off to infinity. SCvx and GuSTO use norm constraints or penalties like this one Malyuta 2022, while TrajOpt uses a box around the current iterate Schulman 2014. Back to the example with Δ = 1 m: the best the point can do is y = −1.0, still 0.5 m short of the fence. The subproblem has no solution, although the real problem has plenty.

Ingredient 4: virtual control, or slack. That dead end is called artificial infeasibility: the subproblem is infeasible only because of the linearisation and the trust region. The fix works like a rental car's late-return fee. You may break a rule, but it costs a lot, so you only do it when you must. Malyuta 2022

For a path constraint, add a slack si ≥ 0 and charge for it in the cost. For the dynamics, SCvx adds a fictitious input νk, the virtual control, with weight λ:

niT(pi − c) ≥ r − si, cost + λ·Σ si
xk+1 = Akxk + Bkuk + ck + Eνk, cost + λ‖ν‖1

In the example, the smallest slack that works is s = 2 − (0.5 + 1) = 0.5 m. At convergence the slack must be zero. A converged answer that still uses virtual control does not solve the real problem; the tutorial calls this a "soft failure". Malyuta 2022

Put together, the loop is short:

p̄ ← initial guess                 # e.g. a straight line
repeat
    linearise dynamics, draw one fence per waypoint around p̄
    solve the convex subproblem (a QP or SOCP):
        min  cost(p) + λ·(total slack)
        s.t. linearised constraints with slack
             ‖p_i − p̄_i‖ ≤ Δ        # trust region
    ρ ← actual drop / predicted drop   # Section 4
    if ρ < ρ0: reject p, shrink Δ
    else:      p̄ ← p; shrink, keep or grow Δ
until the step is tiny and the slack is zero

4. Grading each step: the accuracy ratio, SCvx and GuSTO

Think of a weather forecaster. If her forecasts keep coming true, you start trusting her further ahead. If they miss, you only trust tomorrow's. SCP grades its convex model the same way after every step.

Let J be the real cost, including the penalty for violating the real constraints, and let L be the convex model's version of it. After solving the subproblem from x̄ to x*, compare what happened with what was promised. This is the accuracy ratio:

ρ = [J(x̄) − J(x*)] / [J(x̄) − L(x*)]
= actual drop ÷ predicted drop

The rule uses three thresholds 0 ≤ ρ0 < ρ1 < ρ2 < 1. Below ρ0, the model was badly wrong: reject the step and shrink Δ. Between ρ0 and ρ1, accept but shrink. Between ρ1 and ρ2, accept and keep Δ. Above ρ2, accept and grow Δ, up to a cap. The predicted drop doubles as the stopping test: when it is about zero, nothing is left to gain. Malyuta 2022

A worked example with made-up numbers: J(x̄) = 6.0, the model predicts L(x*) = 5.0, and the real cost turns out to be J(x*) = 5.8. Then ρ = 0.2 / 1.0 = 0.2, which lies between 0.1 and 0.7, so the step is accepted and Δ is kept. If the real cost had been 6.1, then ρ = −0.1: the step made things worse, so it is rejected and Δ shrinks.

This recipe of linearisation, virtual control and a ρ-based trust region is called SCvx (successive convexification). Mao, Szmuk and Açıkmeşe described it, with a convergence analysis, in 2016 Mao 2016. A follow-up claims global convergence with a superlinear rate, and fewer iterations than SQP and a general interior-point solver on a quadrotor problem. Mao 2018 See the SCvx / GuSTO paper card.

GuSTO (Guaranteed Sequential Trajectory Optimization) keeps the same skeleton but changes the safeguards. It targets control-affine systems with drift, handles goal sets and free final time, and moves the state constraints and the trust region into the cost as penalties whose weight grows. Its convergence proof works in continuous time with Pontryagin's maximum principle, so the guarantee does not depend on the discretisation. The guarantee is convergence to a stationary point, not to the global optimum. Bonalli 2019

GuSTO's numbers: in 100 runs of a 12-state free-flyer robot in a mock-up of the space station, started from straight lines, GuSTO and TrajOpt each succeeded 97% of the time, and GuSTO was faster with lower cost. On an 8-state airplane model, from the best initial guess, GuSTO took 0.55 s against TrajOpt's 2.67 s. GuSTO can also reuse the subproblem's dual variables (Day 9) to warm-start a shooting method, which cut run time by 52% on a Dubins car and 74% on the free-flyer. Bonalli 2019

Try it: the widget runs real SCP on a path from (0, 0) to (10, 0) around an obstacle at (5, 0.5) with r = 2, using K = 20 segments. Press Step, or click a table row. Then set Δ to 0.25, and try the "bowed above" start.

Notice: the default view is iteration 1. The straight start runs through the obstacle, and the middle waypoint, 0.5 m from the centre, can move only Δ = 1 m, so it needs 0.5 m of slack (red). Path length goes 10.000 → 10.202 → 10.574 → 10.457 → 10.455 → 10.455 m. The waypoints are collision-free from iteration 2, and SCP stops at iteration 5. With Δ = 0.25 it takes 12 iterations, and the first five need slack. Here ρ reads 1.000 every time, because the fence is conservative and the cost is not linearised. So the model never over-promises, and Δ only sets the pace. In SCvx's main use, linearised nonlinear dynamics, the model can over-promise; then ρ drops below ρ1 and shrinking Δ matters.

5. The honest caveat: the answer depends on the guess

SCP only ever looks near its reference, so it can only promise a local optimum: no nearby path is better, but a different initial guess may find a better one. The widget shows this directly. From a straight line, SCP slides under the obstacle and settles at 10.455 m. From a path bowed above, it settles over the top at 11.248 m, about 0.79 m (7.6%) longer. Neither run made a mistake; they started in different valleys.

You can check both answers by geometry. The shortest continuous path below the obstacle (two tangent lines and an arc) is 10.458 m, and the one above is 11.256 m. The 20-segment answers are slightly shorter than these, because straight segments cut the corner around the arc.

That corner-cutting is a known artefact of the toy. Only the waypoints are constrained, so the segments between them can clip the obstacle. At the end, every waypoint is at least 2.000 m from the centre, yet the closest segment passes at 1.983 m, a 1.7 cm clip. With K = 10 the clip grows to 7 cm. The Malyuta tutorial notes the same clipping in its quadrotor example Malyuta 2022. Real planners inflate obstacles by a margin or check the swept volume between time steps, as TrajOpt does. Schulman 2014

In practice, people manage the guess dependence in three ways. They try several initial guesses, they seed SCP with a rough path from a graph search or sampling planner, or they warm-start from the previous plan, as MPC does. TrajOpt's authors list the strong dependence on initialisation as a main limitation. Schulman 2014 Day 19 shows a way to choose the "valley" globally with convex pieces.

6. SCP for robot arms: TrajOpt, and why CHOMP is different

TrajOpt plans robot-arm motions from the laziest guess possible: a straight line in joint space, which may pass right through a shelf. SCP turns that into a collision-free motion. Schulman 2014

Instead of hard constraints plus slack, TrajOpt moves every violation into the cost with an absolute-value penalty. Write |a|+ = max(a, 0). Its merit function is:

f(x) + μ Σ |gi(x)|+ + μ Σ |hi(x)|

Here f is the smoothness cost, gi ≤ 0 are the inequalities and hi = 0 the equalities. This is an exact (ℓ1) penalty: once the weight μ is large enough, minimising it gives the constrained solution exactly, not approximately. TrajOpt solves a QP inside a box trust region, and multiplies μ by 10 until the constraints hold. Schulman 2014

Collisions use the signed distance sd(A, B) between two shapes: their distance apart, or minus their penetration depth when they overlap. The penalty is |dsafe − sd(A, B)|+, which is linearised through the robot's Jacobian at every iteration. With made-up numbers, dsafe = 5 cm and a gripper 2 cm from the shelf costs μ × 3 cm, and at 8 cm it costs nothing. A swept-volume version checks the space between time steps too. Schulman 2014

Planner (198 arm problems, PR2, 7 joints)Success rateAverage timePath length (normalised)
TrajOpt0.820.19 s1.16
TrajOpt, several initial guesses0.96––
OMPL RRT-Connect (sampling)0.850.62 s1.56
CHOMP-HMC (gradient)0.654.91 s2.04

On 96 full-body problems with 18 degrees of freedom, TrajOpt succeeded 0.73 of the time (0.88 with several initial guesses), against 0.41 for RRT-Connect, taking 2.2 s against 20.3 s. Schulman 2014 See the TrajOpt paper card.

CHOMP is often mentioned in the same breath, but it is not SCP. CHOMP runs covariant gradient descent on a smoothness-plus-obstacle cost. It builds no convex subproblem and uses no trust region. Ratliff 2009 The GuSTO paper groups it with "variational methods" and notes that it does not include dynamics constraints. Bonalli 2019 Think of CHOMP as TrajOpt's gradient cousin.

The same loop fits a car. Linearise the bicycle model around the last plan, turn each nearby obstacle into a halfspace, cap how far each node may move, solve a QP, and repeat. Day 19 replaces "one halfspace per obstacle" with better convex pieces, and Day 20 adds safety filters.

7. Lossless convexification: landing a rocket with one convex solve

Back to the rocket engine with a minimum and a maximum thrust. The allowed thrust vectors form a ring, which is not convex. Powered descent guidance computes the thrust profile for the final landing burn, and it has to handle that ring. Lossless convexification is a relaxation that is proven to give the original problem's global optimum. Açıkmeşe & Ploen 2007

The trick works like a taxi meter. Add a new variable Γ, the thrust you pay fuel for, which may run anywhere between the limits. The actual thrust only has to stay below the meter. A cost-minded passenger never lets the meter run ahead of the pedal.

In symbols, the original constraint and its relaxation are:

original: 0 < ρ1 ≤ ‖T(t)‖ ≤ ρ2
relaxed: ‖T(t)‖ ≤ Γ(t), ρ1 ≤ Γ(t) ≤ ρ2
fuel burn: ṁ(t) = −α Γ(t)

Here T is the thrust vector, m the mass, and α converts thrust into fuel flow. (These ρ1 and ρ2 are thrust limits, as in the papers, not the thresholds of Section 4.) The relaxed set is convex. Under the theorem's conditions, the optimum of the relaxed problem always has ‖T(t)‖ = Γ(t), so it is feasible for the real engine, and globally optimal. A change of variables to the logarithm of the mass, plus time discretisation, turns the whole problem into an SOCP (Day 5), which interior-point solvers (Day 12) handle reliably. Açıkmeşe & Ploen 2007 Blackmore 2010

Blackmore, Açıkmeşe and Scharf give Mars numbers. Gravity is 3.7114 m/s², the lander has a mass of 1905 kg wet and 1505 kg dry, so 400 kg of fuel is on board, and thrust runs from ρ1 = 4972 N to ρ2 = 13260 N. A glide-slope cone (4° here) stops the lander from coming in too low over the terrain. Hovering at full mass needs 1905 × 3.7114 ≈ 7070 N, inside the range. The pair T = 3000 N with Γ = 4972 N is allowed by the relaxation but not by the engine, and the theorem says the optimiser never picks it. Blackmore 2010

In their first case the target is reachable. The optimal landing uses 399.4 kg of fuel with a flight time of 78.4 s. The flight time comes from an outer golden-section search (23 iterations, with 55 time nodes per convex solve), which took 14.3 s in total on a 2.4 GHz MacBook Pro with JPL's G-OPT solver. In the second case the lander starts with an extra 40 m/s sideways. Reaching the target would need at least 414 kg of fuel, more than the 400 kg on board. A minimum-landing-error version of the problem then lands 404 m from the target, after 77.7 s, using all 400 kg. Blackmore 2010 See the lossless convexification paper card.

JPL has flown LCvx-based guidance (G-FOLD) on Masten's Xombie test rocket, including a 750 m divert. Malyuta 2022 On SpaceX, stay with the primary source. Lars Blackmore, writing as a SpaceX engineer, says SpaceX uses CVXGEN to generate flight code for "very high-speed onboard convex optimization", and that the landing trajectory must be computed autonomously "in a fraction of a second". He cites the 2007 and 2010 papers above. Blackmore 2017 He does not publish the formulation. The Malyuta tutorial only hypothesises that LCvx is a close relative of Falcon 9's landing algorithm, and states that SpaceX's methods are undisclosed. We found no public description of SpaceX's current formulation as of Oct 2026. Malyuta 2022

The limits matter. The model is a point mass with constant gravity, the flight time is searched outside the convex solve, and the lossless guarantee holds only for problems whose nonconvexity has the right structure. Otherwise you use SCP, possibly with LCvx inside each subproblem. Malyuta 2022 The Malyuta tutorial card is the best next read; it won the 2023 IEEE Control Systems Magazine Outstanding Paper Award. UW 2024

Going deeper (optional): why the relaxation is lossless

Why can't the optimiser cheat by metering more thrust than it uses? Intuitively, that pays fuel for nothing. But "just lower Γ" is not a proof: Γ cannot go below ρ1, and burning less fuel changes the mass and so the motion. The real proof uses Pontryagin's maximum principle. Along an optimal path, a "costate" vector sets the best thrust direction and size. As long as that vector is not zero over a whole time interval, the best choice puts T on the edge ‖T‖ = Γ. Showing that the costate cannot vanish for a stretch is where the problem's structure is needed: linear dynamics, constant gravity, and the specific constraints. Malyuta et al. walk through the conditions and later extensions. Malyuta 2022

Analogy

SCP is like steering a boat through fog with a short-range sonar. You trust the sonar only within its range (the trust region). You treat each rock as a straight wall facing you (the fence). If no route avoids every wall, you allow yourself a small, expensive scrape (the slack). Then you ping again and redraw the walls. Lossless convexification is the rare harbour whose chart is exact, so one plan is enough.

Explain it to a 10-year-old

You want to walk around a big round pond, but it is foggy and you can only see a few steps ahead. So you put up a straight fence at the edge of the pond nearest to you, and promise to stay behind it. You take a few steps, look again, and move the fence. After a few tries you are around the pond with dry shoes. If you had started on the other side, you would have walked around the other way.

Common misunderstandings

  • "SCP found the optimal trajectory." It found a local optimum. In the widget, a bowed start ends at 11.248 m, while a straight start ends at 10.455 m. The guess picks the valley.
  • "It converged, so it is feasible." Check that the slack and virtual control are zero. Converging with virtual control left over is a soft failure, not a solution.
  • "The waypoints are clear, so the path is clear." The segments between waypoints can clip the obstacle: 1.7 cm with 20 segments, 7 cm with 10. Inflate obstacles or check swept volumes.
  • "Lossless convexification works on any nonconvex problem." It applies to specific problem classes where the maximum-principle argument goes through. Elsewhere, use SCP.
  • "CHOMP is SCP." CHOMP is a covariant gradient method. TrajOpt is SCP, with convex subproblems, a trust region and ℓ1 penalties.
  • "SpaceX lands Falcon 9 with the 2007 algorithm." That is not public. The sourced statement is that SpaceX uses CVXGEN-generated flight code for onboard convex optimisation; the link to LCvx is a hypothesis.

Check yourself

Q1. A waypoint guess sits at p̄ = (5, 0). The obstacle has centre c = (5, 0.5) and radius 2. Which fence does SCP use for this waypoint?

The unit vector from c to p̄ is n = (0, −1), so the fence nT(p − c) ≥ 2 reads −(y − 0.5) ≥ 2, which is y ≤ −1.5. The line y ≥ 2.5 is also outside the disk, but it is the tangent on the far side, facing away from the guess, so it would drag the waypoint across the whole obstacle.

Q2. SCvx computes ρ = 0.05 with thresholds ρ0 = 0, ρ1 = 0.1, ρ2 = 0.7. What does it do?

0.05 lies between ρ0 and ρ1: the real cost did drop, but only by 5% of what the model promised. The step is kept, and the trust region shrinks so the next model is used closer to home. Convergence is judged by the predicted drop being near zero, not by ρ.

Q3. A converged SCP run still uses 0.3 m of slack on one waypoint. What does that mean?

Slack and virtual control are bookkeeping that keeps each subproblem solvable. If they are not zero at the end, the waypoint is still 0.3 m inside the obstacle. Try another initial guess, a larger penalty weight, or check whether the real problem is feasible at all.

Q4. In the widget, a bowed start converges to 11.248 m and a straight start to 10.455 m. Why?

The cost Σ‖pi+1 − pi‖² is convex; the obstacle is what makes the problem nonconvex, with one valley above and one below. Changing Δ changes the pace, not the valley: every Δ from the straight start reaches the same 10.455 m path.

Q5. How does lossless convexification handle the thrust ring ρ1 ≤ ‖T‖ ≤ ρ2?

The lifted set is convex, and the proof shows the optimum sits on its edge ‖T‖ = Γ, so nothing is lost. Dropping the lower bound gives a different problem whose answer may ask for thrust the engine cannot make. A binary variable gives a mixed-integer program (Day 15), which is much harder to solve onboard.

Q6. Which source directly states that SpaceX uses CVXGEN-generated flight code?

Blackmore, writing from SpaceX, makes the statement. The Malyuta tutorial only hypothesises a link between LCvx and Falcon 9 and says SpaceX's methods are undisclosed. The 2007 paper is the method SpaceX's author cites, not a statement about SpaceX.

Recap: things to remember

  1. Direct transcription turns a path into a finite list of node states and inputs, with the dynamics as defect constraints; collocation rules such as the trapezoid define those links.
  2. Obstacles, nonlinear dynamics and minimum-thrust limits are the usual sources of nonconvexity.
  3. SCP repeats four moves: linearise around the last path, replace obstacles by safe halfspaces, limit the step with a trust region, and use penalised slack so every subproblem is solvable. The slack must be zero at the end.
  4. SCvx grows or shrinks the trust region by ρ = actual drop ÷ predicted drop; GuSTO uses penalties and continuous-time guarantees. Both give local, guess-dependent answers.
  5. Lossless convexification lifts the thrust ring with a meter Γ and proves the convex answer is exact: Blackmore 2010's Mars landing used 399.4 kg of fuel in 78.4 s.
