Week 3 · Day 19

Collision avoidance with convex pieces

After today you can explain why obstacle avoidance is nonconvex and name four convex ways around it: OBCA's duality trick, safe corridors, IRIS's convex free-space regions, and Graphs of Convex Sets.

About 60 min · Needs Days 9, 15 and 18 · No CO4A chapter (this day is new in this course)

Today's big idea

The set of places a robot may go has holes in it, so it is not convex. You cannot make the holes go away, but you can work around them. Either carry a small dual "proof of clearance" as an extra variable (OBCA), or cover free space with overlapping convex pieces and plan piece by piece (safe corridors, IRIS, Graphs of Convex Sets). Inside one convex piece, every straight move is safe, so the hard part becomes choosing which pieces to use.

1. Why "stay out of the box" is nonconvex

Picture a car park with one concrete pillar. You can park left of it or right of it. But if you average those two parking spots, you land inside the pillar. That one fact is the whole problem of today.

The free space is every position where the robot touches nothing. On Day 2 a set was convex if the segment between any two of its points stays in the set. Free space around an obstacle fails this test, because the segment between two safe points can pass through the obstacle. So "stay outside" is a nonconvex constraint: averaging two allowed points can break it.

Write the obstacle as a polytope, the set of points that satisfy every face inequality:

O = {x : aiTx ≤ bi, i = 1…m} = {x : Ax ≤ b}

Here ai is the outward normal of face i, bi is its offset, and A stacks the rows aiT. To be outside, you only need to break one face inequality:

x ∉ O  ⇔  maxi (aiTx − bi) > 0

Read it as "beyond face 1 OR beyond face 2 OR …". That is a disjunctive (OR) constraint. Each half-plane is convex, but their union, with the obstacle cut out of the middle, is not. A max of affine functions is convex, and asking a convex function to be large (≥, not ≤) can give a nonconvex set, as it does here.

Numbers: take the square obstacle [−1, 1]2, so A = [I; −I] and b = (1, 1, 1, 1). The points (−2, 0) and (2, 0) are both outside. Their midpoint (0, 0) is inside. One counterexample is enough: this free space is not convex.

2. Three families of fixes

Think of crossing a river. You can list every stepping stone and decide stone by stone which to use. You can start on a rough route and nudge your feet toward safety. Or you can first lay planks across, then walk only on planks. These are the three families of fixes.

The first family keeps the OR exactly with 0/1 switch variables. On Day 15 you met big-M / mixed-integer modelling: one binary per face says "I am beyond this face". It finds the global optimum, but the number of binaries grows with faces × obstacles × time steps, and branch and bound can blow up. The OBCA authors note that integer variables "should generally be avoided" in real-time nonlinear control. Zhang 2021

The second family works locally. On Day 18, sequential convex programming replaced the round obstacle by one straight fence near the current guess, solved a convex problem, and repeated. OBCA (section 3) also belongs here: it keeps the exact shape but makes the constraint smooth, then hands it to a local solver.

The third family is today's main topic. Cover free space with convex pieces. Inside one piece any straight move is safe, so planning becomes "pick the pieces, then solve a convex problem inside them".

FamilyIdeaWhat you getPriceExamples
Binaries (Day 15)One 0/1 per face: "beyond this face"Exact global optimumWorst-case exponential timefootstep MIQP
Local (Day 18)Linearise or smooth near a guessFast, smooth pathsLocal optimum; needs a warm startSCP, TrajOpt, OBCA
Convex pieces (today)Cover free space with convex regionsConvex problem once the pieces are fixedRegions cost time to build and leave some free space outSafe corridors, IRIS, GCS, safe boxes

3. OBCA: distance as a small dual problem

To demand "stay at least 0.5 m from the wall", you need the distance. But distance has no simple formula: it is itself a small optimization, "find the closest point of the obstacle". OBCA (Optimization-Based Collision Avoidance) uses duality from Day 9 to turn that inner problem inside out. Zhang 2021

The intuition is a signed note. Instead of re-measuring the gap at every step, the robot carries a certificate: a straight line that touches the obstacle, plus the claim "I am at least dmin beyond this line". If the claim holds, the robot is safe. The optimizer moves the robot and the note together.

For a point robot at p, strong duality gives the distance as a maximum over multipliers λ, one per face: Zhang 2021, Prop. 1

dist(p, O) = maxλ ⪰ 0 (Ap − b)Tλ  s.t.  ‖ATλ‖2 ≤ 1

So the hard constraint "distance at least dmin" becomes "some λ proves it":

∃ λ ⪰ 0 : (Ap − b)Tλ ≥ dmin
‖ATλ‖2 ≤ 1

Such a λ is a dual certificate (witness). The vector w = ATλ is the normal of a line that touches the obstacle, and (Ap − b)Tλ is how far p sits beyond that line. Any valid λ gives a lower bound on the distance (weak duality). The best λ gives the exact distance (strong duality, which holds here because the constraints are linear).

Numbers, with the square [−1, 1]2 and p = (3, 0.5). Then Ap − b = (2, −0.5, −4, −1.5). The choice λ = (1, 0, 0, 0) picks the face x ≤ 1, has ‖ATλ‖ = 1, and gives value 2, the true distance. The choice λ = (0.71, 0.71, 0, 0) is also valid but gives only (2 − 0.5) × 0.71 = 1.06, a weaker bound. For p = (3, 3), λ = (0.71, 0.71, 0, 0) gives 2√2 ≈ 2.83, the distance to the corner (1, 1).

A car is not a point. OBCA models the car as a fixed shape 𝔹 = {y : Gy ≤ g}, here a 4.7 × 2 m rectangle, rotated by R(x) and shifted by t(x), where x is the car's state. Adding a second multiplier μ for the car's own faces gives the full-shape version: Zhang 2021, Prop. 3

−gTμ + (At(x) − b)Tλ ≥ dmin
GTμ + R(x)TATλ = 0
‖ATλ‖2 ≤ 1,  λ ⪰ 0,  μ ⪰ 0

You add one (λ, μ) pair per obstacle per time step. Every constraint is smooth (square the norm constraint), so a standard nonlinear solver such as IPOPT can handle it. The problem is still nonconvex, through the car dynamics and the rotation R(x), so it needs a good starting guess, a warm start.

In parking, that warm start comes from Hybrid A*, a grid search over (x, y, heading) with car-like motion pieces. Its paths are drivable but jerky; OBCA smooths them. In the paper's test the car had a 2.7 m wheelbase, and it started from 84 poses near a reverse spot (2.6 × 5.2 m) and a parallel spot (2.5 × 6 m). Every run succeeded. With the distance form, average times were 0.60 s (reverse) and 0.87 s (parallel), on a 2013 MacBook Pro with IPOPT. A plain A* warm start, which ignores turning limits, was typically not good enough. Zhang 2021, Table 2

Plain distance is 0 for every overlap, so it cannot say how deep a collision is. OBCA's second form uses signed distance: the distance when apart, minus the penetration depth when overlapping. You get it by changing ‖ATλ‖ ≤ 1 to = 1. Then slack variables can find the least-intrusive path when contact cannot be avoided. The price is a nonconvex equality: 1.03 s and 1.67 s on average in the same tests, and 7.7 s and 9.2 s in the worst case including Hybrid A*. Zhang 2021, Thm 1 More in the OBCA paper entry.

Going deeper (optional): where the dual formula comes from

Let w = p − y be the gap from an obstacle point y to the robot. Then dist(p, O) = min ‖w‖2 subject to A(p − w) ≤ b. The Lagrangian is ‖w‖ + λT(Ap − Aw − b) with λ ⪰ 0. Minimising over w, the term ‖w‖ − (ATλ)Tw is bounded below only if ‖ATλ‖ ≤ 1 (Cauchy–Schwarz), and then its minimum is 0. So the dual function is (Ap − b)Tλ on that set, which is the formula above. Weak duality also has a one-line check: for any y in O, ‖p − y‖ ≥ wT(p − y) ≥ (Ap − b)Tλ when w = ATλ and ‖w‖ ≤ 1. The constraints are linear and the problem is feasible, so the duality gap is zero.

4. Safe flight corridors: plan room by room

If free space cannot be made convex, cover it with convex rooms. Inside one room every straight move is safe. You then plan room by room and only need consecutive rooms to overlap, like stepping stones that touch.

A safe flight corridor is a chain of overlapping convex polyhedra around a rough path, inside which a drone trajectory is optimized. Liu and colleagues built it like this for quadrotors flying through point clouds. The original paper was not checked for this lesson, so the pipeline below comes from the authors' code README and a 2024 description by other researchers: DecompUtil README Wu 2024

  1. Find a rough path of line segments with a grid search (Jump Point Search).
  2. Around each segment, grow an ellipsoid until it touches obstacle points.
  3. At each contact, keep the tangent half-space. Together they form one polyhedron per segment.
  4. The overlapping polyhedra form the corridor.
  5. Optimize the trajectory as a QP that keeps each piece inside its polyhedron.

In formulas, room i is Pi = {x : Aix ≤ bi}, and piece i of the trajectory must satisfy Aix(t) ≤ bi. Those constraints are linear in the trajectory. With a quadratic cost on acceleration or jerk the whole problem is a QP, like the MPC of Day 17. The exact cost, and how the constraint is enforced over time, are in the paper and were not checked here. Liu 2017

Step 3 is worth one number. Say the current ellipsoid is the unit disk at the origin and the closest obstacle point is x* = (2, 1). The wall normal is a = x*/‖x*‖ = (0.894, 0.447) and the offset is b = aTx* = √5 ≈ 2.236. So the room keeps 0.894x + 0.447y ≤ 2.236: the line through x* at right angles to the radius. IRIS uses the same step.

5. IRIS: grow the biggest convex room

Picture blowing up a balloon in a cluttered cupboard. It grows until it presses on the shelves, and the shelves it touches become the walls of its room. IRIS (Iterative Regional Inflation by Semidefinite programming) does this with math: it grows one large obstacle-free polytope, with an ellipse inside, from a seed point. Deits & Tedrake 2015

Describe the ellipse as a stretched unit ball, E = {Cu + d : ‖u‖2 ≤ 1}, with a symmetric matrix C ⪰ 0 and a centre d. Its area (or volume) is proportional to det C. IRIS alternates two convex problems:

  1. Planes (a QP). For each convex obstacle, find its point closest to E, measured after mapping E back to the unit ball. Add the tangent plane there. Skip obstacles already cut off by earlier planes. The planes give a polytope P = {x : Ax ≤ b}.
  2. Ellipse (an SDP). Find the biggest ellipse inside P. This maximum-volume inscribed ellipsoid problem is:

maxC ⪰ 0, d log det C
s.t. ‖Cai‖2 + aiTd ≤ bi,  i = 1…m

Why this constraint? The point of E that reaches farthest in direction ai reaches aiTd + ‖Cai‖. Keeping that below bi keeps the whole ellipse inside face i. log det is concave, so this is a convex problem, in fact an SDP from the zoo of Day 5. Repeat both steps until det C stops growing. The ellipse can only grow, so the loop converges.

Numbers: in the rectangle [−2, 2] × [−1, 1], the biggest ellipse has C = diag(2, 1) and d = 0. For the face x ≤ 2, ‖Ca‖ = 2 ≤ 2, so it touches. Its area is π · 2 · 1 = 6.283, which is 78.5% of the rectangle's area 8.

IRIS is fast. Its run time grows linearly with the number of obstacles, and it converged in seconds with a million obstacles. The closest-point QP took under 20 µs with a code-generated solver. Two limits: obstacles must be convex (split non-convex ones first), and the seed ended up inside the final region only 95% of the time. Deits & Tedrake 2015 See the IRIS paper entry.

For robot arms, the obstacles live in joint space and have no explicit formula. Newer variants handle that case: IRIS-NP2 and IRIS-ZO grow joint-space regions faster, and FIRI (T-RO 2025) speeds up the 2-D and 3-D case. As of Oct 2026 these tools change quickly. Werner 2024 Wang 2025

6. Graphs of Convex Sets: one convex program picks the rooms

Corridors and IRIS give you rooms, but someone still has to choose which rooms to pass through. Think of a road trip. The discrete choice is which towns to drive through. The continuous choice is where exactly you cross each town line. Dijkstra's algorithm solves the first only if road lengths are fixed, and here they depend on the crossing points.

A Graph of Convex Sets (GCS) puts both choices in one problem. Each vertex v holds a convex set Xv and a movable point xv ∈ Xv. Each edge (u, v) has a convex length, here ‖xv − xu‖2. The shortest-path problem is: Marcucci 2024

min over paths and points: Σedges (u,v) on the path ‖xv − xu‖2

If you fix the chain of sets, what is left is convex. Call the chain K1, …, Km, the start S and the goal G. You pick one breakpoint pj in each overlap, or "door":

min Σj=1…m ‖pj − pj−1‖2
p0 = S,  pm = G,  pj ∈ Kj ∩ Kj+1

This convex restriction is an SOCP. Its answer is safe: segment j joins pj−1 and pj, which both lie in the convex box Kj, so the whole segment does too.

Try it: the default view solves every chain from box A (holding the start) to box C (holding the goal) and draws each shortest path. Pick one chain to see its breakpoints and segment lengths. Then tap "Box D1" to remove that box and watch the answer change.

Notice: the 4-box chain A→D1→D2→C (9.6287) beats both 3-box chains, A→F→C (13.6619) and A→B→C (17.2315). Its breakpoints sit on door corners, (3, 4), (3.5, 5) and (3.5, 6), where a taut string would bend. It is 20.4% longer than the blocked straight line of 8. Remove D1 and the best route becomes A→F→C, 13.6619.

The widget tries all three chains. Real maps have thousands of regions and far too many chains to try, and finding the best one is NP-hard in general. GCS writes the choice with one binary φe ∈ {0, 1} per edge, "this edge is used". It then uses a perspective function φ·f(x/φ), a scaled copy of each cost and constraint that switches off cleanly when φe = 0. Marcucci 2024

The convex relaxation loosens φe ∈ {0, 1} to φe ∈ [0, 1]. With Euclidean lengths it is one SOCP. Its optimal cost is a lower bound, and the perspective trick makes it unusually tight. Rounding turns the fractional φ into one path, and the convex restriction of that path gives a real cost. That brackets the true optimum:

Crelax ≤ Copt ≤ Cround

gap ≤ (Cround − Crelax) / Crelax

This optimality gap bound comes free with the solve. In one example of the paper, Crelax = 27.29 and Cround = 28.10, so the path is at most 0.81/27.29 = 2.97% above the best. A mixed-integer solver later showed the true gap was 0%. Marcucci 2023

Robots need smooth curves, not polylines. GCS gives each region a Bézier curve, a polynomial curve that stays inside the convex hull of its control points. Put the control points in a convex region and the whole curve stays in that region, with no sampling. Continuity and velocity limits are linear or conic, so the problem stays an SOCP.

The results are strong. A 2,500-cell maze needed 5,198 binaries instead of 6.25 million for an older formulation, and one SOCP returned the global optimum. For a quadrotor among buildings, 95% of plans were within 1% of the global optimum (worst 2.9%), with a median relaxation time of 3.7 s. On a 7-joint KUKA arm, GCS found shorter paths than a sampling planner (PRM), ran faster than plain PRM, and reached the global optimum on all 5 tasks. These numbers come from the arXiv v1 preprint of the Science Robotics paper and may differ in the published version. Marcucci 2023 See the GCS paper entry.

Limits: the regions must be built first (8 IRIS regions took 53 s for the arm). Full dynamics make the problem nonconvex. Rounding is not guaranteed to find the optimum. Solve times are seconds, not milliseconds. Drake implements the method as GcsTrajectoryOptimization; its SolveConvexRestriction is exactly what the widget does for a fixed chain. Drake docs

import cvxpy as cp, numpy as np
S, G = np.array([1.0, 1.0]), np.array([1.0, 9.0])
# doors of the chain A→D1→D2→C as (lower corner, upper corner)
doors = [((3, 3), (4, 4)), ((3.5, 4.8), (4, 5)), ((3.5, 6), (4.5, 7))]
P = cp.Variable((len(doors), 2))          # one breakpoint per door
cons = []
for j, (lo, hi) in enumerate(doors):
    cons += [P[j] >= np.array(lo), P[j] <= np.array(hi)]
pts = [S] + [P[j] for j in range(len(doors))] + [G]
length = sum(cp.norm(pts[k + 1] - pts[k], 2) for k in range(len(pts) - 1))
cp.Problem(cp.Minimize(length), cons).solve()
print(round(length.value, 4), P.value.round(3))
# expected: 9.6287, breakpoints (3, 4), (3.5, 5), (3.5, 6)

Analogy

GCS is a road trip planner that also chooses where you cross each border. A normal planner adds up fixed road lengths. GCS lets each border crossing slide, so a route through more towns can still be shorter, just as the widget's 4-box chain beats the 3-box ones.

7. Scaling up: fast planning through safe boxes (2024)

A warehouse or a village can need ten thousand safe regions, and then even one GCS relaxation gets slow. Marcucci, Nobel, Tedrake and Boyd traded the optimality bound for speed. They use only axis-aligned boxes, and they split the work into a graph search and a few small convex problems. Marcucci 2024b

  1. Offline: build a graph of which boxes overlap and label its edges with approximate distances, using one convex program.
  2. Online: a weighted shortest-path search gives a box chain and a polygonal path, which is then shortened.
  3. Online: a few convex problems turn the polygon into smooth Bézier curves inside the same boxes.

It is complete: it finds a path if one exists and otherwise proves there is none. It is not guaranteed optimal. With 25,600 boxes, the offline step took 25 s and the online steps 0.12 s (polygon) plus 3.4 s (smooth). For a quadrotor in a village of 10,150 boxes, online planning took 0.22 s plus 7.5 s for a path through 135 boxes. See the safe-boxes paper entry.

The ideas keep moving, as of Oct 2026. GCS* runs an A*-style search over an implicit graph of convex sets. A 2025 paper plans shortest walks, where a path may revisit sets, guided by an SDP lower bound on the cost-to-go. Chia 2024 Morozov 2025

MethodWhat is convexGuaranteeReported time
OBCANothing overall; the collision constraints become smooth and exactLocal optimum from a warm start0.6–0.9 s on average for parking (2013 laptop)
Safe flight corridorThe trajectory QP inside fixed polyhedraStays inside the corridor where the constraints are enforced; quality depends on the rough pathNot checked for this lesson
IRISEach step: a QP for planes, an SDP for the ellipseOne large region per seed, not the largestSeconds even with 106 obstacles
GCSThe relaxation (an SOCP) and each fixed-chain problemCertified gap; often globally optimalSeconds (median 3.7 s for the quadrotor)

Explain it to a 10-year-old

Your room has a big toy box in the middle. You want to walk from the door to your bed without bumping it. First put down a few rugs that do not touch the box, so that each rug touches the next. On one rug you can walk straight anywhere. So you only have to choose which rugs to use, and then walk straight from rug to rug.

Common misunderstandings

  • "OBCA makes collision avoidance convex." It makes the collision constraints smooth and exact. The full problem, with car dynamics and rotation, is still nonconvex, so it finds a local optimum and needs a warm start such as Hybrid A*.
  • "A minimum-distance constraint tells you how deep a collision is." Distance is 0 for every overlap, shallow or deep. To minimise penetration you need signed distance, OBCA's ‖ATλ‖ = 1 form.
  • "Convex pieces cover all of free space." IRIS regions and boxes are inner approximations. They leave some free space out, the seeds matter, and joint-space regions for arms are usually only approximately certified.
  • "Fewest regions means shortest path." In the widget the 4-box chain (9.63) beats both 3-box chains (13.66 and 17.23).
  • "The certified gap is the true gap." It is only an upper bound. In the GCS paper one certified gap of 27.1% hid a true gap of 2.3%.

Check yourself

Q1. Why is "stay outside a square obstacle" a nonconvex constraint?

A convex set must contain the segment between any two of its points, and free space does not. Corners are not the cause: a round obstacle (Day 18) has the same problem. ‖x‖² is convex; the trouble is that we ask it to be large, not small.

Q2. In OBCA, what is the extra variable λ?

λ comes from the dual of the distance problem. A valid λ (λ ⪰ 0, ‖ATλ‖ ≤ 1) with (Ap − b)Tλ ≥ dmin proves the clearance. It is a multiplier, but of the inner distance problem, not of the dynamics.

Q3. Obstacle [−1, 1]² with rows x ≤ 1, y ≤ 1, −x ≤ 1, −y ≤ 1, and p = (3, 0.5), so Ap − b = (2, −0.5, −4, −1.5). Which λ certifies the true distance 2?

(1, 0, 0, 0) gives 2 with ‖ATλ‖ = 1. (0.71, 0.71, 0, 0) is valid too but proves only 1.06, a weaker lower bound. (0, 1, 0, 0) gives −0.5, and (1, 1, 1, 1) gives −4: valid but useless.

Q4. What does IRIS alternate between?

Step (i) puts a tangent plane at each obstacle's closest point to the current ellipsoid (a small QP). Step (ii) solves max log det C inside those planes (an SDP). Sampling and smoothing describe planners like PRM, not IRIS.

Q5. A GCS relaxation costs 27.29 and the rounded path costs 28.10. What can you say?

Crelax ≤ Copt ≤ Cround, so the gap is at most 0.81/27.29 = 2.97%. The bound does not tell you the true gap; in this case a MIP solver showed it was 0%. A relaxation gives a lower bound, not an upper one.

Q6. Why does GCS give each region a Bézier curve?

The convex hull property turns "the whole curve is safe" into a few linear constraints on control points, with no sampling and no gaps between samples. Regions must still overlap so that consecutive curves can join.

Recap: things to remember

  1. Free space has holes, so "stay outside" is an OR over faces and is nonconvex: (−2, 0) and (2, 0) are safe, their midpoint is not.
  2. The fixes are binaries (exact, slow), local methods (fast, need a warm start), and convex pieces (convex once the pieces are chosen).
  3. OBCA writes distance as a dual problem. A multiplier λ with (Ap − b)Tλ ≥ dmin and ‖ATλ‖ ≤ 1 proves clearance, and the constraints are smooth.
  4. Safe corridors and IRIS build convex rooms. IRIS alternates tangent planes (QP) with the biggest inscribed ellipse (SDP).
  5. GCS chooses the rooms and the path in one convex relaxation and certifies the gap. More rooms can mean a shorter path: 9.63 vs 13.66.

  13. Mixed Discrete and Continuous Planning using Shortest Walks in Graphs of Convex Sets, S. Morozov et al., arXiv, 2025 (accessed 2026-10-26).
  14. GcsTrajectoryOptimization class reference, Drake (accessed 2026-10-26).

Week 3 · Day 20

Safety filters & optimization in learning

After today you can build a control-barrier-function QP that minimally corrects any controller to keep a robot safe, and explain how differentiable optimization layers and learned warm starts let neural networks and solvers work together.

About 60 min · Needs Days 10 and 17 · No CO4A chapter (new material)

Today's big idea

Keep the controller you already have, even a neural network, and put a tiny QP between it and the motors. The QP changes the command as little as possible, under one rule: the safety margin h may shrink only slowly as it nears zero, so it never crosses zero. The KKT conditions that solve this QP in one line also let you backpropagate through it. That is how optimization and learning end up in the same loop.

1. The safety filter: a referee between controller and motors

Think of a driving-school car with a second brake pedal on the instructor's side. While the student drives well, the instructor does nothing. When the student heads for trouble, the instructor presses just hard enough to fix it, and no harder. A safety filter is that instructor, written as an optimization problem.

The student is the nominal controller: whatever turns the current state x into a command unom(x). It can be the MPC from Day 17, a hand-tuned PID loop, or a neural-network policy that nobody can verify. The filter does not need to know how it works. It only sees the command and the state.

At every control step the filter solves

u* = argminu ½‖u − unom‖22
subject to: the safety rule holds for u

and sends u* to the motors. The cost measures how much the command was changed, not how large it is. Ames and co-authors describe this as modifying an existing controller "in a minimally invasive fashion". Ames 2019

The safety rule turns out to be linear in u, so the filter is a one-constraint QP (Day 5) with a one-line solution. In today's widget, a planner drives a point robot at 1 m/s past a round obstacle. With the default setting, the filter leaves the planner's command untouched for the first 1.64 s, until the robot is 1.40 m from the obstacle.

2. Barrier functions: you may approach, but slow down

Picture walking toward a wall in the dark, with one rule: each second, you may close at most half of the remaining gap. At 2 m you may walk at 1 m/s. At 20 cm you may walk at only 10 cm/s. You get closer and closer, but you never touch the wall.

To write this down, pick a barrier function h(x), a number that measures your safety margin. The safe set is C = {x : h(x) ≥ 0}. Its edge is where h = 0, and inside it h > 0. A set is forward invariant if every motion that starts inside it stays inside. Being safe means C is forward invariant. Ames 2019

Three barriers you will meet today: h = 5 − x for a wall at x = 5; h = ‖x − c‖2 − r2 for a round obstacle of radius r centred at c; and h = D − 1.8v for a car that keeps a gap D of at least 1.8 seconds' worth of its speed v.

The rule from the wall picture is

ḣ ≥ −γ·h, with γ > 0

In words: far from the edge, h is large and may fall quickly. Near the edge, h is small and may fall only slowly. At the edge, h = 0 and may not fall at all. The rate γ (units 1/s) sets how fast the margin may shrink. The wall walk above is γ = 0.5.

Why can h never cross zero? Take the fastest allowed approach, ḣ = −γh exactly. Its solution is h(t) = h(0)·e−γt, which stays positive forever. Any motion that obeys the rule shrinks h no faster, so it stays positive too.

Now bring in the robot. Most robot models are control-affine: ẋ = f(x) + g(x)u. Here f is the drift (what happens with no input) and g(x) says how the input u pushes the state. The chain rule gives

ḣ = ∇h(x)Tẋ = Lfh(x) + Lgh(x)·u

Lfh = ∇hTf and Lgh = ∇hTg are the Lie derivatives of h: its rate of change along the drift and along the input. The key fact is that ḣ is linear in u. So the rule ḣ ≥ −γh is one linear inequality on u:

Lfh(x) + Lgh(x)·u ≥ −γ·h(x)

h is a control barrier function (CBF) if at every state some input satisfies this inequality. In general, γh may be any extended class-K function α(h): strictly increasing, with α(0) = 0. The main theorem: any Lipschitz controller that always picks such a u keeps C forward invariant, and it pulls the state back if noise pushes it slightly out. Ames 2019

A worked example in 1-D. A robot on a line has ẋ = u and a wall at x = 5, so h = 5 − x and ḣ = −u. The rule −u ≥ −γ(5 − x) becomes

u ≤ γ·h (a speed limit: γ times the gap)

The planner wants unom = 2 m/s. At x = 4 the gap is h = 1 m. With γ = 0.5 the limit is 0.5 m/s, so the filter sends u* = 0.5. With γ = 1 it sends 1. With γ = 5 the limit is 5 m/s, more than the planner wants, so u* = 2 and the filter stays silent. In general u* = min(unom, γh).

How fast does the gap close? If the robot always drives right at the speed limit, then h(t) = h(0)e−γt. From a 2 m gap, one second later it is 1.213 m with γ = 0.5, 0.736 m with γ = 1 and 0.0135 m with γ = 5. A bigger γ lets you get close sooner.

Explain it to a 10-year-old

You ride your bike toward a wall, and the rule is: the closer you are, the slower you must go. Far away you can zoom. Near the wall you have to creep, and right next to it you have to stop. So you can get very close, but you never bump into it.

3. The CBF-QP is a projection with a closed form

Picture a field split by a straight fence. You stand on the wrong side and want the nearest spot on the right side. You walk straight at the fence, at right angles to it, and stop as soon as you reach it. That walk is the whole solution of the safety filter.

Put the pieces together. The CBF-QP is Ames 2019

u* = argminu ½‖u − unom‖22
s.t. Lfh(x) + Lgh(x)·u ≥ −γh(x)

Name the data a = Lgh(x)T (a vector) and b = −γh(x) − Lfh(x) (a number). The constraint reads aTu ≥ b. In the space of inputs that is a half-space, the "right side of the fence". The cost is the squared distance to unom. So u* is the point of the half-space nearest to unom, its projection.

The KKT conditions from Day 10 give the answer. Stationarity says u* − unom = λa for a multiplier λ ≥ 0. Complementary slackness says λ = 0 unless the constraint is tight. Solving the two cases gives CO4A 12-1

λ = max(0, (b − aTunom) / ‖a‖2)
u* = unom + λ·a

If unom already obeys the rule, λ = 0 and the command passes through untouched. Otherwise the filter adds just enough of a to land on the boundary. The CBF tutorial notes this closed form, the min-norm controller, follows from the KKT conditions. No solver is needed. Ames 2019

The correction always points along a = LghT, the direction in which the input raises h fastest. Next to an obstacle, that is straight away from it. Keep this in mind, because it explains the deadlock in Section 5.

Here is a worked 2-D example that matches the widget. A point robot has ẋ = u, so f = 0 and g = I. A disk of radius 1 sits at the origin, so h = ‖x‖2 − 1, a = 2x and Lfh = 0. At x = (−2, 0.2) we get h = 3.04 and a = (−4, 0.4). The planner's unit vector toward the goal (4, 0) is unom = (0.9994, −0.0333), so aTunom = −4.011.

  • γ = 1: b = −3.04. The rule is broken, because −4.011 < −3.04. So λ = 0.971/16.16 = 0.0601 and u* = (0.759, −0.009). The robot slows from 1.00 to 0.76 m/s.
  • γ = 0.5: b = −1.52, λ = 0.154 and u* = (0.383, 0.028). It is slower still, and already steering up, away from the disk.
  • γ = 5: b = −15.2. The rule holds, so u* = unom.

In code, the closed form takes two lines. The CVXPY version handles several barriers or input limits, and its Parameters return in Section 6.

import numpy as np, cvxpy as cp
def cbf_filter(x, u_nom, gamma):      # point robot, unit disk at 0
    a, b = 2*x, -gamma*(x @ x - 1)
    lam = max(0.0, (b - a @ u_nom) / (a @ a))
    return u_nom + lam*a

cbf_filter(np.array([-2, .2]), np.array([.9994, -.0333]), 1.0)
# -> about [0.759, -0.009]

u = cp.Variable(2)                     # the same QP for a solver
un, a, b = cp.Parameter(2), cp.Parameter(2), cp.Parameter()
qp = cp.Problem(cp.Minimize(cp.sum_squares(u - un)), [a @ u >= b])

Try it: the widget starts at γ = 1 with the filter on. Drag the time slider and watch the two arrows: the planner's dashed unom and the solid u that the QP sends. Then try the γ buttons, switch the filter off, and press "Head-on start".

Notice: at γ = 1 the filter stays silent for 1.64 s, then bends the path so the robot passes 0.031 m from the disk and reaches the goal at 11.9 s. Without the filter the robot arrives at 10.0 s, but only by driving 0.75 m into the disk. At t = 3.0 s the planner asks for (1.00, −0.07) and the QP sends (0.45, 0.08) with λ = 0.192. On the chart, the filtered h(x) dips toward 0 but never below it.

Analogy

A safety filter is a strict but lazy copy editor. You hand in your sentence, and the editor checks one rule. If the sentence obeys it, it comes back untouched. If not, the editor makes the smallest change that fixes it and leaves everything else alone. The editor never rewrites your story, which is also why it cannot rescue a story that is heading the wrong way.

4. Adding a goal: the CLF-CBF QP

Picture adaptive cruise control. The driver sets 22 m/s, and then a slow truck appears ahead. Two wishes now collide: "drive at 22 m/s" and "keep a safe gap". The gap must win. The speed wish should give way gracefully, and come back once the road clears.

The "make progress" wish is written with a control Lyapunov function (CLF) V(x). It is an energy-like number that is zero at the goal and that the controller can always make decrease. Its rule mirrors the barrier rule: V̇ ≤ −cV, with c > 0. Ames and co-authors put both rules into one QP, the CLF-CBF QP: Ames 2017

minu, δ ½uTH(x)u + p·δ2

s.t. LfV + LgV·u ≤ −cV + δ (progress)
Lfh + Lgh·u ≥ −γh (safety)

H(x) is a positive definite weight on effort. The relaxation variable δ is a slack on the progress rule, and p > 0 is its price. Both constraints are linear in (u, δ), so this is still a QP.

Why does only the progress rule get a slack? If both rules were hard, they could contradict each other. Then no u satisfies both, and the QP is infeasible. With δ, the progress rule can always be met by paying for a large δ. So the QP has a solution whenever the safety rule alone does, and safety is never traded away. The paper also shows that this controller is Lipschitz continuous, which the safety theorem needs. Ames 2017

Now the paper's cruise-control numbers. The state is the follower's speed vf, the lead car's speed vl and the gap D. The hard rule is the "half the speedometer" headway D ≥ 1.8vf: a gap in metres of half your speed in km/h. So h = D − 1.8vf. The soft goal is V = (vf − 22)2, a desired speed of 22 m/s (79.2 km/h). Starting from (vf, vl, D) = (18, 10, 150), the car cruises at 22 m/s while the gap is large. When the headway rule binds, it settles to the lead car's speed. At 10 m/s the rule asks for a gap of at least 1.8 × 10 = 18 m. Ames 2017

The paper is honest about a catch. Without force limits, the commanded acceleration went past the comfort bounds drawn in its plot. But adding a bound on the wheel force can make the QP infeasible, because braking hard enough may no longer be possible. So the paper builds force-aware barrier functions that stay feasible under braking limits. Ames 2017

5. Tuning knobs and honest limits

γ is a "how late may I brake" knob. A small γ lets the margin shrink only slowly, so the filter brakes early and keeps a wide berth. A large γ lets the robot rush in and brake late. These are the widget's numbers from the default start (−4, 0.5):

SettingClosest gap to the diskFilter first actsReaches the goal
No filter−0.750 m (inside)never10.0 s
γ = 0.50.172 mat t = 0, 3.03 m away13.3 s
γ = 10.031 mat t = 1.64 s, 1.40 m away11.9 s
γ = 50.0004 mat t = 2.84 s, 0.21 m away11.4 s

For a head-on approach at unit speed, the rule breaks once 2‖x‖ > γ(‖x‖2 − 1). So the filter wakes up at a distance (1 + √(1 + γ2))/γ − 1 from the surface: 3.24 m for γ = 0.5, 1.41 m for γ = 1 and 0.22 m for γ = 5.

One warning: the guarantee is for continuous time. A real controller holds u for a step dt, so keep γ·dt well below 1. The widget uses dt = 0.01 s and γ ≤ 10 (see the Going deeper box).

Next comes relative degree, which asks whether the input shows up in ḣ at all. Picture pressing a car's brake pedal. The car's position does not jump. Its speed changes first, and only then its position. If h depends only on position and the input is an acceleration, then ḣ contains no u at all. Lgh = 0, and the rule cannot be enforced through u. The number of times you must differentiate h before u appears is its relative degree. A plain CBF needs relative degree 1.

Take a point mass with position p, velocity v and acceleration input u. The obstacle barrier h = ‖p‖2 − 1 gives ḣ = 2pTv, with no u in it. One more derivative gives ḧ = 2‖v‖2 + 2pTu, where u appears, so the relative degree is 2. Two fixes are common. Fold speed into h, as the headway rule does: v̇f depends on the wheel force u, so ḣ = vl − vf − 1.8v̇f contains u. Or use an exponential (high-order) CBF, which puts a rule on h and its derivatives together. Ames 2019

Now three honest limits. First, h ≥ 0 is the promise, not h ≥ 5 cm. With γ = 5 the widget's robot skims the disk at 0.4 mm. The math is satisfied, but a real bumper would not be. Build the margin into h instead. For a 0.3 m margin, use h = ‖x − c‖2 − (r + 0.3)2.

Second, a filter is not a planner. Press "Head-on start" in the widget. The robot starts at (−4, 0), exactly on the line through the obstacle's centre. It creeps up to (−1, 0), touching the disk, and stays there. The cause is the direction of the correction. Here unom points straight at the centre and a = 2x points straight away from it, so the two are parallel. Adding λa can cancel the forward motion, but it cannot create a sideways one. This stuck state is a deadlock. Off the centre line, a has a small sideways part, and that part steers the default run around the disk. The fix belongs upstream: a planner that picks a side, as on Day 19.

Third, the guarantee is about the model. The proof assumes ẋ = f(x) + g(x)u holds exactly, and tyre slip, actuator delay or a slow control loop break that. The tutorial notes that noise and modelling errors might push the system out of C, and the CBF condition then drives it back. Ames 2019 In practice that means a margin inside h, a conservative γ, and robust CBF variants when the model is uncertain.

Going deeper (optional): why ḣ ≥ −γh keeps h ≥ 0, even with time steps

Continuous time: d/dt(eγth) = eγt(ḣ + γh) ≥ 0. So eγth(t) never decreases, and h(t) ≥ h(0)e−γt ≥ 0. For a general class-K α the same idea works through a comparison lemma.

Discrete time, for the widget's disk: h = ‖x‖2 − 1 is convex, so it lies above its tangent. One Euler step x+ = x + dt·u therefore gives h(x+) ≥ h(x) + dt·∇hTu ≥ (1 − γ·dt)·h(x). With γ·dt ≤ 0.1, each step keeps at least 90% of the margin, so h stays ≥ 0 at every sample. For a non-convex h or drift f ≠ 0 this tidy bound is gone, and you need a smaller dt or a discrete-time CBF.

6. Optimization inside learning: differentiable layers

Picture a clamp: z* = min(q, 1). At q = 0.5, nudging q moves z* by the same amount. At q = 2, the clamp holds z* at 1, and nudging q does nothing. That clamp is the solution of a tiny QP, and its slope (1 or 0) is exactly what backpropagation needs.

The QP is z*(q) = argminz ½z2 − qz subject to z ≤ 1. Its KKT conditions are z − q + λ = 0, λ(z − 1) = 0 and λ ≥ 0. Instead of differentiating a solver's steps, differentiate these equations at the solution. This is implicit differentiation:

dz + dλ = dq
λ·dz + (z − 1)·dλ = 0

At q = 0.5 we have z = 0.5 and λ = 0. The second line forces dλ = 0, so dz/dq = 1. At q = 2 we have z = 1 and λ = 1. The second line forces dz = 0, so dz/dq = 0. Finite differences agree. An active constraint blocks the gradient.

OptNet makes this a neural-network layer. The layer outputs zi+1 = argminz ½zTQz + qTz subject to Az = b and Gz ≤ w, where Q, q, A, b, G and w may come from the previous layer. (The paper writes h for w; we keep h for the barrier.) The backward pass differentiates the KKT system and gets gradients for all six inputs from one linear solve. That solve reuses the factorization that the interior-point solver (primal-dual card) has already computed, so the backward pass is almost free. Amos & Kolter 2017

Its batched GPU solver, qpth, solved 128 QPs of 100 variables and 100 inequalities in 0.18 s, against 4.7 s for Gurobi. The paper also learned the rules of 4×4 mini-Sudoku from examples alone. The limit is cost, which is cubic in the number of variables or constraints. The authors put the practical size below about 1,000 dimensions, and "substantially less" for real time. Amos & Kolter 2017 More on the OptNet paper card.

cvxpylayers removes the hand work. You write the problem in CVXPY with Parameters and wrap it as a PyTorch or TensorFlow layer. The problem must follow DPP (disciplined parametrized programming), CVXPY's rules for where parameters may appear. A parameter times a variable is fine. A product of two parameters times a variable is not, until you replace the product by one new parameter. DPP guarantees that the map from parameters to solver data is affine. Agrawal 2019

Every DPP problem then runs in the ASA form: an affine canonicalizer, a cone solver and an affine retriever. Its derivative is the chain rule through those three pieces. Caching the affine map cut canonicalization from 18.9 ms to 1.49 ms on a logistic-regression example. On a sparse QP with 1,024 variables it ran about 5× faster than qpth. Agrawal 2019 It first shipped with CVXPY 1.1. As of Oct 2026 the latest release is 1.2.0 (May 2026), so check the current API before copying 2019 code. PyPI 2026 See the cvxpylayers paper card.

Differentiable MPC applies the same trick to the controller from Day 17. The MPC becomes the last layer of a policy, and its cost and dynamics become learnable. Gradients come from the KKT conditions of the convex approximation at the solver's fixed point, instead of unrolling every iLQR iteration. The authors report that the backward pass is essentially free. Trained by imitation on a pendulum and a cartpole, it needed less data than a generic neural policy. Amos 2018

The CBF-QP of Section 3 fits here too. In the code above it is a DPP problem in unom, a and b, so a policy can be trained with its own safety filter inside the loop. Remember the clamp, though. Where the filter is active, the derivative of u* with respect to unom is I − aaT/‖a‖2. That matrix wipes out the gradient along a, so the policy gets no signal from pushing harder into the constraint.

7. Learning inside optimization: amortized solves and warm starts

Picture a commuter who drives the same road every day. They do not plan from a blank map each morning. Memory gives a near-perfect first guess, and they only correct for today's traffic. A robot is in the same position, because its MPC solves almost the same problem many times a second.

Amortized optimization learns that memory. A model ŷθ(x) maps the problem's context x (state, goal, obstacles) to an approximate solution of argminy f(y; x). Most of the work is paid once, at training time. Amos 2023 There are two flavours:

  • Fully amortized: one network pass gives the answer, and f is not touched at run time.
  • Semi-amortized: the model runs some solver steps inside. Examples are unrolled gradient steps, learned versions of ISTA (ISTA card), and RLQP, which keeps the OSQP solver inside.

Training can regress onto solved examples, minimizing E‖ŷθ(x) − y*(x)‖2. Or it can minimize the objective itself, E f(ŷθ(x); x), which needs no labels. Amos 2023

The safest use of a prediction is as a warm start, the solver's first guess. Here is why that helps, in numbers. Run gradient descent (Day 6) on f = ½xTQx − bTx with Q = diag(1, 10) and b = (1, 10), so x* = (1, 1). Use step 0.1 and stop when ‖x − x*‖ ≤ 10−6. From x = 0 it takes 132 iterations. From a guess 0.01 off in the slow direction it takes 88, and from 10−4 off it takes 44. Each 100× better guess saves 44 iterations, because the error shrinks by 0.9 per step and 0.944 ≈ 1/100.

On Day 17 the warm start was the previous solution, shifted by one step. A learned warm start replaces or improves that guess. Either way the solver still enforces the constraints, which a network alone cannot promise.

Where does this sit in a driving stack? Each piece of today has a natural place:

LayerWhat the optimizer doesToday's tool
Planner or policy (possibly learned)Proposes the command unom or a trajectoryMPC (Day 17), warm-started or amortized
Safety filterEdits the command as little as possible so the safety rules holdCBF-QP: closed form for one rule, a QP solver such as OSQP for several
Training (offline)Tunes costs, models or policies through the optimizerOptNet, cvxpylayers, differentiable MPC

Keep the claims in proportion to the evidence. The automotive examples in these papers are adaptive cruise control and lane keeping. They were shown in simulation and on small Khepera mobile robots, not on road cars, and the tutorial frames them as driver-assistance examples. Ames 2019 The differentiable-MPC results are on a pendulum and a cartpole. Amos 2018 None of today's sources describes a production vehicle. Treat these as well-founded design patterns, not as a description of any car on the road.

Common misunderstandings

  • "A CBF keeps a safety margin." It guarantees h ≥ 0, not h ≥ some ε. With γ = 5 the widget's robot passes within 0.4 mm. Put the margin inside h, for example ‖x − c‖2 − (r + 0.3)2.
  • "The CBF-QP always has a solution." One rule with no input limits always does. With force limits or several barriers, the half-spaces may not overlap, and the QP is infeasible. That is why the cruise-control paper builds force-aware barriers. Softening the CBF with a slack restores feasibility, but it also gives up the guarantee.
  • "The filter will steer around obstacles." It only adds a push along a = LghT. On the centre line that push is parallel to unom, and the robot freezes at (−1, 0). Route choice belongs to the planner.
  • "A differentiable layer is free." OptNet-style layers cost cubic time in the problem size. Their gradients are zero through active constraints and undefined at kinks, like q = 1 in the clamp. Amos & Kolter 2017
  • "A well-trained network's solution is safe." Amortized predictions carry no feasibility guarantee. Use them as warm starts for a solver that checks the constraints, or pass them through a safety filter.

Check yourself

Q1. What does the CBF-QP minimize at each control step?

The filter's job is to edit the planner as little as possible, so the cost is the squared change. Minimizing ‖u‖2 would ignore what the planner wanted and would happily stop the robot. Safety lives in the constraint, not in the cost.

Q2. A robot has ẋ = u and a wall at x = 5, so h = 5 − x. With γ = 1, the planner asks for unom = 2 m/s at x = 4. What does the filter send?

The rule ḣ ≥ −γh becomes u ≤ γh = 1 × 1 = 1. The planner's 2 m/s breaks it, so the projection gives exactly 1. You would get 2 m/s with γ = 5, where the limit is 5 m/s. Stopping or reversing would change the command more than needed.

Q3. In the widget, you raise γ from 1 to 5. What happens?

γ is how fast h may shrink. With γ = 5 the filter wakes up 0.21 m from the disk instead of 1.40 m, so the robot skims the edge and arrives 0.5 s sooner. It still never enters: h ≥ 0 holds for every γ > 0.

Q4. Why does the CLF-CBF QP put the slack δ on the CLF rule but not on the CBF rule?

Two hard rules can contradict each other, and then the QP has no solution. The slack lets the progress rule bend at a price p·δ2, so safety never has to. Both rules are linear in u, and the QP is convex with or without δ.

Q5. The robot starts at (−4, 0), heading straight through the obstacle's centre toward (4, 0), with the filter on. What happens?

On the centre line, a = 2x points straight back along unom. Adding λa can only cancel forward motion, so the robot slows to a stop at the edge: a deadlock. The guarantee still holds (h ≥ 0), and λ is never negative. Choosing a side is a planner's job.

Q6. How does OptNet compute gradients through a QP layer?

The solution satisfies the KKT equations, so implicit differentiation of those equations gives exact gradients from one linear solve with a matrix that is already factored. Unrolling the iterations also works, but it costs memory and only approximates the answer. Differentiable MPC avoids it for the same reason.

Recap: things to remember

  1. A safety filter solves min ½‖u − unom‖2 subject to the CBF rule at every step. It leaves safe commands untouched and edits unsafe ones minimally.
  2. The rule ḣ ≥ −γh means "approach, but slow down near the edge". It is linear in u for control-affine systems, and it keeps h ≥ 0, because h can shrink no faster than h(0)e−γt.
  3. With one rule, the KKT conditions give u* = unom + λa with λ = max(0, (b − aTunom)/‖a‖2): a half-space projection. The CLF-CBF QP adds a goal with a slack, while safety stays hard.
  4. Know the limits: no margin unless you put it in h, deadlock on the centre line, model error, relative degree, and infeasibility under input limits. γ trades margin (0.172 m at 0.5) for speed (0.0004 m at 5).
  5. Implicit differentiation of the KKT conditions (OptNet, cvxpylayers, differentiable MPC) puts solvers inside networks. Amortized models put networks inside solvers, best as warm starts behind a constraint-checking solver.

Week 3 · Day 21

Solvers in practice & what's next

After today you can pick a modelling tool and a solver for a given problem, diagnose the usual failures (infeasible, unbounded, inaccurate, too slow), and plan what to study next.

About 60 min · Needs Days 5, 12, 13 and 17 · No CO4A chapter (new material)

Today's big idea

You will rarely write a solver yourself. You name the problem's class, write the model in a modelling tool, and hand it to a solver built for that class. Then you do the part no solver does for you: scale the data, read the status, check the answer, and plan for the day it fails.

1. Classify first: the class picks the solver

Analogy

When you are ill you can see a general doctor or a specialist. The specialist is faster and more reliable, but only for their speciality. Solvers work the same way. OSQP specializes in quadratic programs. SCS is a generalist: CVXPY's docs say it handles every class "except mixed-integer". CVXPY docs

So the first job is to name your problem's class exactly. Day 5 built the ladder LP ⊂ QP ⊂ SOCP ⊂ SDP, where each class contains the ones before it. Two labels sit beside the ladder. Add "MI" (mixed-integer) if any variable must be an integer, as on Day 15. Say "NLP" (nonlinear program) if some function is smooth but not convex, as on Day 16.

Pick the narrowest class that fits. A QP solver expects exactly one shape. Here is OSQP's standard form: OSQP docs

minimize ½xTPx + qTx
subject to l ≤ Ax ≤ u

Here x ∈ ℝn holds the decision variables. P ⪰ 0 is the curvature of the cost and q its linear part. The rows of A, with lower bounds l and upper bounds u, hold every constraint. An equality is a row with li = ui, and a one-sided limit uses li = −∞.

Now a worked example. Take a vehicle MPC like Day 17's, with 10 states, 3 inputs and a horizon of 20 steps. It has (10 + 3) × 20 = 260 variables and 10 × 20 = 200 dynamics equalities. A quadratic cost with box limits makes it a QP. It must be re-solved at 100 Hz, which leaves 10 ms per solve on an embedded computer. That calls for a sparse QP solver with warm starts and C code, such as OSQP through CVXPYgen or HPIPM inside acados. Schaller 2022 acados docs

2. The modelling layer: who writes the matrices

You could type P, q, A, l and u by hand. For a 260-variable MPC that means thousands of numbers, and one index slip silently changes the problem. A modelling tool lets you write the math almost as on paper and builds the matrices for you, the way a compiler turns readable code into machine code.

The translation step is called canonicalization: rewriting your model into a solver's standard form. Good tools also check your model on the way. CVXPY checks convexity, and CasADi computes derivatives.

CVXPY (Python) checks convexity with disciplined convex programming (DCP). You build expressions from atoms whose curvature it knows: sum_squares is convex, log is concave. You combine them by rules that keep convexity. If the rules cannot prove your model convex, CVXPY refuses to solve it, even when the model happens to be convex. CVXPY docs

Disciplined parametrized programming (DPP) adds parameters: data that changes between solves, such as the robot's current state. If the model follows the DPP rules, CVXPY canonicalizes once and re-uses that work. With warm_start on, which is the default, the solver can also re-use its matrix factorization. In the docs' example (m = 2000, n = 1000) the second solve drops from 11.14 s to 2.95 s. CVXPY docs

import cvxpy as cp, numpy as np

A = np.array([[1., 2.], [3., 1.]])
b = cp.Parameter(2)                  # data that changes every tick
x = cp.Variable(2)
cons = [x >= 0]
prob = cp.Problem(cp.Minimize(cp.sum_squares(A @ x - b)), cons)
print(prob.is_dcp(), prob.is_dpp())  # True True

b.value = np.array([1., -1.])
prob.solve(solver=cp.CLARABEL)
print(prob.status, x.value)          # optimal, x ≈ [0, 0.2]

b.value = np.array([1., 2.])         # next tick: only b changes
prob.solve(solver=cp.CLARABEL)       # x ≈ [0.6, 0.2]

Check the numbers. Without the bound, the best x would be A−1b = (−0.6, 0.8), which breaks x ≥ 0. So the solver returns x* = (0, 0.2) with cost 1.8. For the next tick, b = (1, 2), the unconstrained answer (0.6, 0.2) is already feasible and the cost is 0.

Four other tools cover most robotics work. Pick by language and by whether your model is convex.

ToolLanguageBest atWorth knowing
CVXPYPythonConvex models checked by DCP; parameters, C code (CVXPYgen), differentiable layers (Day 20)Ships Clarabel, OSQP and SCS CVXPY docs
JuMPJuliaEverything from LP to mixed-integer nonlinearIts docs list each solver's classes and licence JuMP docs
CasADiPython, MATLAB, C++Nonlinear models: automatic differentiation, integrators, NLP and QP plug-ins (IPOPT, qpOASES, HPIPM…), C code exportThe usual front end for nonlinear MPC CasADi
YALMIPMATLAB, OctaveA very wide solver list: LP to SDP, integer and nonlinearIncludes its own global solver, BMIBNB YALMIP
Drake MathematicalProgramC++, PythonRobotics: add variables, costs and constraints; Solve() "will dispatch to the most appropriate solver"IRIS regions and GCS planners (Day 19) Drake docs

3. The solver families: how each one moves

Every solver walks toward the answer, but with different strides. Picture crossing a city. An interior-point method takes a taxi: a few long, expensive rides, each landing very close to the target. A first-order method walks: many cheap steps that start fast but take a while over the last metre. An active-set method guesses which walls you are touching and corrects the guess.

FamilyHow it movesSolversBest for
Interior point (Day 12)A few tens of Newton steps along the central path; each solves one sparse linear systemClarabel, MOSEK, ECOS; IPOPT for NLPs Clarabel docsHigh accuracy and reliable infeasibility detection
First-order splitting (Day 13)Many cheap steps; OSQP factorizes once, PDHG needs only matrix–vector productsOSQP, SCS, PDLP OSQP docsWarm starts, huge problems, GPUs, embedded code; moderate accuracy
Active set (Day 17)Guesses which constraints are tight and updates the guessqpOASES, DAQP qpOASESSmall MPC QPs re-solved from the last answer
Simplex (Day 5)Walks from corner to corner of the LP's polyhedronHiGHS (dual simplex is its default) HiGHS docsLPs that need an exact corner solution
Branch and bound (Day 15)Splits on an integer variable and bounds each branch with a convex relaxationGurobi, MOSEK, SCIP, HiGHS JuMP docsExact answers with integers, when time allows
SQP (Day 16)Solves one QP per step of a nonlinear problemacados (with HPIPM), SNOPT acados docsNonlinear MPC in real time; local answers only

The trade-off fits in one line:

solve time = (number of steps) × (cost of one step)

Interior point wins the first factor and first-order methods win the second. The OSQP paper reports it is "typically ten times faster than competing interior-point methods" on its benchmarks, but by default it stops at moderate accuracy. Clarabel's authors report it is faster and more robust than the solvers they compared, especially when the objective is quadratic. Stellato 2020 Goulart & Chen 2024 See the primal–dual IPM card, the ADMM card and the OSQP paper.

The car's computer cannot run Python, so you need code generation. It writes a small C solver for one problem family, once. On the robot you pass new parameter values each tick, with no parsing and no memory allocation. CVXPYgen does this for any DPP model in CVXPY, with OSQP, SCS or ECOS underneath. OSQP, acados and CasADi can also emit C code. Schaller 2022 CasADi

Here are the CVXPYgen paper's numbers. On a portfolio back-test the generated code was 6× faster than CVXPY at problem size N = 10 and 2.5× faster at N = 100. Including the time to generate and compile, it broke even after about 5,000 solves. A 4-year daily back-test over 100 hyper-parameter settings is 250 × 4 × 100 = 100,000 solves, far past that point. The authors also flew a 14 × 14 cm quadcopter with MPC at 30 Hz on an Intel Atom. Schaller 2022

Try it: choose a problem class, a size and a time budget. The widget looks up this lesson's mapping table and lists modelling tools and solvers, best first, each with a reason, a source and the day to revisit. The size cut-offs are rules of thumb, not sharp limits.

Notice that the default, a small QP with a real-time budget like the 260-variable MPC of Section 1, puts OSQP with CVXPYgen C code first, then qpOASES, HPIPM inside acados and DAQP, and sends you back to Days 13 and 17. Switch the class to SDP and the first line becomes "Keep SDPs out of the loop".

Explain it to a 10-year-old

Choosing a solver is like choosing how to travel. For a short trip you will repeat every day, you ride the same bike and know every turn. For a long trip once a year, you take the train and don't mind the wait. You don't take a plane to the corner shop, and you don't cycle across the ocean.

4. Three knobs: scaling, tolerances and warm starts

Before comparing prices from three countries, you convert them to one currency. Solvers want the same thing: numbers of similar size. A model that mixes metres with micrometres, or newtons with kilonewtons, has entries that differ by a factor of 106. Iterative solvers then crawl, and a tolerance no longer means the same thing for every constraint.

Scaling, also called equilibration, multiplies rows and columns by positive numbers so that all entries are about 1. OSQP solves a scaled copy of your QP: Stellato 2020

P̄ = cDPD, q̄ = cDq, Ā = EAD

Here D and E are positive diagonal matrices and c > 0 rescales the cost. The scaled answer maps back to yours by undoing D and E, so nothing is lost. OSQP picks D and E by a modified Ruiz equilibration. It repeatedly divides each row and column of the KKT matrix by the square root of its largest entry. The default runs 10 passes (scaling = 10). OSQP settings

Here is a number. Take P = diag(100, 0.01) and one constraint row A = [1 1]. The condition number measures how much rounding errors can grow; you met it as κ on Day 6. For this KKT matrix it drops from 100 to 1.15 after a single pass with D = (0.1, 1, 1).

Iterative solvers never land exactly on the optimum. They stop when the leftover errors, the residuals, are small enough. So "optimal" really means "optimal to about 10−3", and you choose the size of that "about". That threshold is the tolerance. For the primal residual, OSQP stops when Stellato 2020

‖Ax − z‖∞ ≤ εabs + εrel·max(‖Ax‖∞, ‖z‖∞)

Here z is OSQP's copy of Ax that already satisfies l ≤ z ≤ u, so Ax − z measures how far the constraints are violated. εabs is an absolute floor, and εrel adds a part that grows with the size of the numbers. A similar test covers the dual residual. OSQP's own defaults are εabs = εrel = 10−3, with up to 4,000 iterations. OSQP settings

A worked example: suppose Ax = (3.0, −250.0) and z = (3.0005, −250.1). The residual is 0.1. The threshold is 0.001 + 0.001 × 250.1 = 0.2511, so OSQP reports "solved" while one constraint is off by 0.1. The relative part dominated because one value was 250, which is one more reason to scale. Defaults also differ between interfaces: as of Oct 2026, CVXPY's docs list eps_abs = 10−5 for OSQP, against OSQP's own 10−3. Always print the tolerances you actually ran with. CVXPY docs

A robot re-solves almost the same problem every tick: the state moved a little and the obstacles barely changed. A warm start starts the solver from last tick's answer, shifted one step along the horizon. It helps in two separate ways. A better first guess means fewer iterations. And if the matrices did not change, factorization caching re-uses the expensive matrix factorization, so only the vectors are new.

The numbers: Day 20's gradient-descent example needed 132 iterations from a cold start, 88 from a guess 10−2 off, and 44 from a guess 10−4 off. CVXPY's example saved about 8.2 s of 11.14 s from caching alone. Interior-point methods gain less from a good first guess. They work best from a well-centred point far from the boundary, and last tick's answer sits right on it. CVXPY docs

5. When it fails: statuses, certificates and your own KKT check

A solver always answers, but not always with "here is x". Treat the status as part of the answer. OSQP's list is typical: solved; solved inaccurate, which means only tolerances 10× looser were met; primal infeasible; dual infeasible (unbounded); maximum iterations; time limit; and non-convex. OSQP warns that it "may not detect non-convexity reliably". CVXPY reports the inaccurate case as optimal_inaccurate. OSQP status values

Use this table as a first-aid kit.

SymptomUsual causeFirst thing to try
Infeasible (primal infeasible)Constraints contradict, e.g. a deadline the speed limit cannot meet, a sign error, or mixed unitsRead the certificate: its nonzero entries name the conflicting constraints. Soften them with slack variables and a penalty (Day 4).
Unbounded (dual infeasible)A missing limit lets the cost fall forever, e.g. a reward on progress with no speed limitAdd the physical limits; check the sign of the objective.
Inaccurate (solved inaccurate, max iterations)Poor scaling, or a problem that is nearly infeasibleFix units, raise the iteration limit, turn on OSQP's polishing, or switch to an interior-point solver such as Clarabel.
Too slowWrong class or solver, or the model is rebuilt every tickUse parameters (DPP) and warm starts, generate C code, or shorten the horizon. Use GPUs only for huge problems.
DCP error in CVXPYThe rules cannot prove the model convexRewrite it with DCP atoms (Day 4), or move to an NLP tool (Day 16).

Polishing is an optional OSQP clean-up step, off by default. It guesses which constraints are active and solves one small linear system for a more accurate answer. OSQP settings In a control loop, every status other than solved needs a planned fallback, such as last tick's plan shifted by one step, or a safe stop. Never send an unchecked x to the actuators.

A good solver doesn't just say "infeasible". It hands you a proof that you can check with one matrix product, like a referee who shows you the rule that was broken. This is Day 9's duality at work. When the primal has no feasible point, the dual can be pushed to +∞ along some direction, and that direction is a certificate of infeasibility.

For constraints Ax = b, x ≥ 0, Farkas' lemma says that exactly one of two things holds: MOSEK Cookbook

(1) some x ≥ 0 has Ax = b, or
(2) some y has ATy ≤ 0 and bTy > 0

The one-line reason why (2) rules out (1): if both held, then bTy = xT(ATy) ≤ 0, because x ≥ 0 and ATy ≤ 0. That contradicts bTy > 0.

Here is the MOSEK Cookbook's example. The constraints are x1 + x2 + 2x3 = 1, −2x1 − x2 + x3 = −0.5, −x1 + 5x3 = −0.1, and x ≥ 0. Take y = (1, 2, −1): add row 1, twice row 2, and minus row 3. The result is −2x1 − x2 − x3 = 0.1, that is, ATy = (−2, −1, −1) and bTy = 0.1. With x ≥ 0 the left side can never be positive, so no feasible x exists. MOSEK Cookbook

OSQP's form l ≤ Ax ≤ u has the same kind of proof: a y with ATy = 0 and uTmax(y, 0) + lTmin(y, 0) < 0. SCS and Clarabel also detect infeasibility. Stellato 2020 SCS docs

Even "solved" deserves a check, and it takes a few lines. On Day 10 you met the KKT conditions. For a convex problem, any point that passes them is optimal, so they make a complete test. For minimizing f(x) subject to x ≥ 0, with a multiplier λ, they read:

∇f(x) − λ = 0 (stationarity)
x ≥ 0, λ ≥ 0, λixi = 0

b.value = np.array([1., -1.])          # the first tick of Section 2
prob.solve(solver=cp.CLARABEL)
x_, lam = x.value, cons[0].dual_value
grad = 2 * A.T @ (A @ x_ - b.value)    # ∇f(x) for f = ‖Ax − b‖²
print(np.abs(grad - lam).max())        # stationarity: want ≈ 0
print(-x_.min(), -lam.min())           # signs: want ≤ about 0
print(abs(lam @ x_))                   # complementarity: want ≈ 0

Do it by hand at x* = (0, 0.2). Then Ax − b = (0.4 − 1, 0.2 + 1) = (−0.6, 1.2), so ∇f = 2AT(Ax − b) = (6, 0). Stationarity forces λ = (6, 0), which is ≥ 0. Complementarity holds, since 6 × 0 = 0 and 0 × 0.2 = 0. The multiplier also has a meaning: loosening x1 ≥ 0 to x1 ≥ −δ would lower the cost by about 6δ. A solver's residuals should be near its tolerance; if one is far larger, distrust the answer.

Common misunderstandings

  • "An NLP solver is the safe choice, since it handles everything." IPOPT and SNOPT treat a convex problem "as general nonlinear", as Drake's docs put it. You give up the certificates and robustness a conic solver offers. Drake docs
  • "OPTIMAL means exact." It means optimal to a tolerance. OSQP's default 10−3 is fine for MPC and loose for science, and "solved inaccurate" is 10× looser still. Report the tolerance with the answer. OSQP status values
  • "A GPU solver is always faster." HiGHS itself says its PDLP on a CPU is "unlikely to be competitive". GPUs pay off on very large sparse problems, not on a 10 ms MPC. HiGHS docs
  • "Warm starts always help." Factorization caching needs unchanged matrices. If A is a parameter, only the first guess helps, and interior-point methods gain little from that. CVXPY docs
  • "Infeasible means the solver is broken." Usually the model is. Read the certificate, check units and signs, and keep a fallback in the control loop for infeasible, max-iteration and time-limit outcomes.

6. The frontier, as of Oct 2026

Picture a factory with 10,000 workers. A job that splits into 10,000 independent pieces finishes fast. A job where each step waits for the one before leaves most workers idle. A GPU is that factory. Interior-point and simplex methods depend on sparse factorizations, which are the second kind of job. A matrix–vector product is the first kind.

PDHG (primal–dual hybrid gradient) is a first-order method that needs only such products. PDLP is PDHG tuned for LPs, with restarts and preconditioning. Its 2025 journal version took on 11 huge LPs with 125 million to 6.3 billion nonzeros. PDLP solved 8 of them to a 1% gap within 6 days, while Gurobi's barrier solved 3 within a 1 TB memory limit. Applegate 2025

The cuPDLP.jl paper moved the whole method onto one GPU. On an NVIDIA H100, at tolerance 10−4 and without presolve, it was 3× faster than Gurobi on medium and 3.7× on large LP relaxations from the MIPLIB benchmark. With Gurobi's presolve it solved 381 of 383 of them. At 10−8 it still trailed Gurobi's barrier. A GPU run also carries a fixed overhead of about a second, so small problems gain nothing. Lu & Yang 2025

Industry adopted the idea quickly. As of Oct 2026:

  • HiGHS ships cuPDLP-C as its "pdlp" solver, which runs on NVIDIA GPUs. HiGHS docs cuPDLP-C 2023
  • Gurobi 13.0 added PDHG for LP with an optional GPU build. The GPU version "matured from the beta state" in 13.0.2. Gurobi 13 notes
  • NVIDIA cuOpt (docs version 26.10) runs GPU PDLP, a GPU barrier and CPU dual simplex at the same time. cuOpt docs
  • For QPs and cones: OSQP 1.0 merged a CUDA backend (cuOSQP), CuClarabel runs interior point on a GPU, and SCS has a cuDSS GPU backend. OSQP releases CuClarabel 2024 SCS docs

Going deeper (optional): the PDHG update

Write the LP as a saddle-point problem with L(x, y) = cTx − yTKx + qTy. PDHG alternates one primal and one dual step, with step sizes τ and σ: Lu & Yang 2025

x⁺ = projX(x − τ(c − KTy))
y⁺ = projY(y + σ(q − K(2x⁺ − x)))

Each projection just clips onto simple bounds, so the only heavy work is one product with KT and one with K. The term 2x⁺ − x extrapolates the primal step, which keeps the method stable. PDLP adds diagonal preconditioning, adaptive restarts, adaptive step sizes, primal-weight updates and infeasibility detection.

The second trend is learning to optimize. A robot solves nearly the same problem 100 times a second, so why not learn the map from situation to solution? Amortized optimization trains a model that predicts solutions across many related problems. The prediction is used directly or as a warm start. Day 20 covered the other direction: optimization layers you can differentiate (OptNet, cvxpylayers). Predictions carry no feasibility guarantee, so in a safety-critical loop use them only as warm starts for a solver that still checks the constraints. Amos 2023

Third, convex pieces at scale. GCS (Day 19) plans through a graph of convex sets with one convex program. A 2024 follow-up restricts the safe sets to boxes and gives up GCS's optimality bound for speed. A quadrotor flew through a village split into 10,150 boxes. After 101 s of offline work, finding the box path took 0.22 s and smoothing it 7.5 s. It is built on CVXPY and Clarabel, the tools of today's lesson. Marcucci 2024 See the safe-boxes paper.

Twenty-one days fit on one page. Each row links back to its lesson.

DayLessonThe one idea to keep
Day 1Why convex?In a convex problem every local minimum is global, so a solver that stops at the bottom of a valley has the answer.
Day 2Convex setsA set is convex if the segment between any two of its points stays inside. Intersections keep convexity.
Day 3Convex functionsThe chord lies above the graph. Test it with tangents or with ∇2f ⪰ 0.
Day 4Convex problemsMinimize a convex function over a convex set. Reshape with slacks, epigraphs and changes of variable.
Day 5The problem zooLP ⊂ QP ⊂ SOCP ⊂ SDP. The narrowest class that fits picks the fastest solver.
Day 6Gradient descentxk+1 = xk − t∇f(xk). The step must stay below 2/L, and κ sets the speed.
Day 7SubgradientsAt a kink, any supporting slope is a subgradient. The subgradient method works but is slow.
Day 8Proximal gradient & accelerationGradient step on the smooth part, prox step on the rest. Momentum turns O(1/k) into O(1/k²).
Day 9DualityThe dual bounds the primal. A zero gap certifies optimality, and an unbounded dual proves infeasibility.
Day 10KKT conditionsStationarity, feasibility, sign and complementarity: for a convex problem, passing them means optimal.
Day 11Newton & quasi-NewtonUse curvature. Newton converges quadratically near the optimum; BFGS approximates the Hessian cheaply.
Day 12Interior-point methodsFollow the central path with Newton steps. The gap m/t shrinks, and solvers finish in a few tens of steps.
Day 13Splitting: dual methods & ADMMSplit the problem, solve the easy parts, coordinate them with prices. Cheap steps, moderate accuracy.
Day 14Frank–Wolfe & coordinate descentFrank–Wolfe replaces projection with a linear step. Coordinate descent updates one variable at a time.
Day 15Mixed-integer programsBinaries model yes/no choices. Branch and bound uses convex relaxations as bounds.
Day 16When it isn't convexLocal minima and saddles appear. SQP, Gauss–Newton and a good starting point are the tools.
Day 17MPC as a QPLinear dynamics, quadratic cost and box limits give a sparse QP, re-solved every tick with warm starts.
Day 18Trajectory optimization & SCPConvexify around the current guess, solve, and repeat inside a trust region.
Day 19Collision avoidance with convex piecesCarve free space into convex regions (IRIS) and let one convex program choose among them (GCS).
Day 20Safety filters & learningA CBF-QP minimally edits a nominal control to stay safe. Optimization layers can be differentiated.
Day 21Solvers in practiceClassify, pick the tool and solver, scale, read the status, check the residuals, and plan a fallback.

Keep CO4A open as your reference. It covers the theory of Weeks 1 and 2 in full, including the proofs this course moved into optional boxes. When a solver surprises you, the answer is usually in one of three places: the problem class, the scaling, or the duality behind its status.

Check yourself

Q1. A 260-variable MPC QP must be solved at 100 Hz on a car's embedded computer. What is the best first choice?

It is a small sparse QP re-solved every 10 ms, so you want a QP specialist that warm-starts and compiles to C. An NLP solver ignores the QP structure and Python adds overhead. GPU solvers carry a fixed overhead that only pays off on huge problems.

Q2. You write an SOCP in CVXPY and call prob.solve() without naming a solver. Which solver does CVXPY pick by default (as of Oct 2026)?

CVXPY calls the solver most specialized to the problem: Clarabel for SOCPs, OSQP for QPs, and SCS as the catch-all. OSQP cannot handle second-order cones. ECOS is an embedded SOCP solver you can choose, but it is not the default, and Gurobi is commercial and not shipped with CVXPY.

Q3. For the constraints Ax = b, x ≥ 0, a solver returns a vector y with ATy ≤ 0 and bTy > 0. What does y prove?

Combine the equations with weights y: (ATy)Tx = bTy. For x ≥ 0 the left side is at most 0, but the right side is positive, so no feasible x exists (Farkas). Unboundedness needs a different certificate, a direction along which the cost falls forever.

Q4. OSQP runs with εabs = εrel = 10−3, and ‖Ax‖∞ ≈ 250. Roughly how large a primal residual can it accept and still report "solved"?

The threshold is εabs + εrel·max(‖Ax‖∞, ‖z‖∞) ≈ 0.001 + 0.001 × 250 ≈ 0.25. The absolute part 0.001 alone would apply only if all values were near zero. Large raw values are one more reason to scale your units.

Q5. Between ticks your MPC changes only the initial state; the matrices stay fixed. Why does warm starting help so much here?

Unchanged matrices mean the expensive KKT factorization can be cached, and only vectors change. The shifted previous solution is also close to the new one, so fewer iterations are needed. Tolerances and checks stay the same.

Q6. A planning LP for a whole delivery network has 109 nonzeros. Which approach is the most promising as of Oct 2026?

At that size, factorizations run out of memory. PDLP solved LPs with up to 6.3 billion nonzeros using only matrix–vector products, and GPU versions now ship in HiGHS, Gurobi 13 and cuOpt. ECOS and qpOASES are built for small embedded problems, and a dense matrix of that size would not fit in memory.

Recap: things to remember

  1. Classify first: LP ⊂ QP ⊂ SOCP ⊂ SDP, plus MI for integers and NLP for smooth nonconvex functions. The narrowest class that fits picks the solver family.
  2. Write the model in a modelling tool: CVXPY (DCP, DPP) for convex models, CasADi for nonlinear ones, Drake for robotics. Use parameters and warm starts for repeated solves, and code generation for embedded targets.
  3. Interior point takes few, accurate steps. First-order methods take many cheap steps, warm-start well and scale to GPUs. Active-set methods suit small, warm-started MPC QPs.
  4. Scale your units, print your tolerances, read every status, and check the KKT residuals yourself. An infeasibility certificate is a proof you can verify with one matrix product.
  5. As of Oct 2026, GPU first-order solvers win on huge LPs, not on small real-time problems.

Algorithms
Every method, on one card.

One card per algorithm, covering what it does in one sentence, when to use it, the update rule, how fast it converges, what each step costs, and the usual pitfalls. Each card links to the day where you can watch it run. Cards are in course order.

Day 6 · first-order

Gradient descent

Repeatedly steps downhill, against the gradient, to minimize a smooth function.

In one sentence

Feel the slope where you stand, take a step downhill whose length is the step size times the steepness, and repeat until the ground is flat.

When to use it

  • f is smooth: its gradient ∇f does not change too fast. Formally ∇f is L-Lipschitz: the slope changes by at most L per unit of distance.
  • Many variables. Each step needs one gradient and O(n) memory, so millions of variables are fine.
  • Moderate accuracy, or a nearly round bowl (well conditioned).
  • Not for kinks such as |x| or ‖x‖1: use the subgradient or proximal gradient card. Not for long, narrow valleys where you need high accuracy: Newton or BFGS take far fewer steps there.

The update

xk+1 = xk − t∇f(xk)

t > 0 is the step size. CO4A 6-1 Example: f(x, y) = ½(x2 + 10y2) at (10, 1) has ∇f = (10, 10). With t = 0.1 the next point is (9, 0). Backtracking picks t for you. It starts at t = 1 and shrinks t by a factor β until f drops by at least a fraction α of what the slope predicts. Boyd and Vandenberghe suggest α between 0.01 and 0.3 and β between 0.1 and 0.8. Boyd & Vandenberghe 2004

x ← x0
repeat
  g ← ∇f(x)
  if ‖g‖ ≤ tol: stop
  t ← 1                                 # backtracking
  while f(x − t·g) > f(x) − α·t·‖g‖²:
    t ← β·t                             # shrink the step
  x ← x − t·g

How fast, and at what cost

SettingRateCost per step
Convex, fixed t ≤ 1/Lf(xk) − f* ≤ ‖x0 − x*‖2/(2tk): O(1/k), so O(1/ε) steps CO4A 6-3-1One gradient, O(n) memory
Convex, backtrackingSame bound with tmin = min{1, β/L} CO4A 6-3-3One gradient plus a few extra f values
Also m-strongly convex, κ = L/mLinear: error × (1 − m/L) per step at t = 1/L CO4A 6-3-4; steps grow roughly like κ Boyd & Vandenberghe 2004One gradient
Any first-order method, worst caseCannot beat O(1/k2) CO4A 6-3-6—

Pitfalls

  • Bigger is not faster. On the example above (L = 10), reaching f ≤ 10−6 takes 85 steps at t = 0.1 and 45 at t = 2/11. At t = 0.2 = 2/L it never settles, and at t = 0.21 it blows up.
  • Zig-zag is normal in a stretched bowl. It is the condition number κ talking, not a bug.
  • The O(1/k) bound is a worst case. On the example it promises 505/k, which would need 5 × 108 steps for 10−6. The real run needs 85.

See it run

Open Day 6: the gd2d widget, pick κ and a step rule, and watch the zig-zag. Related cards: SGD (cheap noisy steps), FISTA (acceleration to 1/k2) and Newton (uses curvature).
