Day 6 · stochastic

Stochastic gradient descent

Gradient descent that uses the gradient of one random data term per step instead of the whole sum.

In one sentence

Instead of surveying the whole town before every step, ask one random passer-by for directions: each answer is cheap and noisy, but on average it points the right way.

When to use it

  • The objective is a sum of m terms, f(x) = Σi fi(x), one per data point, and m is large. Training a model on many lane-marking images is a typical case.
  • You want fast early progress and low accuracy is fine. SGD does well far from the optimum. CMU 10-725 2016
  • Not when you need a precise answer: it struggles near the optimum. CO4A 8-2-4 For small m, use full gradients (gradient descent) or L-BFGS.

The update

xk = xk−1 − tk∇fik(xk−1)

The index ik is drawn at random (the usual choice) or taken in a fixed cycle. m stochastic steps cost about as much as one full-gradient step. CO4A 6-5 Example: f(x) = Σ ½(x − ai)2 with a = (1, 2, 3, 6) has its minimum at the mean, x* = 3. Cyclic SGD with a fixed t = 0.25 from 0 never settles: after 200 passes it still visits 2.94, 2.70, 2.78, 3.58. With tk = 1/k each iterate is the running mean of the ai seen so far, and it lands on 3.

x ← x0
for k = 1, 2, …
  i ← random index in 1…m       # or cycle 1, 2, …, m
  t ← t0 / k                    # shrinking step
  x ← x − t·∇f_i(x)

How fast, and at what cost

SettingRateCost per step
Convex, each term G-Lipschitz, fixed tOnly gets close: the cyclic version ends within 5m2G2t/2 of f* CO4A 8-2-2One term's gradient, 1/m of a full gradient
Same, shrinking steps (Σtk = ∞, Σtk2 < ∞)Converges to f* CO4A 8-2-2Same
Steps needed for accuracy εRandom order: O(m2G2/ε2) in expectation. Cyclic: O(m3G2/ε2) CO4A 8-2-3Same

G bounds each term's (sub)gradient; the rates come from the stochastic subgradient method. "In expectation" means on average over the random choices, not for every run. CMU 10-725 2016

Pitfalls

  • A fixed step never settles. It hovers around the optimum, as in the toy example. Shrink tk to converge.
  • f does not drop every step. A single term's gradient is noisy and can point the wrong way.
  • Count epochs, not steps. One pass of m SGD steps costs about one gradient-descent step.

See it run

Open Day 6: the gd2d_sgd widget, which fits a line to 1,000 noisy points with full gradients and with SGD. Related cards: gradient descent and the subgradient method.

Day 7 · nonsmooth

Subgradient method

Like gradient descent, but steps along any subgradient, so it works on convex functions with kinks.

In one sentence

At a kink there is a whole fan of slopes whose lines fit under the graph; pick any one, step against it, and remember the best point you have seen.

When to use it

  • f is convex but has kinks (a maximum of linear pieces, ‖x‖1, a hinge loss), and one subgradient is cheap to compute.
  • Huge problems that need only low accuracy, and dual problems (dual ascent, the Lagrangian bounds of Day 15).
  • An easy-to-project constraint set C (a box, a ball, x ≥ 0)? Use the projected version.
  • Not when f is smooth plus a simple kink, as in the lasso: proximal gradient is far faster. Not when you need high accuracy.

The update

A subgradient g of f at x satisfies f(y) ≥ f(x) + gT(y − x) for every y. For |x| at 0, any g in [−1, 1] works. CO4A 7-1 The set of all of them is the subdifferential ∂f(x).

xk = xk−1 − tkgk−1, gk−1 ∈ ∂f(xk−1)

A step can raise f, so you keep the best value fbest. CO4A 8-1 Step sizes are fixed or shrinking (for example tk = 1/k), set in advance rather than by line search. CO4A 8-1-1 Example: f = |x| from x0 = 1 with t = 0.3 gives 0.7, 0.4, 0.1, −0.2, 0.1, −0.2, … forever, with fbest = 0.1.

x ← x0;  best ← x0
for k = 1, 2, …
  g ← any subgradient of f at x
  t ← t0 / k                 # pre-set, no line search
  x ← x − t·g                # projected: x ← P_C(x − t·g)
  if f(x) < f(best): best ← x
return best

How fast, and at what cost

SettingRateCost per step
Convex, ‖g‖ ≤ G, fixed tfbest stalls within G2t/2 of f* CO4A 8-1-3One subgradient, O(n)
Shrinking steps (Σtk = ∞, Σtk2 < ∞)fbest → f* CO4A 8-1-3Same
Accuracy ε, with R = ‖x0 − x*‖k ≥ R2G2/ε2: O(1/ε2) steps. R = G = 1, ε = 0.01 needs 10,000 CO4A 8-1-4Same

Pitfalls

  • It is not a descent method. Return fbest, not the last point.
  • A fixed step does not reach f*. The |x| run above stalls at 0.1, under the ceiling G2t/2 = 0.15.
  • A kink is not automatically a minimum. x* is optimal exactly when 0 ∈ ∂f(x*). CO4A 7-3-1 max(0.5x, 2x − 1.5) has a kink at 1 with ∂f(1) = [0.5, 2], which does not contain 0.

See it run

Open Day 7: the subgrad widget to see the fan of subgradients at a kink and the zig-zag of fixed steps. Related cards: proximal gradient, which handles kinks exactly, and SGD.

  2. CO4A 8-1 Subgradient method, 8-1-1, 8-1-3 and 8-1-4, CO4A team (accessed 2026-10-26).
  3. Subgradient Method, CMU 10-725 Fall 2016 slides, Ryan Tibshirani (accessed 2026-10-26).
Day 8 · first-order

Proximal gradient (ISTA)

Takes a gradient step on the smooth part of the objective, then a cheap "prox" step that handles the kinky part exactly.

In one sentence

A courier drives the highway (a gradient step on the smooth part) and walks the last block on foot (the prox step for the simple kinky part).

When to use it

  • The objective splits as f(x) = g(x) + h(x). g is convex and smooth (∇g is L-Lipschitz). h is convex, maybe kinky, and has an easy prox.
  • Lasso and sparse regression (h = λ‖x‖1), matrix completion (h = trace norm), and simple constraints (h = 0 inside C and +∞ outside, which gives projected gradient).
  • Not when h has no cheap prox, or when h couples the variables in a hard way (try ADMM). If plain ISTA is too slow, use FISTA.

The update

proxt(z) = argminu (1/2t)‖u − z‖2 + h(u)

xk = proxt(xk−1 − t∇g(xk−1))

The prox finds a point close to z that also keeps h small. It depends only on h. CO4A 9-1 For h = λ‖x‖1 it is soft-thresholding at λt: shrink each entry toward 0 by λt, and set it to 0 if |zi| ≤ λt. Example: g(β) = ½(4 − 2β)2 and λ = 2, so L = 4 and t = ¼. From β = 0 the gradient step gives 2, and soft-thresholding at 0.5 gives 1.5. That is the optimum, since g′(1.5) + λ = −2 + 2 = 0. Special cases: h = 0 gives gradient descent, and h = indicator of C gives projected gradient, x+ = PC(x − t∇g(x)). CO4A 9-4

β ← 0;  t ← 1/L             # L = largest eigenvalue of XᵀX
repeat                      # lasso: ½‖y − Xβ‖² + λ‖β‖₁
  z ← β + t·Xᵀ(y − X·β)     # gradient step
  for each i:               # prox = soft-threshold at λt
    β_i ← sign(z_i)·max(|z_i| − λ·t, 0)
until β stops changing

How fast, and at what cost

SettingRateCost per step
Fixed t ≤ 1/Lf(xk) − f* ≤ ‖x0 − x*‖2/(2tk): O(1/k), like gradient descent CO4A 9-2. f never goes up Beck & Teboulle 2009One ∇g and one prox. The prox is O(n) for ℓ1 but one SVD for the trace norm CO4A 9-3
Backtracking on g onlySame with tmin = min{1, β/L} CO4A 9-2One prox per trial step (about 6.6 per step in the Day 8 lasso)

Pitfalls

  • Threshold at λt, not λ. The zero band is −λt ≤ zi ≤ λt.
  • Count prox calls, not only iterations. One prox can be a full SVD, and backtracking multiplies the calls.

See it run

Open Day 8: the ista widget for the soft-threshold curve, and the ista_fista widget for ISTA against FISTA on a seeded lasso. Related cards: FISTA, coordinate descent (also solves the lasso) and ADMM.

Sources

  1. CO4A 9-1 Proximal gradient descent, 9-2, 9-3 and 9-4, CO4A team (accessed 2026-10-26).
  2. Proximal Gradient Descent and Acceleration, CMU 10-725 Fall 2016 slides, Ryan Tibshirani (accessed 2026-10-26).
  3. A Fast Iterative Shrinkage-Thresholding Algorithm for Linear Inverse Problems, Beck & Teboulle, SIAM J. Imaging Sci. 2(1), 2009 (accessed 2026-10-26).
Day 8 · first-order

Accelerated proximal gradient (FISTA)

Proximal gradient plus momentum: each step first slides along the last move, which lifts the rate from 1/k to 1/k².

In one sentence

Like pushing a swing, small well-timed pushes along the current motion build speed: FISTA keeps part of its last move and then takes an ordinary ISTA step from there.

When to use it

  • The same problems as ISTA: smooth g plus an h with an easy prox. With h = 0 it is accelerated gradient descent.
  • You need many iterations and each prox is cheap.
  • Little gain when you warm-start along a path of λ values, or when the prox is costly. In matrix completion, backtracking needs several SVDs, and the extrapolated point may not be low rank. CO4A 9-5-4

The update

v = xk−1 + ((k − 2)/(k + 1))(xk−1 − xk−2)

xk = proxt(v − t∇g(v))

Start with x−1 = x0. CO4A 9-5-1 The momentum weight is 0 at k = 2, 0.25 at k = 3, 0.73 at k = 10 and 0.97 at k = 100. Beck and Teboulle's original version uses a sequence θ1 = 1, θk+1 = (1 + √(1 + 4θk2))/2 and weight (θk − 1)/θk+1. Both versions reach O(1/k2). Beck & Teboulle 2009

x_prev ← x0;  x ← x0;  t ← 1/L
for k = 1, 2, …
  v ← x + ((k − 2)/(k + 1))·(x − x_prev)   # momentum
  x_prev ← x
  x ← prox_t(v − t·∇g(v))                  # ISTA step from v
  remember the best f(x) so far            # f can go up

How fast, and at what cost

SettingRateCost per step
Fixed t ≤ 1/Lf(xk) − f* ≤ 2‖x0 − x*‖2/(t(k + 1)2): O(1/k2), so O(1/√ε) steps CO4A 9-5-2ISTA's cost plus one vector combination
Bounds for ‖x0 − x*‖2 = 1, t = 1, ε = 10−4FISTA 141 steps, ISTA 5,000—
Any first-order method, worst caseNo better than O(1/k2), so FISTA's rate is the best possible CO4A 6-3-6—
BacktrackingSame order; start each search from the previous t CO4A 9-5-2One prox per trial step

Pitfalls

  • f does not fall every step. These bumps are called "Nesterov ripples". In the Day 8 seeded lasso, FISTA's objective rose on 430 of 1,000 steps, while ISTA's never rose. Report the best value.
  • "Optimal" is a worst-case claim over all smooth convex problems. A particular lasso can converge much faster than either bound.

See it run

Open Day 8: the ista_fista widget and compare the ISTA and FISTA error curves on a seeded lasso. Related cards: ISTA and gradient descent.

Sources

  1. CO4A 9-5-1 Accelerated proximal gradient method, 9-5-2 and 9-5-4, CO4A team (accessed 2026-10-26).
  2. CO4A 6-3-6 Can we do better?, CO4A team (accessed 2026-10-26).
  3. A Fast Iterative Shrinkage-Thresholding Algorithm for Linear Inverse Problems, Beck & Teboulle, SIAM J. Imaging Sci. 2(1), 2009 (accessed 2026-10-26).

Day 11 · second-order

Newton's method

Fits a quadratic bowl to the function from its gradient and Hessian, then jumps to the bottom of that bowl.

In one sentence

Gradient descent walks downhill with a fixed kind of stride; Newton also measures the curvature, fits a bowl, and jumps to its lowest point, so near the answer the number of correct digits roughly doubles every step.

When to use it

  • f is twice differentiable and convex near the answer, so the Hessian ∇2f (the matrix of second derivatives) is positive definite.
  • Up to a few thousand dense variables, or more when the Hessian is sparse or banded. A banded Hessian makes a step O(n). CO4A 14-8
  • High accuracy, or badly scaled problems: Newton is affine invariant, so rescaling the axes does not change its path. CO4A 14-2-2
  • Not for millions of dense variables (a dense Hessian at n = 106 takes 8 TB), for kinks, or when the Hessian is unavailable. Use L-BFGS instead.

The update

xk+1 = xk − tk(∇2f(xk))−1∇f(xk)

t = 1 is pure Newton. Damped Newton picks t by backtracking. CO4A 14-4 The Newton decrement λ2 = ∇fT(∇2f)−1∇f measures progress: λ2/2 is the drop the bowl predicts, which makes a good stopping test. CO4A 14-3 Example: Newton for the root of x2 − 2 from x = 1 gives 1.5, 1.416667, 1.414216, 1.41421356. The errors are 0.086, 0.0025, 2.1·10−6 and 1.6·10−12. CMU 10-725 2016

x ← x0
repeat
  g ← ∇f(x);  H ← ∇²f(x)
  v ← solve H·v = −g          # Cholesky; never form H⁻¹
  λ² ← −gᵀv                   # Newton decrement squared
  if λ²/2 ≤ ε: stop
  t ← 1
  while f(x + t·v) > f(x) + α·t·gᵀv:
    t ← β·t                   # damping
  x ← x + t·v

How fast, and at what cost

SettingRateCost per step
Strongly convex, Lipschitz Hessian, far from x*Damped phase: f drops by at least a fixed amount per step CO4A 14-5O(n2) memory; dense solve O(n3), about 3.3·108 flops at n = 1000 CO4A 14-7
Near x*, t = 1Quadratic: the error roughly squares. About six such steps shrink it by 5·10−20 Boyd & Vandenberghe 2004Same
Self-concordant f (log barriers)A step count with no unknown constants: C(α, β)(f0 − f*) + log log(1/ε) CO4A 14-6-2Same

Pitfalls

  • Pure Newton can diverge. For f(x) = log(ex + e−x) it converges from x0 = 1 but runs off to −2.3·104 from 1.1. Damped Newton from 1.1 converges in 5 steps. Boyd & Vandenberghe 2004
  • Fewer iterations is not less time. A step costs O(n3) against O(n) for gradient descent, and plotted against time Newton's lead shrinks. CO4A 14-7
  • On nonconvex f the Hessian can be indefinite and the step can point uphill. See the SQP and Levenberg–Marquardt cards.

See it run

Open Day 11: the newton widget and compare Newton, gradient descent and BFGS on the same function. Related cards: BFGS, and the barrier method, which runs Newton inside.

Sources

  1. CO4A 14-1 Newton's method, 14-2-2, 14-3, 14-4, 14-5, 14-6-2, 14-7 and 14-8, CO4A team (accessed 2026-10-26).
  2. Newton's Method, CMU 10-725 Fall 2016 slides, Javier Peña (accessed 2026-10-26).
  3. Convex Optimization, §9.5 and Exercise 9.10, Boyd & Vandenberghe, Cambridge UP 2004 (accessed 2026-10-26).
Day 11 · quasi-Newton

BFGS and L-BFGS

Newton-like steps without the Hessian: the method learns the curvature from how the gradient changes between steps.

In one sentence

You can estimate a car's acceleration from two speedometer readings; BFGS estimates curvature the same way from two gradients, and L-BFGS keeps only the last few readings.

When to use it

  • Smooth unconstrained problems where you have gradients but the Hessian is unavailable or too costly.
  • BFGS: up to a few thousand variables, since it stores an n × n matrix. L-BFGS: millions of variables, since it stores only m vector pairs (typically m = 3 to 20). UW CS726 2025 It is the usual workhorse for large smooth problems.
  • Not for kinks: gradient differences across a kink give a meaningless curvature estimate. Not for general constraints.

The update

s = xk+1 − xk, y = ∇f(xk+1) − ∇f(xk)

The new curvature model must reproduce the observed gradient change (the secant equation), and sTy > 0 must hold to keep it positive definite. CO4A 18-1 BFGS updates H, its estimate of the inverse Hessian:

Hk+1 = (I − ρsyT)Hk(I − ρysT) + ρssT

ρ = 1/(yTs), step direction p = −H∇f

A line search picks the step length. CO4A 18-4 Example: true Hessian diag(10, 1), start H = I, step s = (1, 1), so y = (10, 1). One update gives H11 ≈ 0.107, already close to the true 0.1. L-BFGS never forms H. It rebuilds H∇f from the stored pairs with two loops of dot products. CO4A 18-7

q ← ∇f(x)                         # L-BFGS two-loop recursion
for each stored pair, newest first:
  a_i ← (s_iᵀq)/(y_iᵀs_i);   q ← q − a_i·y_i
p ← γ·q,   γ = sᵀy / yᵀy  (newest pair)
for each stored pair, oldest first:
  b ← (y_iᵀp)/(y_iᵀs_i);     p ← p + (a_i − b)·s_i
x_new ← x − t·p                   # t from a line search
store the new (s, y); drop the oldest if more than m

How fast, and at what cost

SettingRateCost per step
BFGS, Wolfe line search, Lipschitz HessianSuperlinear: the error ratio ‖xk+1 − x*‖/‖xk − x*‖ → 0 CO4A 18-6O(n2) memory and work (a dense matrix)
L-BFGS with m pairsOnly linear is guaranteed in general; often fast in practice UW CS726 2025O(mn) memory, about 4mn multiplications
Newton, for comparisonQuadratic near x*O(n3) solve

At n = 106 a dense Hessian needs 8 TB. L-BFGS with m = 10 stores 2·107 numbers, about 160 MB.

Pitfalls

  • Guard the curvature condition. sTy > 0 holds automatically for strictly convex f. Otherwise use a Wolfe line search, or skip the update. CMU 10-725 2016
  • L-BFGS is not BFGS in theory. It trades the superlinear guarantee for memory.
  • No Hessian is needed to start. H0 = I or γI works.

See it run

Open Day 11: the newton widget and follow the BFGS path next to Newton and gradient descent. Related cards: Newton and gradient descent.

  1. CO4A 18-1 Secant equation and curvature condition, 18-4, 18-6 and 18-7, CO4A team (accessed 2026-10-26).
  2. Quasi-Newton Methods, CMU 10-725 Fall 2016 slides, Javier Peña (accessed 2026-10-26).
  3. CS726 Lecture 23: L-BFGS, Yudong Chen, UW–Madison (accessed 2026-10-26).
Day 12 · interior point

Barrier method

Replaces each inequality wall with a smooth log "fence", solves that easier problem with Newton, then stiffens the fence and repeats.

In one sentence

Picture a ball on a tilted table ringed by springy walls: tilting the table more (raising t) rolls the ball toward the best corner without it ever touching a wall.

When to use it

  • Convex problems with smooth inequality constraints hi(x) ≤ 0 (and Ax = b): LP, QP, SOCP, SDP. Small to medium size, high accuracy.
  • You have a strictly feasible start, or can find one with phase I (below).
  • In practice the primal-dual method is usually faster. CO4A 17-2
  • Not when one Newton system is too big to solve. Then use first-order methods such as ADMM or the GPU LP method in the cuPDLP paper.

The update

minimize t·f(x) + φ(x) subject to Ax = b

φ(x) = −Σi log(−hi(x)), i = 1, …, m

φ is the log barrier. It is finite only strictly inside, and it blows up near each wall. CO4A 15-1-2 Its minimizers x*(t) trace the central path, and f(x*(t)) − p* ≤ m/t. CO4A 15-3-2 Example: minimize x subject to x ≥ 0. The barrier problem, minimize tx − log x, gives x*(t) = 1/t, so the error is exactly m/t with m = 1. Phase I finds a start by minimizing s subject to hi(x) ≤ s and Ax = b. If the optimal s is negative, that x is strictly feasible. CO4A 15-7

x ← strictly feasible point      # phase I if needed
t ← t0;   μ ← 10 to 100
repeat
  x ← Newton on t·f(x) + φ(x), starting from x    # centering
  if m/t ≤ ε: stop                # certified gap
  t ← μ·t

How fast, and at what cost

SettingRateCost per step
Exact centeringGap ≤ m/(μkt0) after k outer steps; ⌈log(m/(t0ε))/log μ⌉ outer steps plus the first centering CO4A 15-5A few Newton steps per outer step
Practice: 2000 random LPs, m = 10 to 1000, μ = 100About 21 → 27 Newton steps to cut the gap by 104, while the size grew 100× Boyd & Vandenberghe 2004One linear (KKT) solve per Newton step; grows with size
Day 12 toy LP, 5 constraintsμ = 2: 24 centerings, 35 Newton steps. μ = 50: 5 centerings, 30 stepsTiny 2 × 2 solves

Pitfalls

  • Don't jump to a huge t. The barrier problem becomes badly conditioned. Raise t step by step and warm-start Newton. CO4A 15-4
  • m/t is a bound, not the error. In the toy LP at t = 10 the true gap is 0.197, against a bound of 0.5.
  • The Newton count grows slowly with size, but each step gets more expensive.

See it run

Open Day 12: the centralpath widget, slide t, and watch x*(t) move along the central path to the optimal corner. The centralpath_iters widget counts Newton steps for different μ. Related cards: primal-dual IPM and Newton.

Sources

  1. CO4A 15-1-2 Log barrier function and barrier method, 15-3-2, 15-4, 15-5 and 15-7, CO4A team (accessed 2026-10-26).
  2. CO4A 17-2 Primal-dual interior-point method, CO4A team (accessed 2026-10-26).
  3. Barrier Method, CMU 10-725 Fall 2016 slides, Javier Peña (accessed 2026-10-26).
  4. Convex Optimization, ch. 11, Boyd & Vandenberghe, Cambridge UP 2004 (accessed 2026-10-26).
Day 12 · interior point

Primal-dual interior-point method

Takes one Newton step at a time on slightly relaxed KKT equations, for the primal and dual variables together, and tightens the relaxation as it goes.

In one sentence

The barrier method walks to each station on the central path before heading on; the primal-dual method cuts the corner, one Newton step at a time toward a moving target.

When to use it

  • LP, QP, SOCP and SDP of small to medium size (larger if sparse), when you want high accuracy such as 10−8 in a predictable number of iterations.
  • Equality constraints need not hold at the start: the iterates may be infeasible. CO4A 17-2
  • Not when one Newton system is too big to factor. Then use ADMM or a first-order LP method (cuPDLP paper). Nonconvex problems need the safeguards of an NLP solver (SQP card).

The update

Problem: minimize f(x) subject to hi(x) ≤ 0 and Ax = b, with multipliers u ≥ 0 and v. The method drives three residuals to zero:

rdual = ∇f(x) + ∇h(x)u + ATv

rcent = diag(u)h(x) + τ1, rprim = Ax − b

Only complementary slackness changes from the KKT conditions: uihi = 0 becomes uihi = −τ. CO4A 16-2 The surrogate duality gap is η = −h(x)Tu. Each iteration sets τ = σ·η/m with σ ∈ (0, 1), takes one Newton step on all variables, and backtracks to keep u > 0 and h(x) < 0. CO4A 17-2-3

pick x with h(x) < 0,  u > 0,  any v
repeat
  η ← −h(x)ᵀu;   τ ← σ·η/m            # aim for a smaller gap
  if η, ‖r_dual‖, ‖r_prim‖ ≤ ε: stop
  Δ ← solve the Newton system  ∇r·Δ = −r
  θ ← 0.99 · (largest step ≤ 1 keeping u > 0)
  shrink θ until h(x + θΔx) < 0 and ‖r‖ drops
  (x, u, v) ← (x, u, v) + θ·Δ

How fast, and at what cost

SettingRateCost per step
GeneralUsually faster than the barrier method, better than linear; no inner loop CO4A 17-2One Newton (KKT) factorization
Random LPs, m = 10 to 100015 → 35 iterations to reach 10−8, growing roughly like log m Boyd & Vandenberghe 2004Grows with size and sparsity
Day 12 toy LP, 5 constraints13 iterations to η ≤ 10−8, ending at x = (1, 3), u = (0, 0, 0, 1, 1)Tiny

Pitfalls

  • The iterates are not feasible along the way. Only u > 0 and h(x) < 0 are kept. Ax = b and dual feasibility hold only in the limit.
  • Counts depend on settings. Tolerances, σ and the line-search constants all change the iteration count.
  • SDP needs care. The plain Newton step breaks the symmetry of the matrix variables, so solvers use special scalings such as Nesterov–Todd. CMU 10-725 2016

See it run

Open Day 12: the centralpath_iters widget, which counts Newton steps for the barrier and primal-dual methods on the same LP. Related cards: barrier method and Newton, plus the KKT conditions on Day 10.

Sources

  1. CO4A 17-2 Primal-dual interior-point method and 17-2-3, CO4A team (accessed 2026-10-26).
  2. CO4A 16-2 Optimality conditions, CO4A team (accessed 2026-10-26).
  3. Primal-Dual Interior-Point Methods, CMU 10-725 Fall 2016 slides, Javier Peña (accessed 2026-10-26).
  4. Convex Optimization, §11.7, Boyd & Vandenberghe, Cambridge UP 2004 (accessed 2026-10-26).
Day 13 · dual methods

Dual ascent and the method of multipliers

Solves a constrained problem by putting prices on its constraints: minimize the priced objective, then raise or lower each price by how much its constraint is violated.

In one sentence

A shared charging station posts an electricity price, each robot plans its own charging for that price, and the station raises the price whenever total demand exceeds capacity.

When to use it

  • Linear constraints Ax = b (or ≤ b) that couple otherwise separate pieces, f(x) = Σi fi(xi). Dual ascent then splits into independent subproblems that run in parallel. This is dual decomposition. CO4A 20-2-1
  • The method of multipliers when plain dual ascent is fragile, for example when f is not strictly convex.
  • Not when you want both the parallel split and robustness: that combination is ADMM.

The update

The Lagrangian is L(x, u) = f(x) + uT(Ax − b), where u is the price vector (see Day 9).

xk ∈ argminx L(x, uk−1)

uk = uk−1 + t(Axk − b)

The violation Ax − b is the gradient of the dual function. CO4A 20-1 For ≤ constraints, prices are clipped at zero: u ← max(0, u + t(Ax − b)). CO4A 20-2-2 The method of multipliers adds (ρ/2)‖Ax − b‖2 to L, minimizes that over x, and updates u ← u + ρ(Ax − b). The step exactly ρ makes every iterate satisfy stationarity, so only feasibility is left. CO4A 20-3

Example: minimize ½(x12 + x22) subject to x1 + x2 = 2. At price u each "agent" picks xi = −u. With t = 0.25 from u = 0, x goes 0, 0.5, 0.75, 0.875 toward 1: the error halves each step. The method of multipliers at ρ = 1 cuts it to 1/3 per step.

u ← 0
repeat
  for each block i, in parallel:        # dual decomposition
    x_i ← argmin f_i(x_i) + uᵀA_i x_i
  r ← Σ A_i x_i − b                      # constraint violation
  u ← u + t·r                            # raise price if over-used
until ‖r‖ ≤ ε

How fast, and at what cost

SettingRateCost per step
Dual ascent, f d-strongly convexDual is smooth: O(1/ε) steps; O(log(1/ε)) if ∇f is also L-Lipschitz CO4A 20-1-1One x-minimization (split into parallel pieces) and one product Ax
Method of multipliersMore robust convergence than dual ascent CO4A 20-3One joint x-minimization; the blocks no longer separate

Pitfalls

  • Dual ascent needs strong convexity. Without it the x-step can be unbounded or have many answers.
  • Mind the step. The dual gradient is (‖A‖22/d)-Lipschitz, so t ≤ d/‖A‖22 is safe. In the example, t = 1 makes u bounce 0, −2, 0, −2 forever.
  • The penalty couples the blocks. The method of multipliers loses the parallel split.

See it run

Read Day 13 (its admm widget runs the ADMM version) and Day 9 (the dual function). Related cards: ADMM and the subgradient method.

Sources

  1. CO4A 20-1 Dual (sub)gradient methods, 20-1-1, 20-2-1, 20-2-2 and 20-3, CO4A team (accessed 2026-10-26).
  2. Dual Methods, CMU 10-725 Fall 2016 slides, Ryan Tibshirani (accessed 2026-10-26).
Day 13 · splitting

ADMM

Splits a problem into two easier parts, f(x) and g(z), and alternates: update x, update z, then update a price that pushes them to agree.

In one sentence

Two specialists edit one document in turns, one polishing the wording (f) and one enforcing the style guide (g), while a referee (the dual variable) keeps track of how much they still disagree.

When to use it

  • minimize f(x) + g(z) subject to Ax + Bz = c, where each part alone is easy: the lasso (least squares plus ℓ1), QPs with box constraints, consensus across many machines or robots.
  • Moderate accuracy is enough, and you can factor one matrix and reuse it. The OSQP solver for MPC is built this way (OSQP paper).

The update

Scaled form, with w = u/ρ the running sum of residuals and ρ > 0 a penalty weight:

xk = argminx f(x) + (ρ/2)‖Ax + Bzk−1 − c + wk−1‖2

zk = argminz g(z) + (ρ/2)‖Axk + Bz − c + wk−1‖2

wk = wk−1 + Axk + Bzk − c

The z-step uses the new x, and that order is what makes it ADMM. CO4A 20-4-1 For the lasso the steps are a ridge regression, β ← (XTX + ρI)−1(XTy + ρ(α − w)), then a soft-threshold, α ← Sλ/ρ(β + w), then w ← w + β − α. CO4A 21-3 Example: minimize ½(β − 3)2 + |β|, whose answer is 2. With ρ = 1, β goes 1.5, 1.25, 1.625, 1.813, 1.906 toward 2.

z ← 0;  w ← 0
repeat
  x ← argmin f(x) + (ρ/2)‖Ax + Bz − c + w‖²
  z_old ← z
  z ← argmin g(z) + (ρ/2)‖Ax + Bz − c + w‖²   # uses new x
  r ← Ax + Bz − c                 # primal residual: agree yet?
  w ← w + r
  s ← ρ·AᵀB·(z − z_old)           # dual residual: z settled?
until ‖r‖ ≤ ε_pri and ‖s‖ ≤ ε_dual

How fast, and at what cost

SettingRateCost per step
f, g closed convex, any ρ > 0Residual → 0, objective → p*, dual → u* Boyd et al. 2011One x-solve, one z-solve (often a prox), vector work
PracticeModest accuracy in a few tens of iterations; slow to high accuracy Boyd et al. 2011Lasso: factor XTX + ρI once, O(p3), then O(p2) per step CO4A 21-3
OSQP, linear MPC with 20 states, 10 inputs, horizon 107 ms cold, 2 ms with warm start and factorization caching Stellato 2020Factor once, then cheap vector work and a box projection

Pitfalls

  • Check both residuals. ‖r‖ can be tiny while z is still drifting.
  • ρ matters. In the Day 13 lasso, ρ = 10 took 123 iterations against 16 at ρ = 1. Residual balancing helps: double ρ if ‖r‖ > 10‖s‖, halve it if ‖s‖ > 10‖r‖, and rescale w by ρold/ρnew. Boyd et al. 2011

See it run

Open Day 13: the admm widget, drag ρ, and watch the iteration count trace a U shape. Related cards: method of multipliers and ISTA, plus MPC as a QP on Day 17.

Sources

  1. CO4A 20-4-1 ADMM and CO4A 21-3 Lasso and group lasso, CO4A team (accessed 2026-10-26).
  2. Distributed Optimization and Statistical Learning via the Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers, Boyd, Parikh, Chu, Peleato, Eckstein, Found. Trends ML 3(1), 2011 (accessed 2026-10-26).
  3. ADMM, CMU 10-725 Fall 2016 slides, Ryan Tibshirani (accessed 2026-10-26).
  4. OSQP: An Operator Splitting Solver for Quadratic Programs, Stellato et al., 2020 (accessed 2026-10-26).
Day 14 · projection-free

Frank–Wolfe (conditional gradient)

Stays inside the constraint set without projections: each step finds the best corner for the current linear model and moves part of the way toward it.

In one sentence

You cannot teleport back inside a fenced park, but from any spot you can see which corner post lies furthest downhill and walk part of the way toward it.

When to use it

  • A smooth convex f over a bounded convex set C where minimizing a linear function over C is cheap but projection is costly. Examples: the trace-norm ball (needs only the top singular pair, not a full SVD), ℓ1 balls, polytopes given by their corners. CO4A 22-2
  • You want sparse or low-rank iterates: after k steps, x mixes at most k + 1 corners.
  • Not for high accuracy. Not when projection is easy anyway: then use projected gradient (ISTA card).

The update

sk ∈ argmins ∈ C ∇f(xk)Ts

xk+1 = (1 − γk)xk + γksk, γk = 2/(k + 2)

The first line is the linear minimization oracle (LMO). Here k counts from 0; CO4A's 2/(k + 1) from k = 1 is the same sequence. A mix of two points of C stays in C, so no projection is needed. For the ℓ1 ball of radius τ, the LMO picks the entry with the largest |∂f/∂xi| and returns s = −τ·sign(∂f/∂xi)·ei, an O(n) operation. Jaggi 2013 The same oracle gives a free duality gap: ∇f(x)T(x − s) ≥ f(x) − f*. CO4A 22-2

Example: minimize ‖x − (0.9, 0.5)‖2 over the triangle with corners (0, 0), (1, 0), (0, 1); the optimum is (0.7, 0.3). From (0, 0) the LMO picks (1, 0) and γ0 = 1 jumps there. The next steps zig-zag between corners toward the optimum.

x ← any point in C
for k = 0, 1, 2, …
  g ← ∇f(x)
  s ← argmin over s in C of gᵀs        # LMO: often a corner
  if gᵀ(x − s) ≤ ε: stop               # certified gap
  γ ← 2/(k + 2)
  x ← (1 − γ)·x + γ·s

How fast, and at what cost

SettingRateCost per step
f convex, curvature constant Cf ≤ L·diam(C)2f(xk) − f* ≤ 2Cf/(k + 2): O(1/k) Jaggi 2013One gradient and one LMO
Triangle example, Cf ≤ 4Bound 8/(k + 2) = 0.078 at k = 100; the actual error is 1.3·10−4Pick one of 3 corners
Away-step variant, strongly convex f over a polytopeLinear CO4A 22-4LMO plus an "away" search

Pitfalls

  • It is not projected gradient with a new step rule. It never takes a gradient step.
  • It zig-zags when the optimum lies on an edge. With exact line search on the triangle example the error falls only like 1/k (3.1·10−3 at k = 100).

See it run

Open Day 14: the fwcd widget and step Frank–Wolfe on the triangle, with the dashed arrow showing each chosen corner. Related cards: coordinate descent and projected or proximal gradient.

Sources

  1. CO4A 22-2 Conditional gradient method and 22-4, CO4A team (accessed 2026-10-26).
  2. Revisiting Frank-Wolfe: Projection-Free Sparse Convex Optimization, Martin Jaggi, ICML 2013 (accessed 2026-10-26).
  3. Conditional Gradient (Frank-Wolfe) Method, CMU 10-725 Fall 2016 slides, Javier Peña (accessed 2026-10-26).
Day 14 · first-order

Coordinate descent

Minimizes over one coordinate at a time, holding the others fixed, and cycles through the coordinates.

In one sentence

A taxi that may only drive north–south or east–west: each move is easy, and on the right kind of landscape it still reaches the lowest point.

When to use it

  • f(x) = g(x) + Σi hi(xi): a smooth convex g plus a nonsmooth part that is separable (a sum of one-variable terms). Lasso, elastic net and box constraints fit. Then a point that no single coordinate can improve is a global minimum. CO4A 23-1
  • Cheap closed-form one-variable updates, many features, and warm-started paths over λ (pathwise coordinate descent, as in glmnet). CO4A 23-4
  • Not when the nonsmooth part couples variables, such as |x1 − x2| or total variation: it can get stuck.

The update

xi ← argminxi f(x1, …, xi, …, xn), i = 1, …, n

Always use the newest values of the other coordinates. For the lasso, with Xi the i-th column of X:

βi ← Sλ/‖Xi‖²(XiT(y − X−iβ−i)/‖Xi‖2)

S is soft-thresholding, and X−iβ−i is the fit without feature i. CO4A 23-3 Example: for f = ½(x12 + 2c·x1x2 + x22) the exact updates are x1 = −c·x2 and x2 = −c·x1, so each cycle multiplies the error by c2. At c = 0.9, reaching f ≤ 10−10 takes 52 cycles, against 167 gradient steps with t = 1/L.

β ← 0;  r ← y                     # residual r = y − Xβ
repeat
  for i = 1 … p:
    z ← β_i + X_iᵀr / ‖X_i‖²      # best 1-D fit
    new ← sign(z)·max(|z| − λ/‖X_i‖², 0)
    r ← r − X_i·(new − β_i)       # O(n) residual update
    β_i ← new
until β stops changing

How fast, and at what cost

SettingRateCost per step
Smooth g plus separable h, cyclic orderEvery limit point is a minimizer (Tseng 2001, under mild conditions) CMU 10-725 2016Least squares: one full cycle is O(np), the same as one gradient step CO4A 23-2
Random order, smooth convexO(1/ε); O(log(1/ε)) if strongly convex (Nesterov 2010, as cited by CO4A) CO4A 23One coordinate per step

Pitfalls

  • Coupled kinks break it. For f = |x1 − x2| + 0.1(x12 + x22) from (2, 1), it stops at (1, 1) with f = 0.2, though the minimum is (0, 0) with f = 0.
  • Updating all coordinates at once from old values (Jacobi style) is not coordinate descent and need not converge. CMU 10-725 2016
  • Compare a full cycle with one gradient step, not one coordinate update with one gradient step.

See it run

Open Day 14: the fwcd widget, set the coupling c, and watch the axis-aligned staircase. Related cards: Frank–Wolfe, ISTA and ADMM, which all solve the lasso too.

Sources

  1. CO4A ch. 23 Coordinate descent, sections 23-1 to 23-4, CO4A team (accessed 2026-10-26).
  2. Coordinate Descent, CMU 10-725 Fall 2016 slides, Ryan Tibshirani (accessed 2026-10-26).
Day 15 · integer

Branch and bound

Finds the best integer solution by splitting the problem into branches, bounding each branch with a convex relaxation, and discarding branches that cannot win.

In one sentence

When hunting for the cheapest flight, if even the most optimistic price via Tokyo is above a ticket you already hold, you never look at Tokyo routes again.

When to use it

  • Mixed-integer programs: some variables are 0/1 or whole numbers (on or off, which side of an obstacle, which safe region a footstep lands in), and dropping integrality leaves a convex problem (LP, QP, SOCP).
  • You need a certified optimum or a known gap. Deits and Tedrake plan 10–20 footsteps over 10 convex regions in seconds to a minute this way. Deits & Tedrake 2014 See the footstep paper.
  • Not when a large instance needs a guaranteed fast answer: the worst case is exponential, and integer programs are NP-hard in general. CO4A 24-3

The update

The relaxation drops integrality. Its value bounds the true optimum (from below for a minimization, from above for a maximization). CO4A 24-4 The best integer point found so far, the incumbent, gives the other bound, and you stop when the two meet. A node is pruned if its relaxation is infeasible, if its solution is already integer (record it), or if its bound cannot beat the incumbent. CO4A 24-5

Example (Day 15): a robot carries 11 kg. Parcels are worth $60, $30, $15 and $10 and weigh 4, 9, 5 and 7 kg. The root LP takes 7/9 of parcel B and bounds the value at $83.33. Branch on B. B = 1 gives bound $60. B = 0 gives $77.86, so branch on D: the children give integer plans worth $70 and $75. Now the B = 1 branch is pruned (60 ≤ 75). Best-first search solves 5 LPs (depth-first: 11) instead of checking all 16 subsets.

best ← −∞  (maximization);   open ← {root}
while open is not empty:
  node ← pick one (best bound, or depth first)
  solve its relaxation → value v, point x
  if infeasible or v ≤ best: prune          # bound
  else if x is integer: best ← v            # new incumbent
  else: pick a fractional x_j and add two children:
        x_j ≤ ⌊x_j⌋  and  x_j ≥ ⌈x_j⌉       # branch
return best

How fast, and at what cost

SettingRateCost per step
General integer programExponential in the worst case CO4A 24-3One relaxation per node, warm-started from its parent

Two cuts, xA + xB ≤ 1 and xC + xD ≤ 1 (each pair is too heavy), make the root LP integer at $75 with no branching. Solvers mix such cuts with branching (branch and cut). CO4A 25-1-4

Pitfalls

  • Rounding the LP is not optimal. B = 7/9 rounds up to an overweight bag or down to a $60 plan. The optimum is $75.
  • Keep big-M small. Use the smallest M the variable bounds allow. A huge M weakens the relaxation and the bounds.
  • A valid cut removes only fractional points, never an integer solution.

See it run

Open Day 15: the bnb widget and grow the search tree on the robot knapsack. Related: the footstep paper and the relaxations of Day 4.

Sources

  1. CO4A 24-3 Solving integer programs, 24-4, 24-5 and 25-1-4, CO4A team (accessed 2026-10-26).
  2. Footstep Planning on Uneven Terrain with Mixed-Integer Convex Optimization, Robin Deits & Russ Tedrake, 2014 (accessed 2026-10-26).
Day 16 · nonlinear

Sequential quadratic programming

Solves a nonlinear constrained problem by solving a quadratic program at every step, built from a quadratic model of the Lagrangian and linearized constraints.

In one sentence

Drive a curvy road by fitting a parabola to the next stretch, driving to its bottom, and fitting again.

When to use it

  • Smooth nonlinear programs, minimize f(x) subject to g(x) ≤ 0 and h(x) = 0, with f, g, h twice differentiable and possibly nonconvex.
  • Nonlinear MPC and trajectory optimization. acados' real-time iteration runs one SQP-type iteration, that is one QP, per sampling time. Verschueren 2021
  • Not when you need the global optimum: it finds local solutions. Use multi-start or a convex relaxation. A common alternative for large NLPs is an interior-point solver such as Ipopt, which also aims for a local solution. Ipopt

The update

At the current point xk with multipliers λk, find the step d from the QP:

mind ∇f(xk)Td + ½dT∇2xxL(xk, λk)d

s.t. h(xk) + ∇h(xk)Td = 0

g(xk) + ∇g(xk)Td ≤ 0

L = f + μTg + λTh is the Lagrangian. With equality constraints only, solving this QP is exactly one Newton step on the KKT equations of Day 10. Wikipedia: SQP Example: minimize x1 + x2 on the circle x12 + x22 = 2, from (−1.5, −0.5) with λ = 1. The constraint error goes 0.125, 0.119, 1.8·10−3, 4.9·10−7, 1.8·10−13, roughly squaring each step, and the iterates reach (−1, −1).

x ← x0;  λ ← λ0
repeat
  build the QP: quadratic model of L at (x, λ),
                constraints linearized at x
  (d, λ_qp) ← solve the QP          # λ_qp: new multipliers
  t ← line search on a merit function   # or filter / trust region
  x ← x + t·d;   λ ← λ_qp
until the KKT residual ≤ ε

How fast, and at what cost

SettingRateCost per step
Near a regular local solutionNewton-fast, because the equality case is Newton's method on KKT Wikipedia: SQPDerivatives plus one QP solve
Far from a solutionNeeds a merit function or filter, with a line search or trust region, to make progress Wikipedia: SQPExtra function evaluations
Real-time NMPC (acados RTI)One SQP-type iteration per sampling time, without waiting for convergence Verschueren 2021One structured QP per control tick

Pitfalls

  • A KKT point need not be a minimum. On the circle, (1, 1) passes the first-order test but is the maximum, with f = 2.
  • The Lagrangian's Hessian can be indefinite. Regularize it, or use a positive definite BFGS-type approximation. Wikipedia: SQP
  • The linearized constraints can contradict each other, so the QP is infeasible and the solver needs a fallback.

See it run

Read Day 16, whose gaussnewton widget shows the related least-squares methods. Related cards: Newton, Gauss–Newton and LM and SCP, plus MPC on Day 17.

Sources

  1. Sequential quadratic programming, Wikipedia (accessed 2026-10-26).
  2. acados: a modular open-source framework for fast embedded optimal control, Verschueren et al., Math. Prog. Comp. 2021 (accessed 2026-10-26).
  3. Ipopt home page, COIN-OR (accessed 2026-10-26).
Day 16 · least squares

Gauss–Newton and Levenberg–Marquardt

Fits a nonlinear model to data by repeatedly linearizing the residuals and solving a linear least-squares problem, with a damping knob (LM) that keeps the steps safe.

In one sentence

Gauss–Newton pretends the model is linear near the current guess; Levenberg–Marquardt adds a leash that you loosen when steps go well and shorten after a bad one.

When to use it

  • Nonlinear least squares, minimize F(x) = ½Σi ri(x)2, where each residual ri is a prediction minus a measurement. SLAM, bundle adjustment, camera and lidar calibration, and curve fitting all look like this.
  • Gauss–Newton is the de facto standard for pose-graph SLAM. SE-Sync paper It is fastest when the model fits well (small residuals). LM is safer from a poor start.
  • Not for objectives that are not sums of squares (use Newton or BFGS). It finds only a local minimum, so the start matters.

The update

J = ∂r/∂x is the Jacobian. The gradient of F is JTr, and Gauss–Newton approximates the Hessian by JTJ, dropping the terms that involve second derivatives of r. Wikipedia: Gauss–Newton

Gauss–Newton: (JTJ)δ = −JTr, x ← x + δ

LM: (JTJ + λD)δ = −JTr

D = I (Levenberg) or diag(JTJ) (Marquardt). A small λ gives the Gauss–Newton step. A large λ gives a short step along steepest descent. Madsen et al. 2004 Example (Day 16): fit y = a·ebt to 9 points from (a, b) = (1, 0). Gauss–Newton gives F = 16.82, 7.09, 62.93 (up!), 6.16, 0.359, 0.0773, 0.0761. LM with λ0 = 1 gives 16.82, 5.94, 2.53, 0.144, 0.0762, 0.0761, downhill every step. From (1, −3) Gauss–Newton diverges; LM still converges.

x ← x0;  λ ← 1
repeat
  r ← residuals(x);  J ← Jacobian(x)
  δ ← solve (JᵀJ + λ·D)·δ = −Jᵀr     # λ = 0: Gauss–Newton
  if F(x + δ) < F(x):
    x ← x + δ;  λ ← λ/10             # trust the model more
  else:
    λ ← 10·λ                         # reject; shorter step
until ‖Jᵀr‖ ≤ ε

The ÷10/×10 rule is a simplification. Marquardt's rule uses the ratio of actual to predicted decrease: below 0.25, double λ; above 0.75, divide it by 3. Madsen et al. 2004

How fast, and at what cost

SettingRateCost per step
Gauss–Newton, zero-residual fitQuadratic Wikipedia: Gauss–NewtonJacobian plus one n × n solve
Gauss–Newton, generalLinear; may fail for large residuals or a bad startSame
LM, F(x*) ≈ 0Nearly quadratic at the end Madsen et al. 2004Same, plus re-solves after rejected steps
Bundle adjustment—Eliminate the 3-D points (Schur complement) and solve a small camera system Ceres docs

Pitfalls

  • Gauss–Newton does not always go downhill. F jumped from 7.09 to 62.9 above. Use LM, a trust region or a line search. Ceres docs
  • Don't crank λ up for safety. A fixed λ = 100 had not converged after 200 iterations.
  • Converged is not global. Start from a convex fit: least squares on ln y = ln a + bt gives a start from which Gauss–Newton needs 2 iterations.

See it run

Open Day 16: the gaussnewton widget, pick a start and a method, then step. Related: the SE-Sync paper (certified SLAM), and the Newton and SQP cards.

Sources

  2. Methods for Non-Linear Least Squares Problems, 2nd ed., K. Madsen, H. B. Nielsen, O. Tingleff, DTU 2004 (accessed 2026-10-26).
  3. Solving Non-linear Least Squares, Ceres Solver documentation (accessed 2026-10-26).
  4. SE-Sync: A Certifiably Correct Algorithm for Synchronization over the Special Euclidean Group, Rosen, Carlone, Bandeira, Leonard (accessed 2026-10-26).
Day 18 · nonconvex

Sequential convex programming

Solves a nonconvex problem, such as a collision-free trajectory, as a sequence of convex subproblems built around the current guess and kept inside a trust region.

In one sentence

As on a frozen lake, trust the ice only where you have tapped it: build a convex model near your current plan, move a little, check, and repeat.

When to use it

  • Trajectory optimization with nonlinear dynamics, obstacles or nonconvex control limits: rockets, quadrotors, robot arms, cars. Malyuta 2022
  • You have a reasonable initial guess (a straight line, the last plan) and want a good, dynamically feasible plan quickly.
  • Not when you need a global optimum: the result depends on the start. For special thrust limits, lossless convexification solves a single convex problem exactly (lossless paper).

The update

Around the current guess x̄, linearize the dynamics and the nonconvex constraints. For example, "stay outside the circle" ‖p − c‖ ≥ r becomes a halfspace:

nT(p − c) ≥ r, n = (p̄ − c)/‖p̄ − c‖

Since nT(p − c) ≤ ‖p − c‖ for every p, any point that meets the halfspace also clears the circle. A trust region ‖x − x̄‖ ≤ Δ stops steps from going where the model is wrong. A penalized slack ("virtual control") keeps every subproblem feasible. Then compare the real improvement with the predicted one. If the ratio ρ is low, reject the step and shrink Δ. If it is high, accept it and grow Δ. Malyuta 2022 Example: obstacle center (5, 0.5), r = 2, guess point (5, 0). Then n = (0, −1) and the fence is y ≤ −1.5. With Δ = 1 the point reaches only y = −1, so iteration 1 needs slack 0.5.

x̄ ← initial guess (e.g., a straight line);  Δ ← Δ0
repeat
  build a convex model at x̄: linear dynamics, halfspaces
  x ← solve  min cost + λ·‖slack‖₁
         s.t. model and ‖x − x̄‖ ≤ Δ
  ρ ← actual decrease / predicted decrease
  if ρ is too low: reject x, Δ ← Δ/2
  else: x̄ ← x; grow Δ if ρ is high
until the predicted decrease ≈ 0
check that the slack is 0

How fast, and at what cost

SettingRateCost per step
Plain SCPA heuristic: no global optimality, and the answer depends on the start EE364bOne convex QP or SOCP
SCvx (virtual control and trust region)Global convergence to a stationary point, with a superlinear rate, under assumptions Mao 2018Same
GuSTO, control-affine systemsConverges to a stationary point Bonalli 2019Same
TrajOpt, 198 PR2 arm problems82% success (96% with several starts) Schulman 20140.19 s per problem on average

Pitfalls

  • Not globally optimal. In the Day 18 widget, a guess bowed above the obstacle converges to an 11.248 m path, while a straight-line start finds 10.455 m.
  • Nonzero slack at convergence is a "soft failure". The answer does not solve the real problem. Malyuta 2022
  • Safe waypoints do not mean safe segments. In the widget every waypoint is at least 2.000 m from the center, yet one segment passes at 1.983 m.

See it run

Open Day 18: the scp widget and step the path as it slides under the obstacle. Related: the Malyuta tutorial, SCvx and GuSTO, TrajOpt, and the SQP card.

  2. Successive convexification: a superlinearly convergent algorithm for non-convex optimal control problems, Mao, Szmuk, Xu, Açıkmeşe (accessed 2026-10-26).
  3. GuSTO: Guaranteed Sequential Trajectory Optimization via Sequential Convex Programming, Bonalli, Cauligi, Bylard, Pavone, ICRA 2019 (accessed 2026-10-26).

Papers
Robots that run on convex optimization.

The papers behind Week 3, where convex optimization made robots, rockets, and cars work. Each is explained three ways: in one sentence, for a 10-year-old, and step by step.

2007 · Açıkmeşe, Ploen · J. Guidance, Control, and Dynamics

Convex Programming Approach to Powered Descent Guidance for Mars Landing

Showed that a Mars lander's fuel-optimal landing burn, which looks nonconvex because the engine has a minimum thrust, can be solved exactly as one convex program.

In one sentence

A minimum thrust makes the set of allowed thrusts a ring, so the problem is nonconvex. The paper swaps the ring for a convex set using one extra variable, proves the optimum never uses the extra room, and so gets the true fuel-optimal landing from one second-order cone program.

Explain it to a 10-year-old

A toy rocket's engine has a rule: once it is on, it must push at least "medium" and at most "full". That rule leaves a hole in your choices, and holes make planning hard. So add a fuel meter. The new rule: push no harder than the meter reads, and keep the meter between medium and full. You pay for what the meter reads, not for the push. Paying for push you don't use is a waste, so the cheapest plan always pushes exactly what the meter says. That plan obeys the real rule too.

About the sources for this entry

The 2007 full text could not be opened (the publisher refused access). This entry relies on the paper's abstract plus two later papers that restate its method: Blackmore, Açıkmeşe and Scharf (2010) and the Malyuta et al. tutorial (2022). All numbers below come from the 2010 paper.

The problem

A Mars landing ends with powered descent: the engines fire to fly the lander to the target and set it down softly. The thrust profile must be computed onboard, within seconds, with a guarantee of an answer in bounded time. Açıkmeşe 2007 abstract

The goal is the minimum-fuel profile. Thrust has a maximum ρ2 and, during the burn, a minimum ρ1 > 0. A glide-slope constraint keeps the lander inside a cone above the target. The minimum is the troublemaker. For the 3-D thrust vector Tc, the rule

0 < ρ1 ≤ ‖Tc‖ ≤ ρ2

allows a thick shell with a hole in the middle, which is not convex (Day 2). With the 2010 paper's Mars values, ρ1 = 4972 N and ρ2 = 13260 N, the thrusts (6000, 0, 0) N and (−6000, 0, 0) N are allowed, but their average (0, 0, 0) is not. Blackmore 2010

The key idea

Add a slack variable Γ(t), read "gamma", and replace the shell by two convex constraints:

‖Tc(t)‖ ≤ Γ(t), ρ1 ≤ Γ(t) ≤ ρ2

Fuel is charged for Γ instead of ‖Tc‖: the mass falls at rate αΓ, with α a fixed engine constant. The first constraint is a second-order cone, and the second is a pair of bounds. Blackmore 2010

The new set is bigger. A thrust of 3000 N with Γ = 4972 N passes the relaxed rules, though the engine cannot make 3000 N. The theorem, proved with Pontryagin's maximum principle, says the optimum never does this: ‖Tc(t)‖ = Γ(t) at every time. Malyuta 2022

So the relaxed optimum obeys the real limits. No original plan can beat it, because the relaxation allows everything the original allows. Nothing is lost, which is why this is called lossless convexification.

How it works

  1. Model the lander as a point mass: 3-D position and velocity, constant gravity, and a mass that falls as fuel burns. An inner loop handles attitude.
  2. Relax the thrust bounds as above.
  3. Change variables using the logarithm of the mass. This removes the division of thrust by mass from the dynamics. Malyuta 2022
  4. Split time into N steps (Day 18). The result is, in the abstract's words, "a finite-dimensional convex optimization problem, specifically … second-order cone programming" (Day 5).
  5. Solve it with an interior-point method (Day 12) in polynomial time. The time of flight tf is searched outside the convex solve; the 2010 paper uses a golden-section search.

Results

The 2010 follow-up uses the same relaxation with g = 3.7114 m/s², a wet mass of 1905 kg and a dry mass of 1505 kg (400 kg of fuel). Hovering at full mass needs 1905 × 3.7114 ≈ 7070 N, inside the thrust range. Blackmore 2010

  • Reachable target: 399.4 kg of fuel, tf = 78.4 s and 55 time nodes. The search took 23 golden-section iterations and 14.3 s in total on a 2.4 GHz MacBook Pro with JPL's G-OPT solver.
  • Unreachable target, which would need at least 414 kg: the minimum-landing-error version lands 404 m away using all 400 kg.

Why it mattered

The Malyuta tutorial calls it "the first time that convex optimization was shown to be applicable to PDG" (powered-descent guidance). It gave a polynomial-time method with guaranteed convergence. It also underlies JPL's G-FOLD flight tests on Masten's Xombie rocket, including a 750 m divert. Malyuta 2022

Lars Blackmore of SpaceX cites the paper in a 2017 chapter, which states that "SpaceX uses CVXGEN (Mattingley and Boyd 2012) to generate customized flight code" for "very high-speed onboard convex optimization". Blackmore 2017 The chapter does not say which problem that code solves. The Malyuta tutorial only hypothesizes a close link to the Falcon 9 landing algorithm.

Limitations

  • Point-mass model, constant gravity, no aerodynamics in the base form.
  • The time of flight is searched outside the convex solve.
  • The guarantee needs this problem structure. Later work added state and pointing constraints and drag. Malyuta 2022
  • Solve times in 2010 were seconds, not milliseconds.

How to read the paper

Read the 2007 abstract, then the 2010 paper. Its Problem 2 and equations 11–13 hold the same relaxation, and its Section V has the Mars examples. For the picture, see Part I of the Malyuta tutorial and its sidebar figure S1, which shows the thrust ring and its relaxation.

Where it appears in the course

Day 18 uses it as the main example of lossless convexification. Day 2 shows why a ring is not convex, Day 5 introduces SOCPs, and Day 12 solves them.

Check yourself

Q1. What makes the original powered-descent problem nonconvex?

The minimum turns the allowed set into a ring with a hole. The glide slope is tempting, but it is a convex cone and does no harm.

Q2. The relaxation allows 3000 N of thrust with Γ = 4972 N, which the engine cannot produce. Why is that harmless?

The extra room exists, but the optimum never uses it. No rounding is needed: the relaxed optimum already fits the real engine.

Q3. What does Blackmore's 2017 chapter, written at SpaceX, actually state?

That is the chapter's statement. It does not say which problem the flight code solves, so "Falcon 9 runs the 2007 algorithm" goes beyond the source.

2014 · Deits, Tedrake · IEEE-RAS Humanoids

Footstep Planning on Uneven Terrain with Mixed-Integer Convex Optimization

Planned where a humanoid robot puts each foot by letting yes/no variables pick a convex safe patch for every step, then solved the whole plan to proven global optimality.

In one sentence

Cut the walkable ground into a few convex safe regions, and let binary variables pick one region, and one piece of a sin/cos approximation, for each footstep. What remains is convex, so a mixed-integer solver returns the globally best plan or proves that none exists.

Explain it to a 10-year-old

To cross a stream on stepping stones, you choose which stone each foot goes on. Once the stones are picked, finding the exact spot on each one is easy, like sliding your foot around a flat rock. The hard part is the picking, because there are so many ways to pick. The computer skips any group of choices that cannot beat its best plan so far. So in the end it can say "this is the best plan" or "there is no way across".

The problem

A humanoid such as Atlas must choose x, y, z and a yaw angle θ for each of N footsteps toward a goal. Each step must avoid obstacles and be reachable from the last one. Deits 2014 Both rules are nonconvex. The floor around an obstacle has a hole in it (Day 2), and turning the foot brings in sin θ and cos θ.

Earlier planners each gave something up. Graph search (A*, RRT) over a fixed menu of steps trades menu size against coverage. The authors' own nonconvex optimizer from the 2013 DARPA Robotics Challenge had no optimality guarantee and could not route around obstacles. QP planners fixed the foot angles and ignored obstacles.

The key idea

Let integer variables absorb every nonconvex part, so the rest is convex once they are fixed. Branch and bound (Day 15, branch-and-bound card) then returns the global optimum or proves that no plan exists.

Obstacles become region choices. The companion IRIS algorithm covers the walkable floor with R convex obstacle-free regions. Each is a polytope in (x, y, yaw) on a flat terrain plane. Step j gets one binary Hr,j per region:

Hr,j = 1 ⇒ Arfj ≤ br, Σr Hr,j = 1

Here fj is the pose of step j, and Arf ≤ br describes region r. The sum puts each step in exactly one region, and the implication is written with big-M or indicator constraints. With 10 regions and 20 steps that is only 200 region binaries. The older drone pattern (Richards et al.) needed one binary per obstacle face. Deits 2014

Rotation becomes a piece choice. Variables sj and cj stand in for sin θj and cos θj, and more binaries pick one straight piece of each curve. The pieces never overstate how far the foot can reach.

Reach becomes two discs. Each step must lie where two discs, placed in the previous foot's frame, overlap. These are convex quadratic constraints. So the problem is a mixed-integer quadratically constrained QP (MIQCQP), the authors' own term. It is not a plain MIQP, which would have only linear constraints.

How it works

  1. Grow the regions with IRIS, from seed points that a human picked.
  2. Fix N step slots. A trim binary tj = 1 pins step j to the current foot position, and a negative cost qt rewards plans with fewer real steps.
  3. Minimize distance to the goal pose g, the trim reward and step size, with weight matrices Qg and Qr:

    (fN − g)TQg(fN − g) + Σj qttj

    + Σj (fj+1 − fj)TQr(fj+1 − fj)

  4. Add the region implications, the sin/cos pieces, the reach discs, the "exactly one" sums and bounds.
  5. Solve with Gurobi in MATLAB, inside the Drake toolbox. Mosek and CPLEX also worked, but Gurobi was generally faster.

Results

  • With 10–20 footsteps and 10 regions, solves took a few seconds to one minute on an Intel i7 2.9 GHz laptop. A few steps took "well under one second". Deits 2014
  • Every plan shown was within 0.1% of the global optimum, as reported by Gurobi. That is the gap between the best plan and a proven lower bound.
  • In simulation, Atlas climbs a pedestal in one stride. It detours when the pedestal is twice its maximum step height, and turns sideways through a narrow gap.
  • On real LIDAR scans of cinderblocks, 7 regions covered the walkable tops. Atlas's stride was 40 cm at most, about 20 cm nominal.

Why it mattered

To the authors' knowledge, it was the first method to solve a whole footstep plan to global optimality with guaranteed obstacle avoidance. It is also complete within its model: "infeasible" means no plan exists. Precomputed convex safe sets plus one binary choice per contact became a standard way to plan contacts in robotics.

Limitations

  • It needs enough regions, and seeding them by hand "clearly sacrifices autonomy", in the authors' words.
  • Each region must be flat terrain.
  • Only foot placements are checked for collisions, not the swing between them.
  • Up to a minute is too slow for long horizons while walking.
  • It is optimal only within the model. The sin/cos pieces shrink the reach away from multiples of π/2.
  • Worst-case solve time grows exponentially with steps and regions.

How to read the paper

Read Section II in order. Part A (assigning steps to regions) is the core trick, Part B (reachability) has the sin/cos pieces and the discs, Part C covers the trim variables, and Part D the complete formulation. Then read Section III's results. Section IV lists the limits.

Where it appears in the course

Day 15 uses it as the robotics example of binaries and branch and bound. Day 19 returns to convex safe pieces, and the IRIS paper shows how the regions are grown.

Check yourself

Q1. In the planner, what does Hr,j = 1 mean?

Hr,j = 1 switches on region r's constraints for step j. Trimming has its own binary, tj.

Q2. Why do the authors call the problem an MIQCQP rather than an MIQP?

An MIQP has a quadratic cost but only linear constraints. The disc constraints are quadratic, hence "quadratically constrained".

Q3. Gurobi reports a plan within 0.1% of the global optimum. What does that mean?

Branch and bound keeps a best plan and a lower bound, and the gap between them is the certificate. Obstacle avoidance is never traded away.

Sources

  1. Footstep Planning on Uneven Terrain with Mixed-Integer Convex Optimization (author PDF), Robin Deits & Russ Tedrake, MIT CSAIL, Humanoids 2014 (accessed 2026-10-26).
  2. Published version (DOI), IEEE-RAS Humanoids 2014 (accessed 2026-10-26).
  3. Computing Large Convex Regions of Obstacle-Free Space through Semidefinite Programming (IRIS), Deits & Tedrake, MIT CSAIL (abstract read; accessed 2026-10-26).
2014 · Schulman, Duan, Ho, Lee, Awwal, Bradlow, Pan, Patil, Goldberg, Abbeel · Int. J. Robotics Research

Motion Planning with Sequential Convex Optimization and Convex Collision Checking

Turned robot-arm motion planning into a loop of small convex QPs that push a straight-line guess out of collision, finding short, smooth paths in a fraction of a second.

In one sentence

Start from a straight-line path that may pass through obstacles. Then repeatedly solve a convex QP in which collisions are a linearized penalty on signed distance and each step stays inside a box trust region, raising the penalty until the path is collision-free.

Explain it to a 10-year-old

Stretch a rubber band straight from one hand to the other, right through a table leg. That band is a path that crashes. Now nudge it a little away from the leg, and nudge again. Each nudge is small, so you can guess where the band will go. After a few nudges it bends around the leg. TrajOpt plans robot-arm motions this way, and each nudge is a small, easy math problem.

The problem

A robot arm with 7 joints, or a whole robot with 18 or even 34, must move between two poses without hitting anything. The plan is a list of joint angles at T time steps. The authors wanted short, smooth, collision-free paths, found quickly from a straight-line guess that may pass right through obstacles. Schulman 2014

The no-collision rule is nonconvex, because the space outside an obstacle has a hole in it (Day 16). The rivals were sampling planners such as RRT, which give longer paths, and CHOMP, a gradient method on a smoothness-plus-obstacle cost.

The key idea

Use sequential convex optimization. Around the current path, build a convex model and solve it as a QP, but move only within a small box called the trust region. Then repeat (SCP card). Three choices make this work for robots.

Exact ℓ1 penalties. Instead of enforcing gi(x) ≤ 0 and hi(x) = 0 strictly, TrajOpt adds their violations to the cost:

f(x) + μ Σi |gi(x)|+ + μ Σi |hi(x)|

Here |a|+ = max(a, 0) and μ is a penalty weight. With μ large enough, the minimizer satisfies the constraints, which is why the penalty is called exact. Every subproblem stays feasible, even from a guess deep in collision.

Collisions as a hinge. The signed distance sd between two shapes is their gap, or minus their overlap depth. TrajOpt penalizes |dsafe − sd|+ for each nearby pair, where dsafe is a safety margin. With illustrative numbers, take dsafe = 5 cm: a 2 cm overlap costs 7 cm times μ, and a 10 cm gap costs nothing. The signed distance is linearized through the robot's Jacobian, so it becomes linear in the joint angles.

Safety between time steps. TrajOpt also checks the convex hull of a link at two neighbouring time steps, which covers the volume it sweeps in between.

How it works

  1. Start from a straight line in joint space, collision or not.
  2. Convexify around the current path, with linearized constraints inside ℓ1 penalties.
  3. Solve the QP inside the box trust region.
  4. Compare the true improvement with the model's predicted improvement. If the ratio beats a threshold, accept and grow the box. Otherwise shrink it and solve again.
  5. If constraints are still violated when steps stop helping, multiply μ by 10 and go back to step 2.
  6. In the benchmarks, stop after 40 iterations, or when the improvement ratio or box size falls below 10−4.

Distance queries use the Bullet physics library, and the QPs go to Gurobi or BPMPD.

Results

On 198 arm problems for the PR2 robot (7 joints, T = 11), on an Intel i7 at 3.5 GHz: Schulman 2014, Table I

PlannerSuccess rateAverage timePath length (normalized)
TrajOpt0.820.19 s1.16
OMPL RRTConnect0.850.62 s1.56
CHOMP (HMC variant)0.654.91 s2.04

With several initial guesses, TrajOpt's success rose to 0.96. On 96 whole-body problems with 18 joints, it succeeded on 0.73 (0.88 with several guesses) against 0.41 for RRTConnect, in 2.2 s against 20.3 s.

Why it mattered

It showed that sequential convex optimization is a practical, fast planner for arms and humanoids, and it came with open-source BSD code. TrajOpt project page Many later SCP methods in robotics build on it or compare against it, including GuSTO.

Limitations

  • Results depend strongly on the initial guess, and several guesses are often needed.
  • There is no guarantee of a collision-free path, since the constraint is nonconvex.
  • It gets stuck when obstacles push waypoints in conflicting directions.
  • Self-collisions are checked only at the discrete time steps.
  • Like all SCP, it finds a local optimum (Day 16).

How to read the paper

Start with Section III and Algorithm 1: the whole solver loop is there. Then read Section IV on the no-collision constraint, where Fig. 3 shows the hinge penalty. Section V has the benchmark tables. Read Section IX on initialization before you use the method. Sections VII and VIII are optional.

Where it appears in the course

Day 18 uses it as the SCP example in manipulation. Day 16 explains why the initial guess matters, and Day 19 covers convex collision checking.

Check yourself

Q1. How does TrajOpt handle the no-collision constraint?

The hinge is zero beyond the margin and grows with penetration. Binary region choices belong to the footstep paper.

Q2. Why can TrajOpt start from a straight line through an obstacle?

With hard constraints, a guess deep in collision could make the QP infeasible. Penalties turn violation into cost, and raising μ drives it to zero.

Q3. Which statement matches the 198 PR2 arm problems?

From one guess it succeeded on 82%, just below RRTConnect's 85%. Several guesses lifted it to 96%, and its paths were the shortest.

  3. Journal version (DOI), OpenAlex, DOI 10.1177/0278364914528132 (accessed 2026-10-26).

2019 · Bonalli, Cauligi, Bylard, Pavone (GuSTO, ICRA) · with Mao, Szmuk, Açıkmeşe (SCvx, CDC 2016)

SCvx and GuSTO: Sequential Convex Programming with Convergence Guarantees

Two closely related recipes that make the "linearize, solve a convex problem, repeat" loop safe to use on robots and spacecraft, with proofs that it converges.

In one sentence

Both methods linearize around the last trajectory, solve a convex subproblem inside a trust region, and use slack (virtual control in SCvx, soft penalties in GuSTO) so every subproblem has a solution. A predicted-versus-actual test accepts or rejects each step, and proofs show the loop converges to a stationary, locally optimal point.

Explain it to a 10-year-old

You are walking in fog with a map that is only right near you, so you step only as far as you can see. If the ground matched the map, take bigger steps next time; if not, smaller ones. Sometimes the map says "no way through" only because you can't see far. Then you may cheat a little, but you pay a big fine, so you stop cheating as soon as you can.

The problem

Sequential convex programming (SCP) means: linearize around your current trajectory, solve the convex subproblem, move, repeat (Day 18, SCP card). Done naively, it breaks in two ways. Malyuta 2022

Artificial infeasibility means the linearized subproblem has no solution though the real problem does. Say a point sits 0.5 m from the centre of a round obstacle of radius 2 m and may move at most 1 m. The linearized rule puts the safe line 1.5 m away, so the point falls 0.5 m short. Artificial unboundedness means that, without a step limit, a linear model can promise endless improvement.

The theory had a gap too. SCP methods popular in robotics, such as TrajOpt, lacked guarantees for general dynamics and free final time. Methods with guarantees did not handle collision constraints well. Bonalli 2019

The key idea

SCvx (Mao, Szmuk and Açıkmeşe, 2016) adds a virtual control ν, a fictitious input that may break the linearized dynamics at a price. Mao 2016

xk+1 = Akxk + Bkuk + ck + Eνk

Ak, Bk and ck come from linearizing around the last trajectory, and E says where ν enters. The cost gains λ‖ν‖1 with a large weight λ. A slack on the obstacle rule works the same way: in the example, 0.5 m of slack makes the first subproblem feasible, and the next iteration needs none. At convergence the slack must be zero; otherwise the result is a "soft failure".

SCvx also judges each step by comparing the real improvement with the promised one:

ρ = (J(x̄) − J(x*)) ÷ (J(x̄) − L(x*))

J is the real penalized cost, L its convex model, x̄ the current trajectory and x* the subproblem's answer. Take example thresholds ρ0 = 0, ρ1 = 0.1 and ρ2 = 0.7. If J(x̄) = 6.0, L(x*) = 5.0 and J(x*) = 5.8, then ρ = 0.2 / 1.0 = 0.2: accept and keep the trust region. If J(x*) were 6.1, ρ = −0.1: reject and shrink.

GuSTO (Bonalli, Cauligi, Bylard and Pavone, 2019) keeps the loop but moves state constraints, such as collision avoidance, and the trust region into the cost as soft penalties whose weight grows. It covers control-affine dynamics with drift, ẋ = f0(x) + Σi uifi(x), plus goal sets and free final time. Its proof works in continuous time with Pontryagin's maximum principle, so it does not depend on how finely time is split. The subproblem's dual variables can also warm-start a fast shooting method. Bonalli 2019

Both guarantees are about reaching a stationary point, one that meets the first-order optimality conditions, not the global optimum. A later SCvx paper claims "global convergence" with a superlinear rate. There, "global" means from any starting guess, not to the best trajectory. Mao 2018

How it works

  1. Pick an initial guess; a straight line, even through obstacles, is common.
  2. Linearize and discretize. GuSTO's experiments use a trapezoidal rule with 30–40 nodes.
  3. Solve the convex subproblem (a QP or SOCP) with the trust region and slack or penalties.
  4. Run the acceptance test, accept or reject, and resize the trust region. GuSTO also raises the penalty weight.
  5. GuSTO only: optionally try a shooting method from the dual variables, at under 1 ms per try.
  6. Stop when the predicted improvement and the slack are both about zero.

Results

  • NASA's Astrobee free-flyer (a 12-D model) in a mock-up of the ISS, 100 trials from straight-line guesses: GuSTO and TrajOpt each succeeded 97% of the time, with GuSTO faster and lower in cost. Mao et al.'s method failed often. Bonalli 2019
  • An 8-D airplane with its best initialization: GuSTO took 0.55 s against TrajOpt's 2.67 s, and improved the cost by 55% against TrajOpt's 49%.
  • The shooting warm start cut solve time by 52% on a Dubins car and 74% on the free-flyer.
  • In the Malyuta tutorial's quadrotor example, SCvx and GuSTO were "equally fast". GuSTO's subproblem had 542 variables against 640, because it has no dynamics virtual control. Malyuta 2022

Why it mattered

These papers brought SCP with proofs into mainstream robotics at speeds comparable to TrajOpt. SCvx and GuSTO are the two SCP methods the Malyuta tutorial teaches, with open-source code. A practitioner can now say why the loop stopped and what kind of point it found.

Limitations

  • A stationary point is not the global optimum, and another guess may do better.
  • GuSTO assumes control-affine dynamics.
  • On the airplane, straight-line guesses failed for all three methods.
  • Testing was mostly in simulation, with a small hardware demo.
  • Slack can stay nonzero, and the weights and thresholds need tuning.

How to read the paper

Start with Part II of the Malyuta tutorial: Fig. 16 shows SCvx's update rule and Fig. 17 GuSTO's. Then read the GuSTO paper's Sections II-B, III-A and IV-B (with Fig. 3). Leave the proofs in Section III-B and the appendix for later. The SCvx paper is a short CDC 2016 paper with the convergence analysis.

Where it appears in the course

Day 18 builds the trust region, virtual control and ρ test step by step. Day 16 explains stationary points, and Day 19 uses SCP for collision avoidance.

Check yourself

Q1. What is SCvx's virtual control for?

It patches artificial infeasibility, and a big penalty pushes it to zero. It works alongside the trust region, not instead of it.

Q2. SCvx computes ρ = 0.05 with ρ0 = 0, ρ1 = 0.1 and ρ2 = 0.7. What does it do?

0.05 lies between ρ0 and ρ1. The step helped, so keep it, but the model was too optimistic, so step shorter next time.

Q3. What does GuSTO's guarantee promise?

It is a local guarantee. On the airplane, straight-line guesses failed for every method.

2019 · Rosen, Carlone, Bandeira, Leonard · Int. J. Robotics Research

SE-Sync: A Certifiably Correct Algorithm for Synchronization over the Special Euclidean Group

Solved pose-graph SLAM, a nonconvex problem, through a convex semidefinite relaxation that is usually exact, and returned a certificate proving the answer is the global optimum.

In one sentence

Remove the translations in closed form, relax the remaining rotation problem to a semidefinite program that is exact when noise is moderate, solve that SDP fast with a low-rank Riemannian method, round, and check that the result reaches the SDP's lower bound, which proves global optimality.

Explain it to a 10-year-old

You walk around a building with a step counter and a compass, writing notes like "from the door, the stairs are 3 steps north". The notes are a little wrong, and you want the map that fits them best. The usual way fixes a guessed map bit by bit, and it might get stuck on a wrong map without knowing. SE-Sync also solves a looser puzzle whose score no real map can beat: a floor. If your map's score sits on the floor, nothing better exists.

The problem

In pose-graph SLAM, a robot estimates its poses x1, …, xn along a route, each a rotation Ri plus a translation ti. The data are noisy relative measurements: odometry between neighbours, plus loop closures when it revisits a place. Rosen 2017 Under the paper's noise model, the maximum-likelihood estimate (MLE) solves

min Σij κij‖Rj − RiR̃ij‖F2

+ τij‖tj − ti − Rit̃ij‖22

over ti ∈ ℝd and rotations Ri ∈ SO(d). The tilde marks a measurement, κij and τij are confidence weights, and ‖·‖F is the Frobenius norm.

The rotation constraint makes this nonconvex. The 2-D rotations by +90° and −90° are [[0, −1], [1, 0]] and [[0, 1], [−1, 0]], and their average is the zero matrix, not a rotation. The standard solver, Gauss–Newton (Gauss–Newton card), needs a good start, can stop in a local minimum, and cannot tell when it has.

The key idea

First eliminate the translations: for fixed rotations, they come from a linear least-squares solve. Then stack R = [R1 … Rn] and form Z = RTR, whose (i, j) block is RiTRj. The cost becomes linear in Z. The relaxation keeps two properties every such Z has and drops the hard one, that Z must factor into rotations:

min tr(Q̃Z) s.t. Z ⪰ 0, Zii = Id

Q̃ is a fixed data matrix and Zii are the d × d diagonal blocks. This convex semidefinite program (SDP) (Day 5) comes from Lagrangian duality (Day 9). Every true set of rotations gives a feasible Z, so the SDP's value pSDP is a lower bound on the MLE cost. Rosen 2017

Two results make this useful. Below a critical noise level, the SDP has a unique solution Z* = R*TR*, which gives the exact global MLE. And you can check it afterwards: if a rounded estimate's cost equals pSDP, it is provably the global optimum. If not, the gap bounds how far off it can be.

How it works

General interior-point SDP solvers stall beyond a few thousand dimensions, and real SLAM problems are one to two orders of magnitude larger. SE-Sync uses the problem's structure instead.

  1. Low rank. Write Z = YTY, where each block of Y is an r × d matrix with orthonormal columns and r is much smaller than dn. Then Z ⪰ 0 holds automatically. This is the Burer–Monteiro idea.
  2. Riemannian Staircase. Find a second-order critical point at rank r. If it is rank-deficient, it solves the SDP. Otherwise raise r and repeat, starting from r = 5. The authors note that one or two "stairs" typically suffice.
  3. Solve each level with a truncated-Newton trust-region method that uses only Hessian-vector products (Day 11).
  4. Round with a rank-d SVD, project each block onto SO(d), and recover the translations in closed form.
  5. Certify by comparing the estimate's cost with pSDP.

Results

The runs used MATLAB on a 2.8 GHz laptop, against Gauss–Newton started from the standard chordal initialization. On six 3-D SLAM benchmarks, both methods reached the same cost, but only SE-Sync's answer was certified, with a suboptimality bound of at most 5.6 × 10−11. Rosen 2017, Table 1

DatasetPosesGauss–NewtonSE-SyncSpeed-up
sphere250014.98 s2.81 s5.3×
torus500031.94 s5.67 s5.6×
grid8000130.35 s22.37 s5.8×
garage166117.81 s5.33 s3.3×
cubicle5750136.86 s13.08 s10.5×
rim10195575.42 s36.66 s15.7×

So the speed-ups ran from 3.3× to 15.7×. In simulated cube worlds, the relaxation stayed exact up to about 15° RMS rotation noise, roughly 10 times typical sensor noise by the authors' estimate.

Why it mattered

SE-Sync made "certifiably correct" estimation practical in robotics. A standard nonconvex robot problem could be solved to global optimality, with a proof, faster than the local methods in use. It needs no good initial guess to reach the global optimum, though a good guess still saves time.

Limitations

  • Exactness holds only below a noise threshold. Above it you get a feasible estimate and a bound, but no certificate.
  • It assumes isotropic Gaussian and Langevin noise and no outliers.
  • In the worst case the Staircase can climb to rank dn + 1.
  • It covers pose graphs only, not landmarks or camera projection models.
  • The numbers here come from the arXiv v2 preprint and may differ from the IJRR version.

How to read the paper

Read Section 1 and Section 2.2 (the problem). In Section 3, skim 3.1 and read 3.2 slowly: Problem 7 and the exactness result are the heart of the paper. Sections 4.1.2 (the Staircase) and 4.2 (rounding) explain the speed. Then read Section 5, with Fig. 2 for the noise threshold and Table 1 for the benchmarks. The manifold background in Section 2.1 can wait.

Where it appears in the course

Day 16 uses it as the main example of a convex relaxation solving a nonconvex robot problem. Day 5 introduces SDPs and Day 9 the duality behind the bound.

Check yourself

Q1. Why is the pose-graph MLE nonconvex?

The cost is a sum of squares, and the translations are easy least squares. The rotation set is the hard part, as the ±90° example shows.

Q2. What does SE-Sync's certificate tell you?

No estimate can beat the floor, so touching it proves optimality. Above the noise threshold you get a bound instead.

Q3. On the six SLAM benchmarks, how did SE-Sync compare with Gauss–Newton?

Table 1 gives 3.3× (garage) to 15.7× (rim) at the same objective. The extra value is the proof, not a lower cost.

Sources
