  2. arXiv abstract page and version history, arXiv (accessed 2026-10-26).
  3. Journal version (DOI; publisher page not read), IJRR, 2019 (accessed 2026-10-26).
2020 · Stellato, Banjac, Goulart, Bemporad, Boyd · Math. Prog. Computation

OSQP: An Operator Splitting Solver for Quadratic Programs

A free ADMM-based QP solver that factors one matrix once and then iterates with cheap vector steps, which makes it fast for MPC loops and embedded code.

In one sentence

Run ADMM on the QP "min ½xTPx + qTx subject to l ≤ Ax ≤ u" with a splitting whose only linear system keeps the same matrix at almost every iteration. Factor it once, and each iteration is a cheap solve plus a clip to the box [l, u], with infeasibility detection and warm starts built in.

Explain it to a 10-year-old

Sorting a huge pile of LEGO, the slow part is building a sorting tray. Once the tray exists, each round is quick: drop pieces in, and push back any piece that sticks out. Tomorrow's pile is similar, so you keep the tray and start from yesterday's bins. OSQP builds its tray (a matrix factorization) once. A robot's controller gets a new, similar pile every few milliseconds, so the trick pays off again and again.

The problem

A quadratic program (QP) has a convex quadratic cost and linear constraints. OSQP writes every QP in one form: Stellato 2020

min ½xTPx + qTx s.t. l ≤ Ax ≤ u

P is positive semidefinite (P ⪰ 0), so the cost is a convex bowl. Each row of A gets a lower bound in l and an upper bound in u. Setting li = ui makes an equality. For a car, the steering limit −0.5 ≤ δ ≤ 0.5 rad is one row.

Model predictive control solves one such QP every control cycle, and consecutive QPs differ only a little (Day 17). The authors wanted a solver that is robust (P may be singular), detects infeasible problems, reuses work and runs on embedded hardware. Interior-point methods (Day 12) are accurate, but their linear-system matrix changes at every iteration, so the expensive factorization is repeated.

The key idea

OSQP runs ADMM (Day 13, ADMM card) on a copy z = Ax of the constraint values. The splitting makes the only linear system use the same matrix at almost every iteration:

K = [ P + σI AT ; A −ρ−1I ]

Here σ and ρ are positive step parameters. K is quasi-definite (positive definite top-left block, negative definite bottom-right), so it always has an LDLT factorization. Factor K once, and every later iteration costs two triangular solves, some vector additions and a clip. Stellato 2020

How it works

  1. Setup. Scale the data and factor K once.
  2. Solve. With the saved factor, solve K·(x̃, ν) = (σxk − q, zk − ρ−1yk). Set z̃ = zk + ρ−1(ν − yk) and xk+1 = αx̃ + (1 − α)xk, with α = 1.6.
  3. Clip onto the box:

    zk+1 = Π[l,u](αz̃ + (1 − α)zk + ρ−1yk)

    With l = −0.5 and u = 0.5, the clip sends 0.8 to 0.5 and leaves −0.2 alone.
  4. Dual update. yk+1 = yk + ρ(αz̃ + (1 − α)zk − zk+1).
  5. Check. Stop when the residuals are small. Differences of successive iterates certify primal or dual infeasibility.
  6. Polish (optional): guess the active constraints and solve one equality-constrained QP for high accuracy.

The paper's defaults are σ = 10−6, α = 1.6 and an adaptive ρ. Changing ρ forces a new factorization, hence "almost" every iteration. For a new problem with the same P and A, keep the factor and warm-start from (x*, Ax*, y*). The generated embedded C code is malloc-free, library-free and division-free. OSQP docs

Results

On 1400 benchmark QPs (7 classes, up to 104 variables and 105 constraints), times are normalized so the fastest solver scores 1.00, and failures count as 1000 s. Runs were single-threaded on an Intel Xeon cluster. Stellato 2020, Table 1

SolverTime, low accuracy (10−3)Time, high accuracy (10−5)Failures, low / high
OSQP1.0001.0000% / 0%
GUROBI4.2851.8861.4% / 1.4%
MOSEK2.5226.2340.07% / 11.0%
ECOS28.84752.71820.7% / 45.6%
qpOASES149.93266.25431.9% / 31.7%

In the MPC test (Table 7), warm starting plus factorization caching cut the time from 7 ms to 2 ms with 20 states, and from 67 ms to 22 ms with 80. At 80 states the iteration count barely moved (32.0 to 31.75), so most of the gain came from reusing the factorization.

Why it mattered

OSQP made a robust, free (Apache 2.0), dependency-free QP solver available from C, Python, Matlab, Julia, R and Rust, with embedded code generation. The authors reported "tens of thousands of users" in 2020. Stellato 2020 It became a standard backend for MPC prototypes. OSQP MPC example

Limitations

  • As a first-order method, it gives moderate accuracy unless polishing works. Polishing succeeded on 42.8% of problems at low accuracy and 83.2% at high.
  • On hard, badly scaled problems (the Maros–Mészáros set), GUROBI is faster. OSQP's normalized time there is 1.464 at low accuracy and 5.247 at high.
  • Choosing ρ is "still an open research question", in the paper's words.
  • The benchmarks ran on server CPUs, not microcontrollers.
  • Defaults have changed: the docs now list rho 0.1 and polishing off, as of Oct 2026. OSQP settings

How to read the paper

Read Section 1.3 for the pitch, then Section 3: 3.1 explains the quasi-definite system, and 3.2 gives Algorithm 1, the whole solver in a few lines. Section 3.3 on infeasibility is short and worth it. Skip Sections 4 and 5 (polishing, parameters) on a first pass. MPC users need Section 6 on warm starts and caching. In Section 8, see Table 1, then Table 7.

Where it appears in the course

Day 17 builds an MPC problem as an OSQP QP. Day 13 covers the ADMM underneath, and Day 21 compares solvers in practice.

Check yourself

Q1. What makes each OSQP iteration cheap?

After one factorization, an iteration is triangular solves, vector updates and a clip. The benchmarks are single-threaded CPU runs.

Q2. In the MPC test, the time at 80 states fell from 67 ms to 22 ms. Where did most of the gain come from?

The iteration count hardly moved at that size, so the saving is the skipped factorization, not fewer iterations.

Q3. The clip step projects onto [l, u] with l = −0.5 and u = 0.5. Where does 0.8 go?

A box projection moves each entry to the nearest allowed value. 0.8 is above u, so it becomes 0.5.

2022 · Malyuta, Reynolds, Szmuk, Lew, Bonalli, Pavone, Açıkmeşe · IEEE Control Systems Magazine

Convex Optimization for Trajectory Generation: A Tutorial on Generating Dynamically Feasible Trajectories Reliably and Efficiently

A 68-page tutorial on the two main ways to plan vehicle trajectories with convex optimization, lossless convexification and sequential convex programming, with theory, worked examples and code.

In one sentence

If a trajectory problem's nonconvexity has a special structure, lossless convexification solves it exactly with one convex program. Otherwise, sequential convex programming (SCvx or GuSTO) solves a chain of convex approximations with trust regions and slack, and converges to a locally optimal trajectory.

Explain it to a 10-year-old

Think of a cookbook for rocket and drone paths. Chapter one: some hard puzzles have a secret easy twin with the same answer, and you learn to spot them. Chapter two: for the other puzzles, solve a chain of easy ones, each a small fix to the last. Chapter three: three full recipes, a rocket landing, a drone dodging obstacles and a robot floating in a space station, with code you can run.

The problem

Rockets, spacecraft, drones and ground robots need trajectories that obey their dynamics and limits. These problems are nonconvex for three common reasons: nonconvex control limits (a minimum engine thrust), nonconvex state limits (keeping out of obstacles) and nonlinear dynamics. Malyuta 2022

Onboard use needs speed and reliability, which favours convex optimization (Day 1). Practitioners lacked one implementable account of how to make convex methods handle these nonconvex problems.

The key idea

The tutorial offers two routes. In its own image, lossless convexification is "a surgical knife to remove acute nonconvexity", and SCP is "a catch-all sledgehammer". Malyuta 2022

Route 1: lossless convexification (LCvx). When the nonconvexity has a special structure, a convex relaxation can be proved to give the original problem's global optimum. One convex solve does the job. The classic case is the thrust ring of the Açıkmeşe & Ploen paper.

Route 2: sequential convex programming (SCP). Otherwise, linearize around a guess, add a trust region and slack, solve, and iterate. The tutorial teaches two such methods, SCvx and GuSTO, each guaranteed to converge to a locally optimal point.

How it works

  1. Part I, LCvx. The theory for nonconvex input constraints such as the thrust ring, then for some state constraints, then LCvx embedded inside SCP. The proofs use Pontryagin's maximum principle.
  2. Part II, SCP. A generic loop of starting, iterating and stopping (Fig. 11). Time discretization, the two failure modes (artificial infeasibility and unboundedness) and their cures. Then SCvx's ρ-ratio trust-region rule (Fig. 16) and GuSTO's penalties and acceptance rule (Fig. 17).
  3. Part III, examples. A 3-DoF rocket landing with LCvx, a quadrotor flying around obstacles, and a 6-DoF free-flyer in a space station, the last two solved with both SCvx and GuSTO. The code reproduces every plot and offers a CVX-like interface to both methods.

Results

As a tutorial, its results are worked examples rather than new benchmarks. It runs 68 pages with 42 figures and 5 tables. arXiv 2106.09125

  • Quadrotor example: 30 time nodes, 15 iterations, ECOS on an Intel i5-7200U laptop. SCvx's subproblem has 640 variables and GuSTO's 542, because GuSTO has no dynamics virtual control (Table 3). The two are "equally fast", roughly 1 s in total as read from the axes of Fig. 24. Malyuta 2022
  • Flight record it reports: JPL's LCvx-based tests on Masten's Xombie rocket, including a 750 m divert (Fig. 18), and a NASA–Blue Origin partnership testing an SCP algorithm aboard New Shepard.
  • It won the 2023 IEEE Control Systems Magazine Outstanding Paper Award. UW news 2024

Why it mattered

It is the standard entry point to convex trajectory optimization. It gathers the theory behind flight-tested methods in one notation, with code that reproduces every figure. A reader can go from "why is this nonconvex?" to running SCvx on their own vehicle model.

Limitations

  • It focuses on the authors' own methods. It is not a neutral benchmark against SQP or IPOPT-based methods (SQP card).
  • SCP can converge to local optima, or to "soft failure" points where the slack never reaches zero.
  • LCvx covers only narrow problem classes.
  • Its industry remarks are hedged. It writes "we hypothesize that LCvx is also a close relative of the SpaceX Falcon 9 terminal landing algorithm" and notes that SpaceX's methods are undisclosed. Treat those lines as hypotheses.

How to read the paper

Read it in passes. Pass 1: the introduction and Fig. 11, for the map. Pass 2: Part I up to the rocket-landing relaxation, with sidebar figure S1. Pass 3: Part II on artificial infeasibility and unboundedness, then SCvx (Fig. 16) and GuSTO (Fig. 17). Pass 4: Part III's quadrotor example with the code open beside it. Leave the detailed proofs for a second reading.

Where it appears in the course

Day 18 follows its structure, from direct transcription to lossless convexification. Day 19 uses its obstacle examples, and Day 5 introduces the SOCPs in every subproblem.

Check yourself

Q1. When does lossless convexification apply instead of SCP?

LCvx needs structure plus a proof of exactness. Obstacles and general nonlinear dynamics are where you reach for SCP.

Q2. In the quadrotor example, why is GuSTO's subproblem smaller (542 variables against 640)?

Both use 30 nodes and ECOS. SCvx adds virtual-control variables, while GuSTO uses penalties instead.

Q3. What does the tutorial say about SpaceX?

It labels the remark a hypothesis. The first-hand statement is Blackmore's 2017 chapter, covered in the lossless convexification entry.

2015 · Deits, Tedrake · Algorithmic Foundations of Robotics XI (WAFR 2014)

Computing Large Convex Regions of Obstacle-Free Space Through Semidefinite Programming

IRIS grows one large obstacle-free convex region around a seed point by alternating a tiny QP and an ellipsoid SDP, and it stays fast with a million obstacles.

In one sentence

Put a flat wall between a small ellipsoid and every obstacle, fit the biggest ellipsoid inside the walls, and repeat until it stops growing. The walls then outline a big convex "room" that a planner can use as plain linear constraints.

Explain it to a 10-year-old

You stand in a messy playroom with a balloon. You put a flat sheet of cardboard between the balloon and each nearby toy. Then you blow the balloon up as big as it can go without pushing through a sheet. With the bigger balloon, you move the sheets out as far as the toys allow, and blow again. Soon the balloon stops growing. The sheets now fence off a big toy-free space where you can walk in any straight line.

The problem

Free space around obstacles is not convex. Two safe points can have an unsafe point between them, like two people on opposite sides of a pillar (Day 19). Convex solvers need convex constraints, so a planner needs another way in.

The authors came to this from footstep planning for the Atlas humanoid. They turned steep terrain cells into obstacles and wanted convex patches where an optimizer could place each foot. Deits 2015

One idea is to split free space into the fewest convex pieces. That is NP-hard even in 2-D. The paper also argues it is the wrong goal: a few large regions near useful spots beat a complete cover. Deits 2015

The key idea

IRIS (Iterative Regional Inflation by Semidefinite programming) keeps two objects. A polytope P = {x : Ax ≤ b} is the room, with one row of A per wall. An ellipsoid is written as a stretched unit ball:

E = { Cx̃ + d : ‖x̃‖2 ≤ 1 }

Here d is the centre and the matrix C ⪰ 0 does the stretching. The volume of E is proportional to det C, and log det C is concave, so "make E as big as possible" is a convex problem. Deits 2015

Finding the walls and the ellipsoid together is hard. Each one alone is easy. So IRIS alternates: fix the ellipsoid and find walls, then fix the walls and find the biggest ellipsoid.

How it works

  1. Seed. Pick a point q0 in free space, for example where an operator clicked. Start with a tiny ball there: d = q0 and C = εI for a small ε.
  2. Walls, one small QP per obstacle. Map the obstacle into "ball space", x̃ = C−1(x − d), where the ellipsoid becomes the unit ball. Finding the obstacle point nearest the origin there is a tiny QP. Map that point back and put a wall through it, tangent to a grown copy of the ellipsoid. Skip obstacles that an earlier wall already blocks.
  3. Biggest ellipsoid, one SDP. With the walls fixed, solve

    maximize log det C

    s.t. ‖Cai‖2 + aiTd ≤ bi for every wall i

    Here aiT is row i of A. The left side is how far the ellipsoid reaches in direction ai, so each line says "stay behind wall i".
  4. Repeat until det C grows by less than a tolerance. The timing runs used 2%. Deits 2015, Fig. 5

It always stops. The old ellipsoid still fits behind the new walls, and the SDP finds the global maximum, so the volume never drops. The room is bounded, so the volume cannot grow forever. Deits 2015, Sect. 3.5

A worked example: the biggest ellipse inside the rectangle [−2, 2] × [−1, 1] has d = 0 and C = diag(2, 1). Check the wall x ≤ 2: a = (1, 0), so ‖Ca‖ = 2, and 2 + 0 ≤ 2 holds exactly. The area is π·2·1 ≈ 6.28, which is 78.5% of the rectangle's area of 8.

Results

Each closest-point QP is tiny. A solver generated by CVXGEN handled a typical 8-vertex 3-D obstacle in under 20 µs on an Intel i7, while MOSEK and Gurobi needed over 1 ms. The SDPs went to MOSEK. Deits 2015

The scaling test ran 1,200 times in MATLAB, in 2-D and 3-D, with 10 to 106 obstacles. Time grew about linearly with the obstacle count, and with a million obstacles a region converged in seconds. Deits 2015, Fig. 5 The wall step is linear work, but the number of walls needed stayed nearly constant, so the SDP took nearly constant time.

The seed ended up inside the final region 95% of the time. The method also ran in 3-D, in the 3-D configuration space of a rod-shaped robot, and in a 4-D example. Deits 2015

Why it mattered

IRIS made "cover free space with convex pieces" practical. Its regions feed mixed-integer footstep planning (footstep paper) and Graphs of Convex Sets (GCS paper), where Drake's IrisInConfigurationSpace builds regions for a robot arm. Marcucci 2022, arXiv

Faster successors include IRIS-NP2 and IRIS-ZO (ISRR 2024) and FIRI (T-RO 2025), as of Oct 2026. IRIS-ZO 2024 FIRI 2025

Limitations

  • Obstacles must be convex. Non-convex ones are first split into convex pieces.
  • No guarantee of the largest region, or that the seed stays inside (95% in the tests).
  • One region per seed. A human or a heuristic must choose the seeds.
  • For a robot arm, obstacles in configuration space are not explicit polytopes. That needed later extensions.

How to read the paper

Read Sect. 1 with Fig. 1, then Sect. 3.1 (Algorithm 1, five lines) and Fig. 3, which shows three iterations. Sects. 3.3–3.5 give the QP, the SDP and the convergence argument. Finish with Sect. 4 and Fig. 5. Skip Sect. 2 at first. About 40 minutes.

Where it appears in the course

Day 19 uses IRIS as one of three ways to handle collisions. Day 2 covers polytopes and ellipsoids, Day 5 introduces SDPs, the class of the ellipsoid step, and Day 15 uses convex regions in mixed-integer footstep planning.

Check yourself

Q1. Which two problems does IRIS alternate between?

Each round solves a small closest-point QP per obstacle to place walls, then one log-det SDP for the biggest ellipsoid inside them. No sampling or graph search is involved.

Q2. Why can the ellipsoid's volume never decrease from one round to the next?

The old ellipsoid is a feasible point of the new SDP. A globally optimal answer can only be at least as large. Obstacles never disappear; they are just skipped once a wall blocks them.

Q3. The biggest ellipse in the rectangle [−2, 2] × [−1, 1] has C = diag(2, 1). What share of the rectangle does it cover?

The ellipse area is π·2·1 ≈ 6.28 and the rectangle area is 4·2 = 8, so the share is π/4 ≈ 78.5%. An ellipse can never fill a rectangle completely.

Sources

  2. Book chapter (DOI), Crossref: Algorithmic Foundations of Robotics XI, Springer STAR, pp. 109–124, 2015, DOI 10.1007/978-3-319-16595-0_7 (accessed 2026-10-26).
  3. iris-distro, Deits, GitHub: the code linked from the paper (accessed 2026-10-26).

2017 · Ames, Xu, Grizzle, Tabuada · IEEE Trans. Automatic Control

Control Barrier Function Based Quadratic Programs for Safety Critical Systems

Turned "stay safe" into one linear constraint on the control, so a tiny QP at every time step can overrule any controller just enough to keep a car or robot safe.

In one sentence

Write safety as a margin h(x) ≥ 0 that may shrink only slowly near zero, ḣ ≥ −α(h). That rule is linear in the control, so "reach the goal, never break safety" becomes a small QP solved at every step.

Explain it to a 10-year-old

A learner driver has an instructor with a second brake pedal. While the learner drives well, the instructor does nothing. Close to the car in front, the instructor presses the brake a little, and harder the closer they get, so they never bump. When the road clears, the instructor lets go. The CBF-QP is that instructor, written as a tiny math problem the computer solves many times a second.

The problem

Safety and performance often fight. Adaptive cruise control (ACC) wants to hold a set speed, but must slow behind a slower car to keep a safe gap, then speed up when the lead car leaves. Ames 2017

Switching between separate "cruise" and "follow" controllers is fragile. An earlier way of combining safety and goal conditions only worked when both could be met at once. This paper keeps safety strict and lets the goal give way. Ames 2017, Sect. V

The key idea

Take a control-affine system: the state x changes as

ẋ = f(x) + g(x)u

The safe set is C = {x : h(x) ≥ 0}, so h is a safety margin. Along the motion, the margin changes at rate

ḣ = Lfh(x) + Lgh(x)u

Here Lfh = ∇hTf and Lgh = ∇hTg. Notice that ḣ is affine in u. A control barrier function is an h for which some u can always satisfy

Lfh(x) + Lgh(x)u ≥ −α(h(x))

α is increasing with α(0) = 0, for example α(h) = γh. Far from the edge, h may shrink fast. Near the edge, the allowed shrinking goes to zero, so h never crosses zero. Start safe, stay safe: C is forward invariant. Ames 2019, Thm 2

The paper also defines a reciprocal barrier, B = 1/h, which blows up at the edge. This page uses the zeroing form above, as the 2019 tutorial does. Ames 2017, Sects. II–III

How it works

  1. Safety margin. For ACC, the rule "keep half the speedometer" in metres becomes D ≥ 1.8 vf, where D is the gap and vf is your speed. So h = D − 1.8 vf. Ames 2017
  2. Goal. A control Lyapunov function V measures distance from the goal. For ACC, V = (vf − vd)2 with desired speed vd = 22 m/s.
  3. One QP per control step. Solve for the input u and a slack δ:

    minu, δ ½uTHu + pδ2

    s.t. LfV + LgV u ≤ −cV + δ

    Lfh + Lgh u ≥ −α(h)

    The goal row has the slack δ, paid for in the cost with weight p. The safety row has none.
  4. Apply, measure, repeat. The QP has only a few variables, so re-solving it every step is cheap.

The tutorial's version keeps an existing controller and edits its command as little as possible. This is the safety filter: Ames 2019

minu ½‖u − unom‖2 s.t. aTu ≥ b

Here a = Lgh(x)T and b = −α(h) − Lfh. With one constraint and no input bounds, the KKT conditions give a closed form (Day 10). If unom already satisfies the rule, keep it. Otherwise project it onto the half-space:

u* = unom + (b − aTunom) a / ‖a‖2

A worked example: a robot moves as ẋ = u toward a wall at x = 5. So h = 5 − x, ḣ = −u, and with α(h) = γh the rule is u ≤ γh. At x = 4 the margin is h = 1. With nominal u = 2 and γ = 1, the filter outputs u* = min(2, 1) = 1. With γ = 5 the limit is 5, so u = 2 passes untouched.

Results

The ACC simulation starts at (vf, vl, D) = (18 m/s, 10 m/s, 150 m), with a 1650 kg car. The car speeds up toward 22 m/s while the gap is large. As it closes on the slower lead car, it slows to follow at the headway limit, and h stays non-negative throughout. Ames 2017, Fig. 2

There was a catch. With no limit on wheel force, the commanded acceleration went past typical comfort bounds. Simply bounding the force can make the QP infeasible, so the paper builds force-aware barriers. With them, all constraints held. Zeroing barriers gave smoother inputs than reciprocal ones, and lane keeping was shown too. Ames 2017, Sect. VI

Why it mattered

Safety became a cheap per-step QP, the template for modern safety filters around learned or legacy controllers. The 2019 tutorial collects uses in walking on stepping stones, ACC and lane keeping, Segway balancing, and multi-robot autonomy. Ames 2019

Limitations

  • You need a valid barrier, which is hard to build under input limits or for high relative degree. Ames 2019, Sects. III–IV
  • The QP can become infeasible with input bounds or several active constraints.
  • The filter looks one step ahead. It slows motion toward an obstacle but never plans a detour, so a head-on approach can deadlock (Day 20).
  • The guarantee is h ≥ 0, not a margin; put the margin inside h. The proofs assume continuous time and an exact model.

How to read the paper

Start with the 2019 ECC tutorial, Sect. II: definitions, Theorem 2 and the CBF-QP fit in a few pages. Then read the TAC paper's Sect. IV (QPs mediating safety and performance), Sect. V-A (ACC setup) and Sect. VI (Figs. 2, 4, 5). Leave the proofs in Sect. II for later.

Where it appears in the course

Day 20 builds the CBF-QP, its closed form and the widget around it. Day 10 supplies the KKT step behind the closed form, and Day 17 covers MPC, which plans a whole horizon where the filter looks one step ahead.

Check yourself

Q1. In the CLF-CBF QP, why does the slack δ go on the goal (CLF) row and not on the safety (CBF) row?

The slack lets the solver miss the goal rate when it must, and it pays for that in the cost. Safety has no slack, so it is never traded away. Both rows are already linear in u, so convexity does not depend on δ.

Q2. ẋ = u, a wall at x = 5, h = 5 − x and γ = 1. At x = 4 the nominal command is u = 2. What does the filter output?

The rule −u ≥ −γh means u ≤ γh = 1. The nominal 2 breaks it, so the filter clips to the nearest allowed value, 1. It does not stop the robot or reverse it.

Q3. In the ACC simulation without force limits, what went wrong?

Safety held: h stayed non-negative. The problem was the size of the commanded force. Simply bounding it can make the QP infeasible, so the paper designs barriers that respect braking limits.

Sources

  1. Control Barrier Function Based Quadratic Programs for Safety Critical Systems, Ames, Xu, Grizzle & Tabuada, arXiv; PDF v2 (accessed 2026-10-26).
  2. Journal version (DOI), Crossref: IEEE TAC 62(8):3861–3876, 2017 (accessed 2026-10-26).
  3. Control Barrier Functions: Theory and Applications, Ames, Coogan, Egerstedt, Notomista, Sreenath & Tabuada, arXiv; PDF (accessed 2026-10-26).
  4. ECC 2019 tutorial (DOI), Crossref: ECC 2019, pp. 3420–3431, DOI 10.23919/ECC.2019.8796030 (accessed 2026-10-26).
2017 · Amos, Kolter · ICML

OptNet: Differentiable Optimization as a Layer in Neural Networks

Made a quadratic program a layer of a neural network: the forward pass solves the QP, and the backward pass differentiates its KKT conditions.

In one sentence

Let a layer output z*, the solution of a QP whose data can come from earlier layers or be learned. Gradients come from differentiating the KKT conditions at z*, one extra linear solve with a factorization the solver already built.

Explain it to a 10-year-old

A marble rolls to the lowest spot of a bowl that has a little fence inside. Where it stops depends on the bowl's shape and where the fence stands. OptNet lets a computer ask: if I tilt the bowl a bit, or move the fence a bit, how far does the resting spot move? It does not replay the whole roll. It looks only at the resting spot, where everything balances, and works out how the balance shifts. A learning program can then keep reshaping the bowl and the fence until the marble stops where it should.

The problem

Standard layers (linear, convolution, ReLU) are good at smooth patterns. They are bad at hard rules, like "each row of a Sudoku holds each number once". An optimization problem captures such rules naturally, but it was not a building block you could train. Amos 2017

Off-the-shelf QP solvers did not help. Gurobi or CPLEX solve one problem at a time on a CPU and return no gradients. Training needs a whole mini-batch of QPs per step, plus derivatives.

The key idea

Define the layer's output as the solution of a QP:

z* = argminz ½zTQz + qTz

s.t. Az = b, Gz ≤ h

At the solution, the KKT conditions hold (Day 10). The multipliers are ν for the equalities and λ ≥ 0 for the inequalities:

Qz* + q + ATν + GTλ = 0

Az* = b, λi(Gz* − h)i = 0

These equations pin down z*. Nudge the data, differentiate the equations, and you get a linear system for how z* moves. This is implicit differentiation: you never differentiate the solver's steps, only the conditions its answer satisfies. Amos 2017, Sect. 3

A tiny worked example: z*(q) = argmin ½z2 − qz subject to z ≤ 1, so z* = min(q, 1). The KKT conditions are z − q + λ = 0 and λ(z − 1) = 0. At q = 0.5 the constraint is slack, λ = 0, and dz*/dq = 1. At q = 2, z* = 1 and λ = 1. Differentiating gives dz = 0: the active constraint holds z fixed, so no gradient flows.

How it works

  1. Forward. A primal-dual interior-point method (Day 12) solves all QPs in the mini-batch at once on the GPU. The authors released it as the PyTorch library qpth. qpth
  2. Backward. Given the loss gradient with respect to z*, solve one linear system with the KKT matrix. The paper writes closed-form gradients for all of Q, q, A, b, G and h from that one solve.
  3. Reuse. The interior-point method already factored that matrix at its last iteration, so the backward pass is almost free. Amos 2017, Sect. 3.1
  4. Train with Adam like any other layer. The QP data can be fixed, learned directly, or produced by earlier layers.

Results

Speed first. For a batch of 128 random QPs with 100 variables and 100 inequality constraints, qpth on a Titan X GPU took 0.18 s on average. Gurobi on a quad-core i7 took 4.7 s. Amos 2017, Fig. 2

The showcase was 4×4 mini-Sudoku. The model was told nothing about the rules. It saw 9,000 puzzles with solutions and was tested on 1,000 new ones. A 10-layer convolutional network learned the training set and overfit. The OptNet model learned most of the hard constraints and generalized much better. Amos 2017, Fig. 5

OptNet also improved total-variation denoising by learning the difference operator instead of fixing it by hand, and worked as a generic layer on MNIST. Amos 2017, Sect. 4

Why it mattered

It started the field of differentiable optimization layers. The cvxpylayers paper generalized it to any disciplined convex problem. Differentiable MPC used the same fixed-point trick to learn controller costs and dynamics end to end. Amos 2018 For robotics, it means a constraint or a cost inside a controller can be learned from data.

Limitations

  • Cost grows with the cube of the number of variables or constraints, against the square for a linear layer. The authors put the practical limit below 1,000 dimensions, and "substantially less" for real time. Amos 2017, Sect. 3.3
  • QPs only, and the solver uses dense matrices, so sparsity is not exploited.
  • Gradients are zero across active constraints (the toy example) and undefined at degenerate points.
  • Training needs more tuning than usual: rescaling a constraint row and its right side changes the parameters but not the problem.

How to read the paper

Read Sect. 1, then Sect. 3 up to the gradient formulas: that is the whole method. Sect. 3.1 explains the batched solver if you care about implementation. Sect. 3.3 is a short, honest list of limits. In the experiments, read Sect. 4.1 (Fig. 2) and Sect. 4.4 (Sudoku, Fig. 5). Skip the representational-power results in Sect. 3.2 on a first pass.

Where it appears in the course

Day 20 covers optimization layers and differentiable MPC. Day 10 gives the KKT conditions being differentiated, Day 12 the interior-point solver inside, and Day 21 places learning-to-optimize on the frontier.

Check yourself

Q1. How does OptNet compute gradients through a QP layer?

Implicit differentiation needs only the conditions the answer satisfies. Unrolling would also work but costs memory and time for every iteration; OptNet avoids it.

Q2. For z* = min(q, 1), what is dz*/dq at q = 2?

At q = 2 the constraint is active, so small changes in q do not move z*. The derivative is 1 only while the constraint is slack, for q < 1.

Q3. Why not simply call Gurobi inside the layer?

Gurobi solves QPs accurately. The obstacles were batching on a GPU and the missing backward pass, both of which qpth provides.

Sources

  1. OptNet: Differentiable Optimization as a Layer in Neural Networks, Amos & Kolter, ICML 2017, arXiv; PDF v5 (accessed 2026-10-26).
  2. qpth, locuslab, GitHub: the batched differentiable QP solver (accessed 2026-10-26).
  3. Differentiable MPC for End-to-end Planning and Control, Amos et al., NeurIPS 2018, arXiv (accessed 2026-10-26).
  4. Differentiable Convex Optimization Layers, Agrawal et al., NeurIPS 2019, arXiv (accessed 2026-10-26).
2019 · Agrawal, Amos, Barratt, Boyd, Diamond, Kolter · NeurIPS

Differentiable Convex Optimization Layers

Lets you write a convex problem in CVXPY, with Parameters, and use it as a PyTorch or TensorFlow layer that returns gradients of the solution.

In one sentence

A rule set called DPP makes the map from parameters to solver data affine, so every DPP problem runs as canonicalize (affine) → cone solver → retrieve (affine). The derivative is then the chain rule through those three pieces: you write natural math, and the library builds the layer.

Explain it to a 10-year-old

Imagine a super calculator that only understands one strict format. Before, you had to rewrite every question into that format by hand, and one slip gave a wrong answer. cvxpylayers is a translator. You say the question in normal words, it rewrites it for the calculator, gets the answer and translates it back. Because each translation step is simple, it can also tell you how the answer changes if you nudge a number in your question. That second trick is what learning programs need.

The problem

Optimization layers such as OptNet worked, but only for problems written in a rigid canonical form. Users had to transform each problem by hand, which the authors call tedious, error-prone and expert-only. Agrawal 2019

Modelling languages like CVXPY already do that transformation, called canonicalization, for solving (Day 21). But it was not differentiable, and it was redone from scratch for every new parameter value.

The key idea

View a parametrized problem as a function S that maps parameters θ to a solution x*. The paper writes S as a chain of three maps:

x* = S(θ) = R(s(C(θ)))

The canonicalizer C turns θ into cone-program data (A, b, c). The cone solver s returns a solution x̃. The retriever R maps x̃ back to the variables you wrote. If C and R are affine, the problem is in ASA form (affine–solver–affine). Then the chain rule gives the backward pass: Agrawal 2019, Sect. 4

DTS(θ) = DTC(θ) · DTs(A, b, c) · DTR(x̃)

The two affine pieces are just sparse matrices. The hard middle piece, differentiating a cone program, comes from the diffcp package.

DPP (disciplined parametrized programming) is the rule set that guarantees ASA form. It is DCP (Day 3) with two changes. Parameters count as affine, like variables. And a product is allowed only when one side is a constant, or one side is parameter-affine and the other parameter-free. So F x with parameter F and variable x is fine. A product of two parameters times x is not, unless you rewrite it with a new parameter. Agrawal 2019, Sect. 4.1

How it works

  1. Write the problem in CVXPY with cp.Parameter objects and check problem.is_dpp().
  2. Build a CvxpyLayer once. This canonicalizes the problem a single time and stores C and R as sparse matrices.
  3. Call the layer with tensors. New parameter values become (A, b, c) by one sparse multiply, the cone solver runs, and R maps the answer back.
  4. Call backward. diffcp differentiates the cone program, and the transposed sparse maps finish the chain.

Adapted from the paper's Sect. 5 example, which still matches the README's usage pattern as of Oct 2026: cvxpylayers README

import cvxpy as cp, torch
from cvxpylayers.torch import CvxpyLayer
m, n = 20, 10
x = cp.Variable((n, 1))
F = cp.Parameter((m, n)); g = cp.Parameter((m, 1))
lambd = cp.Parameter((1, 1), nonneg=True)
obj = cp.norm(F @ x - g) + lambd * cp.norm(x)
problem = cp.Problem(cp.Minimize(obj), [x >= 0])
assert problem.is_dpp()
layer = CvxpyLayer(problem, parameters=[F, g, lambd], variables=[x])
F_t = torch.randn(m, n, requires_grad=True)
g_t = torch.randn(m, 1, requires_grad=True)
lambd_t = torch.rand(1, 1, requires_grad=True)
x_star, = layer(F_t, g_t, lambd_t)
x_star.sum().backward()   # gradients land in F_t.grad, g_t.grad, lambd_t.grad

Results

Caching the canonicalization paid off at once. Going from CVXPY 1.0.23 to 1.1, canonicalizing the paper's logistic-regression example fell from 18.9 ms to 1.49 ms, and the stochastic-control example from 12.5 ms to 1.39 ms. Agrawal 2019, Table 1

Against OptNet's specialized qpth: on a dense QP (n = 128, batch 128) cvxpylayers was competitive, even with qpth on a GPU. On a sparse QP with n = m = p = 1024 and 1% nonzeros (batch 32), it was about 5 times faster. That QP was too large for qpth's GPU mode. cvxpylayers ran on the CPU, batching with 12 threads. Agrawal 2019, Fig. 3

Two applications show the range: gradients of a classifier's test loss with respect to its training data (data poisoning), and learning a control-Lyapunov policy for stochastic control. Agrawal 2019, Sect. 6

Why it mattered

"Put a convex problem inside a network" became a few lines of code. That opened the door for decision-focused learning, learned MPC costs and quick prototypes of safety layers. The package lives on: cvxpylayers 1.2.0 was released on 2026-05-19, as of Oct 2026, and version 1.0 added GPU back ends. PyPI README

Limitations

  • A general cone solver is slower and less accurate than a specialized one. The authors planned QP solver back ends as future work.
  • The problem must be DPP. Products of parameters must be rewritten, for example xTPx with P a parameter becomes ‖P½x‖2 with P½ as the parameter.
  • The method assumes a unique solution and a differentiable solution map. At kinks, as in OptNet, the gradient may not exist.

How to read the paper

Read Sect. 1 for the motivation, then the start of Sect. 4 for the ASA chain rule. Sect. 4.1 on DPP is the most useful part in practice; its list of non-DPP expressions and their rewrites is worth bookmarking. Then read the code in Sect. 5 and the evaluation in Sect. 7. Skip Sects. 4.2–4.4 unless you are implementing something similar.

Where it appears in the course

Day 20 uses it for optimization layers. Day 21 covers CVXPY, DPP and Parameters as the modelling layer, and Day 3 introduces the DCP rules that DPP extends.

Check yourself

Q1. What does DPP guarantee?

DPP is about how parameters enter the problem. Uniqueness is a separate assumption, and the problem must still be convex.

Q2. Which expression breaks the DPP rules? (p1, p2, F, g and λ ≥ 0 are parameters; x is a variable.)

A product of two parameters is not parameter-affine. Rewrite it with a new parameter p3 = p1p2. The other three are DPP, as the paper's own example shows.

Q3. In ASA form, which piece is not affine?

Solving a cone program is a nonlinear map, and diffcp supplies its derivative. The outer two pieces are affine by design.

  3. cvxpylayers release data, PyPI (accessed 2026-10-26).

2021 · Zhang, Liniger, Borrelli · IEEE Trans. Control Systems Technology

Optimization-Based Collision Avoidance

Used duality to turn "keep this car-shaped box away from that obstacle" into smooth, exact constraints for a standard NLP solver, and showed tight autonomous parking.

In one sentence

Distance between two convex shapes is itself a small convex problem, so by strong duality "distance > dmin" means "some dual multipliers prove it". Add those multipliers as variables, and the non-smooth collision rule becomes a few smooth, exact constraints.

Explain it to a 10-year-old

You want to prove two toys are not touching, without measuring every point. Here is a trick: slide a sheet of paper between them. If it fits with room to spare on both sides, they are not touching. OBCA asks the computer to plan the car's motion and, at the same time, keep carrying such a sheet between the car and every obstacle. If a sheet always fits, the car never crashes.

The problem

Staying outside a polytope is a non-convex, non-smooth constraint. You must be beyond face 1 or face 2 or face 3, which is an OR (Day 19). Distance and signed distance have no closed form, and their gradients jump at corners.

The usual exact fix uses integer variables, which the authors say should generally be avoided for real-time nonlinear control. Shrinking the car to a point inside a ball is simpler, but too conservative for tight parking spots. Zhang 2021

The key idea

Take an obstacle O = {y : Ay ≤ b}. The distance from a point p to O is a convex problem: minimize ‖p − y‖2 over y in O. Its dual problem (Day 9) is Zhang 2021, Prop. 1

dist(p, O) = maxλ (Ap − b)Tλ

s.t. ‖ATλ‖2 ≤ 1, λ ⪰ 0

Weak duality says every feasible λ gives a lower bound on the distance. Strong duality says the best λ gives the distance exactly. So:

dist(p, O) > dmin ⇔

(Ap − b)Tλ > dmin for some feasible λ

That λ is a dual certificate. Geometrically, ATλ is the direction of a separating plane, the sheet of paper. The optimizer moves the robot and the certificate together, and every constraint involved is smooth.

A worked example with the square [−1, 1]2: its rows are x ≤ 1, y ≤ 1, −x ≤ 1, −y ≤ 1. For p = (3, 0.5), Ap − b = (2, −0.5, −4, −1.5). λ = (1, 0, 0, 0) is feasible and gives 2, the true distance. For p = (3, 3), λ = (1/√2, 1/√2, 0, 0) gives 2√2 ≈ 2.83, the distance to the corner (1, 1).

How it works

A car is not a point. Its footprint is a rotated, shifted rectangle E(x) = R(x)𝔹 + t(x). Here 𝔹 = {y : Gy ≤ g} is the rectangle in the car's own frame, R(x) is the rotation and t(x) the position. A second multiplier μ handles the car's own faces: Zhang 2021, Prop. 3

−gTμ + (At(x) − b)Tλ > dmin

GTμ + R(x)TATλ = 0

‖ATλ‖2 ≤ 1, λ ⪰ 0, μ ⪰ 0

  1. Model each obstacle as a union of convex polytopes and the car as a 4.7 × 2 m rectangle.
  2. For every time step and every obstacle, add one (λ, μ) pair and the three constraints above.
  3. Add the dynamics: a kinematic bicycle with wheelbase 2.7 m, steering within ±0.6 rad, acceleration within ±1 m/s2. The cost trades time against control effort.
  4. Warm-start with Hybrid A*, a grid search with car-like motions, and solve the smooth NLP with IPOPT (Day 16).
  5. If a collision cannot be avoided, use the signed-distance form, ‖ATλ‖ = 1, with slack variables. It finds the least-penetrating trajectory.

Results

The parking tests used 84 start poses on a 21 × 4 grid. The reverse spot was 2.6 × 5.2 m and the parallel spot 2.5 × 6 m, both off a 6 m road. Both formulations parked from all 84 starts. Times are on a 2013 MacBook Pro with JuMP and IPOPT. Zhang 2021, Table 2

Mean timeHybrid A* warm startDistance formSigned distance
Reverse parking0.55 s0.60 s1.03 s
Parallel parking0.30 s0.87 s1.67 s

The worst case, Hybrid A* plus the signed-distance form, took 7.7 s for reverse and 9.2 s for parallel parking. The authors still call this real-time parking in tight spaces. A quadcopter crossing a room through a window took about 15 s on average. Zhang 2021, Sects. 5–6

Why it mattered

It gave autonomous-driving and robotics engineers an exact, smooth way to write rectangle-against-polytope collision rules inside standard NLP solvers. The paper's pipeline, a coarse Hybrid A* search followed by OBCA smoothing, fits tight parking well, and the authors' Julia code is public. OBCA code

Limitations

  • The problem is smooth but still non-convex: dynamics, rotations and the λ·R(x) products remain. Solutions are local and need a good warm start. Plain A* paths, which ask the car to slide sideways, typically could not be repaired. Zhang 2021, footnote 4
  • Each obstacle adds multipliers at every time step, so problem size grows with obstacles × horizon.
  • The signed-distance form is slower, roughly twice as slow in the parking tests.
  • Times are seconds, not milliseconds, on 2013 hardware.

How to read the paper

Read Sect. 1, then Sect. 2.4 on why collision constraints are hard. Sect. 3.1 holds the core trick for a point (Prop. 1), about one page. Sect. 4.1 extends it to full shapes (Prop. 3). Then read Sect. 6 on parking with Table 2 and Figs. 4–9. Leave the signed-distance parts (3.2, 4.2) and the quadcopter in Sect. 5 for a second pass.

Where it appears in the course

Day 19 presents OBCA as the first of three escape routes. Day 9 supplies the duality behind the certificate, Day 2 the polytopes and separating planes, and Day 16 the NLP solvers.

Check yourself

Q1. In OBCA, what does the dual vector λ represent?

Any feasible λ gives a lower bound on the distance, and ATλ points along a separating plane. It is a decision variable, not a tuning knob.

Q2. For p = (3, 0.5) and the square [−1, 1]2 with rows x ≤ 1, y ≤ 1, −x ≤ 1, −y ≤ 1, which λ certifies distance 2?

With Ap − b = (2, −0.5, −4, −1.5), λ = (1, 0, 0, 0) gives 2. The choice (½, ½, 0, 0) is feasible but only proves 0.75, and (1, 1, 1, 1) gives a useless negative bound.

Q3. Does OBCA make the parking problem convex?

OBCA trades a non-smooth constraint for smooth ones. The problem as a whole stays non-convex, which is why Hybrid A* warm starts mattered so much.

2023 · Marcucci, Petersen, von Wrangel, Tedrake · Science Robotics

Motion Planning around Obstacles with Convex Optimization

Covers free space with convex regions, links the overlapping ones in a graph, and plans with one convex program whose answer is usually the global optimum, with a certificate.

In one sentence

Write "which regions" and "which exact curve" as one shortest-path problem in a graph of convex sets. Its convex relaxation is so tight that one solve plus cheap rounding usually gives the globally optimal path, with a bound on the gap.

Explain it to a 10-year-old

You walk across a city of parks joined by gates. You must choose which parks to cross and exactly where to pass each gate. GCS chooses both at once. Its trick is to first solve an easy, blurry version that may send 30% of you through one park and 70% through another. Usually the blurry answer already says 100% for one route, and then the computer knows it has the best walk.

The problem

Each planner family has a weak spot. Trajectory optimization gets stuck in local minima in clutter (TrajOpt). Sampling planners struggle in high dimensions and with smoothness, so their paths need post-processing. Mixed-integer planners are exact but slow. Marcucci 2022, arXiv v1

The classic mixed-integer setup gives each trajectory segment a binary for each safe region. If the path might visit every region, that is |I|2 binaries for |I| regions, far too many for big maps.

The key idea

A graph of convex sets has a convex set Xv at each vertex v and a point xv that must lie inside it. An edge e = (u, v) has a convex length ℓe(xu, xv), for example ‖xv − xu‖2. The shortest-path problem chooses the path and the points together:

min Σe ∈ path ℓe(xu, xv), xv ∈ Xv

Plain Dijkstra cannot do this, because edge lengths depend on where you cross. The problem is NP-hard in general. Marcucci 2024, SIAM J. Optim.

The companion SIAM paper writes it as a mixed-integer convex program with a binary φe per edge. Perspective functions (Day 3) let an unused edge drop out cleanly. Relaxing φe ∈ {0, 1} to [0, 1] gives a convex program (an SOCP for Euclidean lengths), and that relaxation is very tight.

It also gives a free bound. The relaxed cost Crelax is a lower bound, and any rounded path's cost Cround is an upper bound: Marcucci 2022, Sect. 4.2

Crelax ≤ Copt ≤ Cround

δrelax = (Cround − Crelax) / Crelax

In the paper's 2-D example, Crelax = 27.29 and Cround = 28.10, so δrelax = 0.81 / 27.29 ≈ 3.0%. The rounded path is certified within 3% of optimal. A mixed-integer solver later confirmed it was exactly optimal.

How it works

  1. Regions. Build convex safe regions, for example with the IRIS paper's method. Every pair of overlapping regions gets edges.
  2. A curve per region. Each region holds a Bézier curve, which stays inside the convex hull of its control points. So control points inside the region keep the whole curve safe, not just samples of it.
  3. Time. A second Bézier curve maps path position to time. Costs on duration, length and energy, and limits on derivatives, are all convex in the control points.
  4. Edges. Continuity of position and derivatives between neighbouring curves is a set of linear equalities.
  5. Solve, round, polish. Solve the convex relaxation (MOSEK), round the fractional edges into one path, re-solve the convex problem for that fixed path, and report δrelax.

Results

All numbers below come from the arXiv v1 preprint of May 2022. The published Science Robotics version may differ slightly. Marcucci 2022, Sect. 7

TestHeadline result
Maze, 50 × 50 = 2,500 cells5,198 binaries instead of 6.25 × 106; a single SOCP returned the globally optimal path
Quadrotor, 100 random building maps95% of plans within 1% of the global optimum, worst 2.9%; relaxation time median 3.7 s, mean 6.4 s, max 31.2 s
KUKA iiwa arm, 7 joints, 5 tasks8 IRIS regions built in 53 s; shorter paths than PRM and shortcut PRM, faster than plain PRM; global optimum on all 5 tasks
Two arms, 14 joints, 3 tasks4.0 s, 8.4 s and 12.9 s

The certificates were often conservative. The largest certified gap on the quadrotor maps was 27.1%, yet that path was only 2.3% from optimal. On the arm, the certified gap averaged 4.1% while the true gap was 0. Marcucci 2022, Sects. 7.3–7.4

Why it mattered

It showed that convex optimization can reliably plan around obstacles with global-optimality certificates, uniting route choice and smoothing in one solve. It started a research line: GCS* for planar pushing (2024), shortest walks in GCS (2025), and the faster safe-boxes planner. GCS* 2024 Shortest walks 2025 Drake ships it as GcsTrajectoryOptimization, as of Oct 2026. Drake docs

Limitations

  • The regions must be built first. For the arm this took 53 s for 8 regions. They came from a fast non-convex method that is reliable in practice but gives no rigorous collision-free certificate. Marcucci 2022, Sect. 7.4
  • Only kinematic limits and derivative bounds stay convex. Full dynamics constraints break convexity.
  • Rounding is not guaranteed to find the optimum; the problem is NP-hard in general. The certificate is an upper bound and can be loose.
  • Solve times are seconds, not milliseconds. MOSEK numerical issues forced a slower, stabler mode. Marcucci 2022, Sect. 7.3

How to read the paper

Section numbers follow arXiv v1; the published article regroups them into Results, Discussion and Methods. Start with Sect. 1 and Fig. 1, the whole method in one picture. Then read Sects. 4.1 (shortest paths in GCS) and 4.2 (rounding and the gap). Sect. 3 on Bézier curves is short, and Sect. 5 builds the graph. For results, read Sects. 7.2 (maze) and 7.4 (arm versus PRM), then Sect. 8 for comparisons with other planners. For theory, read the SIAM paper by Marcucci, Umenberger, Parrilo and Tedrake.

Where it appears in the course

Day 19 builds GCS and its widget, which solves the convex restriction for a fixed chain of boxes. Day 15 explains relaxation, rounding and bounds, Day 5 the SOCP class, and Day 3 the perspective function.

Check yourself

Q1. The relaxation costs 27.29 and the rounded path costs 28.10. What can you guarantee?

The relaxation is a lower bound, so the optimum lies between 27.29 and 28.10. The true gap could be anything from 0 to 3.0%; here it was 0.

Q2. Why do Bézier curves suit GCS?

The convex-hull property turns "the whole curve is safe" into a few linear constraints on control points. Overlaps are still needed to pass from one region to the next.

Q3. In the 2,500-cell maze, how many binary variables did GCS need, against the classic mixed-integer setup?

GCS uses about two binaries per pair of overlapping cells, roughly 2|I|. The classic setup needs |I|2 = 2,5002. That gap is a factor of about 1,200.

2024 · Marcucci, Nobel, Tedrake, Boyd · IEEE Trans. Robotics

Fast Path Planning Through Large Collections of Safe Boxes

Trades GCS's optimality bound for speed: with axis-aligned boxes, a graph search plus a few convex smoothing steps plans through 10,000+ boxes in seconds, and always finds a path if one exists.

In one sentence

With axis-aligned boxes, find the overlaps and build a graph once, offline. Online, a graph search gives a safe polygonal path, and a few small convex problems pull it tight and smooth it into Bézier curves: no optimality bound, but complete and fast.

Explain it to a 10-year-old

Picture a giant playground made of overlapping cardboard boxes you can crawl through. Before anyone plays, a helper marks every spot where two boxes overlap and draws a map of which spots connect. When you want to cross, you first find the shortest chain of spots on the map, like a dot-to-dot. Then you pull the dotted line tight like a string. Finally you round off its corners so you can crawl smoothly without stopping.

The problem

Think of a drone inspecting an industrial plant, or a robot carrying packages through a large warehouse. The map is static but huge. The authors note that, for a flight like theirs, existing methods took a few seconds to plan through fewer than 100 safe boxes. Marcucci 2024 The GCS paper gives tight bounds, but it was not built for maps of thousands of regions.

Exact mixed-integer planning is hopeless at that scale. Its worst-case cost is super-exponential in the number of boxes, and the paper shows CPLEX needing 584 s on even the smallest instance of its scaling study. Marcucci 2024, Sect. VII-D

The key idea

Give up the optimality bound and use the structure of boxes everywhere. Box overlaps are cheap to find, and "stay in a box" is just lower and upper bounds on each coordinate. The planner splits the problem into a discrete part, a graph search, and a continuous part, a few convex optimal-control problems (Day 17).

Safety is exact. The path is a chain of Bézier curves, one per box, with control points inside that box, so the whole path is safe at all times. It is also complete: if a safe path exists it finds one, and otherwise it reports infeasibility. Marcucci 2024, Sect. II

How it works

  1. Offline: the line graph. Find every pair of overlapping boxes. Each overlap becomes a vertex, and two vertices are joined if their overlaps share a box. Each vertex gets a representative point inside its overlap, chosen by one convex program that minimizes the total edge length. Marcucci 2024, Sect. III
  2. Online, polygonal phase. Connect start and goal to the graph and run a shortest-path search. That gives a safe polygonal curve. Then alternate: fix the box sequence and shorten the curve, which is convex; then fix the curve and improve the box sequence. This took 1 to 4 iterations in the scaling study.
  3. Online, smooth phase. Freeze the box sequence. Put one Bézier curve in each box, with derivative continuity at the joins. Shape and traversal times together make a non-convex problem. So alternate two convex ones: fix the times and optimize the shape, then improve the times with a local convex approximation. This took 5 to 6 iterations in the scaling study.

The cost penalizes squared derivatives of the path. For a quadrotor the paper penalizes snap, the fourth derivative, because a smooth flat-output path then gives feasible thrusts and orientations.

Results

Runs used an 8-core 2.4 GHz Intel i9, with CVXPY 1.4.1 and Clarabel 0.6.0. CVXPY's own overhead was removed from the reported times. Marcucci 2024, Sect. VII

ExampleBoxesOfflinePolygonalSmooth
2-D scaling study, largest25,60025 s0.12 s3.4 s
3-D village, quadrotor10,150101 s0.22 s7.5 s

The village has buildings, trees and bushes. Its line graph has 70,907 vertices and 1,022,782 edges, and the final path crosses 135 boxes. The first smooth iteration cut the cost by 84.3%, and the final path cost 99.3% less than the initial guess. Marcucci 2024, Sect. VII-C

On a 9-box toy problem the planner took 17.2 ms with cost 1.0001, essentially the global minimum of 1. The best mixed-integer formulation reached 1.01 and took 439 ms with CPLEX, the fastest of three commercial solvers. Marcucci 2024, Fig. 9

Why it mattered

It shows the convex-pieces idea scaling to city- or warehouse-sized maps, with online times of seconds. It is a practical bridge from GCS theory to deployment, and the code is open source as fastpathplanning. fastpathplanning

Limitations

  • No optimality bound. On the smallest scaling-study map, the mixed-integer path was about three times cheaper, though it took 584 s instead of 43 ms.
  • Boxes only. Axis-aligned boxes describe free space conservatively, and general convex sets would slow the offline steps.
  • The map must be static and known. A changed map means redoing the offline step, 101 s for the village.
  • Online times are still seconds for the largest maps.
  • Adding derivative limits with a fixed final time breaks completeness, unless the final time is also optimized. Marcucci 2024, Sect. VIII

How to read the paper

Look at Fig. 1 and read Sect. I. Sect. II-D outlines all three phases on one page. Sects. III, IV and V each end with the same small example (III-C, IV-C, V-D), so read those examples first and the details second. Then read Sect. VII-B and VII-C for scale, and VII-D for the mixed-integer comparison. Skip the derivations in Sect. V-C on a first pass.

Where it appears in the course

Day 19 ends with this planner as the scaled-up version of GCS. Day 21 lists it on the frontier, Day 14 covers alternating between blocks of variables, and Day 18 covers trajectory optimization more generally.

Check yourself

Q1. What does this planner give up compared with GCS?

The path is still safe at all times and smooth, and the method is complete. What is lost is the certified gap that GCS's relaxation provides.

Q2. In the village example, what must be recomputed when a new start and goal arrive?

The line graph depends only on the boxes, so it is built once. Each new query runs the two online phases.

Q3. Why is the smooth phase solved by alternating two problems?

Times multiply the shape variables, which breaks convexity. Fixing one part makes the other a convex problem. The box sequence is frozen during this phase.

2025 · Lu, Yang · Operations Research

cuPDLP.jl: A GPU Implementation of Restarted Primal-Dual Hybrid Gradient for Linear Programming in Julia

Showed that a first-order LP method running entirely on one GPU can match Gurobi on standard benchmarks, answering "are GPUs useful for LP?" with yes.

In one sentence

PDHG needs only products with the constraint matrix and its transpose, which GPUs do very fast, instead of the factorizations simplex and interior point need. Run every iteration of restarted PDHG on the GPU, and a Julia prototype keeps up with a commercial solver at moderate accuracy.

Explain it to a 10-year-old

Two players play a game. One decides how much of each thing to make. The other sets prices that punish breaking the rules. They take turns making small changes, and when neither wants to change anything, the game's answer is the best plan. Each turn needs only simple multiplications. A GPU is like a classroom of thousands of kids who can each do one multiplication at the same moment, so every turn goes very fast.

The problem

Classic LP solvers, simplex and interior point (Day 12), must solve linear systems by LU or Cholesky factorization. A sparse matrix can have a much denser factorization, which eats memory. Factorizations are also hard to spread over thousands of parallel cores. Lu 2025

So "are GPUs useful for solving linear programming?" was a long-standing open question. GPUs had transformed deep learning, but not LP.

The key idea

Use a method whose main cost is a matrix–vector product. Write the LP as

min cTx s.t. Gx ≥ h, Ax = b, l ≤ x ≤ u

Stack K = [G; A] and q = [h; b]. Dualizing the constraints (Day 9) gives a saddle-point problem. Here x stays in the box X = [l, u], and the multipliers y lie in Y, where the part for G is non-negative:

minx ∈ X maxy ∈ Y cTx − yTKx + qTy

PDHG (primal-dual hybrid gradient) takes a step in x, then a step in y, with step sizes τ and σ: Lu 2025, Sect. 2.1

x+ = projX(x − τ(c − KTy))

y+ = projY(y + σ(q − K(2x+ − x)))

Each step needs one product with K, one with KT, and a clip. No linear system is solved. That is exactly the kind of work a GPU is built for.

A worked example: minimize x subject to x ≥ 1, so c = K = q = 1. The answer is x = 1 with multiplier y = 1. Start at (0, 0) with τ = σ = 0.5:

Stepxy
1−0.51.0
3−0.1252.125
51.01.844
400.9971.006

The pair circles in toward (1, 1) slowly. Plain PDHG is not strong enough on real LPs, so PDLP adds five upgrades: diagonal preconditioning, adaptive restarts, adaptive step sizes, primal-weight updates and infeasibility detection. Lu 2025, Sect. 2.2

How it works

  1. CPU. Read the LP and precondition it, rescaling rows and columns (Day 21).
  2. Copy in. Move the scaled LP to GPU memory, once.
  3. GPU loop. Run restarted PDHG with adaptive steps. The one algorithmic change from CPU PDLP: restarts are triggered by the KKT error, because the old restart test needs a sequential computation. The same order of linear convergence is proved. Lu 2025, Sect. 3
  4. Stop when the relative KKT error, checked on the original LP, falls below 10−4 (moderate) or 10−8 (high accuracy).
  5. Copy out the solution, once.

Results

The tests used an NVIDIA H100 GPU for cuPDLP.jl and a 16-thread Xeon for the CPU solvers, including Gurobi 11.0 with crossover off. The benchmarks were 383 LP relaxations from MIPLIB 2017 and 49 LPs from Mittelmann's set. Lu 2025, Sect. 4

ComparisonResult
Against Gurobi, 10−4, no presolve3× faster on medium instances (4 more solved), 3.7× faster on large ones
With Gurobi presolve381 of 383 solved (99.5%) at 10−4; 97.4% at 10−8
Against Gurobi, 10−8Comparable to primal and dual simplex, behind barrier
Against CPU PDLP in Julia4×, 10× and 20× faster on small, medium and large; 30 more instances solved

The GPU has a cost. Kernel launches add about one second to every solve, while Gurobi finishes about 35% of the instances within one second. Lu 2025, Sect. 4.2

Why it mattered

It was the first evidence that a GPU first-order LP method can match commercial solvers on standard benchmarks. Adoption was fast, as of Oct 2026. HiGHS offers cuPDLP-C, the C rewrite, as its "pdlp" solver on NVIDIA GPUs. HiGHS docs Gurobi 13.0 added PDHG with an optional GPU mode. Gurobi 13.0 notes NVIDIA cuOpt runs GPU PDLP alongside barrier and dual simplex. cuOpt docs

For robotics and driving, this matters for huge planning or fleet LPs solved offline or at low rate. It does not help the small MPC QPs inside a controller.

Limitations

  • LP only. QPs and cone programs need other work, such as the GPU versions of OSQP and Clarabel.
  • Weaker at high accuracy: at 10−8 Gurobi's barrier still wins.
  • About one second of GPU overhead per solve, so small problems gain nothing. HiGHS itself warns that PDLP on a CPU is unlikely to be competitive. HiGHS docs
  • It needs a GPU. The Julia prototype was later rewritten in C as cuPDLP-C. cuPDLP-C 2023

How to read the paper

Read Sect. 1 with Table 1, which compares simplex, barrier and first-order methods. Then read Sect. 2.1 (the PDHG update) and Sect. 2.2 (the five PDLP upgrades, Algorithm 1). Sect. 3.2 shows the two-transfer design and Sect. 3.4 the KKT restarts. In Sect. 4.2, read Fig. 3 and the bulleted findings. Skip the appendix proof at first.

Where it appears in the course

Day 21 places it on the solver frontier. Day 9 gives the Lagrangian behind the saddle point, Day 5 the LP class, and Day 13 the splitting methods it is related to (see the ADMM card).

Check yourself

Q1. Why does PDHG suit a GPU better than simplex or interior point?

PDHG usually needs many more iterations, but each is cheap and parallel. It uses K constantly; it just never factors it.

Q2. Is cuPDLP.jl a good choice for a small MPC QP solved 100 times per second?

It is an LP solver built for very large instances. A small QP in a control loop wants something like OSQP or an active-set solver on the CPU.

Q3. At 10−8 tolerance on the MIPLIB relaxations, how did cuPDLP.jl compare with Gurobi?

High accuracy is where first-order methods struggle. The 20× figure was the speed-up over the CPU version of PDLP, not over Gurobi.
