Glossary
Every term, in plain words.

Tap a term for its meaning and the day that introduces it.

Sets & functions

Affine function

A linear part plus a constant, f(x) = aTx + b, so its graph is flat (a line or a plane). A convex problem allows only affine equality constraints.

Concave function

A function whose negative is convex, so it bends down like a cap. Maximizing a concave function is a convex problem.

Cone

A set that stays inside itself when you stretch any of its points by a factor θ ≥ 0. A convex cone also contains every nonnegative sum of its points.

Convex combination

A weighted average θ1x1 + … + θkxk in which every weight θi ≥ 0 and the weights add up to 1.

Convex function

A bowl-shaped function: the chord between any two points of its graph lies on or above the graph, f(θx + (1 − θ)y) ≤ θf(x) + (1 − θ)f(y) for θ ∈ [0, 1].

Convex hull

The smallest convex set that contains a given set, like a rubber band snapped around the points. It holds every convex combination of them. Written conv S.

Convex set

A set with no dents: the straight segment between any two of its points stays inside the set.

Disciplined convex programming (DCP)

A rule set for building functions from known convex pieces and convexity-preserving moves, so convexity is checked automatically. CVXPY uses it to accept or reject a model.

Ellipsoid

A stretched and rotated ball, {xc + Au : ‖u‖2 ≤ 1}. It is convex, and it is often used to describe uncertainty or a region of free space.

Epigraph

The region on or above a function's graph, epi f = {(x, t) : f(x) ≤ t}. A function is convex exactly when its epigraph is a convex set.

First-order condition

A differentiable f is convex exactly when every tangent plane lies below its graph: f(y) ≥ f(x) + ∇f(x)T(y − x) for all x and y.

Gradient

The vector of partial derivatives ∇f(x), one slope per variable. It points in the direction of fastest increase, so −∇f(x) points downhill.

Hessian

The matrix of second derivatives ∇2f(x), which describes curvature. A twice-differentiable f is convex exactly when ∇2f(x) ⪰ 0 everywhere (the second-order condition).

Hyperplane

A flat wall {x : aTx = b} with normal vector a. It splits space into two halfspaces, such as {x : aTx ≤ b}, and both are convex.

Indicator function

IC(x) is 0 inside the set C and +∞ outside. It turns the rule “x ∈ C” into a cost, and it is convex when C is convex.

Jensen's inequality

For a convex f, the value at an average is at most the average of the values: f(E[x]) ≤ E[f(x)]. It is the chord test applied to many points at once.

L-smooth

The gradient never changes faster than L: ‖∇f(x) − ∇f(y)‖2 ≤ L‖x − y‖2, or ∇2f ⪯ LI. It makes the step size t = 1/L safe for gradient descent.

Norm

A measure of a vector's length ‖x‖. Common ones are ‖x‖1 (sum of absolute entries), ‖x‖2 (straight-line length) and ‖x‖∞ (largest entry). Every norm is convex.

Norm ball

All points within distance r of a centre, {x : ‖x − xc‖ ≤ r}. The ℓ2 ball is round, the ℓ1 ball a diamond and the ℓ∞ ball a square. All are convex.

Perspective function

P(z, t) = z/t for t > 0, the pin-hole camera map, which keeps convex sets convex. The perspective of a function, t·f(x/t), keeps convexity too.

Polyhedron

The intersection of finitely many halfspaces and hyperplanes, {x : Ax ⪯ b, Cx = d}: a flat-sided convex region. A bounded polyhedron is a polytope.

Positive semidefinite (PSD)

A symmetric matrix X with all eigenvalues ≥ 0, written X ⪰ 0. Equivalently, vTXv ≥ 0 for every vector v. The PSD matrices form a convex cone, S+n.

Projection

PC(x), the point of the set C closest to x. For a closed convex C it exists and is unique. For a box it is simple clipping.

Second-order cone

The ice-cream cone {(x, t) : ‖x‖2 ≤ t}. It is a convex cone, and an SOCP keeps affine expressions inside it.

Strictly convex

The chord lies strictly above the graph between any two different points, so there are no flat stretches. A strictly convex function has at most one minimizer.

Strongly convex

At least as curved as a quadratic: f − (m/2)‖x‖22 is still convex for some m > 0, or ∇2f ⪰ mI. It gives a unique minimizer and linear convergence for gradient descent.

Subdifferential

∂f(x), the set of all subgradients at x. At a kink it is a whole fan of slopes, such as [−1, 1] for |x| at 0. Where f is smooth it is just {∇f(x)}.

Subgradient

A slope g whose line or plane through (x, f(x)) never rises above f: f(y) ≥ f(x) + gT(y − x). It replaces the gradient at kinks, where f has no derivative.

Sublevel set

All inputs that score at most α, {x : f(x) ≤ α}. Every sublevel set of a convex function is convex. Functions with only that property are called quasiconvex.

Supporting hyperplane

A flat wall that touches a set at a boundary point while the whole set stays on one side. Every boundary point of a convex set has one.

Problems

Active constraint

An inequality that holds with equality at x, gi(x) = 0: you are touching that fence. Constraints you are not touching push with zero force at the optimum.

Big-M constraint

A constraint loosened by M times a binary variable, so the binary can switch it on or off. M must be large enough to be safe but small enough to keep the relaxation tight.

Box constraint

Each variable has its own lower and upper bound, l ≤ x ≤ u, and nothing more. Projecting onto a box is clipping. An input sitting on its bound is in saturation.

Conic program

Minimize cTx subject to Fx + g ⪯K 0 and Ax = b, for a cone K. The nonnegative orthant gives an LP, the second-order cone an SOCP, and the PSD cone an SDP.

Constraint

A rule the variables must obey, written as an inequality gi(x) ≤ 0 or an equality hj(x) = 0.

Convex optimization problem

Minimize a convex objective subject to convex inequality constraints gi(x) ≤ 0 and affine equality constraints. Then every local minimum is a global minimum.

Cutting plane

A valid inequality, true for every integer-feasible point, that slices off the current fractional LP solution. Gomory and cover cuts are examples. Branch and cut adds cuts inside branch and bound.

Feasible set

The set of all points that satisfy every constraint. A point in it is a feasible point. If it is empty, the problem is infeasible.

Global minimum

A feasible point where no feasible point anywhere has a lower objective value. In a convex problem every local minimum is global.

Integrality gap

The difference between the optimum of the relaxed problem, where fractions are allowed, and the true integer optimum. A small gap means the relaxation's bound is informative.

Lasso

Least squares plus an ℓ1 penalty: minimize ½‖y − Xβ‖22 + λ‖β‖1. The kink at zero drives many coefficients exactly to zero, giving a sparse model.

Linear matrix inequality (LMI)

A constraint x1F1 + … + xnFn + G ⪯ 0: a symmetric matrix that depends affinely on x must stay negative semidefinite. Its feasible set is convex.

Linear program (LP)

Minimize a linear objective cTx subject to linear inequalities and equalities. The feasible set is a polyhedron, and if an optimum exists and the polyhedron has a corner, some vertex is optimal.

Local minimum

A feasible point that no nearby feasible point beats. It may not be the best overall, unless the problem is convex.

LP relaxation

The LP you get by dropping the “must be an integer” (for example 0/1) rule. When minimizing, its optimal value is a lower bound on the integer problem's optimum.

Mixed-integer program (MIP)

A problem in which some variables must be integers, often 0/1 binary switches, and the rest are continuous. MILP and MIQP have linear and quadratic objectives. Integrality makes it nonconvex.

Objective function

The score f(x) you want to make as small as possible, or as large for a maximization. Also called the cost or criterion.

Optimal solution

A feasible point x* that achieves the optimal value p*. Also called a minimizer. A problem may have none, one or many.

Optimal value

The best achievable objective value p* over the feasible set. It is +∞ if the problem is infeasible and −∞ if it is unbounded below.

Optimality gap

In a MIP solver, the distance between the incumbent (the best integer solution found so far) and the best proven bound. A gap of zero means the incumbent is proven optimal.

Optimization variable

The knobs x ∈ ℝn that you get to choose.

Quadratic program (QP)

Minimize a convex quadratic ½xTPx + qTx, with P ⪰ 0, subject to linear constraints. Linear MPC for cars and robots solves one QP per control step.

Relaxation

A problem solved over a bigger feasible set that contains the original one. With more choices, its optimal value is a lower bound on the original optimum.

Second-order cone program (SOCP)

A linear objective with constraints ‖Aix + bi‖2 ≤ ciTx + di, each keeping an affine expression inside the ice-cream cone. It includes LPs and convex QPs.

Semidefinite program (SDP)

A linear objective with a linear matrix inequality constraint, so a matrix built from the variables must stay PSD. LPs and SOCPs are special cases.

Slack variable

An extra variable s ≥ 0 that measures the room left in an inequality, turning Gx ⪯ h into Gx + s = h.

Standard form

The agreed way to write a problem: minimize f(x) subject to gi(x) ≤ 0 and hj(x) = 0. It is convex when f and every gi are convex and every hj is affine.

Methods

Active-set method

A solver family that guesses which inequality constraints are tight, solves the resulting equality-constrained problem, and corrects the guess. It suits small, warm-started MPC QPs.

Alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM)

For min f(x) + g(z) s.t. Ax + Bz = c: minimize the augmented Lagrangian over x, then over z, then update the price. OSQP runs on it.

card

Backtracking line search

Start with a step t, then shrink it by a factor β until f drops enough: f(x − t∇f) ≤ f(x) − αt‖∇f‖2. That test is the Armijo, or sufficient-decrease, condition.

Barrier method

Solve a sequence of barrier problems, minimize t·f(x) + φ(x), each by Newton's method from the last answer, multiplying t by a factor μ each round. It follows the central path.

card

BFGS

The standard quasi-Newton update: a rank-two correction of the curvature estimate that satisfies the secant equation and stays positive definite. L-BFGS keeps only the last m step pairs.

card

Branch and bound (B&B)

An exact method for integer problems: split on a fractional variable, bound each piece with a relaxation, and prune pieces that are infeasible or cannot beat the incumbent.

card

Central path

The curve of barrier minimizers x*(t) as t grows from 0 to ∞. On it the duality gap equals m/t, so it leads to the optimum through the inside of the feasible set.

Condition number

κ = L/m, the ratio of the largest to the smallest curvature: how stretched the bowl is. A large κ makes gradient descent zig-zag and slow, and amplifies numerical errors.

Coordinate descent

Minimize over one coordinate (or block) at a time, keeping the others fixed, and cycle through them. It is very fast for the lasso, where each coordinate step is a soft-threshold.

card

Dual ascent

Solve a problem through its dual: minimize the Lagrangian over x at the current prices u, then move u along the constraint residual Ax − b. Also called dual (sub)gradient ascent.

card

First-order method

A method that learns about f only through gradients or subgradients. Each new point lies in x0 plus the span of past gradients. Steps are cheap, but you need many.

FISTA

ISTA plus Nesterov momentum: each step starts from a point pushed a little further along the last move. It improves the rate from O(1/k) to O(1/k2) at almost no extra cost.

card

Frank–Wolfe method

Also called conditional gradient. A linear minimization oracle returns the best point s of C for the cost ∇f(x)Ts, then x ← (1 − γ)x + γs. No projection is needed.

card

Gradient descent (GD)

Repeat xk+1 = xk − t∇f(xk): step against the slope, scaled by a step size t (Day 1 writes η). The simplest first-order method; Day 1 meets it, Day 6 studies it.

card

Interior-point method

A method that replaces inequality walls by a smooth barrier and follows the central path through the inside of the feasible set. It takes a few tens of Newton steps, each costly but accurate.

ISTA

Iterative soft-thresholding: proximal gradient descent for the lasso. Take a gradient step on the least-squares part, then soft-threshold for the ℓ1 part.

card

Linear convergence

The error shrinks by a constant factor c < 1 each step, so it falls along a straight line on a log plot. Gradient descent achieves it on strongly convex problems.

Log barrier

φ(x) = −Σ log(−hi(x)), a smooth penalty that is defined only strictly inside the feasible set and blows up at every wall. It stands in for the hard inequality constraints.

Method of multipliers

Dual ascent on the augmented Lagrangian, with the penalty ρ as the step size. It converges under weaker conditions than plain dual ascent, but the x-step no longer splits into pieces.

card

Newton's method

Fit a quadratic bowl to f at x and jump to its bottom: Δx = −(∇2f(x))−1∇f(x). Damped Newton picks the step length by backtracking. Near the optimum convergence is quadratic.

card

PDHG

Primal–dual hybrid gradient: a first-order method that needs only products with the constraint matrix and its transpose, so it runs well on GPUs. PDLP is PDHG tuned for LPs.

Primal-dual interior-point method

Newton steps on the perturbed KKT equations in the primal x and the duals together. It aims each step at a moving target on the central path instead of fully re-centering.

card

Proximal gradient descent

For a composite objective g(x) + h(x), with g smooth and h simple: take a gradient step on g, then apply the proximal operator of h. With h = IC it is projected gradient descent.

card

Proximal operator

proxt(x) = argminz (1/2t)‖x − z‖22 + h(z): a point that balances staying near x against making h small. For an indicator it is projection; for λ‖·‖1, soft-thresholding.

Quadratic convergence

The error roughly squares each step, so the number of correct digits doubles. Newton's method converges this way once it is close to the optimum.

Quasi-Newton method

Newton-like steps with an approximate Hessian built from gradient changes. Each update must satisfy the secant equation B+s = y. SR1, DFP and BFGS are the classic updates.

card

Residual

How much a group of equations or conditions is violated. Interior-point methods track primal, dual and centrality residuals; ADMM stops once its primal and dual residuals fall below a tolerance.

Soft-thresholding

Sλ(x) shrinks each entry toward 0 by λ and sets anything within ±λ to exactly 0. It is the proximal operator of λ‖x‖1, which is why the lasso gives sparse answers.

Step size

t > 0, how far each step moves along the search direction; machine learning calls it the learning rate. Common choices are a fixed step, backtracking, and diminishing steps.

Stochastic gradient descent (SGD)

Gradient descent that uses the gradient of one random term (or a minibatch) of a sum f = Σfi per step. Steps are cheap but noisy, so step sizes usually shrink over time.

card

Subgradient method

x ← x − t·g with any subgradient g ∈ ∂f(x). It is not a descent method, so you keep the best value seen. It needs O(1/ε2) iterations, against O(1/ε) for gradient descent.

card

Sublinear rate

An error that falls like a constant over k, such as O(1/k): slower than any fixed shrink factor. One more correct digit costs about ten times more steps.

Superlinear convergence

The ratio between successive errors goes to 0: faster than linear, slower than quadratic. BFGS converges this way near the optimum.

Warm start

Start a solver from the solution of a nearby problem, such as the previous λ on a path or the previous MPC time step. It often cuts the number of iterations sharply.

Duality

Augmented Lagrangian

The Lagrangian plus a quadratic penalty on the constraint residual: Lρ(x, u) = f(x) + uT(Ax − b) + (ρ/2)‖Ax − b‖22. The penalty ρ makes dual methods robust.

Certificate of infeasibility

A vector that proves no feasible point exists. For Ax = b, x ≥ 0, Farkas' lemma says exactly one holds: a feasible x exists, or some y has ATy ≤ 0 and bTy > 0.

Complementary slackness

A KKT condition: λihi(x) = 0 for every inequality. Either the constraint is tight or its multiplier is zero, so an untouched fence pushes with zero force.

Conjugate function

f*(y) = supx (yTx − f(x)), the largest gap between the line yTx and the graph of f. It is convex even when f is not, and duals are often written with it.

Dual cone

K* = {y : yTx ≥ 0 for all x ∈ K}: all vectors that make a non-obtuse angle with every vector of K. Weights from it pick out the minimal (Pareto-optimal) points.

Dual feasible

Multipliers (u, v) with u ⪰ 0 and g(u, v) > −∞. Every dual-feasible point gives a lower bound on the primal optimum p*.

Dual norm

‖z‖* = max{zTx : ‖x‖ ≤ 1}, how large zTx gets over the original unit ball. The dual of ‖·‖1 is ‖·‖∞, and ‖·‖2 is its own dual.

Dual problem

Maximize the dual function g(u, v) subject to u ⪰ 0: the search for the best lower bound on the original, or primal, problem. It is always a convex problem.

Duality gap

f(x) − g(u, v) for a feasible x and a dual-feasible (u, v). It is never negative and bounds how far f(x) is from optimal, so solvers use it to decide when to stop.

KKT conditions

Four checks at a point: stationarity, primal feasibility, dual feasibility (λ ⪰ 0) and complementary slackness. For convex problems they are sufficient for optimality, and necessary when strong duality holds.

Lagrange dual function

g(u, v) = min over x of the Lagrangian L(x, u, v). It is always concave and, for u ⪰ 0, always a lower bound on p*, even when the problem is not convex.

Lagrange multiplier

The price on one constraint, also called a dual variable: ui ≥ 0 for an inequality, and vj of any sign for an equality. At the optimum it is the force that constraint exerts.

Lagrangian

The objective plus priced constraints: L(x, u, v) = f(x) + Σuihi(x) + Σvjℓj(x). On the feasible set, with u ⪰ 0, it never exceeds f(x).

Lagrangian relaxation

Move hard constraints into the objective with prices u ≥ 0 and solve the easier problem that is left. Each price vector gives a bound on the original optimum.

Slater's condition

If a convex problem has a strictly feasible point, strong duality holds: p* = d*. Affine inequalities may hold with equality; only the curved rules need room to spare.

Stationarity

A KKT condition: ∇f(x) + Σλi∇hi(x) + Σνj∇ℓj(x) = 0. The downhill pull of the objective is exactly balanced by the pushes of the constraints.

Strictly feasible

A point that satisfies every inequality with room to spare, hi(x) < 0, and every equality exactly. Slater's condition asks for one.

Strong duality

The primal and dual optimal values are equal, d* = p*, so the optimal duality gap is zero. Convex problems that satisfy Slater's condition have it.

Weak duality

d* ≤ p* for every problem, convex or not: the best lower bound never exceeds the true optimum. The difference p* − d* is the optimal duality gap.

Beyond convex & robotics

Amortized optimization

Learn a model that maps a problem's context (state, goal, obstacles) to an approximate solution, paying most of the cost once at training time. Its output can warm-start a solver.

CBF-QP

A safety filter solved every control step: minimize ‖u − unom‖2 subject to the CBF condition, which is linear in u. It changes the nominal command only when it must.

Constraint qualification

A regularity condition on the constraints that makes the KKT conditions necessary at a local optimum. The common one, LICQ, asks that the gradients of the active constraints be linearly independent.

Control barrier function (CBF)

A margin function h, with safe set h(x) ≥ 0, such that some input can always keep ḣ ≥ −γh. Enforcing that rule keeps the safe set forward invariant: once inside, you stay inside.

Direct transcription

Turn a continuous trajectory into a finite problem: chop time into K steps, make the state and input at each node unknowns, and enforce the dynamics between nodes as defect constraints.

Factorization caching

Reusing one matrix factorization for every solve because the problem matrices never change, only vectors such as the current state. It is why OSQP suits sparse MPC.

Gauss–Newton

For nonlinear least squares: linearize the residuals with their Jacobian J and solve a linear least-squares step, which approximates the Hessian by JTJ. Standard in SLAM and bundle adjustment.

card

Graph of Convex Sets (GCS)

A graph whose vertices are convex regions, each holding a movable point, with convex edge costs that depend on those points. Its convex relaxation, tightened by perspective functions, plans paths with a lower bound.

IPOPT

An open-source interior-point solver for general nonlinear programs, using a barrier, a line search and a filter. It finds a local solution and needs twice-differentiable functions.

IRIS

Iterative Regional Inflation by Semidefinite programming. From a seed point it alternates two convex problems, growing a large obstacle-free polytope with an ellipse inside, to give convex regions for planning.

Kinematic bicycle model

A car model with one front and one rear wheel and no tyre forces, only geometry. For small angles it links lateral acceleration to steering: u ≈ (V2/L)·δ.

Levenberg–Marquardt (LM)

Gauss–Newton plus a damping term λ that shortens risky steps. The gain ratio, actual over predicted decrease, decides whether to accept a step and whether to loosen or tighten λ.

card

Lossless convexification

A relaxation that is proven to give the original problem's global optimum. In rocket landing (powered descent guidance) it turns the nonconvex thrust ring into a convex SOCP.

Model predictive control (MPC)

Control by repeatedly solving a finite-horizon optimal-control problem from the current state, applying only the first input, and re-planning at the next tick (receding horizon). With linear models it is a QP.

Modelling tool

Software that turns the math you write into solver-ready matrices (canonicalization), such as CVXPY, JuMP, CasADi, YALMIP or Drake. You state the problem; it calls a solver.

Nonlinear least squares

Minimize the sum of squared nonlinear residuals, ½‖r(x)‖22, where each residual is prediction minus measurement. Pose-graph SLAM and bundle adjustment are examples.

Nonlinear program (NLP)

An optimization problem with a nonlinear, possibly nonconvex, objective or constraints. Solvers usually find only a local optimum, so the starting point matters.

OBCA

Optimization-Based Collision Avoidance: it rewrites “stay at least dmin from the obstacle” with dual variables that certify the distance, giving smooth constraints. Hybrid A* warm-starts it in parking.

OptNet

A neural-network layer whose output is the solution of a QP. Its gradients come from implicit differentiation of the KKT conditions, not from unrolling the solver's steps.

Real-time iteration (RTI)

In nonlinear MPC, do one SQP iteration, a single QP, per sample instead of solving the NLP fully, starting from the previous plan.

Saddle point

A stationary point that is a minimum in some directions and a maximum in others, like a mountain pass. Its Hessian has both positive and negative eigenvalues.

Safe flight corridor

A chain of overlapping convex polyhedra around a coarse path through free space. Keeping each trajectory segment inside its corridor avoids collisions with convex constraints only.

Safety filter

An optimizer between the controller and the motors that minimally edits the nominal command so a safety rule holds. A CBF-QP is the standard example.

SDP relaxation

Replace a hard nonconvex problem by a semidefinite program over a larger set, which gives a lower bound. When the relaxation is exact, as in SE-Sync below a noise threshold, it yields the global optimum.

Sequential convex programming (SCP)

Repeatedly replace a nonconvex problem by a convex approximation around the current guess and solve it inside a trust region. It is a workhorse of trajectory optimization.

card

Sequential quadratic programming (SQP)

Solve a nonlinear program by repeatedly solving a QP model built from the Lagrangian's Hessian and linearized constraints. A merit function or filter judges each step.

card

Signed distance

The distance between two shapes when they are apart, and minus their penetration depth when they overlap. Collision constraints keep it above a safety margin.

Trajectory optimization

Choosing a whole time-indexed path of states and inputs at once, minimizing a cost subject to the dynamics, input limits and obstacles.

Trust region

A region around the current point where the local model is trusted, such as |xi − xi(k)| ≤ ρi. It grows when the model predicts well and shrinks when it does not.

Virtual control

A fictitious slack input added to the linearized dynamics so SCP subproblems stay feasible, at a heavy cost. It must vanish at convergence. SCvx uses it.
